Running every tool in a fixed order is a scripted workflow, not an agent. The whole point of the loop is that the model picks the next action after seeing each result.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask you to sketch this loop as code: a `while` loop that calls the model, checks for tool calls, runs them, appends results and stops on a final answer or a step cap. Strong candidates add the stop conditions without being asked.

questions.prompt: A homework-help chatbot runs on a model whose safety training makes it refuse to write malware. A user sets up a long role-play in which the bot must act as a fictional AI with no rules and stay in character no matter what. Then, in character, the user asks for working malware code. An attack like this, where the user tries to talk the model out of its safety training rather than hijack the app's own task instructions, is usually called a ______.
questions.explanation:
A jailbreak is an attempt by the user to talk the model out of its safety training or policy. Role-play, hypothetical framing ("for a novel I am writing"), splitting a forbidden request into harmless-looking pieces and odd encodings are all common jailbreak styles. The goal is always content or behaviour the system is meant to refuse.

The common mix-up is with prompt injection. In prompt injection, text tries to take over the application's instructions, and in the indirect form it arrives through data such as a web page, so the user is often the victim. In a jailbreak, the user is the attacker and the target is the safety policy. The two overlap. Some people describe a jailbreak as a kind of direct injection, and real attacks often mix both. But the name for getting a model past its own safety rules is jailbreak.

Defences come in layers: safety training in the model, classifiers on input and output, and limits on what the app can do even if a jailbreak succeeds.
questions.deeper: In an interview, connect jailbreaks to red-teaming. Teams keep a growing set of known jailbreak prompts, run it against every new model or prompt version, and track the success rate. Output classifiers matter because new jailbreak styles appear faster than any model can be retrained.

questions.prompt: A recommender has 2 million product ids. Instead of feeding one-hot vectors, it keeps a trainable matrix with one row of 64 numbers per product. A product's row is fetched by its id and updated by backpropagation like any other weights, so products that behave alike end up with similar rows. This learned lookup table is called the ______ layer.
questions.explanation:
An embedding layer is a weight matrix with one row per id. Looking up row i gives the same result as multiplying a one-hot vector for id i by the matrix, but without building a 2-million-long vector, so it is far cheaper. Because the rows are trained by the task loss, products that play similar roles, such as ones bought by the same users, drift toward nearby vectors.

A common wrong answer is one-hot encoding. That is the sparse input the embedding replaces. It has no learned values and puts every product at the same distance from every other product. Another is feature hashing, which maps many ids into fewer buckets to save memory but is a fixed function, not a learned table. Hashing is sometimes placed in front of an embedding to shrink it, which is where the two get mixed up.
questions.deeper: For large catalogues the embedding table can hold most of a model's parameters, here 2 million × 64 = 128 million. Interviewers may ask how you handle ids never seen in training, with answers such as a shared unknown row, hashing into buckets, or building the vector from content features.

questions.prompt: A k-nearest-neighbours model recommends similar products using 15 dense features, and it works well. The team then adds 3,000 one-hot and word-count features. Now, for most products, the nearest and farthest neighbours sit at almost the same distance, and the recommendations look random. The general effect where data becomes sparse and distances lose their contrast as the number of dimensions grows is called the ______.
questions.explanation:
As you add dimensions, the space grows so fast that a fixed number of points becomes very spread out. For many kinds of data the distances between random pairs of points also bunch together, so the ratio of farthest to nearest distance moves toward 1. kNN only works if near really means similar. Here most of the 3,000 new features carry little signal, and each one adds a bit of random distance that drowns out the 15 useful features.

A frequent wrong answer is overfitting. The two are linked, since sparse data makes overfitting easier, but the effect in the prompt is about the geometry of distance, not about a model memorising training rows. Another is sparsity, which describes one symptom rather than the effect itself. The fixes all reduce the effective number of dimensions: drop weak features, use PCA, or learn a compact embedding and measure distance there.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like candidates who connect this to retrieval. Vector search works on embeddings of a few hundred dimensions because the embedding is trained so that distance carries meaning. Raw one-hot vectors of thousands of dimensions rarely do, so methods that rely on distance, such as kNN and k-means, suffer most.

questions.prompt: An online furniture shop adds a chatbot that answers questions about orders, deliveries and returns. Under the EU AI Act's risk-based approach, where does this system most likely sit?
options: High-risk: it needs a conformity assessment and human oversight first.
Prohibited: it could sway buyers, so it cannot be offered in the EU.
Minimal risk: the Act places no specific duties on customer chatbots.
Limited risk: people must be told they are talking to an AI system.
questions.explanation:
The EU AI Act sorts AI systems by the harm they could do. A chatbot that talks to the public falls under transparency duties, often called the limited-risk tier. The main obligation is that people are told they are dealing with an AI, unless that is already obvious from the context.

High-risk covers uses listed in the Act where errors can seriously affect people's lives or rights, such as credit scoring, access to education, hiring and essential public services. Answering questions about furniture deliveries is not on that list. Prohibited practices are a short list of unacceptable uses, such as social scoring and manipulation that distorts behaviour in a way that causes significant harm. Ordinary sales help does not reach that bar. Minimal risk is the tier for systems such as spam filters, with no specific duties. It is the close miss here, but a system that talks directly with people carries the transparency duty, so it sits one tier up.
questions.deeper: The tier depends on the use, not the technology. The same language model could power this chatbot and also a tool that screens job applicants, which would be high-risk. In interviews, a strong candidate asks what decision the system feeds before naming a tier.

questions.prompt: A hospital has only 600 labelled patient records and builds a random forest to predict readmission. Each tree trains on rows drawn at random with replacement, so roughly a third of the records never reach any given tree. Scoring each record using only the trees that never saw it gives the ______ error, a built-in validation estimate.
questions.explanation:
When you draw n rows with replacement from n rows, each row has a (1 − 1/n)ⁿ chance of never being picked, which is close to 1/e ≈ 0.37 for large n. Those left-out rows are the tree's out-of-bag rows. For each record, you combine predictions only from the trees that did not train on it and compare with the true label. Averaged over all records, this gives the out-of-bag error.

It behaves much like cross-validation but costs almost nothing, since no extra models are trained. That helps here, where holding out a separate validation set from only 600 records would waste scarce data.

A common mix-up is with training error. Scoring a record with all the trees, including those that trained on it, gives an optimistic number. Another is treating it as a final test score. If you tune many settings against the out-of-bag error, it becomes optimistic too, so keep an untouched test set.
questions.deeper: In scikit-learn you get it by setting `oob_score=True`. A good interview point is that it assumes rows are independent. If one patient has several admissions, a tree can train on one of them and be scored on a near-copy, which makes the estimate optimistic. A split grouped by patient is safer.

questions.prompt: A fine-tuning method keeps a pretrained weight matrix W frozen and unquantized at its original precision, and learns an update ΔW = BA, where B and A are thin matrices of rank r, much smaller than the dimensions of W. Only A and B are trained. This method is called ______.
questions.explanation:
LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, assumes the change needed to adapt a model to a new task has low rank. Instead of updating W directly, it trains two thin matrices whose product BA has the same shape as W. For a 4,096 × 4,096 layer, full fine-tuning updates about 16.8 million weights. With r = 8, B is 4,096 × 8 and A is 8 × 4,096, which is 65,536 weights, about 0.4% of the layer. After training, BA can be merged into W, so inference costs nothing extra.

A common mix-up is with QLoRA, which uses the same low-rank update but stores the frozen base model in 4-bit precision. The prompt says the base stays unquantized at its original precision, which rules it out. Adapters and prefix tuning are also parameter-efficient, but they add new layers or tokens rather than a low-rank update to existing weights.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask which layers to apply LoRA to and how to pick the rank. A strong answer mentions the attention projections as a common start, trying a few ranks on a validation set, and the serving benefit: one base model can host many small task adapters and swap them per request.

questions.prompt: A bank's data team is deciding which of its models need a real-time prediction service and which can run as scheduled batch jobs. Which use case needs online serving?
options: Scoring each card payment for fraud while the customer waits at the checkout page
Scoring every customer's churn risk for a retention email that goes out each Monday
Forecasting tomorrow's cash demand at each branch so cash can be delivered overnight
Scoring all credit card accounts each month to pick who gets a credit limit increase
questions.explanation:
The deciding question is when the prediction is needed and whether the inputs exist in advance. A fraud check at checkout must use details of a payment that did not exist a second ago, and the customer is waiting for an approve or decline. Only an online service that scores the request as it arrives can do that.

The other three can all be computed ahead of time. The Monday churn email needs scores once a week, so a weekly batch job scores every customer and the email system reads the results. The branch cash forecast is needed once a day, before overnight delivery, so a nightly job fits. The monthly limit review covers every account on a schedule, which is a classic batch workload. Batch scoring is usually cheaper and simpler to run, retry and audit, so it is the default when nothing forces real time.
questions.deeper: Many systems mix both. A strong candidate might precompute slow features or candidate lists in batch and do a light online step at request time. Interviewers also like the point that online serving adds latency targets, autoscaling and on-call duty, so it should be chosen for a reason.

questions.prompt: A recipe app recommends dishes from user ratings using matrix factorisation. New users and newly added recipes both get poor recommendations. Which strategies help with this cold-start problem? Select all that apply.
options: Ask new users to pick a few cuisines or diets at sign-up and seed their recommendations from those
Score new recipes from their ingredients, text and photo embeddings before any ratings exist
Show each new recipe to a small, controlled share of users so that early ratings for it arrive quickly
Look up each new user's factorisation embedding, which the model fits from their profile at sign-up time
Hide new recipes until they have 100 ratings, so the model only ever ranks items that are well measured
Raise the number of latent factors so the model has enough room to represent new users and new recipes
questions.explanation:
Matrix factorisation learns an embedding for each user and each recipe from their ratings. With no ratings there is nothing to learn from, so cold start needs other signals or a way to gather data fast.

Onboarding questions give a new user a starting profile from day one. Content features let the system score a recipe by what it is, using its ingredients, text and photo, instead of by who rated it. A small exploration budget shows new recipes to some users so real feedback arrives quickly, and it is how many production systems handle new items.

The idea of an embedding fitted from the profile at sign-up is false. Matrix factorisation fits the embedding to a user's ratings, not their profile, and at sign-up there are none, so it would be random or a default vector. More latent factors do not help either. They give the model more capacity to fit existing ratings, but a user or recipe with no ratings still has nothing to fit. Hiding recipes until they reach 100 ratings creates a trap. Hidden recipes cannot be rated, so many will never reach 100 and new content stays invisible.
questions.deeper: A strong answer separates user cold start from item cold start, since the fixes differ. It may also mention hybrid models that blend content features with collaborative signals, so a new item starts from a content-based embedding that moves toward a learned one as ratings arrive. Popular dishes by region are a simple, strong fallback.

questions.prompt: Four GPUs train a product-recommendation model with data parallelism. The model fits easily on one GPU. What happens on each training step?
options: Each GPU holds a full copy of the model and runs its own slice of the batch, then the GPUs average gradients so every copy makes the same update.
Each GPU holds a quarter of the layers and passes its activations to the next GPU, so the batch flows through the model like an assembly line.
Each GPU trains its own copy on its own share of the data with no syncing, and the four sets of weights are averaged once when training ends.
Each GPU holds a quarter of every weight matrix, and the GPUs exchange partial results inside each layer to build the full output for the batch.
questions.explanation:
In data parallelism, every GPU keeps a complete copy of the model. The batch is split, so with a batch of 256 each GPU runs 64 examples through its own forward and backward pass. The GPUs then average their gradients with an all-reduce, and every copy applies the same averaged gradient. The copies stay identical, and the result matches training on the full batch of 256 on one device.

The option about passing activations from GPU to GPU describes pipeline parallelism, which splits the layers into stages and is used when a model is too large for one device. The option about splitting every weight matrix describes tensor parallelism, another way to fit a large model. The option about averaging weights only at the end describes training separate models. Without syncing on every step the copies drift apart, and averaging the weights of separately trained networks usually gives a poor model.
questions.deeper: Data parallelism is the first scaling tool to reach for when the model fits on one GPU. Its cost is the gradient all-reduce each step, which modern frameworks overlap with the backward pass. Interviewers often follow up by asking what you would change when the model no longer fits.

questions.prompt: A camera model watches forests for wildfire smoke, and smoke is the positive class. One morning it raises a smoke alert, but the image only shows fog. In the model's confusion matrix, this case is counted as a ______.
questions.explanation:
Read the name in two parts. The second word is what the model predicted: it said smoke, the positive class, so the case is a positive. The first word says whether that prediction was right: there was no smoke, so it was false. Together that makes a false positive. In statistics it is also called a type I error, or in plain words a false alarm.

The common mistake is to answer false negative, reasoning that fog is a negative thing or that the truth was negative. The name follows the prediction, not the truth. A false negative would be the opposite case: real smoke that the model missed. False positives push precision down, because precision divides by everything the model flagged. False negatives push recall down, because recall divides by everything that was really there.
questions.deeper: For a wildfire system the two errors have very different costs. A false positive sends a crew to look at fog, while a false negative lets a fire grow. Interviewers often ask you to name both cells and say which one the business would rather pay for.

questions.prompt: A clinic's patient-message system starts with a small, cheap model call that labels each incoming message as a prescription refill, an appointment change or a clinical question. Each label then sends the message to its own prompt and tools, built only for that kind of request. This workflow pattern, where a classification step decides which specialized handler takes a request, is called ______.
questions.explanation:
Routing splits the work in two. First, one step classifies the input. Then the input goes to a handler built for that class. Each handler can have a tight prompt and only the tools it needs, so the refill handler never sees appointment tools, and a prompt change for one class does not break the others. The classifier can be a small model, an LLM call or plain rules.

The common mix-up is with orchestrator-workers. There, a central model breaks one task into subtasks it decides on the fly, hands each to a worker, then combines the results. Routing makes one choice at the start and sends the whole request down one path. Another mix-up is prompt chaining, which runs the same fixed steps in sequence on every input with no branching. Routing is also a natural place to send easy requests to a cheaper model and hard ones to a stronger model.
questions.deeper: In practice, log the router's choice and measure its accuracy on its own, since a wrong route sends a patient to a handler that cannot help. Strong designs add a fallback class for unclear messages that goes to a person, which matters a lot when a misrouted clinical question could be urgent.

questions.prompt: In a semantic search system, a query embedding a and a document embedding b are scored with Σ aᵢbᵢ. The score is large when the two vectors point in a similar direction and are long. This operation is called the ______ of a and b.
questions.explanation:
The dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them up: a · b = Σ aᵢbᵢ. Geometrically it equals |a| × |b| × cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. So it grows when the vectors point the same way and also when they are long.

The common mix-up is with cosine similarity. Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by both lengths, a · b / (|a| |b|), which keeps only the angle and always lies between −1 and 1. The plain sum Σ aᵢbᵢ has no division, so it is the dot product. The two give the same ranking only when the document vectors all have the same length, for example when every embedding is normalized to length 1.

This is why the choice matters in search. With raw dot products, a document whose embedding happens to be long can rank high for many queries, even if its direction is only a loose match.
questions.deeper: Vector databases usually let you choose dot product, cosine or Euclidean distance. A strong candidate checks what the embedding model was trained with. If embeddings are normalized, all three give the same ranking and the dot product is the cheapest. Matrix multiplication is just many dot products computed at once.

questions.prompt: A sepsis screening dataset has one row per patient, and 3% of patients are positive. To make sure the train, validation and test sets each hold close to 3% positives instead of leaving it to chance, you use a ______ split.
questions.explanation:
A stratified split samples separately within each class, so every part keeps the original class share. With rare positives this matters. Say there are 1,000 patients and 30 positives, and the test set is 200 patients. A plain random split expects 6 positives in test, but by chance it could hold 2 or 10, and recall measured on 2 positives is close to meaningless. Stratifying fixes the count at about 6. In scikit-learn you pass `stratify=y` to `train_test_split` or use `StratifiedKFold`.

The common mistake is answering "balanced". A balanced split forces 50% positives, which no longer looks like the 3% the model will face, so precision and every other metric read from it would be wrong.
questions.deeper: Stratification and grouping can be needed together. If patients could have several visits, you would use `StratifiedGroupKFold` to keep each patient on one side and the class share steady. Interviewers like candidates who notice both constraints.

questions.prompt:
Using NumPy 2.x, a fraud team adds up the value of large transactions that a rule has flagged. What does the last line return? Give a whole number.

```python
import numpy as np
amounts = np.array([120, 15, 980, 40, 610, 75])
flagged = np.array([False, False, True, False, True, True])
amounts[flagged & (amounts > 100)].sum()
```
questions.explanation:
Work out each mask, then combine them element by element with `&`.

- `flagged` is True at positions 2, 4 and 5, which hold 980, 610 and 75.
- `amounts > 100` is True at positions 0, 2 and 4, which hold 120, 980 and 610.
- Both are True only at positions 2 and 4.

Indexing with that mask keeps 980 and 610, and the sum is 1590.

The most common slip is to answer 2. That is the result of summing the mask itself, `(flagged & (amounts > 100)).sum()`, which counts the True values instead of adding the amounts. Others forget one condition and get 1665, the sum of every flagged amount, or 1710, the sum of every amount over 100. The parentheses matter as well. `&` binds more tightly than `>`, so without them Python would compute `flagged & amounts` first, which is not what you mean.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask why `flagged and amounts > 100` fails. Python's `and` needs one True or False for the whole array, so NumPy raises a ValueError. Use `&`, `|` and `~` for element-wise logic, and wrap each comparison in parentheses.

questions.prompt: An insurer tests its claims agent in a sandbox. A test passes if, at the end, the claim record holds the right status and payout. Every test passes. Reading the traces, an engineer finds that in some passing runs the agent opened the records of two unrelated policyholders, and in others it called the payout calculator nine times with slightly different inputs. What should the team change about its evaluation?
options: Replace the outcome check with a trajectory check that requires every run to match one reference sequence of tool calls exactly.
Also grade the trajectory: which tools ran, in what order and with what arguments, since the outcome check misses these.
Nothing, since a correct final claim record shows that every step the agent took to reach it was also acceptable.
Grade the agent's closing message to the claims handler instead, since it describes each step the agent took.
questions.explanation:
Outcome grading asks one question: did the world end up in the right state? It is the best main signal, because many different paths can be correct. But it is blind to how the agent got there. Opening unrelated customers' records is a privacy problem, and nine calculator calls waste time and money, yet both runs still pass. Adding trajectory checks catches these: tool choice, order, arguments, and calls that should never happen at all.

Requiring an exact match to one reference sequence goes too far the other way. Agents often reach the same correct state by different valid routes, so that check would fail good runs. A better trajectory check looks for forbidden calls, wrong arguments and wasted steps. Saying the correct end state proves every step was fine is the exact mistake these traces expose. Grading the closing message grades what the agent says it did, not what it did, and agents can misreport their own actions.
questions.deeper: In interviews, say you use the outcome check as the main score and trajectory checks as guards. Guards cover safety rules such as never touching unrelated records, budgets such as a cap on tool calls, and argument checks. A common follow-up is how to grade trajectories at scale: rule-based checks on the trace for hard rules, plus an LLM judge or human review for softer judgment.

questions.prompt: A ride-hailing app sends 2% of its arrival-time prediction traffic to a new model as a canary. The service handles 500 requests per second in total. The new model has a bug that returns a bad estimate on 4% of the requests it serves. The canary runs for 45 minutes before the team rolls it back. How many requests received a bad estimate? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation:
Work out the total traffic first, then take the canary's share of it, then the share of that which went wrong.

- Seconds in the canary: 45 × 60 = 2,700
- Total requests: 500 × 2,700 = 1,350,000
- Requests sent to the canary: 1,350,000 × 0.02 = 27,000
- Bad estimates: 27,000 × 0.04 = 1,080

The common mistake is to forget the canary share and multiply total traffic by the error rate. That gives 54,000, which is what a full rollout of the same buggy model would have caused over 45 minutes. The gap between 1,080 and 54,000 is the point of a canary. It limits the damage while you learn whether the new model is safe. Another slip is mixing units, for example multiplying requests per second by 45 minutes without converting to seconds.
questions.deeper: In an interview, a strong answer adds the other side of the trade. A 2% canary limits harm but also collects data slowly, so a rare failure may need hours to show up. Teams often start at 1 to 5%, then step up to 25% and 50% once error rate and latency hold steady at each stage.

questions.prompt:
An airport tests a model that flags checked bags for a manual search. On 5,000 test bags the results are:

- Flagged, bag held a banned item: 36
- Not flagged, bag held a banned item: 4
- Flagged, bag was clean: 248
- Not flagged, bag was clean: 4,712

What is the model's specificity? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Specificity is the share of truly negative cases that the model correctly leaves alone: TN / (TN + FP). Here the negatives are the clean bags. There are 4,712 + 248 = 4,960 of them, and the model left 4,712 unflagged. So specificity is 4,712 / 4,960 = 0.95.

Recall is the same idea for the positive class: TP / (TP + FN) = 36 / (36 + 4) = 0.90. Together the two describe how the model treats each true class on its own.

The most common mistake is to divide by all 5,000 bags, which gives 4,712 / 5,000 ≈ 0.94. That puts the bags with banned items into the denominator, even though specificity is only about clean bags. Another slip is to use the flagged column, 36 / (36 + 248) ≈ 0.13, which is precision. Notice how that low precision sits beside a high specificity. With so many clean bags, even 5% of them flagged swamps the 36 real hits.
questions.deeper: Recall and specificity each look inside one true class, so they stay the same if banned items become rarer or more common, as long as the model behaves the same on each kind of bag. Precision does not. That is why screening teams quote recall and specificity for the test itself, then work out flag volume for the traffic they really see.

questions.prompt: A support team puts three labelled example tickets at the start of every prompt, and an LLM's routing accuracy rises from 71% to 84%. A product manager asks whether the model has now learned the categories. Which answer is correct?
options: No weights changed. The examples only steer predictions for the request that holds them, so they must be resent, and their order and format can matter.
Yes. The provider briefly fine-tunes a copy of the model on the examples it sees, so after a few requests the examples can safely be dropped from the prompt.
Partly. Attention updates the model's weights during the forward pass, and those updates stay in place for the rest of that user's session with the model.
No weights changed, but the model averages the examples, so their order and wording do not matter and only the number of examples affects the results.
questions.explanation:
Few-shot prompting is in-context learning. The examples are just more input tokens. The model reads them in the same forward pass as the new ticket and uses them to infer the task and the output format, but no weights are updated. Once the request ends, nothing is kept, so every future request must include the examples again, which also adds tokens and cost.

The option about the provider fine-tuning a copy describes a training job, which only happens if you run one. The option about attention updating weights confuses activations with parameters. Attention computes temporary values from the input, and chat apps only seem to remember because they resend the history each turn. The option claiming order and wording do not matter is the tempting one, since its first half is right. In practice, few-shot results can shift noticeably when you reorder the examples, change their format or change the balance of labels, so the model is not simply averaging them.
questions.deeper: In an interview, add how you would make few-shot robust: pick examples that cover the hard categories, keep one consistent format, test a few orderings on a held-out set, or retrieve the most similar labelled tickets for each request. If the example block grows large, prompt caching or fine-tuning may become cheaper.

questions.prompt: You are distilling a large 10-class product-defect image classifier into a small model for factory cameras. On most training images the teacher puts more than 0.99 probability on a single class. A colleague suggests dividing both models' logits by a temperature T = 4 inside the distillation loss. What is the main benefit?
options: The teacher's probabilities for the wrong classes become large enough to learn from, so the student sees which defects the teacher finds similar to each other.
The teacher becomes even more confident in its top class, so the student trains on cleaner targets than the human labels, which contain some annotation mistakes.
The softened outputs add random noise to the teacher's targets, which acts as a regularizer and stops the student from copying the teacher too closely.
The gradients of the distillation loss grow by a factor of T², so the student learns faster and the loss can be added to the label loss without a weight.
questions.explanation:
Softmax with temperature computes softmax(z / T). Dividing the logits by T > 1 shrinks the gaps between them, which flattens the distribution. Take three logits of 10, 4 and 1. At T = 1 the probabilities are about 0.997, 0.0025 and 0.0001, almost a hard label. At T = 4 they become about 0.75, 0.17 and 0.08. Now the student can see that the teacher rates the second class as far more plausible than the third, for example that a scratch looks more like a dent than like a missing part. This similarity structure, sometimes called dark knowledge, is what makes soft targets more informative than labels.

The option about more confidence has the effect backwards. Raising T makes the teacher less confident. The option about random noise is wrong because temperature is a fixed rescaling, with nothing random about it. The option about gradients also has it backwards. Gradients of the softened loss shrink by about 1 / T², which is why the standard recipe multiplies that loss by T² before mixing it with the label loss.
questions.deeper: In interviews, mention that T is a tuning knob. Too high and the targets flatten toward uniform and lose the ranking, too low and they collapse to hard labels. Teams often try values from about 2 to 10 and tune the weight between the soft and hard losses on a validation set.

questions.subtopic: online metrics for a recommender launch
questions.prompt: A short-video app will A/B test a new recommender for four weeks before deciding whether to launch it. The new model was trained to maximise clicks. Which metrics belong in the launch decision as success or guardrail metrics? Select all that apply.
options: The share of users in each arm who come back 7 and 28 days after first being exposed to it
How many distinct creators and topics make up each user's watch time in each arm
The rate of "not interested" taps, reports and hides per 1,000 videos shown in each arm
Click-through rate as the single launch criterion, since it has the most data and moves fastest
The average click probability the new model predicts for the videos it shows in each arm
Offline NDCG of the new model on last month's logs, recomputed for each week of the test
questions.explanation:
A model trained on clicks will probably raise clicks, so clicks alone cannot tell you whether the app got better. Return rate at 7 and 28 days measures lasting value, and the longer window catches novelty effects that fade. Creator and topic diversity is a guardrail against a narrow, repetitive feed that may win in week one and bore users by week four. Negative feedback rates catch clickbait and harmful content, which can raise clicks while users grow annoyed.

Using click-through rate as the only criterion is the trap: it is easy to game with sensational thumbnails, and it is the very thing the model was trained to push up. The model's own predicted click probability is not a measurement of users at all. It differs between arms because the models differ, so comparing it says nothing about outcomes. Offline NDCG on old logs does not change during an online test and is biased toward the old model's choices, so it has no place in an online launch decision.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like to ask what you do if clicks rise but 28-day return falls. A strong answer treats the long-term metric as the decision maker and digs into segments. Some teams also keep a small long-running holdout to measure effects that take months, such as creator supply and user churn.

questions.prompt: Readings from a gas turbine form a ring of normal operation around a central blob of faulty states, so no straight line separates them. An SVM that compares points with the Gaussian similarity exp(−γ‖x − z‖²) still finds a curved boundary. It computes inner products as if the points had been mapped into a much higher-dimensional space, without ever building the mapped features. This shortcut is called the ______.
questions.explanation:
Training and prediction for an SVM use the data only through inner products between pairs of points, xᵢ · xⱼ. The kernel trick swaps each inner product for a kernel function K(xᵢ, xⱼ) that equals the inner product after some mapping φ, without ever computing φ. The RBF kernel, K(x, z) = exp(−γ‖x − z‖²), matches a mapping with infinitely many dimensions, so building those features is impossible, yet the kernel needs just one distance calculation.

In the mapped space a flat boundary can separate the ring from the blob. Back in the original space that flat boundary shows up as a curve.

The common mistake is to think the SVM explicitly creates polynomial or other extra features. That is ordinary feature expansion. It works, but the feature count explodes: all polynomial terms up to degree 3 of 100 inputs give more than 170,000 columns. The kernel trick avoids that cost. The price is that kernel SVMs work with a matrix over pairs of training points, so training gets slow once the data reaches hundreds of thousands of rows.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask what γ does in the RBF kernel. A large γ makes each point's influence very local and gives wiggly boundaries that can overfit, while a small γ gives smooth ones. γ and C are tuned together, usually on a log-scale grid. On large datasets teams switch to linear models on approximate kernel features.

questions.prompt: A ride-hailing team is cleaning a table of 2 million trips, with duration, distance and fare, before training a fare model. Which steps are sensible for finding and handling outliers? Select all that apply.
options: Drop the trips the current model predicts worst, since large errors mean the rows are bad data
Flag trips more than 1.5 IQRs below the first quartile or above the third, then inspect them
Check domain limits, such as fares below zero or average speeds above 200 km/h
Flag values with a z-score beyond ±3 on columns that are roughly bell-shaped
Delete every row outside the 1st to 99th percentile of each column, without looking at them
questions.explanation:
The IQR rule flags points far outside the middle half of the data and is robust, because quartiles barely move when extreme values are added. Inspecting the flags matters, since a long airport trip is extreme but real. Domain limits catch values that are impossible rather than just rare: a negative fare or a car averaging 300 km/h is a logging error, whatever the statistics say. A z-score cut at ±3 works on roughly bell-shaped columns, though very large outliers inflate the standard deviation and can hide themselves.

Blindly deleting the tails of every column removes 2% per column, including real long trips and surge fares, which are exactly the cases a fare model must price well. It also leaves the model untrained on its most expensive mistakes. Dropping the rows the current model gets most wrong is circular. It deletes hard but valid trips and makes the model look better than it is.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like the follow-up: what do you do with a real but extreme value? Options include capping, a log transform, a robust loss such as Huber, or a separate model for that segment. Deletion is for values you have confirmed are errors.

questions.prompt: A support-ticket router predicts probabilities of 0.60 for billing, 0.25 for technical and 0.15 for account. The ticket is really a technical one. What is the cross-entropy loss for this ticket, using the natural log? Give the answer as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
For one example with a single true class, cross-entropy only looks at the probability given to that class: loss = −ln(p_true). The true class is technical, so p_true = 0.25 and the loss is −ln(0.25) = ln(4) ≈ 1.386, which rounds to 1.39.

The other two probabilities still matter, but only indirectly. Softmax ties all three together, so training that pushes technical up also pushes billing and account down.

The most common mistake is to plug in the model's top prediction, 0.60, which gives −ln(0.60) ≈ 0.51. That measures how sure the model is of its own guess, not how well it did on the true label. Another slip is to use log base 10, which gives about 0.60. A perfect prediction, p_true = 1, gives a loss of 0, and the loss grows without limit as p_true falls toward 0.
questions.deeper: Averaged over a dataset, this is the log loss, and it punishes confident mistakes hard. A ticket where the true class gets 0.01 costs about 4.6, as much as many well-handled tickets put together. Interviewers like candidates who connect this to label noise, since a few mislabelled examples can dominate the average loss.

questions.prompt: Scanned invoices go through an LLM that pulls out the supplier name, invoice date and total, and the result is loaded into an accounting system. About 3% of replies fail to parse. Some wrap the JSON in a sentence, and some leave out the total field. What is the most reliable fix?
options: Enforce a JSON schema through structured output or a tool call, then validate each reply and retry the failures.
Add "Return ONLY valid JSON" in capitals to the prompt, then regex out the first brace-delimited block of each reply.
Set the temperature to 0, so the model gives the same well-formed JSON structure every time it reads one of the invoices.
Ask the model for plain text instead, then make a second LLM call that converts that text into JSON before it is loaded.
questions.explanation:
Schema-constrained output limits which tokens the model can produce, so the reply always parses and always has the required fields. Tool calling with a JSON schema for the arguments works in a similar way, though some setups treat the schema as a strong hint rather than a hard rule. Validation is still needed, because a schema guarantees the shape and not the content. A total of -40 or a date in 2087 is valid JSON. When a check fails, retry with the error message included, and after a few failures send the invoice to a human queue.

A stronger prompt lowers the failure rate but guarantees nothing, and a regex that grabs the first brace block breaks on nested objects and happily accepts a reply with a missing field. Temperature 0 makes output less random, but the most likely token sequence can still be malformed, and every invoice is a new input anyway. A second LLM call to convert text into JSON adds cost and latency and has exactly the same failure mode as the first call.
questions.deeper: In an interview, separate three layers: format (does it parse), schema (are the right fields there with the right types) and business rules (does the total equal the sum of line items). Constrained decoding handles the first two. Only your own code handles the third.

questions.prompt: Users who turn on an app's dark mode keep using the app 20% longer than users who do not. A product manager proposes switching dark mode on for everyone to raise retention. What is the main flaw in this reasoning, and the best next step?
questions.explanation:
Dark mode users are not a random group. People who explore settings tend to be engaged, long-time users, and those same users would stay longer anyway. Engagement is a confounder: it drives both dark mode use and retention, so the 20% gap can appear even if dark mode does nothing. A randomized test breaks this link. If dark mode is switched on for a random half of users, engagement is balanced across the two groups on average, so any retention gap is caused by dark mode.

The option asking for a larger observational dataset fixes the wrong problem. More data shrinks random noise but keeps the same confounding, so you just get a more precise biased number. The reverse-causation option has a fair point, since long-time users have more chances to find the setting, but it jumps to the claim that the change must hurt, which nothing here shows. The option calling the gap strong evidence confuses a large correlation with a causal effect. A big gap can come entirely from who chooses the feature.
questions.deeper: When a randomized test is not possible, interviewers expect you to mention ways to adjust for confounders, such as matching users on engagement and tenure. A strong candidate also notes that switching dark mode on for everyone turns a choice into a default, which is a different treatment from the one users picked for themselves.
options: The sample may be too small to trust, so gather a larger observational dataset and check again.
Retention may cause dark mode use, so the change will surely hurt and the idea should be dropped.
Committed users may be likelier both to find the setting and to stay, so run a randomized test.
Nothing is wrong, since a gap as large as 20% is strong enough evidence of a causal effect.

questions.prompt: You have budget for 9 training runs to tune a gradient-boosted model's learning rate and its column sample rate. From past projects you know the learning rate matters far more than the column sample rate. Why is random search usually a better use of the 9 runs than a 3 × 3 grid?
options: Random search tries 9 different learning rates, while the grid tests only 3, each repeated 3 times.
Random search uses earlier results to choose the next trial, so it moves toward the best region quickly.
Random search is sure to hit the best setting, while a grid can step right over it between its points.
Random search trains each run on a random sample of rows, so it fits more runs into the same budget.
questions.explanation:
In a 3 × 3 grid, each of the 3 learning rates is paired with 3 column sample rates. Since the column rate barely matters, those 3 runs give almost the same result, so 6 of the 9 runs teach you little. Random search draws both values fresh for every run, so all 9 runs land on different learning rates. You explore the axis that matters 3 times as finely for the same cost. The more unimportant hyperparameters there are, the bigger this advantage gets.

Using earlier results to pick the next trial describes Bayesian optimisation and other adaptive methods. Plain random search draws every trial independently. Random search has no guarantee of hitting the best setting. It can miss too, it just covers the important axis better on average. Training on a sample of rows is a separate budget trick used by methods such as successive halving. It is not what makes random search beat a grid.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds that the learning rate should be sampled on a log scale, for example between 0.001 and 0.3, so small values get fair coverage. Many teams start with random search, then switch to Bayesian optimisation once they know roughly where the good region is.

questions.prompt: A job-ad delivery model shows senior engineering ads to men far more often than to women. The team lists possible fixes and the stage of the pipeline each belongs to. Which pairings are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Reweighing training examples so group and label look independent in the weighted data is a pre-processing fix.
Adding a fairness penalty to the training loss so the gap counts as error is an in-processing fix.
Setting a separate score threshold for each group on the already trained model is a post-processing fix.
Adversarial debiasing, where a second network tries to guess gender from the model's outputs during training, is a post-processing fix.
Resampling the training data so both groups appear equally often is a post-processing fix.
Relabelling some training examples so both groups have similar positive rates is an in-processing fix.
questions.explanation:
The three stages are defined by what you change. Pre-processing changes the data before training. In-processing changes how the model learns. Post-processing changes how a trained model's outputs become decisions.

Reweighing gives each example a weight so that, in the weighted data, group and label are independent. It touches only the data, so it is pre-processing. A fairness penalty in the loss changes the training objective, which makes it in-processing. Per-group thresholds leave the model alone and only change the cut-off applied to its scores, so they are post-processing.

Adversarial debiasing is wrong as post-processing because the adversary is trained together with the main model and its loss shapes the main model's weights. That is in-processing. Resampling the training data, like reweighing, changes the data before training, so it is pre-processing. Relabelling, sometimes called massaging, flips a few labels before training starts. It edits the data, not the learning algorithm, so it is also pre-processing, not in-processing. Per-group thresholds need no retraining at all, which is why they are the fastest fix to try.
questions.deeper: Each stage has a catch. Post-processing needs the protected attribute at decision time, which can be unlawful in hiring or ads for jobs. In-processing needs it during training. A strong candidate names the stage, the data it needs and the legal check before suggesting one.

questions.prompt:
A teammate evaluates a churn model with this scikit-learn code. What is wrong, and what is the best fix?

```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
scores = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X_scaled, y, cv=5)
```
options: The scaler is fit on all rows, held-out folds included. Wrap the scaler and model in a Pipeline and cross-validate that.
Nothing leaks, because the scaler never looks at `y`. The scores are a fair estimate of new data, so the code can stay as it is.
The scaler should be refit on each validation fold inside the loop, so that every fold is scaled by its own mean and variance.
The folds are not stratified, so class balance varies between them. Pass `cv=StratifiedKFold(5)` to keep the scaling consistent.
questions.explanation:
`fit_transform(X)` computes the mean and standard deviation from all rows before cross-validation starts. So in every fold, the validation rows have already shaped the scaling of the training rows, and the model gets a small peek at data it is later scored on. With a Pipeline, `cross_val_score` refits the scaler on the four training folds each time and only applies it to the held-out fold. That matches production, where the scaler never sees future data.

The claim that nothing leaks because the scaler never sees `y` is the trap. Leakage is any information from the evaluation data reaching training, labels or not. With a plain scaler the effect is often small, but the same habit with imputers, target encoders or feature selection can inflate scores a lot. Refitting on each validation fold is wrong the other way: held-out rows should be transformed with training statistics, never used to fit. Stratification is not the problem either. For a classifier, `cv=5` already uses stratified folds, and it says nothing about where the scaler was fit.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like to ask which steps belong inside the Pipeline. The answer is anything that learns from data: scalers, imputers, encoders and feature selectors. A good habit is to make the Pipeline the object you tune with GridSearchCV, so every candidate in the search is scored without leakage.

questions.subtopic: naming the error of too-simple models
questions.prompt: A straight-line model predicts house prices from floor area alone. Prices really curve upward for large homes, so training and validation error are both high and close together. The bias-variance decomposition splits expected error into three named terms. The term for error that comes from a model being too simple to capture the true pattern is called ______.
questions.explanation:
Bias is the error from wrong assumptions built into the model. A straight line cannot bend, so however much data you give it, it will keep missing the curve for large homes. That is why training error stays high: the model is wrong even on data it has seen. Validation error is close to training error because the model is too simple to memorise anything.

The common mix-up is with variance. Variance is the error from a model being too sensitive to the particular training set, which shows up as low training error and much higher validation error. Some people also answer underfitting. Underfitting is the name of the situation, not one of the three terms. The decomposition is bias squared plus variance plus irreducible noise, and bias is the term that causes underfitting. Adding a squared term or a tree-based model would cut bias here, while more data alone would not help much.
questions.deeper: In interviews, tie the term to a fix. High bias calls for more capacity or better features, not more rows. A useful check is whether training error is far from a reasonable target, such as human-level error or the error of a stronger reference model.

questions.prompt: In RLHF, human raters compare pairs of responses to the same prompt and pick the better one. A separate model is trained on these comparisons to give any response a single score, and the policy is optimized against that score during reinforcement learning. This model is called the ______.
questions.explanation:
The reward model turns human preferences into a number the RL algorithm can use. It is usually a transformer like the policy, with the output layer replaced by a head that gives one scalar. It is trained so that the preferred response in each pair scores higher than the rejected one, often with the loss -log σ(r_preferred - r_rejected). During PPO, the policy generates responses and the reward model scores them, which is far cheaper than asking humans each time.

A common mistake is to answer "value model" or "critic". In PPO the critic estimates how much reward to expect from a point partway through a response, to make updates less noisy. It learns from the reward model's scores and does not judge quality itself. Another mix-up is the "reference model", the frozen copy of the starting policy that the KL penalty compares against.
questions.deeper: Because the policy is optimized against the reward model, its flaws become the policy's flaws. Interviewers may ask how you would check a reward model: its accuracy on held-out preference pairs, whether it simply prefers longer answers, and whether its scores still agree with humans on outputs from the newly trained policy.

questions.prompt: An online store wants to A/B test a new checkout on revenue per user, with about 50,000 users in each arm. Revenue per user is very skewed: most users spend nothing and a few spend thousands. A colleague says a z-test on the difference in means is invalid because revenue is not normally distributed. What is the best reply?
questions.explanation:
The z-test compares two sample means. What it needs is for each mean to be close to normal across repeated samples. The central limit theorem says the mean of many independent values is close to normal whatever the shape of the individual values, as long as their variance is finite. With 50,000 users per arm, the averages are close enough to normal for the test to work, even though single users' revenue is far from normal.

The option claiming the revenue values become normal misreads the theorem. The data keeps its skewed shape however many users you collect. Only the sampling distribution of the average becomes normal. The option about symmetric data is wrong because the theorem has no symmetry condition, though strong skew does mean you need more data before the approximation is good. A rank-based test would also answer a different question, whether one arm tends to rank higher, not whether average revenue rose. Log-transforming changes the question too. The mean of log revenue tracks the geometric mean, not average revenue, so it no longer tests the number the business cares about, and the many zero values need special handling.

One real caveat: a few huge spenders inflate the variance, so the test may need a lot of data to have useful power.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds practical fixes for heavy-tailed metrics: capping extreme values, variance reduction with pre-experiment data such as CUPED, or a bootstrap to check the interval. They also check that the unit of randomization matches the unit of analysis, since many orders from one user are not independent.
options: The colleague is right, so log-transform revenue first and then run the z-test on the logged values.
The test needs the averages to be near normal, not the raw values, and 50,000 users per arm gives that.
The central limit theorem makes the revenue values close to normal once each arm has enough users in it.
The central limit theorem only holds for symmetric data, so skewed revenue needs a rank-based test.

questions.prompt: A legal document classifier is retrained each week. Each round, the team sends labelers the unlabelled documents where the model's top predicted probability is lowest, the ones closest to a coin flip between classes. This active learning strategy is called ______ sampling.
questions.explanation:
Uncertainty sampling picks the examples the model is least sure about, because a label there is most likely to change the decision boundary. A document the model already scores at 0.99 teaches it little. A document at 0.4 versus 0.35 sits right where the model is confused. Using the lowest top probability, as here, is the least-confidence version. Margin sampling, the gap between the top two classes, and entropy over all classes are close variants.

A common wrong answer is random sampling, which is the baseline active learning tries to beat. Another is "diversity sampling", which picks examples that cover different parts of the data rather than the uncertain ones. The two are often combined, because pure uncertainty sampling can pick many near-identical confusing documents or chase noisy outliers.
questions.deeper: Keep a separate random, labelled test set. Data picked by active learning is deliberately unrepresentative, so scores measured on it mislead. Interviewers also like hearing that model scores must be reasonably calibrated for least-confidence picks to mean much.

questions.prompt: A marketplace checks new product listings with a two-stage cascade. Every listing first goes through a small model that costs $0.30 per 1,000 listings. The small model escalates 18% of listings to a large model that costs $6.00 per 1,000 listings, and escalated listings still pay for the small model. What is the average cost per 1,000 listings, in dollars to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation:
Every listing pays for the small model, and only the escalated share also pays for the large one.

- Small model on all listings: $0.30 per 1,000.
- Large model on 18% of them: 0.18 × $6.00 = $1.08 per 1,000.
- Total: $0.30 + $1.08 = $1.38 per 1,000 listings.

The common mistake is to treat the stages as a split, as if 82% used the small model and 18% the large one: 0.82 × 0.30 + 0.18 × 6.00 ≈ $1.33. That forgets that escalated listings ran through the small model first. The same logic applies to latency: escalated requests wait for both models, so average latency is the small model's time plus 18% of the large model's time.
questions.deeper: Compare against running the large model on everything, $6.00 per 1,000, and the cascade is over four times cheaper. Interviewers then ask what the escalation rate depends on. The answer is the confidence threshold, so a strong candidate shows how cost and accuracy move as that threshold changes.

questions.prompt: A bank's loan default model has been live for a year. Monitoring shows the mix of applicants looks the same as in training: income, debt ratio and age have barely moved. But applicants with a given profile now default more often than the model predicts. What best describes this change?
options: Concept drift: the same inputs now lead to different outcomes, so P(y | x) has changed.
Data drift: the inputs have moved away from the training data, so P(x) is now different.
Training-serving skew: production computes the features differently from the training pipeline.
Overfitting: the model memorised its training set, and this only shows up after months live.
questions.explanation:
The clue is that the inputs look the same, but the outcome for the same inputs has changed. That is concept drift. The relationship the model learned, the chance of default given a profile, is no longer true. A recession or a change in lending rules can do this without changing who applies.

Data drift, also called covariate shift, means P(x) moves, for example a sudden wave of younger applicants. Monitoring says the inputs have barely moved, so that does not fit. Training-serving skew is a pipeline bug where features are built differently in production. It usually shows up as odd feature values from the first day, not as a gradual rise in defaults for the same profiles. Overfitting shows up as a gap between training and held-out scores before launch. It does not explain a model that was fine for months and then got worse.
questions.deeper: Concept drift is the harder kind to catch, because input monitoring cannot see it. You need labels, or a fast proxy for them, to notice. A strong answer adds that the usual fix is retraining on recent data, sometimes with more weight on recent rows, and checking whether the features still capture what drives the outcome.

questions.prompt: A PyTorch model has dropout and batch norm layers, and you are writing its inference code. Which statements about `model.eval()` and `torch.no_grad()` are true? Select all that apply.
options: `model.eval()` makes dropout layers pass their inputs through unchanged
`model.eval()` makes batch norm use its stored running mean and variance
`model.eval()` on its own stops autograd from recording operations
`torch.no_grad()` switches batch norm to its stored running statistics
Inside `torch.no_grad()`, no autograd graph is built, which saves memory
`model.eval()` freezes the weights so `optimizer.step()` cannot change them
questions.explanation:
The two do separate jobs, and inference code usually needs both. `model.eval()` sets a flag that changes how some layers behave. Dropout stops dropping units and becomes a pass-through. PyTorch scales activations up during training instead, so no rescaling is needed at test time. Batch norm stops using the current batch's statistics and uses the running mean and variance it collected in training, so a prediction does not depend on what else is in the batch.

`torch.no_grad()` turns off gradient tracking. Operations inside it are not recorded, so the activations kept for the backward pass are not stored, which saves memory and time.

The statements that mix the two up are false. `eval()` alone still builds a graph, which is why forgetting `no_grad()` wastes memory. `no_grad()` alone leaves dropout and batch norm in training mode, which gives noisy, batch-dependent predictions. Neither one freezes weights. After `eval()`, gradients still flow and `optimizer.step()` still updates parameters. Freezing means setting `requires_grad=False` on parameters or leaving them out of the optimizer.
questions.deeper: A common follow-up asks about `torch.inference_mode()`, a stricter and slightly faster cousin of `no_grad()` for pure inference. Another classic bug is forgetting to call `model.train()` after a validation loop, so the rest of training runs with dropout off and batch norm statistics no longer updating.

questions.prompt: Using sentence embeddings as features, a kNN classifier labels support tickets as urgent or not. With k = 1 it scores 100% on training data and 74% on validation. If you raise k to 15, what is the most likely change?
options: Training accuracy will likely fall and validation accuracy rise, since a larger k smooths the boundary.
Training and validation accuracy will likely both rise, since each vote then draws on more labelled tickets.
Validation accuracy will likely fall, since a larger k makes the model follow single noisy points more closely.
Very little will likely change, since k only affects prediction speed and not the shape of the boundary.
questions.explanation:
With k = 1, each training point is its own nearest neighbour, so training accuracy is 100% by construction, unless two identical tickets carry different labels. The boundary bends around every single ticket, mislabelled ones included. That is high variance: a slightly different training set would give quite different predictions.

Raising k makes each prediction a vote among 15 neighbours, so one odd or mislabelled ticket gets outvoted. The boundary becomes smoother. Training accuracy usually drops, since points can now be outvoted by their neighbours, while validation accuracy often rises. Push k too high and the model underfits, drifting toward predicting the majority class everywhere.

Training accuracy cannot rise from 100%, and drawing on more tickets does not always help, because distant neighbours may come from a different region. Following single noisy points closely describes a small k, so that option has the direction backwards. And k changes the shape of the boundary, not just the speed of prediction.
questions.deeper: Pick k with cross-validation, and use an odd k for two classes to avoid ties. A strong candidate also mentions distance weighting, where nearer neighbours get more say, and notes that kNN prediction cost grows with the training set, so production systems use approximate nearest neighbour indexes.

questions.prompt: An IT helpdesk assistant built on a general-purpose LLM gives generic or made-up answers about the company's VPN setup. The real setup is described in internal wiki pages that change every few weeks. The team adds a step that fetches the most relevant wiki pages and puts them in the prompt before the model answers. What does this step mainly give them?
options: Answers based on the current internal pages, with links to the source, and no retraining when the pages change.
A model whose weights absorb the wiki pages each time a user asks, so it learns the VPN setup a little more over time.
Freedom from the context window limit, because fetched pages are kept in the model's memory instead of the prompt.
A guarantee of correct answers, since the model can only write sentences found word for word in the pages.
questions.explanation:
Retrieval puts the relevant wiki pages in front of the model at the moment of the question. The model then answers from text it can see, so the answer can follow the current setup and point to the page it came from. When the wiki changes, you update the search index, and the next answer uses the new text. No training run is needed. This is how a general model gets fresh and private knowledge cheaply.

The option about weights absorbing the pages describes fine-tuning or online learning, not retrieval. A RAG system leaves the weights untouched, which is exactly why it is cheap to keep up to date. Retrieval does not escape the context window either. Fetched pages go into the prompt and use up that window, which is why you retrieve a few relevant chunks rather than the whole wiki. Finally, retrieval reduces made-up answers but does not guarantee correct ones. The model can still misread a page, blend two pages or add facts of its own, so you still check that answers are grounded in the retrieved text.
questions.deeper: In an interview, name the three gains together: fresh knowledge, private knowledge and citations a user can check. Then name the costs. Retrieval can miss the right page, retrieved text adds tokens and latency, and the index needs access controls so the bot never quotes a page the user is not allowed to read.

questions.prompt:
A hospital tests a sepsis alert model on two age groups.

- Under 65: 80 true positives, 20 false negatives, 30 false positives, 270 true negatives.
- 65 and over: 54 true positives, 21 false negatives, 100 false positives, 400 true negatives.

Equalized odds asks for equal true positive rates (TPR) and equal false positive rates (FPR) across groups. Report the equalized odds gap, defined here as the larger of the absolute TPR gap and the absolute FPR gap. Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Work out both rates for each group. TPR is TP / (TP + FN), the share of real sepsis cases that get an alert. FPR is FP / (FP + TN), the share of patients without sepsis who get an alert anyway.

- Under 65: TPR = 80 / 100 = 0.80, FPR = 30 / 300 = 0.10.
- 65 and over: TPR = 54 / 75 = 0.72, FPR = 100 / 500 = 0.20.

The TPR gap is 0.08 and the FPR gap is 0.10, so the equalized odds gap is 0.10. Older patients get twice the rate of false alarms, and they also miss out on more true alerts.

The most common mistake is to stop after the TPR and answer 0.08. That checks equal opportunity, which only looks at people who really have the condition. Equalized odds also needs the error rate among people who do not. Another slip is to compute FP / (FP + TP), which is the share of alerts that are false. That gives 0.27 and 0.65 here, a different quantity that answers a different question.
questions.deeper: With only 75 older patients who had sepsis, a TPR gap of 0.08 could be noise, so a strong candidate adds confidence intervals before acting. They would also ask which error hurts more in this ward. A missed sepsis case can be fatal, while extra false alarms cost staff time and feed alert fatigue.

questions.prompt: A banking chatbot's intent classifier outputs logits of 3.0 for "check balance", 1.0 for "transfer money" and 0.0 for "report fraud". What softmax probability does it give "check balance"? Use e ≈ 2.71828 and give the answer as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Softmax turns logits into probabilities by exponentiating each one and dividing by the total.

- e³ ≈ 20.086
- e¹ ≈ 2.718
- e⁰ = 1
- Sum ≈ 20.086 + 2.718 + 1 = 23.804
- P(check balance) ≈ 20.086 / 23.804 ≈ 0.84

The other two intents get about 0.11 and 0.04, and all three add up to 1.

The common mistake is to divide the logits directly: 3 / (3 + 1 + 0) = 0.75. That skips the exponent, which is what makes softmax favour the largest logit more strongly than a plain ratio would. Plain division also breaks for negative logits, which it cannot turn into probabilities. Only the gaps between logits matter. A gap of 2 means a ratio of e² ≈ 7.4 between two probabilities, whatever the logits' absolute values are.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often follow up with temperature. Dividing every logit by a temperature T above 1 flattens the distribution, and T below 1 sharpens it. The same idea controls randomness in LLM sampling and is used to calibrate classifiers after training, where a single T is fitted on validation data.

questions.prompt: Suppose a data-cleaning agent completes a job in 20 steps, one after another. Each step succeeds with probability 0.97, independently of the others, and the job fails if any single step fails. What percentage of jobs succeed end to end? Give the answer as a percentage to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation:
The job succeeds only if all 20 steps succeed. Because the steps are independent, you multiply their success probabilities: 0.97 raised to the power 20.

- 0.97² = 0.9409
- 0.97⁴ = 0.9409² ≈ 0.8853
- 0.97⁵ ≈ 0.8853 × 0.97 ≈ 0.8587
- 0.97¹⁰ ≈ 0.8587² ≈ 0.7374
- 0.97²⁰ ≈ 0.7374² ≈ 0.5438, which is 54.4%

The most common mistake is to feel that 97% per step is "high" and expect most jobs to pass. Almost half fail. A second mistake is to subtract the error rates linearly: 20 × 3% = 60% failure, giving 40% success. That shortcut only works when the total error is small. For larger totals it overcounts, because once a job has failed, a second failure in the same job does not fail it again.

The same maths shows why small per-step gains matter so much. At 0.99 per step, 20 steps give about 81.8% success.
questions.deeper: Interviewers may turn it around: what per-step rate gives 90% over 20 steps? The answer is 0.9^(1/20) ≈ 0.995. In practice agents beat this simple product by checking their own work and retrying failed steps, which breaks the assumption that one failure ends the job.

questions.prompt: A logistics company serves a 20-billion-parameter model with 8-bit weights (1 byte per parameter) on one GPU whose memory bandwidth is 1.8 TB/s, where 1 TB = 10¹² bytes. For a single user, each new token requires reading every weight from memory once. Ignoring the KV cache and all other memory traffic, what is the upper bound on tokens per second for that one stream? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation:
At batch size 1, decoding is limited by how fast the weights can be streamed from memory, because each token needs every weight but does very little math with it.

- Bytes read per token: 20 × 10⁹ parameters × 1 byte = 20 × 10⁹ bytes
- Bandwidth: 1.8 × 10¹² bytes per second
- Ceiling: 1.8 × 10¹² / 20 × 10⁹ = 90 tokens per second

The common mistake is to use 2 bytes per parameter out of habit, which gives 45 tokens per second. That is the fp16 figure, and halving the bytes is exactly why 8-bit weights double the ceiling. Another mistake is to work from the GPU's compute rate. That gives a number many times higher, which is not reachable because memory runs out first.

Real systems land below this bound because of KV cache reads, kernel overheads and bandwidth that is never fully used.
questions.deeper: This back-of-the-envelope bound is a favourite in LLM serving interviews. It tells you quickly whether a latency target is even possible on given hardware. A strong candidate adds that the bound is per stream: batching many users shares the same weight reads, so total throughput can be far higher than 90 tokens per second.

questions.prompt: A model flags faulty sensor readings on a wind farm. In the test set, 5% of readings are faulty. The model scores a PR-AUC (average precision) of 0.30, and a teammate says that is worse than a coin flip. What PR-AUC would a model with random scores get on this test set, in expectation?
options: About 0.05, the share of faulty readings, so 0.30 is about six times the random level.
About 0.50, the same as the random ROC-AUC, so 0.30 means the model ranks worse than chance.
About 0.00, because random scores almost never put a faulty reading at the top of the list.
About 0.95, the share of normal readings, because random scores get most of those right.
questions.explanation:
With random scores, the readings above any threshold are a random sample of the test set, so about 5% of them are faulty at every threshold. Precision stays near 0.05 all the way along the recall axis, and the area under that flat line is about 0.05. So the baseline for PR-AUC is the positive rate, and 0.30 is a real gain over it.

The option claiming 0.50 mixes up the two curves. ROC-AUC has a random baseline of 0.5 whatever the class mix, but PR-AUC does not. The option claiming 0.00 forgets that precision is a share, not a count. Random scores still put some faulty readings near the top, about 5% of whatever is flagged. The option claiming 0.95 uses the wrong class. Precision and recall here are about the faulty class, so the normal readings do not set the baseline.
questions.deeper: Always say the positive rate next to a PR-AUC. A score of 0.30 is strong when positives are 1% and weak when they are 25%. It also means PR-AUC values from test sets with different class mixes cannot be compared directly.

questions.prompt: An energy company trains a usage-forecasting model on household smart-meter data. It uses a training method with a formal guarantee: adding or removing any one household's data changes the probability of any possible output by at most a factor of exp(ε), where a smaller ε means stronger protection. This guarantee is called ______.
questions.explanation:
Differential privacy promises that the output looks almost the same whether or not any one person's data was used. So an attacker who sees the model learns very little about any single household. ε, the privacy budget, sets how close the two cases must be. For model training the usual method is DP-SGD: clip each example's gradient so no one record can push too hard, then add random noise before each update. Stronger privacy, a smaller ε, usually costs some accuracy.

The common wrong answer is k-anonymity. That is a property of a released table, where each person is indistinguishable from at least k − 1 others on certain columns. It gives no bound on how much one record can change a trained model, and it can break when combined with outside data. Federated learning is another near miss. It keeps raw data on devices but gives no formal limit on what the shared updates reveal.
questions.deeper: A good interview point is that ε adds up. Each training run or query on the same data spends more of the budget, so teams track total privacy loss. Ask what ε value is planned and why, since a very large ε offers little real protection even though the method is technically differentially private.

questions.prompt: An online retailer has three language tasks: tagging support tickets into 20 categories, translating product manuals from German into Spanish, and writing open-ended marketing copy from a short brief. Which assignment matches what each transformer architecture was designed for?
options: Encoder-only for ticket tagging, encoder-decoder for manual translation, decoder-only for marketing copy.
Decoder-only for ticket tagging, encoder-only for manual translation, encoder-decoder for marketing copy.
Encoder-decoder for ticket tagging, decoder-only for manual translation, encoder-only for marketing copy.
Encoder-decoder for ticket tagging, encoder-only for manual translation, decoder-only for marketing copy.
questions.explanation:
An encoder-only model reads the whole ticket with attention in both directions and produces rich representations. A small classification head on top predicts the category, which is exactly what it was built for. An encoder-decoder model reads the full source sentence with the encoder, then the decoder writes the target language one token at a time while attending back to the source, which is the classic shape of translation. A decoder-only model is trained to continue text, so open-ended writing from a short brief is its natural job.

Every other assignment puts the encoder-only model on a generation task. That cannot work as designed, because an encoder outputs one vector per input token and has no step that writes new tokens. Those options also give tagging to a generative model. That can be made to work, but it wastes compute on generating text when a single label is all you need.
questions.deeper: In practice, large decoder-only models now handle all three tasks through prompting. A strong candidate still knows the tradeoff: a small fine-tuned encoder classifier is often far cheaper and faster for high-volume tagging, and an interviewer may ask when that beats prompting a large general model.

questions.prompt: An insurance claims assistant answers adjusters' questions from retrieved policy clauses. A reviewer checks each answer sentence by sentence and asks one thing: is every claim supported by the retrieved clauses, whether or not it happens to be true in the world? This property of an answer is called ______.
questions.explanation:
Groundedness, also called faithfulness, asks whether each statement in the answer can be traced to the retrieved text. It is checked against the context the model was given, not against the outside world. That is what makes it useful for a RAG system. If an answer contains a claim the clauses do not support, the model added it from memory or made it up, and an adjuster cannot verify it from the sources.

The common mistake is to answer "accuracy" or "correctness". Those compare the answer with the truth or with a reference answer, and the two ideas can come apart. If the retriever returns an outdated clause, an answer can be fully grounded and still wrong. If the model answers from general knowledge, it can be correct and still ungrounded, which is a problem in a regulated setting where every answer must be traceable. "Relevance" is also different.
