questions.deeper: A strong candidate notes the cost of randomisation: shuffled results hurt bookings, so the slice is kept small or only swaps neighbouring positions. They may also mention that propensity weights get large for low slots, so teams clip them to keep training stable.

questions.prompt: An intent classifier for a support bot scores 91% accuracy on a 12,000-ticket test set. Before launch, the team wants to know whether it fails for particular groups, such as users writing in Portuguese or tickets sent from the mobile app. Which practices are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Report accuracy for each language and channel, side by side with the overall 91%.
Show how many test tickets each slice has, with an interval, so a 40-ticket slice is read with care.
For slices well below 91%, read a sample of their misclassified tickets to find the cause.
Report the plain average of the per-slice accuracies as the overall accuracy, so each group counts once.
Leave out every slice with fewer than 200 test tickets, since such small slices tell you nothing.
Measure each slice on the training set instead, since it has far more tickets per slice than the test set.
questions.explanation:
Slice evaluation exists because a good overall number can hide a group where the model fails. Putting per-slice accuracy next to the overall figure shows which groups lag. Sample size matters because a slice of 40 tickets has a 95% interval of roughly ±12 points around 80% accuracy, so a gap that size may be noise. Reading the errors in a weak slice turns a number into a cause, such as missing training data in one language.

The plain average of slice accuracies is a macro average. It is a useful extra view, but calling it overall accuracy is wrong, since it no longer matches the share of all tickets classified correctly. Dropping small slices hides exactly the groups most likely to be underserved. The better move is to report them with wide intervals and collect more data. Training-set accuracy is inflated by fitting, so it cannot show how the model does on new tickets from any group.
questions.deeper: In practice, slice definitions are agreed before results come in, and new slices found while digging are treated as hypotheses to confirm on fresh data. Interviewers also like hearing that slice metrics belong in monitoring after launch, not only in the pre-launch report.

questions.prompt: After an A/B test, an analyst checks the result separately in 12 user segments, running a test at a significance level of 0.05 in each one. Suppose the change truly has no effect in any segment and the 12 tests are independent. What is the probability that at least one segment shows a significant result? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Work with the complement. When there is no effect, each test correctly stays non-significant with probability 1 − 0.05 = 0.95. With 12 independent tests, all of them stay quiet with probability 0.95¹² ≈ 0.540. So at least one false positive happens with probability 1 − 0.540 = 0.46.

The common mistake is to add the error rates: 12 × 0.05 = 0.60. That sum is an upper bound, not the true probability, because it double counts the cases where several tests fire together. With enough tests the sum even goes above 1, which no probability can.

The standard fix is the Bonferroni correction: test each segment at α / m = 0.05 / 12 ≈ 0.0042. Then the chance of at least one false positive across all 12 segments is at most 0.05. It is simple and safe but conservative, so it lowers the power in each segment.
questions.deeper: Segment hunting is a common way teams fool themselves: one of twelve segments "wins" and gets a launch. A strong candidate says the segments should be chosen before the test, corrected with Bonferroni or a false discovery rate method such as Benjamini-Hochberg, and that a surprise segment result needs a fresh test to confirm it.

questions.prompt:
Using pandas 3.x, what number does the last line return? Give a whole number.

```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"user": ["a", "b", "c"], "score": [10, 20, 30]})
df[df["score"] > 15]["score"] = 0
sub = df[df["score"] > 15]
sub.loc[:, "score"] = 99
df.loc[df["user"] == "c", "score"] += 5
df["score"].sum()
```
questions.explanation:
Under copy-on-write in pandas 3, every result of indexing behaves as its own copy. Only a single-step assignment on `df` itself, such as `df.loc[...] = ...`, changes `df`.

- The third line is chained assignment. `df[df["score"] > 15]` builds a new object, and setting `"score"` on it never reaches `df`. pandas 3 warns about this, and the scores stay 10, 20 and 30.
- `sub` is a separate frame. Setting its scores to 99 changes `sub` only.
- The `.loc` line changes `df` directly, so user c goes from 30 to 35.

The sum is 10 + 20 + 35 = 65.

The common mistake comes from older pandas habits, where chained assignment sometimes did update the original. If you believe the third line works, b and c become 0, then c becomes 5, and you get 15. If you believe `sub` is a view, b and c become 99, c then becomes 104, and you get 213.
questions.deeper: In an interview, say what copy-on-write buys you: no more guessing about SettingWithCopyWarning, and cheap copies, because data is only copied when one side is written to. The rule to remember is one step: write `df.loc[mask, col] = value`, never `df[mask][col] = value`.

questions.prompt: A linear regression for apartment rent includes an intercept and one-hot columns for all four districts in the city. Every row has exactly one district column set to 1, so the four columns always add up to the intercept column. The coefficients then have no unique least-squares solution. This problem is known as the ______ trap.
questions.explanation:
One-hot columns are also called dummy variables, and keeping all of them alongside an intercept is the dummy variable trap. The four district columns sum to 1 on every row, exactly like the intercept column, so the columns are perfectly collinear. You could add 100 to the intercept and subtract 100 from every district coefficient and get identical predictions, so there is no single best set of weights.

A common wrong answer is "multicollinearity". That is the underlying cause, perfect multicollinearity, but the named pitfall is the dummy variable trap. The usual fix is to drop one category, which becomes the reference level, with `drop="first"` in `OneHotEncoder` or `drop_first=True` in `pd.get_dummies`. Each remaining coefficient then reads as the rent difference from that reference district. Removing the intercept or adding ridge regularization also gives a unique solution.
questions.deeper: scikit-learn's `LinearRegression` will not crash here. Its solver returns one of the infinitely many solutions, so predictions look fine but the coefficients cannot be interpreted. Tree models are not affected, so dropping a column matters mainly for linear and logistic models.

questions.subtopic: approvals that are not rubber stamps
questions.prompt: A CRM agent proposes changes to customer records, such as merging duplicates, updating addresses and deleting stale contacts. Every change needs a human click on "Approve". Reviewers handle about 400 requests a day, approve 99.7% of them, and take a median of 3 seconds each. Last week a reviewer approved a request summarized as "clean up duplicates" that deleted 2,000 live contacts. How would you redesign the approval step?
questions.answer: The approvals have become a rubber stamp, so I would make fewer of them and make each one count. First, show the exact effect, not the agent's summary: which records change, a before and after diff, and how many rows are touched. Second, sort actions by risk. Small, reversible edits such as one address fix could run automatically with a log and an undo. Similar low-risk items, such as twenty duplicate merges, could be reviewed as one batch. Large or irreversible actions, such as deletes above a set count, get a detailed review and perhaps a second approver. Third, enforce it in code: the approval is tied to the exact action shown, and a bulk delete above the limit cannot run without it. Finally, I would watch review times and approval rates, and keep backups or soft deletes so mistakes can be undone.
points: Show the exact change and its size, not the agent's own summary
Tier by risk: auto-run small reversible actions, batch similar low-risk ones
Escalate large or irreversible actions to detailed or second-person review
Enforce limits in code and tie each approval to the exact action shown
Make actions reversible and monitor review behaviour over time
questions.explanation:
A 99.7% approval rate at 3 seconds each is a sign of approval fatigue. When nearly every request is fine, people stop reading, and the one dangerous request gets the same click as the rest. The fix is not to tell reviewers to try harder. It is to put fewer, clearer decisions in front of them.

The most common mistake is to add more approvals, which feeds the fatigue. A second mistake is to keep showing the agent's own description. "Clean up duplicates" was the agent's summary, and it hid that 2,000 live contacts would go. A reviewer can only catch what they are shown, so the screen must show the real effect: counts, a sample of records and a clear diff. Tiering by risk puts attention where a mistake is costly and lets routine edits flow. Enforcement in code matters because a rule such as "never bulk delete without review" should not rely on the agent asking politely. Reversibility is the last line of defence when review still misses something.
questions.deeper: Some teams test their reviewers by slipping a known-bad request into the queue now and then and tracking whether it gets caught. In interviews, saying that human review needs its own monitoring is a strong signal of production experience.

questions.prompt: A retailer retrains its demand model every month. To test that policy, the team pretends it is the start of January, trains only on data from before then and scores January. Then it moves forward a month and repeats, so every month of the past year is scored by a model that saw only earlier data. This way of evaluating a model as if it had been deployed in the past is called ______.
questions.explanation:
Backtesting replays history in time order. At each past cutoff the model is trained only on what would have been known then, and tested on the period that followed. Because it repeats across many cutoffs, it shows how the whole retraining policy would have performed, including months when patterns shifted, not just how one model does on one test set. The terms walk-forward validation and time series cross-validation describe the same idea and are accepted.

The common mistake is to answer k-fold cross-validation. Standard k-fold shuffles rows into folds, so a model can be trained on March and tested on January, using the future to predict the past. That inflates scores for any problem where patterns change over time. Backtesting keeps the arrow of time, which is why its scores are usually lower and more honest.
questions.deeper: Interviewers may ask about gaps. If labels arrive late or features use trailing windows, leave a buffer between the training cutoff and the test period, matching the delay the live system will have. A strong candidate also reports the spread of scores across months, not just the average.

questions.prompt: For which of these datasets would a random row-level train and test split put closely related rows on both sides, so the test score comes out over-optimistic? Select all that apply.
options: A churn table with one row per customer per month, where most customers appear in 12 monthly rows
A product photo set where most items were shot several times from nearly the same angle
Minute-by-minute sensor readings from 20 pumps, used to predict a failure in the coming week
A loan table with one row per applicant, each person appearing once, all from the same quarter
One record per patient, sampled at random, with the class rate kept equal in both splits
questions.explanation:
A random split is only honest when rows are independent draws, so that each test row is new to the model.

The churn table breaks this. A customer's 12 monthly rows share the same identity, habits and often the same label, so the model can recognise the customer instead of learning churn patterns. Split by customer instead. The photo set breaks it too. Near-identical shots of one item land on both sides, and the model scores well by matching a photo it has nearly seen. Group by item. The pump readings break it in two ways. Readings a minute apart are almost the same, and every minute in a week before a failure shares one label. Split by time, and ideally by pump as well.

The loan table has one row per person from a single period, so a random split is fine. The patient records are also independent. Keeping the class rate equal is stratification, which changes how rows are divided but does not link any two rows together.
questions.deeper: In scikit-learn, GroupKFold and GroupShuffleSplit keep a group on one side. A strong candidate asks how the model will be used: if it must work on new customers or new pumps, the test set should contain only unseen ones. Near-duplicate detection, such as perceptual hashing for images, is worth running before any split.

questions.prompt: A retailer runs k-means with k = 2 on six store locations, given as (x, y) in km: P1 (2, 3), P2 (3, 4), P3 (4, 2), P4 (9, 8), P5 (10, 9) and P6 (6, 5). The starting centroids are A = (3, 3) and B = (9, 9). Do one assignment step using Euclidean distance, then one centroid update. What is the x-coordinate of the new centroid A? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
In the assignment step each point joins its nearest centroid. P1, P2 and P3 are all within about 1.4 km of A and far from B. P4 and P5 are each 1 km from B. The only point that needs care is P6 at (6, 5).

Distance from P6 to A: √((6 − 3)² + (5 − 3)²) = √13 ≈ 3.61.

Distance from P6 to B: √((6 − 9)² + (5 − 9)²) = √25 = 5.

So P6 joins A. In the update step each centroid moves to the mean of its points. Cluster A now holds P1, P2, P3 and P6, so its new x is (2 + 3 + 4 + 6) / 4 = 15 / 4 = 3.75. Its new y is (3 + 4 + 2 + 5) / 4 = 3.5.

The common mistake is to judge P6 by eye. It looks like it sits between the groups, so people send it to B or leave it out. Either way cluster A keeps only P1 to P3 and its x comes out as (2 + 3 + 4) / 3 = 3.00. Always compute the distance for borderline points.
questions.deeper: k-means repeats these two steps until no point changes cluster. Each step can only lower the within-cluster sum of squares, so it always converges, but to a local minimum that depends on the start. That is why libraries use k-means++ seeding and several restarts. An interviewer may ask why the mean is the point that minimises the summed squared distance.

questions.prompt: A contract-review assistant handles very long documents, and the KV cache of a single long request uses too much GPU memory. Which of these changes reduce the KV cache memory one request can take, with the number of layers and the head size unchanged? Select all that apply.
options: Moving to a version of the model trained with 8 key-value heads in place of 32
Storing the cached keys and values as 8-bit numbers instead of 16-bit floats
Capping each request's context at 8,192 tokens instead of 32,768 tokens
Quantizing the model weights to 4 bits while keeping the cache in 16-bit floats
Computing attention with FlashAttention instead of the standard kernels
Raising the batch size so that more requests share each forward pass
questions.explanation:
KV cache memory for one request is 2 × layers × key-value heads × head size × tokens × bytes per number. With layers and head size fixed, the levers are key-value heads, bytes per number and tokens.

Grouped-query attention with 8 key-value heads instead of 32 cuts the cache to a quarter, because several query heads share each cached key and value head. An 8-bit cache halves the bytes per number. A context cap of 8,192 tokens instead of 32,768 cuts the worst-case cache per request to a quarter.

Quantizing the weights frees memory for the cache, which helps overall, but the cache of one request stays exactly the same size. FlashAttention avoids storing the n × n attention score matrix during the computation, yet the keys and values it reads are cached just as before. A larger batch serves more requests at once, so total cache memory goes up, while each request's share is unchanged.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds the tradeoffs. Grouped-query attention needs a model trained or adapted for it, an 8-bit cache can slightly hurt quality on long contexts, and a context cap may cut off parts of long contracts, so it may need chunking or retrieval instead.

questions.prompt: A bank's loan model approves 30% of applicants in group X and 30% of applicants in group Y. Among applicants who would actually repay, it approves 60% in group X but only 40% in group Y. Which statement is correct?
options: It meets demographic parity but fails equal opportunity, since true repayers are approved at unequal rates.
It meets equal opportunity, since applicants in both groups are approved at the same overall rate of 30%.
It meets both criteria, since equal approval rates also mean equal approval rates among those who would repay.
It fails demographic parity, since applicants who would repay are approved at a higher rate in group X.
questions.explanation:
Demographic parity asks only whether each group is approved at the same overall rate. Both groups get 30%, so it holds. Equal opportunity asks whether people who truly deserve a yes, here those who would repay, get one at the same rate. That is the true positive rate, 60% against 40%, so it fails.

The option claiming equal opportunity holds uses the overall rate, which is the parity test, not the opportunity test. The option claiming both hold assumes equal approval rates force equal true positive rates. They do not, because the groups can differ in how many applicants would repay and in how many non-repayers get approved. The option claiming parity fails applies the opportunity test to the parity criterion.

The two goals can pull against each other. When repayment rates differ between groups, equal approval rates usually push true positive rates apart. Getting both at once generally means accepting different false positive rates per group.
questions.deeper: There is no single fair metric. In an interview, say which harm matters for the use case. In lending, qualified applicants being refused points toward equal opportunity. Then say who should decide the trade-off: legal, policy and affected groups, not only the ML team.

questions.prompt: Inside each transformer block, every token's activation vector is normalized on its own: subtract the mean of that vector's features, divide by their standard deviation, then apply a learned scale and shift. No statistics are shared across the examples in a batch. This normalization is called ______.
questions.explanation:
Layer normalization computes the mean and standard deviation over the features of a single token's vector, so each token is normalized independently of every other token and every other example. That makes it behave the same at any batch size and any sequence length, in training and at inference.

The common wrong answer is batch normalization. Batch norm computes statistics for each feature across the examples in a batch and keeps running averages for use at inference. That fits transformers poorly. Sequences have different lengths, and padding tokens would pollute the batch statistics. Batches of long sequences are often small, so the estimates are noisy. During generation the model processes one new token at a time, where batch statistics make little sense, and running averages from training may not match what the model sees in production. RMSNorm is also ruled out, since it skips the mean subtraction and the shift that the prompt describes.
questions.deeper: Many recent LLMs use RMSNorm, a lighter variant that skips the mean subtraction and the shift and only divides by the root mean square. A likely follow-up is pre-norm versus post-norm: placing the normalization before each sublayer, as most modern models do, makes deep transformers train more stably.

questions.prompt: You download an open base language model and type "How do I reset my router?" It replies with more questions, as if continuing a forum page, instead of answering. Explain why, and walk through the training stages that turn a base model into a chat assistant and what each stage changes.
questions.answer: The base model was only pretrained on next-token prediction over a huge text corpus. It learned language and a lot of knowledge, but to it a question is just text to continue, and on the web a question is often followed by more questions. Supervised fine-tuning then trains it on curated prompt and response pairs in a chat format, so it learns to answer, follow instructions and stop at the end of its turn. Preference tuning, with RLHF or DPO, uses comparisons between pairs of replies to push it toward answers people rate as more helpful, honest and safe, such as admitting uncertainty or declining harmful requests. Most knowledge comes from pretraining. The later stages mainly change behaviour, format and tone, using far less data. Pushed too far, preference tuning can make a model verbose or overly cautious.
points: Pretraining on next-token prediction gives knowledge and language skill but no habit of answering
A base model continues text, so a question can be followed by more questions
Supervised fine-tuning on prompt and response pairs in a chat format teaches instruction following and turn-taking
Preference tuning such as RLHF or DPO uses compared replies to improve helpfulness, honesty and safety
Later stages change behaviour more than knowledge and use far less data than pretraining
Over-tuning on preferences can cause verbosity, over-refusal or reward hacking
questions.explanation:
The key idea is that each stage has a different job. Pretraining is the expensive part, run on trillions of tokens, and it is where the model learns grammar, facts and reasoning patterns. Its only goal is to predict the next token, so it imitates whatever usually comes next on the web, which explains the forum-style reply.

Supervised fine-tuning uses a much smaller set of high-quality examples, often tens of thousands, written in a fixed chat template. It teaches the shape of a helpful answer. Preference tuning then refines choices that are hard to show with single examples, such as which of two correct answers is clearer or safer.

The common mistake is to think fine-tuning is where the model learns its knowledge. Facts added only in fine-tuning are learned unreliably and can even raise hallucination. Another mistake is to describe RLHF as the whole process, skipping the supervised stage that makes preference tuning work.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often follow up with why a chat model needs its exact chat template at inference, or why a base model is sometimes the better starting point for your own fine-tune. A strong candidate also mentions that a few examples in the prompt can make a base model answer, without any training.

questions.prompt: A hospital group wants to add discharge-note summaries to its records system. It expects about 4,000 notes a day, each a few thousand tokens long, and a summary may take up to an hour to appear. One option is a hosted LLM API. The other is running an open-weight model on its own GPUs. How would you decide between them?
questions.answer: I would compare the two on data control, quality, cost at this volume, latency and operating burden. Data control comes first because these notes hold patient health data. For the API I would check whether the contract covers health data, whether the provider keeps or trains on inputs, and where data is processed. If those terms are not acceptable, self-hosting may be the only option. Next I would test both on a labelled set of real notes, since a smaller open model may summarize less well. On cost, 4,000 notes a day is modest. Pay-per-token pricing is likely cheaper than GPUs that sit mostly idle, unless volume grows or other workloads share the hardware. Latency barely matters because a one-hour window allows batch processing. Finally, self-hosting needs people to run serving, scaling, security patches, monitoring and model upgrades, and that staff cost belongs in the comparison.
points: Data control first: health data, retention, training use, processing location
Compare quality on a labelled set of real notes
Cost at 4,000 a day: per-token pricing versus mostly idle GPUs
Latency matters little with a one-hour batch window
Self-hosting adds staff and operating burden: serving, patches, upgrades, on-call
questions.explanation:
The decision is a set of tradeoffs, and the volume, the data and the latency needs in the prompt each push in a direction. The most common mistake is to decide on one factor alone. Some candidates say "self-host, because health data must never leave the building" without checking whether a hosted API can offer acceptable contract terms, processing location and no retention. Others say "use the API, because it is cheaper" without asking whether the terms allow health data at all, which can rule the API out before cost matters.

A second mistake is to compare GPU rental with the API bill and stop there. A self-hosted model needs engineers to keep it running, patched and monitored, and at modest volume that cost often exceeds the hardware. The picture changes with scale. At 4,000 notes a day a GPU sits idle much of the time, but at many times that volume, or when several workloads share the hardware, self-hosting can win. A good answer says what would change the decision.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate proposes a cheap experiment: run 200 real notes through both options, have clinicians score the summaries, and estimate monthly cost for each from measured token counts and GPU throughput. They might also put the model behind a common interface so the hospital can switch later without rewriting the feature.

questions.prompt: An ad-click model is checked each day with a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test per feature, comparing about 5 million of yesterday's requests with a 1 million row training sample. Most days, 40 of the 60 features come back with p < 0.001. Yet click-through rate and calibration are steady, and the flagged features' histograms look almost identical to training. What is the best change to the drift alerting?
options: Alert on the size of each shift, such as PSI or a distribution distance, with a set threshold
Apply a Bonferroni correction across the 60 features so each test uses a much stricter cut-off
Retrain the model every day, since the tests show that most of the inputs keep drifting
Replace the KS test with a chi-squared test on binned values, which reacts less to noise
questions.explanation:
A p-value answers "is there any difference at all?", not "is the difference big enough to matter?". With samples this large the test can see tiny gaps. With 5 million rows against 1 million, a largest gap of only about 0.002 between the two CDFs already gives p < 0.001. Real traffic is never an exact copy of the training sample, so almost every feature gets flagged. The fix is to alert on an effect size, such as PSI or a distance between distributions, with a threshold tied to what has hurt the model before.

Bonferroni treats this as a many-tests problem. It moves the cut-off from 0.001 to about 0.00002, but with millions of rows the p-values for harmless shifts are far smaller than that, so most alerts stay. Daily retraining reacts to noise. Click-through rate and calibration are steady, so nothing shows the model is being hurt. A chi-squared test on bins is still a significance test, and it has the same problem as the sample grows.
questions.deeper: A good follow-up is to ask what threshold to use. Strong candidates calibrate it on history: replay past months, see what PSI or distance values came before real performance drops, and set the alert just below that. Some teams also run the test on a fixed-size random sample, which keeps its sensitivity steady as traffic grows.

questions.prompt: A one-weight model predicts ŷ = w × x and uses the loss L(w) = (w × x − y)². For a single example with x = 2 and y = 10, the current weight is w = 3 and the learning rate is 0.05. What is w after one gradient descent step? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
The gradient of L(w) = (w × x − y)² with respect to w uses the chain rule: dL/dw = 2 × (w × x − y) × x.

With the numbers: the prediction is 3 × 2 = 6, the error is 6 − 10 = −4, so dL/dw = 2 × (−4) × 2 = −16. The update rule is w_new = w − learning rate × gradient = 3 − 0.05 × (−16) = 3 + 0.8 = 3.80.

The negative gradient means the loss falls as w grows, so the step moves w up, which makes sense because the model is predicting too low. The two common mistakes are dropping the inner factor x from the chain rule, which gives a gradient of −8 and w = 3.40, and adding the gradient instead of subtracting it, which gives w = 2.20 and moves the wrong way.
questions.deeper: Checking the new loss is a good habit: with w = 3.8 the prediction is 7.6, so the squared error drops from 16 to 5.76. Interviewers may ask what happens with a learning rate of 0.5. The step would overshoot to w = 11 and the loss would grow, which is how divergence looks.

questions.prompt:
Using pandas 3.x, a click log is joined to an ad table that, by mistake, lists ad 1 twice. How many rows does `out` have? Give a whole number.

```python
import pandas as pd
clicks = pd.DataFrame({"ad_id": [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3], "ts": range(6)})
ads = pd.DataFrame({"ad_id": [1, 1, 3, 4], "campaign": ["a", "b", "c", "d"]})
out = clicks.merge(ads, on="ad_id", how="left")
len(out)
```
questions.explanation:
A left merge keeps every row of `clicks` and pairs it with every matching row of `ads`. Work key by key:

- ad 1: 2 clicks × 2 ad rows = 4 rows
- ad 2: 1 click with no match, kept once with a missing campaign = 1 row
- ad 3: 3 clicks × 1 ad row = 3 rows
- ad 4 exists only in `ads`, so a left join drops it

That gives 4 + 1 + 3 = 8.

The most common mistake is to answer 6, believing a left join never changes the row count. That only holds when the right table's keys are unique. Duplicate keys on the right multiply the matching left rows. Others answer 7, which is what an inner join gives because it drops ad 2, or 9, which counts ad 4 as if it were an outer join.
questions.deeper: Silent row growth after a merge is a classic cause of inflated metrics, such as clicks counted twice. Pass `validate="many_to_one"` so pandas raises an error when the right keys are not unique, and compare `len()` before and after every join in a feature pipeline.

questions.prompt: A health insurer is about to launch an LLM assistant that answers members' questions using their own claim records. You are asked to plan the red teaming. Which plan is strongest?
options: Probe leaks, jailbreaks, unsafe advice and bias, and turn each failure into a regression test.
Probe jailbreaks only, since nearly every other harm starts with getting past the guardrails.
Probe leaks, jailbreaks, unsafe advice and bias in one big session the week before launch.
Have the prompt authors probe every harm type, since they know their own prompts' weak points.
questions.explanation:
Red teaming means deliberately trying to make the system fail in the ways that would hurt people most. For this product that means jailbreaks, leaks of another member's claims, unsafe medical or coverage advice, and answers that treat members differently by group. Each prompt that causes a failure becomes a test case. The set is rerun on every model, prompt or retrieval change, so a fixed failure that comes back is caught before release.

A focus on jailbreaks alone misses failures that need no jailbreak. An assistant can leak data through a retrieval bug or give harmful advice to a perfectly polite question. A single session before launch can cover every harm type and still only find today's problems. Without saved tests, a later model or prompt change can bring a fixed failure back, and real members are the ones who find it. Prompt authors can also cover every harm type, but they share their own blind spots and tend to test the cases they already designed for. Good red teams include outsiders and domain experts, here clinicians and claims staff.
questions.deeper: Interviewers may ask how you would scale this. Strong answers mention using an LLM to generate attack variants of each human finding, scoring outputs with a mix of rules and an LLM judge, and tracking failure rate per harm category as a release gate.

questions.prompt: A video streaming service builds each user's home page with a ranking service. During a recent incident the ranking service timed out for 15 minutes and home pages took 8 seconds to load. Which are sound parts of the fallback design? Select all that apply.
options: Serve the user's last ranked home page from a cache, as long as it is no more than a day old
Serve a list of titles popular in the user's region when no cached page exists for that user
Show an empty row in place of recommendations and skip logging, so the page loads and no alerts fire
Retry the ranking call in a tight loop until it answers, keeping the page request open the whole time
Count every fallback served and alert when the share of fallback pages rises above a set level
Fill missing features with zeros and keep scoring, without marking those requests as degraded
questions.explanation:
A good fallback gives users something reasonable quickly and makes the failure visible to the team. A recent cached page is personal and cheap to serve, and the age limit stops it from showing stale content for days. Popular titles by region are a safe default for users with no cache, such as new sign-ups. Counting fallbacks and alerting on their rate turns a silent degradation into an incident someone can fix.

An empty row with no logging hides the failure, so the outage could run for hours unnoticed while engagement drops. Retrying in a tight loop holds the page open, which is exactly how a timeout turns into 8-second page loads, and the extra calls pile more load onto a service that is already struggling. Retries need a short timeout, a small limit and backoff. Scoring with zeros in place of missing features can be a fair fallback if the model was trained to handle it, but doing it without marking the requests means nobody knows the scores are degraded, and those requests also pollute the training logs.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate pairs fallbacks with timeouts: give the ranking call, say, 150 ms, then fall back, so a slow dependency cannot drag the whole page down. They also mark fallback impressions in the logs so they are excluded from or flagged in training data, since they were not chosen by the model.

questions.prompt: A job board predicts the advertised salary of each posting. Salaries are right-skewed, with a long tail of executive roles. The team trains a linear regression on `np.log1p(salary)` instead of the raw salary. How should they turn the model's outputs back into dollars?
options: Multiply each output by the mean training salary to restore units
Apply `np.expm1`, which computes exp(x) − 1 and reverses `np.log1p`
Apply `np.exp` and then add 1, which reverses the `np.log1p` step
Apply `np.log1p` once more, which maps the outputs back into dollars
questions.explanation:
`np.log1p(x)` computes log(1 + x). To undo it, take the exponential and then subtract 1, which is exactly what `np.expm1` does. The log helps here because salary errors are roughly proportional (a $10,000 miss matters more on a $40,000 role than on a $400,000 one), and because the long executive tail no longer dominates the squared loss.

Adding 1 after `np.exp` gets the sign backwards. The error is tiny for salaries but would be large for a target near zero, such as a count. Applying `np.log1p` again compresses the outputs further instead of reversing them. Multiplying by the mean salary has no mathematical link to the log and produces nonsense values.

One more point: the model predicts the mean of the log salary. Undoing the log gives something close to the median for similar postings, which sits below their mean salary. If you need mean dollars, apply a correction such as Duan's smearing.
questions.deeper: scikit-learn's `TransformedTargetRegressor(func=np.log1p, inverse_func=np.expm1)` handles both directions so no one forgets. Interviewers may ask why metrics should be reported in dollars after the inverse, not on the log scale, since the business cares about dollar errors.

questions.subtopic: batch norm in training vs inference
questions.prompt: A team trains a CNN to spot cracks in high-resolution road scans. Memory allows only 2 images per batch, and the network uses batch normalization. Training loss falls nicely, but after calling `model.eval()` the validation predictions are poor. Oddly, the same validation images score much better when the model is left in training mode and fed in batches of 2. What is the most likely cause?
options: Training normalized with the noisy statistics of 2 images per batch, but eval mode uses running averages that do not match what the layers learned.
Eval mode switches batch normalization off entirely, so at inference the layers receive raw activations at a scale never seen during training.
Eval mode recomputes the mean and variance over the whole validation set in one pass, and those statistics sit far from the ones gathered in training.
Switching to eval mode resets the learned scale and shift in every batch norm layer back to their starting values of 1 and 0, undoing what training learned.
questions.explanation:
In training mode, batch norm normalizes each channel with the mean and variance of the current batch and also updates running averages of those statistics. In eval mode it uses the running averages instead, so a prediction does not depend on which other images share the batch. With only 2 images per batch, the batch statistics jump around from step to step, and the network learns to work with those noisy, batch-specific values. The smoothed running averages give the layers inputs unlike anything they saw in training, so eval mode underperforms. Feeding batches of 2 in training mode recreates the training conditions, which is why it looks better, but each prediction then depends on its batch partner, which is not usable in production.

Eval mode does not switch normalization off. It only changes which statistics are used. It does not compute fresh statistics over the validation set either, since that would make predictions depend on the test data. The learned scale and shift, γ and β, are ordinary trained parameters and stay exactly as trained. Common fixes are group or layer normalization, which do not depend on batch size, or synchronized batch norm across GPUs for a larger effective batch.
questions.deeper: When fine-tuning a pretrained CNN with tiny batches, many teams freeze the batch norm layers so the running statistics from pretraining stay fixed. Detection and segmentation models, which often train with only 1 or 2 images per GPU, commonly use group norm or frozen batch norm for exactly this reason.

questions.prompt: A team is tuning text generation for a product-description writer. Which statements about decoding settings are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Greedy decoding picks the most likely next token at every step, so it involves no random sampling.
A temperature above 1 flattens the next-token distribution, so less likely tokens are chosen more often.
Top-p sampling with p = 0.9 samples from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to at least 0.9.
Lowering the temperature toward 0 makes the output more varied, because it removes the bias toward common tokens.
Top-p sampling keeps the same number of candidate tokens at every step, however peaked the distribution is.
Greedy decoding is guaranteed to return the most likely complete sequence for the given prompt.
questions.explanation:
Greedy decoding takes the highest-probability token at each step, so it has no sampling randomness, and the same input gives the same output apart from small numerical effects on some hardware. Temperature divides the logits before the softmax. A value above 1 shrinks the gaps between logits and flattens the distribution, so unlikely tokens get picked more often and the text becomes more varied. Top-p, or nucleus, sampling sorts tokens by probability, keeps the smallest set whose total reaches p, and samples from that set.

Lowering the temperature does the opposite of what the false statement claims. It sharpens the distribution, and as it nears 0 sampling approaches greedy decoding, so output becomes less varied. Keeping a fixed number of candidates describes top-k. Top-p adapts: when the model is confident, a few tokens reach 0.9, and when it is unsure, many tokens are needed. Greedy is only best one step at a time. A slightly less likely first token can lead to a much more likely full sequence, which is why beam search exists.
questions.deeper: For product descriptions, a strong answer picks settings per field: greedy or a low temperature where facts such as sizes and materials must be exact and consistent, and a moderate temperature with top-p for the creative copy. Interviewers often follow up on why greedy text can become repetitive and how repetition penalties help.

questions.prompt: A music streaming app plans an even 50/50 split for an A/B test of a new playlist screen. After a week, control has 503,912 users and treatment has 496,088. A chi-square test comparing these counts with the planned split gives p < 0.0001. Before reading any business metric, the team flags this problem, which usually points to a bug in assignment or logging. The problem is called a ______.
questions.explanation:
A sample ratio mismatch means the users who ended up in each arm do not match the split you planned, by more than chance allows. With 1,000,000 users and a fair 50/50 coin, the count in one arm has a standard deviation of √(1,000,000 × 0.5 × 0.5) = 500. Control is 3,912 above 500,000, nearly 8 standard deviations, and the chi-square value is about 61. That is not luck.

The common mistake is to wave the gap away because 50.4% against 49.6% looks close to even. At large sample sizes even small percentage gaps are far outside chance. The other mistake is to call it selection bias or Simpson's paradox. Those are broader ideas. SRM is the specific check on counts per arm, and when it fails, the users that are missing from one arm are usually not missing at random, for example users whose app crashed before the treatment screen logged them. That biases every metric, so the result should not be trusted until the cause is found.
questions.deeper: Mature experiment platforms run the SRM check automatically and block results when it fails. Common causes include bot filtering that hits one arm more, redirects that drop users, and a treatment that crashes for some devices before the exposure event fires.

questions.prompt: A code-completion service adds speculative decoding. A small draft model proposes the next 4 tokens, and then the large model checks them. Completions now come back faster, and their quality is no worse than before. Which description of the mechanism explains both results?
options: The large model scores all 4 drafts in one forward pass, keeps them up to the first one it rejects, and replaces that one with a token chosen by the large model itself.
The draft model writes the completion, and the large model checks a random sample of its tokens, regenerating only the spans where the two models disagree with each other.
The large model still runs one forward pass per token, but the drafted guesses let it skip the softmax over the whole vocabulary, which is the costly part of each step.
Both models generate a full completion in parallel, and the service returns whichever of the two completions the large model gives the higher total log-probability.
questions.explanation:
Speculative decoding works because checking tokens is cheaper than generating them. A large model's decoding step is limited by reading all of its weights from memory, and it yields one token. Scoring 4 drafted tokens in one forward pass reads the weights once, so it costs about the same as a single step. That is the speed-up.

Quality holds because of the accept rule. With greedy decoding, a drafted token is kept only if it matches the large model's own top choice. With sampling, a token is kept with probability min(1, p / q), where p is the large model's probability and q is the draft's, and the first rejected token is replaced by a sample from the large model's leftover distribution. This makes the output follow exactly the large model's distribution. If all 4 are accepted, the same pass also gives a fifth token.

Checking only a random sample would let the draft model's mistakes through, so quality would drop. Skipping the softmax saves almost nothing, since the cost is in the weight reads, and one pass per token gives no speed-up. Generating two full completions in parallel is slower, and returning the draft's completion would change the output.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask when speculative decoding stops helping. The answer is when the draft is often rejected, when the draft model itself is slow, or at large batch sizes, where decoding is no longer memory-bound and the spare compute the trick relies on is gone.

questions.prompt: An insurer trains a model to flag claims that need manual review. The team plots a learning curve from 10,000 to 400,000 training rows. Since about 80,000 rows, training error has stayed near 11% and validation error near 12%, and both lines are flat. The product goal is 5% error. A vendor offers another 400,000 labelled claims for a high price. What should the team conclude?
options: Hold off on buying. Both curves are flat at a high error, so the model needs more capacity or better features.
Buy the data. Validation error is still above training error, and more rows will close that gap down to 5%.
Buy the data. The model is overfitting, and more labelled rows are the standard first fix for overfitting.
Hold off on buying. The 1-point gap shows overfitting, so stronger regularization is the next thing the team should try.
questions.explanation:
When both curves have been flat for hundreds of thousands of rows and sit close together, the model has learned about as much as it can from this kind of data. More rows just extend a flat line. The remaining problem is the distance between 11% training error and the 5% goal, which is bias. The model is too simple, or the features do not carry enough signal. Error analysis, better features or a more flexible model are the levers that can move training error down.

The option about closing the gap misreads the numbers. The gap is only 1 point, so closing it fully would bring validation error to about 11%, still far from 5%. Calling this overfitting is wrong because overfitting shows low training error and a large gap, the opposite of this picture. Stronger regularization would make an underfitting model even simpler and push both errors up.
questions.deeper: More data is worth buying when validation error is still falling at the right edge of the curve, or when there is a large train to validation gap. A strong candidate also asks whether the new rows differ in kind, such as a new region or product line. Data that covers new cases can help even when the curve looks flat.

questions.prompt: A logistics company gives its operations agent one tool, `run_sql(query)`, which runs any SQL against the warehouse database. The tool description says only "Runs SQL." When a query fails, the tool returns a 60-line Python stack trace. In traces, the agent guesses table names, misreads errors and often retries the same broken query. Which redesign would help the agent most?
options: Add narrow tools like `get_shipment_status(tracking_id)` with clear descriptions, and return short errors with a fix hint.
Keep `run_sql` but return the full stack trace plus the database logs on failure, so the agent has every detail it could need to debug the query.
Merge every action into one `do_task(instruction)` tool, so the agent has fewer choices to make and can never pick the wrong tool by mistake.
Return an empty result whenever a query fails, so error text never distracts the agent from its task.
questions.explanation:
A model decides when and how to use a tool from its name, its description and its parameter schema, much like a new developer reading API docs. A narrow tool such as `get_shipment_status` puts the right tables and joins in code once, so the agent no longer has to guess the database schema. A typed parameter like `tracking_id` makes bad calls less likely, and a scoped tool is also safer than open SQL. Errors are input to the agent's next step. A message such as "No shipment with tracking ID ABC123. IDs start with TRK followed by 8 digits." gives it a clear way to recover.

A longer stack trace plus logs adds tokens and noise and buries the one line that matters. A single `do_task` tool does not remove the choice, it hides it inside free text with no schema, which is harder to check and to debug. Returning an empty result on failure is the most dangerous option, because the agent cannot tell "no data" from "the query broke" and may report a wrong answer with confidence.
questions.deeper: In practice, teams improve tools by reading agent traces and watching where the model gets confused, the same way you would watch a user test a product. A strong candidate also mentions returning only the fields the agent needs and paging large results, since huge tool outputs waste context.

questions.prompt: A recipe app predicts star ratings with a matrix factorisation model that has bias terms. The global mean rating is 3.6. A user has bias +0.3 and a recipe has bias −0.4. The user's latent vector is (0.8, −0.5, 1.2) and the recipe's is (0.5, 0.6, 0.3). The prediction is the global mean plus both biases plus the dot product of the two vectors. What rating does the model predict for this user and recipe? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
The model is r̂ = μ + b_u + b_i + p_u · q_i.

Dot product, one factor at a time: 0.8 × 0.5 = 0.40, then −0.5 × 0.6 = −0.30, then 1.2 × 0.3 = 0.36. The sum is 0.40 − 0.30 + 0.36 = 0.46.

Add the rest: 3.6 + 0.3 − 0.4 + 0.46 = 3.96.

The most common slip is losing the minus sign on the middle factor. That gives 0.40 + 0.30 + 0.36 = 1.06 and a prediction of 4.56. Another is leaving out the global mean, which gives 0.36, nowhere near a star rating.

Each part has a meaning. The biases capture that this user rates 0.3 stars above average and this recipe gets 0.4 below average from everyone. The dot product adds the personal fit. Here the third factor, where both vectors are positive, does most of the work, while the second factor, which the user dislikes and the recipe has, pulls the prediction down.
questions.deeper: In an interview, explain that the biases and vectors are learned by minimising squared error on known ratings with L2 regularisation, using SGD or alternating least squares. A good follow-up is cold start: a brand-new recipe has no learned bias or vector, so you fall back on the global mean plus the user bias, or on content features.

questions.prompt: A phone keyboard learns next-word suggestions with federated learning. A product manager writes: "Users' typing never leaves their phones, so the system is private by design." Which response is most accurate?
options: Raw text stays on the phone, and averaging updates on the server makes them impossible to trace back.
Phones upload their typed text in encrypted form, and the server decrypts it to train the shared model.
Raw text stays on the phone, but the shared model updates can still leak details of what a user typed.
Privacy is not a concern here, since next-word models are too small to memorize any one user's text.
questions.explanation:
In federated learning each phone trains on its own data and sends back only a model update, such as gradients or new weights. The server combines the updates into a shared model. Raw text never moves, which is a real gain. But an update is computed from that text. Research has shown that individual updates can be partly inverted to recover inputs, and the final model can memorize rare strings such as a typed card number.

The option about averaging is the close miss. In plain federated learning the server receives each update separately and averages them afterwards, so it can inspect any single one. Hiding individual updates needs secure aggregation, where the server only ever sees the sum. Even then, the combined model can leak without differential privacy noise. The option about encrypted uploads describes central training, not federated learning. Small models can still memorize unusual sequences, so model size is no guarantee.
questions.deeper: A strong answer names the layered defences: secure aggregation, clipping each update and adding noise for differential privacy, and a minimum number of devices per round. It also notes that federated learning makes debugging harder, because engineers cannot look at the data the model trains on.

questions.prompt: Using scikit-learn 1.x, you want a churn experiment to give the same numbers on every run. In which of these steps does `random_state` actually control randomness? Select all that apply.
options: `train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)` with its default shuffling
`KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True)` used as the `cv` of a grid search
`RandomForestClassifier`, which bootstraps rows and samples features
`KFold(n_splits=5)` with `shuffle` left at its default value
`StandardScaler`, fit on the training rows before the model
`LinearRegression`, fit by ordinary least squares on the same data
questions.explanation:
`random_state` matters wherever a step draws random numbers.

- `train_test_split` shuffles rows before cutting by default, so the seed decides which rows land in the test set.
- `KFold` with `shuffle=True` shuffles before forming folds, so the seed decides fold membership and therefore every cross-validation score.
- A random forest draws a bootstrap sample of rows for each tree and a random subset of features at each split. Without a fixed seed, two fits give different trees and slightly different predictions.

The other three have nothing random to control. `KFold` without shuffling cuts the data into consecutive blocks in order. Recent scikit-learn versions even raise an error if you pass `random_state` with `shuffle=False`, because it would have no effect. `StandardScaler` computes a mean and standard deviation, which are fixed by the data. `LinearRegression` solves least squares directly and has no `random_state` parameter at all. Model initialization is another source of randomness the seed controls, for example in `MLPClassifier` or `KMeans`.
questions.deeper: A useful detail: passing an int gives the same draws on every call, while passing a shared `np.random.RandomState` object gives different draws each time it is used. For full reproducibility, also fix library versions and note that `n_jobs` and GPU code can add their own nondeterminism.

questions.subtopic: a shell tool or narrow tools
questions.prompt: An accounts-payable agent only ever needs to do four things: look up an invoice, list overdue invoices, mark an invoice as paid, and email a vendor a copy. One engineer proposes four narrow tools. Another proposes a single shell tool with the finance system's command-line client and a full-access login, because it can do anything. Which choice is better, and why?
options: The shell, since a model writes shell commands more reliably than it chooses between several tools with typed arguments.
Narrow tools, since the tasks are few and known, and each tool can validate inputs and hold only the access it needs.
The shell, since running it inside a container removes the risk of giving the agent a full-access finance login.
Narrow tools, since agents that have a shell or code tool cannot be traced, evaluated or monitored in production.
questions.explanation:
When the set of tasks is small and known, narrow tools win on both safety and reliability. Each tool can check its inputs, such as refusing to mark an invoice paid twice, and carry only the access its task needs, which is least privilege. Typed arguments are also easy to validate and easy to test.

The container option mixes up two risks. A sandbox protects the machine the agent runs on, but the full-access login still reaches the real finance system, so one wrong or injected command could change or delete any record. Models can be good at shell commands, but nothing here needs that flexibility, and a free-form command has far more ways to go wrong than a typed call with a few fields. Agents with shell tools can be traced and evaluated perfectly well, since every command and its output can be logged. A general shell is the better fit for open-ended work, such as data analysis or coding inside a sandbox with no production credentials.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like a nuanced answer. General tools are powerful when tasks are open-ended, and many coding agents rely on them. The deciding questions are what the worst possible command could do and whether the task set is known. A middle path is a code tool in a sandbox for analysis, plus narrow tools for any action that changes real money or records.

questions.prompt: A payments team has millions of card transactions but no fraud labels yet. They want to flag unusual transactions for review. Which methods can do this without labels? Select all that apply.
options: Isolation forest, flagging points that are split off in few steps
Local outlier factor, flagging points in much sparser areas than their neighbours
An autoencoder, flagging transactions with high reconstruction error
Logistic regression with class weights, trained to predict the fraud flag
SMOTE oversampling of the fraud class, followed by a random forest
A t-test comparing the amounts of fraud and genuine transactions
questions.explanation:
All three keys learn what normal looks like from the data alone and score how far each point is from it.

An isolation forest builds random trees that split on random features and values. Odd points sit far from the crowd, so they get isolated in only a few splits, and a short average path means a high anomaly score. Local outlier factor compares how dense the area around a point is with the density around its neighbours, which catches points that are unusual locally. An autoencoder learns to compress and rebuild transactions. Since most traffic is normal, it rebuilds normal patterns well and rare ones badly, so high reconstruction error flags them.

The other three all need a fraud label. Logistic regression has nothing to predict without one. SMOTE creates synthetic examples of a labelled minority class, so it cannot run when no rows are marked as fraud. A t-test compares two labelled groups and is a test, not a way to score single transactions.
questions.deeper: In production these scores feed an analyst queue, and the analysts' decisions become the first labels. A strong candidate explains the move from unsupervised scoring to a supervised model once enough labels exist, and warns that unusual is not the same as fraud. Big but legitimate purchases will also look odd.

questions.prompt: You train a transformer from scratch to route support tickets, using Adam with a peak learning rate of 3 × 10⁻⁴. Starting at the peak rate makes the loss spike in the first few hundred steps and sometimes diverge. A schedule with linear warmup over 2,000 steps, then cosine decay to near zero, trains smoothly. Which statement best explains why this schedule works?
options: Early gradients and Adam's moment estimates are unreliable, so full-size steps can throw the weights into an unstable region. Later decay shrinks the steps so the weights can settle.
Adam's bias correction makes the first updates far too small, so warmup ramps the rate up to make up for it. Later decay then undoes that extra boost once the moment estimates have become stable.
Small early steps stop the network from memorizing the first batches it sees, which cuts overfitting. Later decay does the job of weight decay, so no separate regularizer is needed.
Small early steps give the batch norm running statistics time to settle before big updates arrive. Later decay keeps those running statistics from drifting as training goes on.
questions.explanation:
At the start the weights are random, gradients are large and change quickly, and Adam's second-moment estimate is built from only a handful of steps, so the per-weight step sizes are noisy. Taking full-size steps in that state can push the model into a region where activations and the loss blow up, and transformers are known to be sensitive to this. Warmup keeps the steps small until the gradient statistics and the model are calmer. Decay at the end does a different job. Late in training, large steps bounce around the bottom of a valley, so shrinking them lets the weights settle and usually lowers the final loss.

The option about bias correction has it backwards. Bias correction removes the shrinkage caused by starting the moments at zero, so the first Adam steps are already close to full size, which is part of why warmup helps. The option about memorizing early batches confuses step size with regularization, and decay does not replace weight decay. The option about batch norm does not fit, because transformers use layer norm, which keeps no running statistics.
questions.deeper: A typical follow-up asks how long warmup should be. Common practice is a few hundred to a few thousand steps, or a few percent of the run. You can add that Adam variants such as RAdam try to fix the early variance problem directly, and that warmup also helps in fine-tuning, where large early steps can erase pretrained knowledge.

questions.prompt: A news site writes 6 candidate headlines for each article. Most articles get nearly all their readers in the first 24 hours. The team wants to pick headlines by click-through rate. Why does a multi-armed bandit suit this better than a fixed 6-way A/B test?
options: A bandit gives a more precise and unbiased estimate of how much each headline differs than an equal traffic split does.
A bandit moves traffic to stronger headlines while the test runs, so fewer readers of a short-lived article see weak ones.
A bandit needs no click data to start, so it can choose the best headline before the article has been published.
A bandit avoids novelty effects, because it keeps showing all six headlines equally often until the article finally expires.
questions.explanation:
A fixed A/B test gives each headline one sixth of the traffic until the end, then you switch to the winner. For an article that is only read for a day, "the end" comes after most readers have gone, so five sixths of them saw weaker headlines. A bandit learns as it goes. As clicks come in it shifts traffic toward headlines that are doing well, while still testing the others a little. Less traffic is wasted on losers, which is called lower regret.

The claim about precise estimates is backwards. Because a bandit starves weak arms of traffic, its estimates of their click rates are noisy and its data is not an equal random split, so a fixed test is better when you need a clean measure of the difference. A bandit still needs clicks to learn, so it cannot pick a winner before publishing. And keeping all six arms at equal traffic describes the fixed test, not a bandit.
questions.deeper: The rule of thumb interviewers want: use a bandit when you care about reward during the test and the decision is short-lived or repeated often, such as headlines, thumbnails or promotions. Use a fixed A/B test when you need a trustworthy effect size and guardrail metrics for a lasting launch decision.

questions.prompt: A help-desk software company runs one shared vector index for all its business customers, and each chunk is tagged with a tenant id. A query searches the whole index for the top 10 chunks, then drops any chunk that belongs to another tenant. A small tenant owns 0.5% of all chunks, and its users often get only 0 to 2 chunks back, even for questions their own docs answer well. What is the best fix?
options: Apply the tenant filter inside the search, so the top 10 are chosen only from that tenant's own chunks.
Add the tenant's name to the query text, so the embedding pulls the search toward that tenant's chunks.
Raise the similarity cut-off, so weak matches from other tenants are dropped earlier in the search.
Lower the embedding dimension, so each tenant's chunks form a tight cluster the search reaches first.
questions.explanation:
Filtering after the search spends the top 10 on chunks the user can never see. With 99.5% of chunks owned by other tenants, the 10 nearest neighbours of a question are usually someone else's documents, even when the tenant's own docs answer it well. Removing them afterwards leaves a handful or nothing. Filtering during the search limits the candidates to the tenant's chunks first, so all 10 slots go to chunks this user may see. Most vector databases support this as filtered search, and very large tenants are sometimes given their own partition or index.

Putting the tenant name in the query only nudges the embedding. It guarantees nothing, and other tenants' chunks still crowd the top 10. A higher similarity cut-off removes results without adding any, so the shortage gets worse. A smaller dimension does not make tenants cluster, because embeddings group text by meaning, and two companies' password-reset articles look alike whoever owns them.

Filtering inside the search is also the safer design. Tenant isolation should be enforced by the search itself, not by a cleanup step someone could forget.
questions.deeper: A good follow-up is how very selective filters interact with an approximate index. A graph built over all chunks can struggle when only 0.5% of nodes are allowed, so recall can drop. Systems handle this by switching to exact search over the small filtered set, or by partitioning by tenant. Measure recall per tenant, not just overall.

questions.prompt: A subscription app retrains its churn model each month. This month's retrained model scores 0.84 AUC on a random 20% split of its own training window. The production model scored 0.81 AUC on its test set when it launched a year ago. The team lead asks whether to promote the new model. What should happen first?
options: Score both models on the same recent holdout that neither trained on, then decide
Promote the new model now, since 0.84 against 0.81 is a clear three-point AUC gain
Keep the production model, since a year of live use shows it is safer than a new one
Score both models on the launch test set from a year ago, since it is already labelled
questions.explanation:
The two AUC numbers come from different test sets, a year apart, drawn from different customers and conditions. A gap between them could come entirely from one test set being easier than the other. A fair champion-challenger comparison scores both models on the same data, which should be recent and later than either model's training data. The challenger is promoted only if it wins by a margin agreed in advance.

Promoting on 0.84 against 0.81 trusts a comparison that is not like for like. The random split also mixes rows from the whole window, which tends to flatter the score compared with testing on later months. Keeping the production model because it has a track record ignores the chance that it has decayed over the year, which is why the team retrains at all. Reusing the year-old launch test set does put both models on the same data, but that data is stale. It shows how each would have done a year ago, not on today's customers, and if the new model's training window covers those months, it has already seen the test rows.
questions.deeper: Many teams automate this in the pipeline: the registry holds the champion, each retrain registers a challenger, and promotion needs a win on the shared holdout plus no big drop on key slices. Interviewers may ask what to do on a tie. A common answer is to keep the champion, since change has its own risk.

questions.prompt: An email team is choosing between Naive Bayes and logistic regression for a spam filter. Explain the difference between a generative and a discriminative classifier, say which camp each of these two models is in, and describe a practical case where the generative view helps.
questions.answer: A discriminative model learns p(y given x) directly, or just a decision boundary. Logistic regression is discriminative. It fits weights that map an email's features straight to the probability of spam. A generative model learns how the data is produced: p(x given y) and p(y), which together give p(x, y). It then uses Bayes' rule to get p(y given x). Naive Bayes is generative. It estimates how often each word appears in spam and in normal mail, assuming words are independent given the class. The generative view helps when labelled data is scarce. Its strong assumptions leave few parameters, so it tends to get close to its own best accuracy with far fewer examples, though that best is often lower than logistic regression's. It also copes with missing features, and p(x) can hint at unusual emails. With plenty of data the discriminative model usually wins, because it does not spend effort modelling x and is not hurt by a wrong independence assumption.
points: Discriminative models learn p(y given x) or a boundary directly
Generative models learn p(x given y) and p(y), then apply Bayes' rule
Logistic regression is discriminative and Naive Bayes is generative
Generative helps with little data, missing features or spotting unusual inputs
With lots of data, discriminative models usually reach lower error
questions.explanation:
The difference is what gets modelled. A discriminative model only cares about the boundary between classes. A generative model describes each class fully, so it can say how likely an input is under each class and turn that into a prediction with Bayes' rule.

A common mistake is to think generative only means models that produce images or text. Any model of p(x given y) is generative, even a word-count model like Naive Bayes. Another is to call Naive Bayes discriminative because it outputs a class. The output is the same kind of thing, but the route to it is different.

The tradeoff is classic. Naive Bayes makes a strong and usually wrong assumption, that words are independent given the class. That assumption is a kind of bias that helps when data is small, because there are few parameters to estimate. Ng and Jordan's well-known comparison showed this as a tendency, not a guarantee: Naive Bayes neared its own lowest error with far fewer examples, but that lowest error was often higher. As data grows, the bias starts to cost more than it saves, and logistic regression pulls ahead. Its probabilities are also usually better calibrated, while Naive Bayes tends to push scores toward 0 and 1.
questions.deeper: Interviewers may connect this to modern models. A language model is generative over text, while a fine-tuned classifier head is discriminative. A good follow-up answer: with few labels, start with a generative or prior-heavy model, then switch to a discriminative one once labelled data piles up, comparing both on the same validation set.

questions.prompt: A summarization service runs batches of 8 requests. In one batch, a single request needs 500 output tokens and the other seven need about 50. With static batching, the seven short slots sit idle for about 450 decode steps while new requests wait in the queue. What does continuous batching do differently?
options: When a request finishes, a waiting request takes its slot at the next decode step, so the batch stays full while the long request keeps going.
It sorts waiting requests by expected output length before each batch starts, so requests of similar length are always grouped together.
It splits the long request into chunks of 50 tokens and spreads them across the free slots, so all eight slots finish their work at the same time.
It runs every request in its own forward pass as soon as it arrives, so no request ever waits for another one and the batch idea is dropped.
questions.explanation:
Continuous batching makes scheduling decisions at every decode step instead of once per batch. After about 50 steps, the seven short requests finish, and their slots are given to requests from the queue at the next step. The long request carries on alongside them. The GPU keeps working on a full batch, and new requests start almost at once instead of waiting about 450 steps.

Sorting by expected length is a separate trick, sometimes called bucketing. It needs output lengths to be known in advance, which they are not, since the model decides when to stop. Splitting one request into chunks across slots cannot work, because each token depends on the one before it, so a single sequence must be generated in order. Running each request alone gives up batching, and with it the reuse of each weight read across many requests, so total throughput falls sharply.
questions.deeper: Interviewers sometimes ask what makes this hard to build. Sequences in the batch have different lengths and different KV caches, so the engine needs attention kernels that handle ragged batches and a cache that can grow and shrink per request without wasting memory.

questions.prompt: A factory's defect classifier is trained on sensor readings where 2% of parts are defective. An engineer applies SMOTE to the whole dataset, then runs 5-fold cross-validation and gets a defect recall of 0.93. On the next month of parts from the same line, with the same 2% defect rate, recall is 0.58. What is the most likely problem?
options: SMOTE copies existing defects exactly, so the model memorised them, and random oversampling would avoid this
SMOTE was not also applied to next month's parts, so the live class mix no longer matches the training data
SMOTE interpolates between defective and normal parts, which blurs the boundary the model needs to learn
Synthetic defects came from rows that later sat in validation folds, so SMOTE must run per training fold
questions.explanation:
SMOTE makes a synthetic minority row by picking a real defect, picking one of its nearest defect neighbours, and placing a new point on the line between them. Run on the whole dataset, a validation fold can contain real defects whose near-copies sit in training, and synthetic points built from training defects. Both are easy to classify, so cross-validated recall is inflated. Resampling must happen inside each training fold, which `imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline` does for you.

SMOTE does not copy rows exactly. Random oversampling does, so switching to it would not help. You never resample validation, test or live data, because those must keep the real 2% mix you will face. And SMOTE interpolates between minority neighbours, not between a defect and a normal part. Interpolation can still create points in the majority region when defects are scattered, but that is not what explains the gap here.
questions.deeper: Mention in interviews that SMOTE often adds little over class weights for tree models, and that it distorts predicted probabilities, so recalibrate if the scores are used as real chances. The rule generalises: any step that learns from data runs only on the training fold.

questions.prompt: To estimate how often a support bot hallucinates, reviewers check 500 randomly sampled answers and mark 90 of them as hallucinated. Using the normal approximation with z = 1.96, what is the lower end of the 95% confidence interval for the hallucination rate? Give it as a decimal to 3 places.
questions.explanation:
The observed rate is p̂ = 90 / 500 = 0.18. Its standard error is √(p̂(1 − p̂) / n) = √(0.18 × 0.82 / 500) = √0.0002952 ≈ 0.01718. The margin of error is 1.96 × 0.01718 ≈ 0.0337. The interval is 0.18 ± 0.0337, which runs from about 0.146 to 0.214, so the lower end is 0.146.

The most common mistake is to leave n out of the standard error and use √(0.18 × 0.82) ≈ 0.384, which gives a nonsense interval that dips below zero. Another is to forget the square root and use 0.18 × 0.82 / 500 ≈ 0.0003 as the standard error. That is the variance, and it gives an interval far too narrow.

The normal approximation works here because both n p̂ = 90 and n(1 − p̂) = 410 are well above 10. For rare events, such as 2 hallucinations in 500 answers, a Wilson interval is the safer choice.
questions.deeper: Reporting "an 18% hallucination rate" without an interval invites bad calls. If a new prompt scores 16% on another 500 answers, the two intervals overlap heavily and the change may be noise. Halving the margin needs four times as many reviewed answers, which is often the real cost question in LLM evaluation.

questions.subtopic: choosing a threshold from business costs
questions.prompt: A telecom company has a churn model that outputs a probability for each customer. The retention team can make at most 300 calls a week. Each call costs $15. A churner who gets a call stays 25% of the time, and a customer who stays is worth $400. Calling a customer who was not going to churn gains nothing. How would you choose the score threshold for who gets a call?
questions.answer: I would set the threshold from expected value, not from 0.5. A call to a customer with churn probability p is worth p × 0.25 × $400 = $100p and costs $15, so it pays off when p is above 0.15. That is the break-even threshold. Capacity also binds. If more than 300 customers score above 0.15, I would call the 300 highest scores, so the real threshold becomes the 300th score. If fewer clear 0.15, I would call only those and leave spare capacity unused. This only works if the probabilities are calibrated, so I would check a reliability plot first. Then I would confirm the value with a holdout group that gets no calls, and revisit the threshold when costs, save rates or the score distribution change.
points: Compare the cost of a wasted call with the value lost from a missed churner
Break-even probability is cost divided by value times save rate, here 0.15
The 300-call cap means taking the top 300 scores when many clear break-even
Scores must be calibrated for the break-even rule to hold
Validate with a no-call holdout and update the threshold as inputs change
questions.explanation:
The threshold is a business decision, so it should come from what each mistake costs. A false positive wastes a $15 call. A missed churner who could have been saved loses the expected value of the call, which is 0.25 × $400 = $100 for a sure churner. Setting p × 100 = 15 gives p = 0.15. Above that, a call is worth more than it costs on average.

The common mistake is to keep the default 0.5 or to pick the threshold that maximises F1. Both ignore the costs. Here 0.5 would skip many customers who are worth calling.
