The second mistake is to forget the capacity cap. When demand exceeds 300 calls, you rank by score and stop at 300, and the cap, not the break-even point, sets the cut. Finally, the break-even rule assumes a score of 0.2 really means a 20% chance of churn. An uncalibrated model breaks that link.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate notes that the 25% save rate is not the same for everyone. Some customers would stay anyway and some cannot be saved. Uplift modelling targets the customers whose behaviour the call actually changes, which often beats ranking by churn risk alone.

questions.prompt: Attention computes softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k)V. A teammate writing a custom attention layer with d_k = 128 drops the √d_k term, and training becomes slower and less stable. Why does the scaling matter?
options: Unscaled dot products have variance that grows with d_k, so softmax saturates toward one-hot weights with tiny gradients. Dividing by √d_k brings it back near 1.
Dividing by √d_k turns each dot product into a cosine similarity, so every score stays between −1 and 1 however long the query and key vectors grow during training.
Without the √d_k term the attention weights in each row no longer sum to 1, so each output is a biased weighted average of the value vectors and its scale drifts.
Dividing by √d_k cuts the cost of building the score matrix from O(n²·d_k) to O(n²), so the layer runs faster and fits much longer sequences into GPU memory.
questions.explanation:
If the components of q and k are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product is a sum of d_k terms, each with variance 1, so it has variance d_k. With d_k = 128, typical scores have a standard deviation of about 11. A softmax over scores that far apart puts almost all weight on one key, and in that saturated region its gradients are close to zero, so learning slows and becomes unstable. Dividing by √128 brings the standard deviation back to about 1.

The cosine option is wrong because cosine similarity divides by the vectors' lengths, not by a fixed constant, so scaled scores can still take any size. The option about rows summing to 1 is wrong because softmax always normalizes each row, with or without scaling. The option about compute is wrong because dividing by a constant is a cheap elementwise step that changes neither the O(n²·d_k) cost nor the memory use.
questions.deeper: A good follow-up: the scaling acts like a fixed temperature on the softmax. Some large models also normalize queries and keys before the dot product to keep scores bounded. Interviewers may ask you to derive the variance d_k on a whiteboard, which only needs the fact that the variances of independent terms add.

questions.prompt: A support bot uses a router. 70% of requests go to a small model, and the other 30% go straight to a large model. Of the requests the small model answers, 10% fail an automatic quality check and are re-sent to the large model, so those requests pay for both calls. Suppose a small-model call costs $0.002 and a large-model call costs $0.03. What is the model cost per 1,000 requests, in dollars, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation:
Count the calls to each model, then price them.

- Small-model calls: 70% of 1,000 = 700. Cost: 700 × $0.002 = $1.40.
- Large-model calls sent directly: 30% of 1,000 = 300.
- Large-model calls from escalation: 10% of 700 = 70.
- Large-model calls in total: 300 + 70 = 370. Cost: 370 × $0.03 = $11.10.
- Total: $1.40 + $11.10 = $12.50 per 1,000 requests.

Sending every request to the large model would cost $30.00, so routing cuts the bill by more than half. The common mistake is to ignore the escalated requests and answer $10.40. Escalation looks small at 7% of traffic, but each escalated request adds a large call that costs 15 times a small one. Another slip is to drop the small-model cost for escalated requests and answer $12.36. Those 70 requests were already answered by the small model before the check failed, so they pay for both calls.
questions.deeper: The escalation rate is the number to watch. If the small model fails the check 40% of the time, the saving shrinks fast, and those users wait for two calls. Interviewers may ask what makes a good check, such as schema validation, a confidence score or a cheap classifier trained on past failures.

questions.prompt: A bank trains a loan default model on its past loans. Outcomes exist only for applicants the old policy approved, about 40% of everyone who applied. Explain how this biases the model when it scores all new applicants, and describe ways to reduce the bias.
questions.answer: The model only sees outcomes for loans the old policy approved, so it learns default patterns inside that approved group. Rejected applicants, often thinner files or riskier profiles, have no labels, so the model never learns how they behave. When it scores everyone who applies, it can be badly wrong on exactly those profiles. It often underestimates their risk, because the few approved members of a risky group were the ones that looked best on other signals. Ways to reduce the bias: approve a small random slice of would-be rejects under a loss budget to collect unbiased labels, reweight approved loans by the inverse of their approval probability if the old policy's scores were logged, and use credit bureau outcomes for rejected applicants who borrowed elsewhere. Reject inference methods help only roughly. Finally, evaluate on the full applicant population, not just on held-out approved loans.
points: Labels exist only for approved applicants, a non-random sample chosen by the old policy
The model can misjudge, often underrate, risk for profiles that were usually rejected
Collect unbiased labels by approving a small random or controlled slice of would-be rejects
Reweight by inverse approval probability, or use outside outcome data such as bureau records
Evaluate on all applicants, and treat reject inference as a rough fix
questions.explanation:
This is selection bias: the training sample was picked by a process tied to the outcome. The old policy approved people it judged safe, so the labelled data covers mainly low-risk regions. Inside a risky segment, the approved few were chosen on extra evidence, so their default rate understates the segment's true rate. A model trained on them carries that optimism to new applicants.

The common mistake is to check the model on a held-out set of approved loans and conclude it works. That test set has the same bias, so it hides the problem. Another mistake is to think more data from the same process fixes it. More approved loans still say nothing about the rejected region. Random approvals cost money, which is why they run on a small, capped slice, but they are the cleanest source of truth. Reweighting needs the old approval probabilities, and outside data needs legal and privacy checks.
questions.deeper: There is also a feedback loop: the new model decides who gets approved next, so its blind spots shape the next training set. Interviewers like candidates who mention that the same pattern appears in fraud, where blocked transactions never get labels, and in recommenders, which only see clicks on items they showed.

questions.prompt: A ticket classifier scores 88% accuracy on a validation set of 2,500 rows. A rival model scores 89% on the same rows, and you want to know how big the noise is. Treat each row as an independent trial. Using SE = √(p(1 − p) / n), compute the half-width of an approximate 95% interval, 1.96 × SE, for the 88% accuracy. Give the half-width in percentage points to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation:
Step by step: p(1 − p) = 0.88 × 0.12 = 0.1056. Divide by n: 0.1056 / 2,500 = 0.00004224. The square root gives SE ≈ 0.0065, which is 0.65 percentage points. Multiply by 1.96 to get about 1.27 percentage points. So the interval for 88% runs from roughly 86.7% to 89.3%.

The rival's 89% sits inside that range, so a 1-point gain is about the size of the noise from 2,500 rows. On these numbers alone it is weak evidence. Common slips are stopping at SE (0.65) without the 1.96, or forgetting the square root, which gives a tiny and wrong figure.

There is a subtlety a strong candidate raises. Both models were scored on the same rows, so a paired test is sharper than comparing two intervals. It looks only at rows where the models disagree. If the rival fixes 40 rows and breaks 15, that pattern can be convincing even though the intervals overlap.
questions.deeper: McNemar's test or a paired bootstrap over rows are the usual tools for this. In interviews, also mention the reverse problem: to detect a 1-point gain reliably you need many more rows, and the required size grows with the square of the precision you want, so halving the SE takes four times the data.

questions.prompt: A support team uses logistic regression to predict whether a ticket will be escalated. The model's score is z = −2.0 + 0.5 × (previous tickets in the last 90 days) + 1.0 × (enterprise plan, 1 if yes and 0 if no). A ticket arrives from an enterprise customer with 3 previous tickets. What is the predicted probability of escalation? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Logistic regression first builds a linear score, called the logit or log-odds, then passes it through the sigmoid to get a probability.

Step 1, the score: z = −2.0 + 0.5 × 3 + 1.0 × 1 = −2.0 + 1.5 + 1.0 = 0.5.

Step 2, the sigmoid: p = 1 / (1 + exp(−0.5)) = 1 / (1 + 0.607) = 1 / 1.607 ≈ 0.622, which rounds to 0.62.

The common mistake is to stop at step 1 and report 0.5 as the probability. The score lives on the log-odds scale, where 0 means a 50% chance. A related slip is to read the 0.5 coefficient as "each previous ticket adds 0.5 to the probability". It adds 0.5 to the log-odds, which multiplies the odds by exp(0.5) ≈ 1.65. How far that moves the probability depends on where you start, since the sigmoid is steep near 0.5 and flat near 0 and 1.
questions.deeper: The odds-ratio reading is a favourite follow-up. exp(coefficient) is the factor by which the odds change for a one-unit rise in a feature, here about 1.65 per previous ticket and about 2.72 for the enterprise plan. Stakeholders usually find "1.65 times the odds" easier to use than raw log-odds.

questions.prompt: An LLM endpoint for a travel-booking assistant switches from static batching, where a batch runs until its longest request finishes, to continuous batching. Request lengths vary a lot. Which of these improve as a result? Select all that apply.
options: Total tokens generated per second across all users
Share of batch slots doing useful work at each decode step
Time a new request waits in the queue before it starts
Decode speed of one request running alone on an idle server
Size of the KV cache that each sequence needs per token
Time per output token for each request as more requests join
questions.explanation:
Continuous batching schedules at the level of single decode steps. When one request finishes, a waiting request takes its slot at the next step. That keeps the batch full, so the GPU does more useful work per weight read. This raises total throughput and GPU use. New requests no longer wait for the slowest member of the current batch to finish, so queue wait drops a lot, especially when lengths vary.

It does not make a lone request faster. With nothing else running, each decode step is limited by reading the weights, and batching changes nothing about that. The KV cache per token is set by the model's layers, heads and precision, not by the scheduler. Time per output token for each request actually rises slightly as the batch grows, because each step has more work to do. The trade is a small slowdown per request for a large gain in total throughput and much shorter waits.
questions.deeper: A good interview point is that continuous batching works best with a KV cache allocated in small blocks, since requests join and leave at different lengths. Teams usually cap the batch size or token budget per step so that per-token latency stays within the target.

questions.prompt: A utility company fine-tunes a language model on five years of customer support chats. In testing, a prompt written like the opening of a real chat gets the model to complete it with a real customer's full home address. Which plan best reduces this risk before launch?
options: Lower the sampling temperature, since memorized text mostly appears under random sampling.
Scrub personal data from the chats, drop duplicates, and filter outputs for personal data.
Add a system prompt telling the model it must never reveal anyone's personal details.
Train for more epochs so the model generalizes beyond any one specific support conversation.
questions.explanation:
Language models can memorize and repeat training text word for word, especially text that is rare and specific, like an address, or that appears many times. The fix works at three points. Scrubbing personal data from the chats removes the source. Removing duplicate chats cuts repetition, which is a major driver of memorization. An output filter catches anything that still slips through.

Lowering temperature does not help and can make things worse. Memorized text is often the most likely continuation, so greedy decoding is a common way extraction attacks recover it. A system prompt asks the model to behave, but the address is still stored in its weights and a clever prompt or jailbreak can draw it out. Training for more epochs shows the model each chat more times, which increases memorization instead of reducing it.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds an extraction test to the pre-launch checks: prompt the model with prefixes of real training records and measure how often it completes them exactly. For high-risk data, fine-tuning with differential privacy gives a formal bound, at some cost to quality.

questions.prompt: A team predicts house sale prices. On the training data R² is 0.91. On a held-out test set from a later year, scikit-learn's `r2_score` returns −0.15. What does the negative test score mean?
options: The model's test predictions have more squared error than predicting the test set's mean price for every house.
R² cannot be below zero, so the test score points to a bug in how the metric was computed on the test set.
The model explains 15% of the price variance on the test set, but with predictions that run the wrong way.
The model needs more features, since adding features always raises R² on any data set, test sets included.
questions.explanation:
R² is 1 − SS_res / SS_tot. SS_res is the squared error of the model's predictions, and SS_tot is the squared error of always predicting the mean of the actual values. A score below zero means SS_res is larger than SS_tot, so the model does worse than that constant guess. With a training R² of 0.91, the likely causes are overfitting or a shift in prices between the years.

The belief that R² cannot be negative comes from least squares fits with an intercept, scored on their own training data, where the fit can always fall back to the mean. On new data there is no such floor. Reading −0.15 as 15% explained the wrong way is not how R² works. It is simply a worse-than-baseline score. Adding features never lowers training R² for least squares, but on a test set extra features often make things worse by adding variance.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like to follow up with adjusted R², which penalises extra features, and with why a later-year test set is the honest one. If prices rose overall, the model may be biased low across the board. Plotting residuals against time or predicted price usually shows this quickly.

questions.prompt:
One attention head has d_k = 4. A query attends over three tokens:

- q = [2, 0, 2, 0]
- k₁ = [1, 0, 1, 0], v₁ = [4, 0]
- k₂ = [0, 1, 0, 1], v₂ = [0, 8]
- k₃ = [1, 0, 0, 0], v₃ = [2, 2]

The head computes softmax(q·kᵢ / √d_k) and outputs the weighted sum of the values. What is the first component of the output vector? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
First the raw dot products: q·k₁ = 2 + 2 = 4, q·k₂ = 0 and q·k₃ = 2. Divide by √4 = 2 to get scores 2, 0 and 1.

Next the softmax. e² ≈ 7.389, e⁰ = 1 and e¹ ≈ 2.718, which sum to about 11.107. The weights are 7.389 / 11.107 ≈ 0.665, 1 / 11.107 ≈ 0.090 and 2.718 / 11.107 ≈ 0.245. They add up to 1, as softmax weights must.

Finally the output is the weighted sum of the values. Its first component is 0.665 × 4 + 0.090 × 0 + 0.245 × 2 ≈ 2.661 + 0.489 ≈ 3.15.

The most common mistake is to skip the √d_k step. Using the raw scores 4, 0 and 2 gives weights of about 0.867, 0.016 and 0.117 and an output of about 3.70. The softmax is not linear, so the missing division does not cancel out. It makes the weights more peaked. Another slip is to weight the keys instead of the values. The keys only decide the weights. The values are what gets mixed.
questions.deeper: Working one query by hand is a common whiteboard warm-up. A strong candidate then says that a real layer does this for every query at once as softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k)V, and checks the second output component too. It is 0.090 × 8 + 0.245 × 2 ≈ 1.21, and most of it comes from the token with the smallest weight, because its value is large. A weight says how much a token counts, not how much it adds.

questions.prompt:
Using NumPy 2.x, a scoring job keeps five model scores in one array and takes two pieces out of it. What does the last line print?

```python
import numpy as np
scores = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
middle = scores[1:3]
picked = scores[[3, 4]]
middle[0] = -1
picked[0] = -2
print(scores.tolist())
```
questions.explanation:
A basic slice such as `scores[1:3]` is a view. It points at the same memory as `scores`, just with a different start and length. So `middle[0] = -1` writes straight into `scores[1]`.

Indexing with a list, `scores[[3, 4]]`, is fancy indexing, and it always builds a new array. The picked items could be in any order or repeated, so NumPy cannot describe them as a start, stop and step over the old memory. It copies them instead. Writing to `picked` changes only `picked`, and `scores[3]` stays 40.

The option where both writes show up assumes every index result is a view. The option where nothing changes assumes every result is a copy, which is how pandas 3 behaves under copy-on-write, but not plain NumPy. The option where only the fourth score changes has the two rules the wrong way round. Boolean masks count as fancy indexing too, so `scores[scores > 25]` is also a copy.
questions.deeper: When unsure, ask NumPy: `np.shares_memory(scores, middle)` is True and the same call on `picked` is False. Note that assigning through fancy indexing on the original, as in `scores[[3, 4]] = -2`, does write in place. Only reading with fancy indexing makes a copy.

questions.prompt: An analyst computes Pearson correlations between features in a churn dataset. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation:
Pearson correlation measures linear association after centring and scaling each variable. Converting dollars to cents multiplies by 100, a positive linear change that the scaling undoes, so every correlation stays the same. Because Pearson correlation works with products of deviations, one point far from the rest can dominate the sums and create a strong correlation out of almost nothing. Spearman correlation is Pearson correlation on the ranks, and a strictly increasing transform such as a log of positive values keeps every rank, so Spearman is unchanged.

Zero correlation only rules out a linear relationship. If y = x² with x spread evenly around zero, y depends fully on x, yet the Pearson correlation is zero. Multiplying by −1 is linear but flips the direction, so the correlation keeps its size and changes sign. Finally, the share of variance explained in a simple linear fit is r², not r. A correlation of 0.9 explains 0.81, or 81%, of the variance.
questions.deeper: Before trusting a correlation matrix, plot the pairs that matter. An interviewer may show a scatter plot with one outlier and ask what the correlation would be without it. Spearman correlation is a sensible default for skewed features such as spend or session counts.
options: A Pearson correlation of zero means the two features are independent.
Converting a feature from dollars to cents leaves its correlations unchanged.
Multiplying a feature by −1 leaves its correlations with others unchanged.
A single extreme customer can turn a near-zero correlation into a strong one.
A correlation of 0.9 means one feature explains 90% of the other's variance.
Spearman correlation is unchanged by any strictly increasing transform of a feature.

questions.prompt: A hotel pricing model uses a feature holding competitors' average room price, refreshed every night by an upstream job. Nine days ago that job broke. Since then the feature pipeline has quietly reused the last value it had for each hotel. The pricing service showed no errors and normal latency, and booking labels take about 30 days to arrive. Which check would have caught this problem soonest?
options: A weekly comparison of model accuracy against booking outcomes as soon as their labels arrive
Alerts on the pricing service's HTTP error rate and p99 latency, paging when either crosses its limit
A freshness check that alerts when a feature's source has not updated within its expected window
A schema check that every request contains each expected feature with the correct data type
questions.explanation:
A stale feature looks perfectly valid. The values are numbers in the right range, the type is right and the service runs fine, so only a check that asks when the data last changed will notice. A freshness check compares each feature's last update time with how often it should update, here once a night, and would have fired after the first missed run.

Accuracy against outcomes would catch the damage eventually, but labels take about 30 days, so the model would have priced on old data for weeks first. Error rate and latency watch the service, not the data, and the service was healthy throughout. A schema check confirms each feature is present with the right type, and a reused old price passes it easily.

The same idea covers the other common silent failure, a feature that suddenly arrives empty and gets filled with a default. A completeness check on null or default-value rates against their normal level catches that one.
questions.deeper: In interviews, name freshness and completeness together as part of a data contract for each feature, with an expected update cadence and a normal null rate. A good follow-up is what the service should do when a check fails, such as falling back to a simpler model or a safe default price, rather than serving on stale inputs.

questions.prompt: A crop-monitoring model takes 100×100 satellite tiles. Its first convolution layer uses a 7×7 kernel, a stride of 3, and 2 pixels of zero padding on every side, with 32 output channels. What is the height of the output feature map (the width is the same)? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation:
The output size of a convolution is ⌊(n + 2p − k) / s⌋ + 1, where n is the input size, k the kernel size, s the stride and p the padding on each side.

- Padded size: 100 + 2 × 2 = 104
- Room for the kernel to move: 104 − 7 = 97
- Steps of 3: 97 / 3 ≈ 32.33, which rounds down to 32
- Add 1 for the starting position: 32 + 1 = 33

The output is 33 × 33 with 32 channels. The channel count does not affect the height or width.

The +1 counts the kernel's first position before any step is taken, and forgetting it gives 32. Adding the padding once instead of twice gives ⌊95 / 3⌋ + 1 = 32 as well. Rounding 32.33 up instead of down gives 34. The floor is there because the kernel can only start at positions where it fits fully inside the padded input. Leftover pixels at the far edge are simply skipped.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like to chain this through a few layers or ask for the padding that keeps the size unchanged. For stride 1 and an odd kernel size k, that is p = (k − 1) / 2, often called same padding. A shape mismatch at the first linear layer after the convolutions is a classic bug, so print the shapes once before training.

questions.prompt: A purchasing agent calls a supplier's `create_order` API. The request times out, so the runtime retries it. Later the team finds two identical orders: the first request had actually gone through. The fix is to generate one unique value per intended order and send it with the first attempt and every retry, so the supplier carries out the order only once. That value is usually called the request's ______ key.
questions.explanation:
An idempotency key makes a call that changes something safe to repeat. The client creates the key once for one intended action and sends it with every attempt. The server stores the keys it has processed. If a request arrives with a key it has seen, it returns the stored result instead of creating a second order. A timeout is the classic case: the client cannot tell whether the request failed or only the response was lost, and the key makes the retry safe either way.

The common mistake is to reach for an ordinary request ID or trace ID and generate a fresh one for each attempt. A per-attempt ID is useful for logging, but the server sees two different values and creates two orders. The key must stay the same across retries of one action and change only for a genuinely new action. It also only works if the server supports it. If the supplier's API has no such feature, the agent should look up whether the order exists before retrying.
questions.deeper: With agents there is a twist. If the model, rather than the runtime, decides to call `create_order` again after an error, a new key may be generated and the duplicate comes back. Strong designs derive the key in code from the task and step, not from the model's output.

questions.prompt: An interviewer says "Design a system that detects fake reviews on our marketplace" and then waits. What would you pin down in the first few minutes before drawing any components, and why does each point matter?
questions.answer: Start with the business goal: protecting buyers from misleading ratings, catching paid review rings, or both. That decides what counts as success. Agree a main metric tied to it, such as the share of fake reviews buyers actually see, plus a guardrail like the rate of genuine reviews wrongly removed, since honest sellers suffer from false alarms. Ask about scale: reviews per day, peak rate and the size of the catalogue. Ask whether a review must be checked before it is published or whether a batch check a few hours later is fine, because that sets the latency budget and the whole serving design. Ask where labels come from: moderator decisions, user reports or confirmed fraud rings, and how trustworthy they are. Finally ask about constraints and what exists today, such as reviewer capacity, privacy rules and current rules, which become the baseline to beat. Repeat these back as stated assumptions before designing.
points: Business goal, which defines success
A main metric plus a guardrail for the cost of false alarms
Scale: volume, peak rate, catalogue size
Latency: real time before publishing or batch afterwards
Label source and quality
Constraints and the current baseline to beat
questions.explanation:
Each question changes the design. A real-time check before publishing needs a fast model and features ready in milliseconds, while a batch job can run heavy graph analysis over reviewer networks. Labels decide whether you can train a supervised model at all or must start with rules and anomaly detection. Scale sets how much compute and human review you can afford. And without a metric agreed up front, you cannot justify any trade-off later.

The common mistake is to jump straight to a model, such as "I would fine-tune a text classifier on review text". That skips the facts that decide whether text is even the right signal. Many fake reviews read naturally, and the stronger signal is often behaviour: accounts created together, bursts of five-star reviews, or reviewers who only rate one seller.

Asking too many questions is also a mistake. Interviewers want a few sharp ones, then stated assumptions so the design can move on.
questions.deeper: A useful habit is to write the assumptions on the board, such as "2 million reviews a day, batch check within an hour, labels from moderators". The interviewer can correct them, and you can point back to them when justifying each choice later. A simple baseline, such as rules on account age and review bursts, shows you think about what to beat.

questions.prompt: A speech-to-text model runs on GPU servers behind a load balancer, with autoscaling set to add a server when average CPU use passes 70%. During a traffic spike, p95 latency triples and request queues grow, but CPU use stays near 25% and no servers are added. A new server takes about 6 minutes to boot and load the model. Which change best fixes this?
options: Lower the CPU target to 20% so the autoscaler reacts sooner, and keep the rest of the setup as it is
Scale on queue depth or in-flight requests per server, and keep warm spare servers for the slow start
Scale on GPU memory use per server, since a busy server holds more data in memory than an idle one
Keep scaling on CPU but give each server more CPU cores, so the CPU no longer limits how fast it serves
questions.explanation:
The heavy work happens on the GPU, while the CPU mostly moves data in and out. So CPU use can sit low while the GPU is saturated and requests pile up. Queue depth or concurrent requests per server measure what drives latency directly: how much work is waiting. A 6-minute start-up also means any scale-out arrives late, so you keep some warm headroom, or scale earlier, to absorb a spike while new servers load.

Lowering the CPU target to 20% would add servers in this spike, but only by luck. The signal still does not track GPU load, so it would scale out when the GPU is idle and miss spikes that barely raise CPU use. GPU memory is mostly taken by the model weights and buffers reserved at start-up, so it stays nearly flat whether the server is busy or idle. Adding CPU cores does nothing when the CPU was never the bottleneck.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often follow up on targets. A good answer sets the queue or concurrency target from the latency objective, for example the number of in-flight requests a server can hold while keeping p95 under the agreed limit. It also mentions scaling down slowly, since removing a server that took 6 minutes to warm up and then needing it back is costly.

questions.prompt: An ad click-through model is trained with a very high learning rate for its first few thousand steps. Afterwards, many hidden units with ReLU activations output exactly 0 for every training example, and their incoming weights and biases no longer change at all. Units stuck in this state are called ______ ReLUs.
questions.explanation:
A ReLU outputs max(0, z). If a large update pushes a unit's weights or bias so far that z is below 0 for every input, the unit always outputs 0 and its local gradient is always 0. No gradient reaches its incoming weights, so nothing pulls it back. The unit is dead. It still costs memory and compute but adds nothing to the prediction. High learning rates are the usual trigger, because one oversized step can throw a unit into that region.

A common wrong answer is vanishing. Vanishing gradients shrink gradually across many layers, as with saturating sigmoids, and slow learning everywhere. A dead ReLU is a hard zero in one unit, and it can happen in a shallow network too. Another wrong answer is saturated, which fits sigmoid or tanh units stuck near their flat ends, where the gradient is small but not exactly zero.
questions.deeper: To diagnose it, log the share of units in each layer that output zero across a whole validation batch. Fixes include a lower learning rate or warmup, He initialization, and activations with a nonzero slope for negative inputs, such as Leaky ReLU or GELU. A dead unit recovers only if earlier layers happen to shift its inputs back above zero.

questions.prompt: A team prunes a transformer text classifier by zeroing the 50% of individual weights with the smallest magnitudes, then fine-tunes briefly. Accuracy holds, but GPU inference latency barely changes, and the saved model, stored as dense matrices, is the same size. What explains this, and what would give a real speed-up?
options: The zeros are scattered, so dense matrix kernels still multiply every entry. Removing whole attention heads or hidden units shrinks the matrices and cuts latency.
Zeroed weights are only skipped after several more epochs of fine-tuning, so a longer fine-tune after pruning is what will finally bring the inference latency down.
Latency in this model is set by the embedding lookup rather than the matrix multiplications, so pruning inside the transformer layers cannot reduce it at all.
Pruning only cuts training cost, since the backward pass does most of the multiplications. Inference speed needs quantization and cannot come from any pruning.
questions.explanation:
Unstructured pruning zeros individual weights wherever they are small, so the zeros land in random places. A dense matrix multiply on a GPU does not check for zeros. It multiplies every entry, zero or not, so the work and the memory traffic stay the same. Unless you store the weights in a sparse format and use kernels built for it, and sparsity is usually far above 50% before those win on a GPU, there is no speed-up.

Structured pruning removes whole units: attention heads, rows of a feed-forward layer, or entire layers. The matrices that remain are smaller but still dense, so the standard fast kernels run on less data and latency falls.

The option about fine-tuning longer is wrong because training does not change how the kernels run. Zeros stay zeros that get multiplied. The embedding lookup is cheap next to the many matrix multiplications in each transformer layer, so it does not set latency here. Pruning does not only help training. Structured pruning is a standard way to speed up inference, and it can be combined with quantization.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate mentions a middle ground: semi-structured patterns, such as 2 zeros in every block of 4 weights, which some accelerators can run faster. They also note that structured pruning usually costs more accuracy than unstructured at the same sparsity, so it needs fine-tuning and a careful check on slices.

questions.prompt: A documentation search merges a BM25 ranking and a vector ranking with reciprocal rank fusion. Each document's fused score is the sum, over the lists it appears in, of 1 / (k + rank), where rank starts at 1 and k = 60. Document A is ranked 1st by BM25 and does not appear in the vector list. Document B is ranked 4th by BM25 and 3rd by the vector search. What is document B's fused score? Give it as a decimal to 4 places.
questions.explanation:
Add one term for each list the document appears in.

- BM25 term: 1 / (60 + 4) = 1/64 ≈ 0.015625
- Vector term: 1 / (60 + 3) = 1/63 ≈ 0.015873
- Fused score: 0.015625 + 0.015873 ≈ 0.031498, which is 0.0315

Document A gets only 1 / (60 + 1) ≈ 0.0164, so B ranks above A even though A topped one list. RRF rewards documents that both retrievers agree on.

The most common mistake is to leave out k and add 1/4 + 1/3 ≈ 0.5833. Without k, the gap between rank 1 and rank 2 is huge, so the top result of a single list would dominate the merge. The constant k flattens the curve, so ranks 1, 2 and 3 count almost equally. Another slip is to average the two terms instead of adding them, which gives about 0.0157 and no longer rewards agreement between the lists. Notice also that RRF uses only ranks, so you never need to put BM25 scores and cosine scores on a common scale.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like to ask why you fuse ranks instead of raw scores. BM25 scores are unbounded and vary by query, while cosine scores sit in a narrow band, so adding them directly lets one side dominate. RRF sidesteps this. Weighted versions exist when one retriever is clearly stronger, and k is worth a quick test on your own queries.

questions.prompt:
This pandas 3.x feature step runs on a 5-million-row orders table, and it takes hours. `order_date` and `signup_date` are datetime columns. Review it and explain how you would make it fast.

```python
df["days_since_signup"] = df.apply(
    lambda r: (r["order_date"] - r["signup_date"]).days, axis=1)
df["user_orders"] = df.apply(
    lambda r: (df["user_id"] == r["user_id"]).sum(), axis=1)
df["big_order"] = df.apply(
    lambda r: 1 if r["amount"] > 100 else 0, axis=1)
```
questions.answer: All three lines use `apply` with `axis=1`, which builds a Series for every row and calls a Python function on it, so nothing runs at NumPy speed. The second line is far worse. For every row it compares the whole `user_id` column, which is O(n²), about 25 trillion comparisons at 5 million rows. I would replace each line with a column operation. `(df["order_date"] - df["signup_date"]).dt.days` subtracts the date columns in one call. `df.groupby("user_id")["user_id"].transform("size")` counts orders per user in one pass and puts the count back on each row. `(df["amount"] > 100).astype(int)` turns a vectorized comparison into 0 and 1. Before switching, I would check the dtypes and confirm the new columns match the old ones on a sample, then time each step to see what is left.
points: Row-wise apply calls Python once per row, so it is not vectorized
The per-row scan of the whole user_id column is O(n²) and dominates
Use column subtraction with .dt.days for the date feature
Use groupby with transform("size") to count orders per user
Use a vectorized comparison cast to int for the flag
Check that the new columns match the old ones before swapping
questions.explanation:
The key insight is that the three slow lines are not equally slow. The date and flag lines are O(n) but pay Python overhead per row, so vectorizing them gives a large constant speed-up. The user count line is O(n²), because each of 5 million rows scans 5 million values. No amount of hardware fixes that. It needs a different algorithm, and a groupby is one pass over the data.

The common mistake is to reach for parallel tools, such as multiprocessing or a parallel apply library, or for `np.vectorize`. Spreading an O(n²) loop across 8 cores still leaves an O(n²) loop, and `np.vectorize` still calls Python per element. Another weaker answer rewrites the count as a groupby `agg` and then merges it back, which works but costs an extra join compared with `transform`.

A careful reviewer also confirms the dates are true datetime64 columns. If they are strings, the first fix is `pd.to_datetime` once, not per row.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate also flags a leakage risk. `user_orders` counts all of a user's orders, including ones placed after the current order. If the model predicts at order time, the feature should be the count so far, such as `df.sort_values("order_date").groupby("user_id").cumcount()`.

questions.prompt: You run PCA on unscaled housing data with two features: sale price in dollars (variance about 10¹⁰) and number of rooms (variance about 2). The first principal component explains 99.99% of the variance. What is the best reading of this result?
options: The first component lies almost along the price axis, because PCA follows variance measured in raw units.
Price and room count are almost perfectly correlated, so one component is enough to capture both features.
The data is truly one-dimensional, so the second component carries no information and can be dropped safely.
PCA stopped before converging, and more iterations would spread the variance more evenly across components.
questions.explanation:
Principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, ordered by their eigenvalues, which are the variances along each direction. Covariance is measured in the raw units. A variance of 10¹⁰ against a variance of 2 means the direction of greatest spread is almost exactly the price axis, whatever the link between the two features. The 99.99% says more about dollars than about structure.

Near-perfect correlation would produce the same number, but nothing here shows it. You would see the same result with price and rooms completely unrelated. That also rules out the claim that the data is one-dimensional. The room count, which is surely useful, is sitting in the second component, so dropping it throws away a real feature. PCA is usually solved exactly with an eigendecomposition or SVD, and approximate solvers aim at the same components, so more iterations would not change how the variance splits. The fix is to standardise both features first, which is the same as running PCA on the correlation matrix.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate states the rule plainly: standardise before PCA unless the features share a unit and their raw spread is meaningful, such as pixel intensities. Fit the scaler and PCA on training data only, then apply both to new data. Interviewers may also ask how to choose the number of components from a cumulative explained variance plot.

questions.prompt: A biotech team has 400 patients and 20,000 gene expression features. They pick the 50 genes most correlated with the outcome using all 400 patients, then run 5-fold cross-validation of a logistic regression on those 50 genes and get AUC 0.93. As a sanity check, they shuffle the labels and rerun the whole procedure. AUC is still 0.90. What should they change?
options: Pick genes with an L1-penalised model fit once on all 400 patients, then cross-validate as before
Keep the top 500 genes instead of the top 50, so the selection depends less on random chance
Redo the gene ranking inside each training fold, such as a step in a scikit-learn `Pipeline`
Swap the correlation filter for recursive feature elimination, run once on all 400 patients first
questions.explanation:
With shuffled labels there is no real signal, so an honest procedure should score about 0.5. Getting 0.90 proves the evaluation is broken. With 20,000 genes and 400 patients, some genes correlate with any labels by pure chance. Ranking them on all patients picks those lucky genes using the validation patients' labels too, so each validation fold has already been used to choose the features. The fix is to treat selection as part of training: rerun it on the training part of each fold. A `Pipeline` with `SelectKBest` and the model does this automatically.

Recursive feature elimination is a wrapper method and an L1 penalty is an embedded method, but run once on all patients both leak in exactly the same way. The choice of filter, wrapper or embedded does not matter if it sees the validation labels. Keeping 500 genes still selects them on all the data, so it still leaks.
questions.deeper: Interviewers love the shuffled-label test because it is cheap and decisive. If selection settings such as k are tuned too, use nested cross-validation, with tuning in the inner loop and the honest estimate from the outer loop.

questions.prompt:
A help-centre search is tested on five queries. Each query has one or more relevant articles, found at these ranks:

- Query 1: rank 1
- Query 2: ranks 3 and 5
- Query 3: no relevant article in the top 10
- Query 4: ranks 2 and 4
- Query 5: rank 4

A query with no relevant article in the top 10 scores 0. What is the mean reciprocal rank? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Reciprocal rank uses only the first relevant result for each query and scores it as 1 divided by its rank. The later relevant results for queries 2 and 4 do not count.

- Query 1: 1 / 1 = 1.000
- Query 2: 1 / 3 ≈ 0.333
- Query 3: 0
- Query 4: 1 / 2 = 0.500
- Query 5: 1 / 4 = 0.250

The sum is about 2.083, and the mean over 5 queries is about 0.42.

One common mistake is to drop query 3 and average over four queries. That gives about 0.52 and hides the query that failed completely. Another is to average the first ranks and then invert, turning ranks 1, 3, 2 and 4 into a mean rank of 2.5 and a score of 0.40. That is not the same calculation, and a single deep result can swing it a lot. A third slip is to add 1/5 and 1/4 for the extra relevant articles in queries 2 and 4.
questions.deeper: MRR suits tasks where the user wants one answer, such as a help article or a known product page. It ignores every relevant result after the first, so it fits poorly when users read several results. For the retriever in an LLM app, teams often report MRR next to recall@k.

questions.prompt: An ad server keeps a Beta distribution over the click rate of each of its creatives, updated after every impression. For each request it draws one random value from every creative's distribution and shows the creative with the highest draw. This bandit method is called ______.
questions.explanation:
Thompson sampling picks each arm with the probability that it is the best one, given the data so far. Drawing one sample from each posterior and taking the largest does exactly that. A creative with few impressions has a wide Beta distribution, so it sometimes draws a high value and gets shown, which is exploration. A creative with many impressions has a narrow distribution near its true rate, so it wins only if it really is strong. Exploration fades on its own as evidence builds up.

The common mistake is to answer UCB, upper confidence bound. UCB also favours uncertain arms, but it does so deterministically: it adds a bonus based on how few times an arm has been tried and picks the highest score, with no random draw. Epsilon-greedy is also wrong here, since it explores by picking a uniformly random arm a fixed share of the time and keeps no distribution at all.
questions.deeper: Thompson sampling is popular in production because it is simple and handles delayed rewards well. With click data the Beta prior is easy: start at Beta(1, 1), add 1 to the first number for each click and 1 to the second for each non-click. A follow-up is how to add context, such as user features, which leads to contextual bandits.

questions.prompt: A ridge regression model predicts delivery times from 300 features. With almost no penalty, its training error is far below its validation error. You refit it many times, raising the L2 strength λ step by step from near zero to a very large value. Which pattern should you expect?
options: Training error rises steadily, validation error falls then rises, and the weights shrink toward zero.
Training error falls steadily, validation error falls then rises, and the weights grow steadily larger.
Training error rises steadily, validation error keeps falling, and most weights become exactly zero.
Training and validation error both fall steadily, and the weights shrink but never reach zero.
questions.explanation:
Raising λ makes large weights more expensive, so the model is less free to fit the training data. Training error can only go up as λ grows, and the size of the weights can only go down. Validation error traces a U shape. At near zero penalty the model overfits, as the big gap shows. A moderate λ removes much more variance than the bias it adds, so validation error falls. At a very large λ every weight is pushed close to zero and the model predicts roughly the average delivery time, so it underfits and validation error climbs again. You pick λ at the bottom of the U.

Training error falling with a stronger penalty, and weights growing, both have the effect backwards. Validation error cannot keep falling forever, because the far end of the sweep is a near-constant model. Exact zeros are L1 behaviour. L2 shrinks weights smoothly without zeroing them. Both errors falling steadily cannot happen, since training error never improves when the penalty grows.
questions.deeper: In practice you sweep λ on a log scale, for example 10⁻⁴ to 10⁴, and plot both curves. An interviewer may ask why features must be standardised first: the penalty treats all weights alike, so a feature measured in metres and one in kilometres would be shrunk very differently.

questions.prompt: A telecom churn model explains one customer's score with SHAP. The base value is 0.20. The contributions are: month-to-month contract +0.25, tenure of 3 months +0.10, no support calls −0.05. A manager says: "Move this customer to an annual contract and their churn score will fall by 0.25." Which statement is correct?
options: The score is 0.50, and switching will lower it by exactly 0.25, because SHAP values are additive.
The score is 0.30, and switching will cut it by 0.25, leaving a churn score of only 0.05.
The score is 0.50, and the manager is right as long as the features are not correlated.
The score is 0.50, but the 0.25 is credit relative to the average, not the effect of a switch.
questions.explanation:
SHAP contributions add up from the base value: 0.20 + 0.25 + 0.10 − 0.05 = 0.50. But each contribution measures how far knowing that feature moves the prediction away from the average over a background set of customers. That background mixes all contract types. The +0.25 compares month-to-month with that mix, not with an annual contract, and it says nothing about how the other contributions would shift if the contract changed.

Additivity is about how the explanation of one prediction adds up. It does not turn a contribution into the change you get from editing a feature, so the option claiming an exact 0.25 drop is wrong. The option giving 0.30 forgets the base value. Uncorrelated features do not rescue the manager either. Even in a purely additive model, switching to annual removes the +0.25 and adds the annual contract's own contribution, which is usually negative, so the drop would differ from 0.25.

To see what the model predicts after a switch, re-score the customer with an annual contract.
questions.deeper: Even the re-scored number is only what the model predicts, not what the customer will do. Customers who choose annual contracts differ from those who are pushed into one. A strong candidate separates explanation, model what-if and causal effect, and suggests an experiment such as a randomized retention offer for the last one.

questions.prompt: Depth-2 decision trees give a churn model 0.70 AUC on both training and validation data. You can turn it into an ensemble of 300 such shallow trees, either by bagging or by gradient boosting. Which is more likely to raise validation AUC, and why?
options: Bagging, because averaging many shallow trees lowers their shared bias as well as their variance.
Boosting, because it trains its trees independently on bootstrap samples, which cuts variance.
Boosting, because each new shallow tree fits what the earlier trees still get wrong, cutting bias.
Bagging, because each bootstrap sample shows a tree rows it has never seen, which fixes underfitting.
questions.explanation:
Equal training and validation scores at a modest level point to high bias. Depth-2 trees are too simple to capture the patterns, and they are not overfitting. Boosting attacks bias directly. Each new tree is fit to what the current ensemble still gets wrong, the residuals or gradients, so the combined model builds complex patterns out of many simple pieces.

Bagging averages trees trained independently on bootstrap samples. Averaging reduces variance, but every tree has much the same bias, and the average of many similarly biased trees keeps that bias. So the option claiming bagging lowers the shared bias is wrong. The one saying bootstrap samples show new rows is wrong too, since a bootstrap sample only reuses rows from the same dataset. The option crediting boosting with independent bootstrap training describes bagging. Boosting trains in sequence, and each tree depends on the ones before it.
questions.deeper: The mirror case is a deep tree that overfits, where bagging or a random forest is the natural choice. A strong candidate also notes that boosting can overfit if it runs too long, which is why it is paired with a small learning rate and early stopping. Adding more trees to a random forest does not overfit in the same way.

questions.prompt: A customer-support agent can read customer records, send emails to customers and issue refunds through tools. In testing it once looped for 400 steps on a confusing ticket, and once refunded the same order twice. Which safeguards should be in place before it goes live? Select all that apply.
options: A hard cap on steps and on token spend per ticket, after which the agent stops and hands the ticket to a person.
Human approval before irreversible actions, such as a refund above a set amount or an email sent to many customers.
A refund tool that enforces limits itself: a maximum amount and a check that the order has not already been refunded.
A line in the system prompt saying "Never refund more than $200", relied on as the main control for large refunds.
Automatic retries on any failed tool call, repeated until the call succeeds, so that no ticket is left half done.
questions.explanation:
Each of the three keys enforces a rule outside the model, which is the point of a safeguard. A step and spend cap turns the 400-step loop into a bounded failure with a clean hand-off. Human approval for irreversible actions keeps a person in the loop exactly where mistakes are expensive and cannot be undone. Limits inside the refund tool stop a double refund even when the model is confused, because the tool checks the order's state before acting, and a maximum amount caps the damage from any single call.

A system prompt rule is guidance, not enforcement. The model can misread it, and a prompt injection in a customer email could override it, so it must not be the main control for something that moves money. Retrying every failed call until it succeeds is how runaway loops start. Some errors, such as "order not found" or "refund already issued", will never succeed on retry. Retries should be limited, used only for temporary errors such as timeouts, and safe to repeat.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like the word idempotent here. A refund call that carries a unique request ID can be retried safely, because the payment system ignores a repeat of the same ID. A strong answer also mentions logging every tool call so incidents can be audited later.

questions.prompt: A model has 28 layers and width 3,072. A team applies LoRA with rank r = 16 to two matrices in every layer: the query projection, which is 3,072 × 3,072, and the MLP up-projection, which maps 3,072 inputs to 8,192 outputs. How many trainable parameters does LoRA add in total? Give the answer in millions to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation:
LoRA replaces the update to a d_in × d_out matrix with two thin matrices. One is d_in × r and the other is r × d_out, so the trainable count is r × (d_in + d_out).

Query projection: 16 × (3,072 + 3,072) = 16 × 6,144 = 98,304.
Up-projection: 16 × (3,072 + 8,192) = 16 × 11,264 = 180,224.
Per layer: 98,304 + 180,224 = 278,528.
Across 28 layers: 278,528 × 28 = 7,798,784, which is about 7.80 million.

For comparison, fully fine-tuning those same matrices would train 28 × (3,072 × 3,072 + 3,072 × 8,192) ≈ 969 million weights, so LoRA trains about 0.8% as many.

The most common mistake is to multiply r × d_in × d_out, as if one matrix had all three sizes. That gives a number larger than the original matrix, which defeats the purpose. Another slip is to use r × 2 × 3,072 for the up-projection as if it were square, which undercounts it.
questions.deeper: Trainable parameters are only part of the memory story. A strong candidate notes that the frozen base weights and the activations still dominate GPU memory, which is why QLoRA also quantizes the base. Optimizer state is where LoRA saves most, since it is kept only for the small adapter weights.

questions.prompt:
A fraud-scoring API logged these 20 response times in milliseconds:

120, 95, 110, 480, 105, 130, 98, 115, 125, 102, 140, 108, 118, 900, 112, 100, 135, 122, 128, 107

Use the nearest-rank method: sort the values, and the p-th percentile is the value at position ⌈p / 100 × n⌉, counting from 1. How many milliseconds higher is the p95 latency than the p50 latency? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation:
Sort the 20 values: 95, 98, 100, 102, 105, 107, 108, 110, 112, 115, 118, 120, 122, 125, 128, 130, 135, 140, 480, 900.

- p50: position ⌈0.50 × 20⌉ = 10, which is 115 ms
- p95: position ⌈0.95 × 20⌉ = 19, which is 480 ms
- Difference: 480 − 115 = 365 ms

The common mistake is to take p95 as the largest value, 900 ms. With 20 values, the 19th is the 95th percentile, and the 20th is the maximum. Another slip is to use a different percentile rule. Interpolating between ranks, as many libraries do by default, gives a p95 of 501 ms and a p50 of 116.5 ms, which is why the prompt fixes the method.

Notice what the numbers say. The typical request takes about 115 ms, but the slowest 2 of the 20 take four times as long or more. The mean is about 172.5 ms, which describes neither group. Users remember the slow requests, and a page that makes several calls in a row hits the tail far more often than 1 time in 20.
questions.deeper: Latency targets are usually written on p95 or p99, not the mean. A strong candidate adds that percentiles cannot be averaged across servers or time windows. To get a fleet-wide p95, you merge the raw data or histograms first. They would also look for the cause of the 480 and 900 ms outliers, such as garbage-collection pauses, cold caches or slow downstream calls.

questions.prompt: A hospital team checks the calibration of a readmission model. They sort 20,000 test patients into 10 equal-width bins by predicted probability and plot a reliability diagram: mean predicted probability on the x-axis and the observed readmission rate on the y-axis. They also report expected calibration error (ECE). Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A bin plotted below the diagonal is one where the model predicted more readmissions than actually happened.
ECE weights each bin's gap by its share of patients, so a large gap in a nearly empty bin adds very little.
A model that gives every patient the overall readmission rate can have ECE near 0 while ranking no one usefully.
A bin plotted above the diagonal is one where the model's scores are too high and should be pulled down.
ECE comes out the same whatever number of bins you choose, so the bin count does not need reporting.
If recalibration lowers ECE, the model's ROC-AUC must have gone up by a similar amount as well.
questions.explanation:
A point below the diagonal has an x value (what the model predicted) higher than its y value (what happened). If patients in a bin were scored 0.40 on average but only 25% were readmitted, the model overestimates risk there, and its scores for that bin should be pulled down. ECE is the weighted average of the gaps |observed − predicted| across bins, with each bin weighted by the share of patients in it, so a 30-point gap in a bin with 15 patients barely moves it. And calibration is not discrimination. A model that predicts the base rate for everyone is perfectly calibrated on average but cannot separate high-risk from low-risk patients.

The option about points above the diagonal has it backwards. There the observed rate is higher than predicted, so the scores are too low. ECE does depend on the binning: more bins means fewer patients per bin and noisier gaps, which tends to push ECE up, so the bin count should be reported. Finally, a monotonic recalibration such as Platt scaling keeps the order of the scores, so ROC-AUC stays the same while ECE falls.
questions.deeper: In an interview, pair ECE with the diagram itself and a count per bin. A single ECE number hides where the miscalibration sits, and for a readmission model the high-risk bins usually drive care decisions. A strong candidate also mentions equal-count bins, which avoid near-empty bins at the extremes.

questions.prompt: A job board wants to flag duplicate job postings and also sort postings into 15 categories. You have a pretrained sentence encoder that turns text into 768-number vectors, and a few hundred hand-labeled examples for each task. How would you use the encoder's embeddings for both tasks, and how would you decide whether they are good enough or need fine-tuning?
questions.answer: I would embed each posting with the frozen encoder, using the pooling it was trained with, and L2-normalize the vectors. For duplicates, I would compare postings by cosine similarity, find each posting's nearest neighbours with a vector index, and flag pairs above a threshold that I tune on the labeled pairs, reporting precision and recall. For categories, I would train a logistic regression on the frozen embeddings, a linear probe, and measure macro-F1 on a held-out split. To judge quality, I would compare both against a simple TF-IDF baseline and read the nearest neighbours of some postings by hand, looking for failures such as matching on company boilerplate instead of the job itself. If the encoder clearly loses to the baseline or misses domain jargon, I would fine-tune it on in-domain pairs or on the category labels.
points: Embed with the frozen encoder and normalize the vectors
Duplicates: cosine similarity with a threshold tuned on labeled pairs, measured by precision and recall
Categories: train a linear probe on frozen embeddings and score it on a held-out split
Compare against a simple baseline and inspect nearest neighbours by hand
Fine-tune on in-domain data only if the frozen embeddings fall short
questions.explanation:
Pretrained embeddings place texts with similar meaning close together, so many tasks need only a light layer on top. A linear probe is a strong first test because it is cheap and shows how much useful information the frozen vectors already hold. A probe that does well means the encoder already separates the categories. A probe that does poorly means fine-tuning or a different encoder is needed.

The common mistake is to judge embeddings by eye on a few hand-picked pairs, or to pick a cosine threshold such as 0.8 without measuring it. Similarity scores depend on the encoder, and many encoders give unrelated texts scores well above zero, so a threshold only means something once it is tuned on labeled pairs. Another mistake is to ignore what the text contains. Job postings share long legal and benefits sections, which can make two different jobs at one company look like duplicates. Embedding only the title and duties, or stripping boilerplate first, often matters more than the choice of encoder. Also check truncation, since long postings can exceed the encoder's input limit and lose their key details.
questions.deeper: In production, a two-stage setup is common: cheap embedding search proposes candidate duplicates, then a cross-encoder or rules confirm them. Interviewers may ask what happens when you upgrade the encoder, since every stored vector must then be recomputed, because vectors from two models are not comparable.

questions.subtopic: what a good tool result contains
questions.prompt: A home-goods shop gives its shopping agent a `search_products(query)` tool. Today it returns the full HTML of up to 50 matching product pages, and the agent often loses track of what the user asked for. What should a redesigned tool result contain? Select all that apply.
options: A few useful fields per product, such as name, price and stock, instead of every field the system stores.
Each product's full description and all its customer reviews, so the agent never needs a second call.
A product id for each result, so the agent can pass it straight to follow-up tools like `add_to_basket`.
Internal debug data such as query plans and cache timings, so the agent can tune its own searches.
A note when results are cut off, such as "showing 10 of 240, add a filter to narrow the list".
Results silently trimmed to the first 10, with no note, so that the context always stays small.
questions.explanation:
A tool result becomes part of the model's context, so every token in it competes with the user's request and the agent's plan. A good result returns what the next decision needs and little else. A few fields per product let the agent compare options. Ids let it act on a choice without copying names or guessing, so a follow-up call like `add_to_basket` gets an exact reference. A truncation note tells the agent more results exist and how to reach them, so it can refine the search instead of assuming the first 10 are everything.

Full descriptions and every review for each result repeat the current problem in a cleaner form. For dozens of products that is still thousands of tokens, which bury the few facts that matter and pull attention away from the user's request. Saving one follow-up call is not worth paying that cost on every search. Debug data helps engineers, not the agent, which cannot change query plans, so it is pure noise. Silent trimming keeps the context small but misleads the agent. It will treat the 10 results as the whole catalogue and may tell the user an item does not exist.
questions.deeper: A useful idea to mention in interviews: design tool results for a model reader the way you design an API for a developer. Some teams add a detail-level argument, short by default and full on request, so the agent can drill into one product without every search paying that cost. Measure the change with task success and tokens per run.

questions.prompt: A model with width d_model = 768 uses 12 attention heads of size 64 in each layer instead of one head of size 768. What does this split mainly gain?
options: It cuts the attention compute by about a factor of 12, because each head works on vectors that are 12 times smaller than the full width.
Each head has its own projections and softmax, so heads can attend to different tokens for different reasons at about the same total cost.
Each head reads a different slice of the sequence, so together the 12 heads can handle an input about 12 times longer than one head could.
The 12 heads share one set of weights and their outputs are averaged, which lowers the variance of the attention scores like an ensemble.
questions.explanation:
A single head produces one softmax distribution per token, so it has to blend every kind of relationship into one set of weights. With 12 heads, each has its own query, key and value projections, so one head can track the subject of a verb while another follows a pronoun back to its noun. The head outputs are concatenated and passed through an output projection, so the model can combine these views.

The compute option is wrong because the total stays about the same: 12 heads of size 64 do the same projection work as one head of size 768, and the score matrices add up to a similar cost. The option about slices of the sequence is wrong because every head sees every token. Heads split the feature width, not the positions, so context length does not change. The ensemble option is wrong twice: heads have separate weights, and their outputs are concatenated rather than averaged.
questions.deeper: Interviewers sometimes ask whether all heads are needed. Studies that prune heads find many can be removed with little loss, which suggests some redundancy. A strong candidate also mentions grouped-query attention, where several query heads share one key and value head to shrink the KV cache during inference.

questions.prompt: A clinic screens blood test results for a kidney condition with a linear SVM on 15 standardised lab values. A new teammate asks what the model is actually optimising and what the C setting does. Explain the maximum-margin idea, what support vectors are, and how raising or lowering C changes the model.
questions.answer: Many boundaries can separate the two classes. A linear SVM picks the one with the widest margin, the gap between the boundary and the nearest training points of each class. A wide margin leaves room for new patients whose values differ a little from the training data, so it tends to generalise better. The support vectors are the training points that sit on the margin or inside it, including any on the wrong side. Only they decide where the boundary goes. Moving any other point slightly changes nothing. Real data overlaps, so the soft-margin SVM lets points violate the margin at a cost, and C sets that cost. A large C punishes violations heavily, giving a narrow margin that hugs the training data and can overfit. A small C accepts more violations in exchange for a wider margin, which means stronger regularisation and usually more support vectors. I would tune C with cross-validation.
points: Picks the separating boundary with the widest margin to the nearest points
Support vectors sit on or inside the margin, and only they set the boundary
Soft margin allows violations, and C is the penalty on them
Large C: narrow margin, fewer training errors, risk of overfitting
Small C: wider margin, more violations, stronger regularisation
Tune C with cross-validation on scaled features
questions.explanation:
The SVM objective makes the idea concrete. It minimises ½‖w‖² + C × Σξᵢ. The margin width is 2 / ‖w‖, and each ξᵢ measures how far point i falls inside the margin or past the boundary. Shrinking ‖w‖ widens the margin, the second term charges for violations, and C decides which of the two wins.

The most common mistake is to read C like the regularisation strength λ in ridge or lasso. It works the other way round. C multiplies the error term, so raising C means weaker regularisation and a model that bends to fit noisy or mislabelled training points. With a few wrong lab labels, a very large C chases them and generalises worse.

A second slip is to think every training point shapes the boundary. Points safely outside the margin get zero weight in the solution, so deleting them leaves the same model. For kernel SVMs this is also why prediction cost grows with the number of support vectors rather than with the size of the training set.
questions.deeper: A strong answer adds that SVMs need scaled features, because the margin is measured in raw distance, and that SVM scores are not probabilities, so you calibrate them, for example with Platt scaling, before setting a clinical threshold. A good follow-up is class imbalance, which per-class weights on C can handle.

questions.prompt: A payments company has a new fraud model with strong offline results. Before a full launch, the team wants to learn how the model's own decisions affect chargebacks and complaints from wrongly declined customers on real traffic. They also want to keep the damage small if the model turns out to be bad. Which rollout fits best?
options: A canary release that sends a small share of live traffic to the new model and widens it while metrics hold.
A shadow deployment that scores all live traffic with the new model while the old model's decisions are used.
A blue-green switch that moves all traffic to the new model at once and keeps the old one ready for rollback.
A backtest that replays last month's logged transactions through the new model and compares the scores.
questions.explanation:
The team wants to see the effect of the new model's decisions, and that only happens if some customers actually get those decisions. A canary does this for a small slice of traffic, say 1 to 5%, so a bad model can only hurt a few customers before it is rolled back. If chargebacks and complaints look fine, the share grows step by step.

A shadow deployment answers a different question. It is safe and shows latency, errors and how often the two models disagree, but its decisions are never acted on. No customer is declined by it, so you cannot see the chargebacks or complaints it would cause. A blue-green switch does give real outcomes, but it exposes every customer at once, which breaks the need to keep the damage small. A backtest only has outcomes for what the old model decided. A transaction the old model declined has no chargeback record, so you cannot tell what would have happened if the new model had approved it.
questions.deeper: A common pattern uses both in order: shadow first to check latency, errors and score agreement at no risk, then a canary to measure real outcomes. Interviewers like to hear the rollback trigger agreed in advance, for example the decline rate or p99 latency crossing a set limit, so nobody argues about it in the middle of an incident.

questions.prompt: An electronics parts distributor runs vector search over its catalogue. Customers who type a part number such as "RX-4471-B" often get parts with similar-looking codes or generic parts of the same type, while the exact part ranks low or is missing. Paraphrased queries such as "small voltage regulator for a 5 volt hobby board" work well. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Embeddings capture general meaning and blur rare codes, so add BM25 keyword search and fuse its ranking with the vector one.
The vector index is approximate, so switching to exact nearest-neighbour search will put the exact codes at the top.
The embeddings are too short to hold codes, so doubling the dimension will let each vector store the exact part number.
Vector search is the wrong tool, so replace it with BM25 alone, which handles both exact codes and paraphrased queries.
questions.explanation:
An embedding model is trained to place texts with similar meaning close together. A code like RX-4471-B carries little meaning to learn. The tokenizer splits it into fragments, and its vector lands near other codes that share fragments, or near the generic product type. So the exact match can lose to look-alikes. BM25 scores exact term overlap and gives extra weight to rare terms, which is exactly what a part number is. Running both searches and fusing the two rankings keeps the semantic matches and adds the exact ones.

Exact nearest-neighbour search only removes approximation error. It still ranks by the same embedding similarity, so if the vectors place look-alike codes closer, exact search returns them too. Doubling the dimension does not give a vector a slot for exact strings, because the model still learns meaning, not spelling. Replacing vector search with BM25 fixes the codes but breaks the paraphrased queries that work today. BM25 only matches words that actually appear in the product text, so a query about a "hobby board" misses a listing that never uses those words.
questions.deeper: Strong candidates say the blend needs tuning on real traffic, for example a test set split into code-style queries and natural-language queries, with recall measured on each. Some teams also spot identifier-shaped queries with a simple pattern and send them straight to an exact lookup before any search runs.

questions.subtopic: a credit model approves one group less
questions.prompt: A journalist reports that your bank's credit-card approval model approves applicants from one ethnic group at about half the rate of others. The model does not use ethnicity as a feature. You lead the response. What do you do, and in what order?
questions.answer: First, verify the claim. Get or carefully estimate group membership for an audit sample, within privacy rules, and measure approval rates, the disparate impact ratio, and outcomes where they exist, such as default rates among approved applicants, noting that rejected applicants have no repayment record. Check whether the gap is statistically solid and how much remains after legitimate factors such as income and existing debt. Second, find the cause. Look at the labels, since past approvals may carry past bias, at how well the group is represented in training data, and at proxy features such as postcode, using SHAP or removing features to see what drives the gap. Third, choose a fix with legal and compliance: drop or rework proxies, reweigh data, or retrain with a fairness constraint, then re-measure both fairness and default rates. Finally, record the finding, fix and trade-offs in the model card, add group metrics to monitoring, and give a clear public answer.
points: Verify first: approval rates and error rates by group on a proper audit sample
Getting group labels for the audit needs care under privacy rules
Check labels, representation and proxy features to find the cause
Choose a fix with legal and compliance, then re-measure fairness and default rates
Document in the model card, monitor group metrics, and communicate clearly
questions.explanation:
The order matters. Measuring comes before fixing, because a raw approval gap can have several causes and each needs a different remedy. If the gap comes from biased past decisions in the labels, reweighing or new labels help. If it comes from a proxy feature, removing or reworking that feature helps. If it shrinks a lot once income and debt are accounted for, the team must still show those factors are needed for the business and are not proxies themselves.

The most common mistake is to defend the model because ethnicity is not a feature. Proxies can carry the same signal, and regulators and courts look at outcomes, not just inputs. The opposite mistake is jumping straight to per-group thresholds before knowing the cause, which may be unlawful and hides the real problem. A further gap is the audit itself. Banks often do not hold ethnicity data, so getting it through a voluntary survey or a careful statistical estimate is real work, and that data must be protected. Under the EU AI Act, credit scoring of individuals is a high-risk use, so documentation and monitoring are duties, not extras.
questions.deeper: Senior candidates also talk about the people side: who owns the decision on which fairness metric to target, how to brief the journalist honestly without overclaiming, and how to offer affected applicants a review. Keeping the audit reproducible means the same check can run after every retrain.

questions.prompt: Using scikit-learn 1.x, a fraud dataset has 2,000 rows, and 6% of them are fraud. You split it with `train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.15, stratify=y, random_state=7)`. How many fraud rows land in the test set? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation:
Work in three steps.

1. Fraud rows overall: 6% of 2,000 = 120, so 1,880 rows are legitimate.
2. Test set size: 0.15 × 2,000 = 300 rows.
3. With `stratify=y`, each class is split in the same proportion, so the test set gets 0.15 × 120 = 18 fraud rows and 282 legitimate ones. That keeps the test fraud rate at 18 / 300 = 6%, the same as the full data.

The common mistake is to read `test_size` as the training share and answer 0.85 × 120 = 102, which is the number of fraud rows left in training. Another is to think the answer depends on `random_state`. With stratification the counts per class are fixed, and the seed only decides which particular rows go where. Without `stratify`, the count would vary from seed to seed around 18, and with rare classes it can drift far enough to make test metrics unstable.
questions.deeper: When the numbers do not divide evenly, scikit-learn rounds the split sizes and allocates leftovers across classes, so counts can be off by one. For very rare classes, use `StratifiedKFold` and report the spread across folds, since 18 positives give a noisy estimate of recall.

questions.prompt: Training and inference code almost always works with log probabilities instead of raw probabilities. Explain why.
questions.explanation:
