The core issue is that probabilities multiply. A model that gives each of 1,000 tokens a probability of 0.1 assigns the whole sequence 0.1¹⁰⁰⁰ = 10⁻¹⁰⁰⁰. A 64-bit float bottoms out near 10⁻³⁰⁸, so the product becomes exactly zero and you can no longer compare sequences or take gradients. In log space the same quantity is 1,000 × ln 0.1 ≈ −2,303, an ordinary number.

The common incomplete answer stops at underflow. A strong answer also explains why the switch is safe and useful. Log is strictly increasing, so the parameters that maximize the log-likelihood also maximize the likelihood. The sum form makes the loss an average over examples, which is exactly what mini-batch gradient descent estimates. And the negative mean log-likelihood of the correct labels is the cross-entropy, which ties the everyday loss to maximum likelihood.

Another gap is forgetting overflow. Computing softmax directly can overflow when logits are large, so libraries use log-sum-exp: log Σ exp(zᵢ) = m + log Σ exp(zᵢ − m), where m is the largest logit.
questions.deeper: This shows up directly in code. Use a fused loss that takes raw logits and applies log-softmax inside, instead of applying softmax and then taking a log yourself. Perplexity for language models is just exp of the mean negative log-likelihood per token, so it comes from the same sum.
questions.answer: There are three main reasons. First, numerical stability. The likelihood of a dataset or a long token sequence is a product of many probabilities below 1. With enough terms the product falls below the smallest number a float can hold and underflows to zero. Its log is a sum of moderate negative numbers, which stays well within range. Second, sums are easier to work with than products. The log turns the product into a sum over examples, so the gradient is a sum of per-example gradients, which suits mini-batch training. Because log is strictly increasing, maximizing the log-likelihood picks the same parameters as maximizing the likelihood. Third, the negative mean log-likelihood of the correct labels is exactly the cross-entropy loss, so minimizing cross-entropy is maximum likelihood. Frameworks also compute log-softmax with the log-sum-exp trick, subtracting the largest logit before exponentiating to avoid overflow.
points: Products of many small probabilities underflow to zero in floating point
Logs turn products into sums, so gradients add up over examples
Log is increasing, so the best parameters do not change
The negative mean log-likelihood is the cross-entropy loss
Log-sum-exp keeps softmax and its log numerically stable

questions.prompt: Your team wants to predict delivery arrival times with a large sequence model trained on GPS traces. Before that work starts, a senior engineer asks for a simple baseline. Which baselines would you build, and what does having one tell the team?
questions.answer: I would build a few cheap baselines: the historical median time for each route and hour, distance divided by typical speed for that road type, and a linear or small gradient-boosted model on a handful of features such as distance, hour and weekday. Each takes hours, not weeks. Together they set the bar. The large model is only worth its cost in compute, latency and upkeep if it beats them by a margin the business cares about. Building one also exercises the whole pipeline end to end, from data extraction and labels to the split and the metric, so bugs show up early. A baseline that scores suspiciously well points to leakage. One that already meets the product target may mean the complex model is not needed. Later it serves as a fallback in production and a sanity check when a new model's numbers look odd.
points: Name concrete simple baselines, such as historical medians or a linear model
Sets the bar the complex model must beat by a meaningful margin
Tests data, labels, split and metric end to end early
A suspiciously strong baseline flags leakage or an easy problem
May already meet the target, saving the complex build
Serves as a fallback and a sanity check in production
questions.explanation:
Without a baseline, a number like 6 minutes of mean absolute error means nothing. It could be excellent or worse than a lookup table. A baseline turns the complex model's score into a gain, and the gain is what justifies the extra cost.

The most common weak answer names a single baseline, such as the global average arrival time, and stops there. That is a fair floor, but domain heuristics such as route medians, plus a simple learned model, set a far more useful bar. Another weak answer treats the baseline as a formality. Its biggest value is often finding problems: a broken join, labels that include the wait at the depot, or a time leak in the split. Those bugs are far cheaper to find with a model that trains in seconds than with one that trains for days.

A strong answer also says when the baseline changes the plan. If the route median already gives an error the dispatch team accepts, the sequence model needs a clear business case before it is built.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask what you would do if the large model beats the baseline by only 2%. A good answer weighs that gain against serving cost, latency and maintenance, and checks whether the gain holds across segments such as rural routes and peak hours, rather than in the overall average alone.

questions.prompt: A dermatology startup trains an image classifier on 20,000 skin-lesion photos from 3,000 patients. Most patients have 3 to 10 photos, often of the same lesion from different angles. The photos were split 80/20 at random. Validation AUC is 0.94. On photos of 400 new patients from the same clinics and cameras, taken the following month, AUC is 0.79. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?
options: The label mix differs by chance, so stratify the random photo split by diagnosis
The model is overfitting, so add stronger augmentation and keep the same random split
Photos of one patient sit in both sets, so use a group split keyed on patient ID
The validation set is too small, so hold out 40% of the photos at random instead
questions.explanation:
A random split over photos puts different shots of the same patient, often the same lesion, on both sides. The model can then recognise the patient from skin tone, lesion shape or lighting and recall the label it saw in training. Validation measures how well it recognises people it has already met, not how it handles new ones. The new patients came from the same clinics and cameras, which rules out a change in equipment and points at the split. The fix is to split by patient ID, so all of a patient's photos land on one side. Expect validation AUC to fall toward 0.79. That lower number is the honest one.

A bigger random holdout still mixes the same patients across both sets, so it stays inflated. Stratifying by diagnosis keeps the label share equal but still splits patients across sets. Stronger augmentation may help a model that overfits, but a contaminated validation set cannot show you whether it worked, so the split has to be fixed first.
questions.deeper: In scikit-learn, `GroupKFold`, `StratifiedGroupKFold` and `GroupShuffleSplit` take a `groups` array for this. A good interview follow-up is which unit to group by. Pick the unit the model must generalise to in production: the patient here, the user for a recommender, the store for a store-level forecast.

questions.prompt: A news app has 20 million daily active users. Each user opens the feed 5 times a day on average, and each open sends 2 requests to the recommendation service. Peak-hour traffic is 3 times the daily average rate. Using 86,400 seconds in a day, what peak load in requests per second must the service handle? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation:
Work out the daily total, turn it into a per-second average, then scale up to the peak.

- Requests per day: 20,000,000 × 5 × 2 = 200,000,000
- Average rate: 200,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 2,314.8 requests per second
- Peak rate: 2,314.8 × 3 ≈ 6,944 requests per second

The most common mistake is to stop at the average, about 2,315. A service sized for the average falls over every evening, because traffic bunches into busy hours. Another slip is to forget the 2 requests per open, which gives about 3,472. In a live interview, rounding a day to 100,000 seconds is fine for speed and gives about 6,000, but this question fixes 86,400 so there is one exact answer.
questions.deeper: After the peak, interviewers ask what it means for hardware. If one replica of the ranking model handles 500 requests per second within the latency target, you need about 14 replicas at peak, plus 30 to 50% headroom for spikes and a failed node. Caching popular feeds can cut the load further.

questions.prompt: An internal HR assistant answers policy questions using retrieval over the company handbook. An employee reports that yesterday it gave the wrong number of parental leave weeks. The team only logs each user question and the final answer, so they cannot tell what went wrong. Which per-request trace would best let them find out whether the fault was in retrieval, the prompt or the model?
options: The question, final answer, model version, total latency and an error flag, logged for every request
The final answer and its token cost, plus a nightly snapshot of the whole handbook index and its embeddings
Prompt template version, retrieved passages with document IDs, tool calls, and tokens and latency per step
The question, the final answer, the sampling temperature used and a thumbs-up or thumbs-down rating
questions.explanation:
To debug one bad answer you need to see what the model actually saw and did on that request. The retrieved passages show whether the right handbook section was found. If it was missing, the fault is retrieval. If it was there and the answer still got the number wrong, the prompt or the model is at fault. If the passage itself was out of date, the handbook is. The prompt template version tells you which instructions were in force, since prompts change often. Tool calls, tokens and latency per step complete the picture and also feed cost and speed dashboards.

Model version, total latency and an error flag per request tell you which model answered and that nothing crashed. They still hide what context the model was given, so you cannot tell a retrieval miss from a model mistake. A snapshot of the index shows what could have been retrieved, not what was retrieved for this question, and retrieval results depend on the exact query. A rating and the temperature tell you the answer was bad and how random the sampling was, but not why it was wrong.
questions.deeper: A strong answer ties every step to one trace ID, so a thumbs-down or a complaint links straight to the prompt, context and tool calls behind it. Interviewers may also ask about privacy: traces hold user text, so they need access controls, retention limits and redaction of personal data.

questions.prompt:
Using pandas 3.x, what value does `out` hold after this code runs? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "store": ["a", "a", "b", "b", "b"],
    "sales": [10.0, np.nan, 30.0, np.nan, 60.0],
})
df["sales"] = df["sales"].fillna(df["sales"].mean())
out = df.groupby("store")["sales"].mean()["b"]
```
questions.explanation:
Work through it in two steps.

Step 1: `df["sales"].mean()` skips NaN by default. It averages 10, 30 and 60, which is 100 / 3 ≈ 33.33. Both missing values become 33.33.

Step 2: store b now holds 30, 33.33 and 60. Their mean is 123.33 / 3 ≈ 41.11.

The most common mistake is to think the mean treats NaN as zero, giving 100 / 5 = 20 as the fill value and (30 + 20 + 60) / 3 ≈ 36.67 for store b. Another is to skip the fill in your head and average store b's real values only, (30 + 60) / 2 = 45. Note that the fill uses the global mean, not each store's own mean. Filling by store would need `groupby("store")["sales"].transform("mean")` instead.
questions.deeper: Filling with a mean pulls group averages toward the global average and shrinks variance, which can hide real differences between stores. In an interview, mention adding a was-missing flag column and computing fill values from training data only, so the fill does not leak test information.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain scores its daily demand forecasts with MAPE across 5,000 products. Many products sell only 1 to 3 units a day, and days with zero sales are left out of the metric. The weekly MAPE reads 340% and jumps around even when the forecasts barely change. What is the best diagnosis and fix?
options: Small actuals in the denominator turn tiny misses into huge percentages. Report WAPE, total absolute error over total sales.
MAPE treats over- and under-forecasts the same, which hides forecast bias. Report RMSE, which separates the two kinds of miss.
Products sell on very different scales, which MAPE cannot handle. Report RMSE pooled across all 5,000 products and days instead.
The slow sellers are just noise. Keep MAPE but drop products that sell under 3 units a day from the report.
questions.explanation:
MAPE averages |actual − forecast| / actual. When the actual is 1 unit, forecasting 3 is a 200% error, and a product that sells 1 unit one day and 3 the next swings between 200% and 0% with the same forecast. Slow sellers like this push the average to 340%. WAPE sums the absolute errors over all products and days and divides by total sales once, so a 2-unit miss counts as 2 units, not 200%.

The option about symmetry is wrong twice. MAPE is not symmetric: an under-forecast costs at most 100%, while an over-forecast has no cap, so MAPE quietly rewards forecasting low. RMSE squares away the sign, so it does not separate the two kinds of miss either. Pooled RMSE does not fix scale. It is in units, so high-volume products dominate it, and MAPE was scale-free to begin with. Dropping slow sellers hides products whose stock still has to be planned, rather than fixing the metric.
questions.deeper: Other common choices are MASE, which scales errors by the error of a naive forecast, and reporting error per product family. In an interview, add that you would track bias separately, as the sum of signed errors over total sales, because neither WAPE nor RMSE shows whether forecasts run high or low.

questions.prompt:
Two churn models are compared with 5-fold cross-validation, using the same five folds for both. ROC-AUC per fold:

- Model A: 0.81, 0.86, 0.79, 0.84, 0.80 (mean 0.82)
- Model B: 0.84, 0.82, 0.83, 0.82, 0.84 (mean 0.83)

Which readings are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A's fold scores span 7 points, so its mean alone hides how much its result depends on the split.
B's 0.01 lead in mean is small next to the swings between folds, so it is weak evidence that B is better.
Since both used the same folds, the fold-by-fold differences can be paired, and here they flip sign.
Rerunning with 20 folds instead of 5 would remove the variation between folds and settle the winner.
B's higher mean shows that B will score above A when both are run on the untouched test set.
The five fold scores are independent, so a standard t-test on them gives a trustworthy p-value.
questions.explanation:
A's scores run from 0.79 to 0.86, a 7-point spread, so its 0.82 mean comes with a lot of split-to-split variation that a single number hides. B's lead of 0.01 is far smaller than those swings. The paired view says the same thing: fold by fold, B minus A is +0.03, −0.04, +0.04, −0.02, +0.04. B wins three folds and loses two, so the data does not show a clear winner.

More folds do not remove variance. Each estimate still depends on which rows land where, and with more folds each validation fold gets smaller and noisier. A higher cross-validation mean does not guarantee a higher test score, especially with a gap this small. The t-test claim fails because fold scores are not independent. Any two training sets in 5-fold share three quarters of their rows, so the scores are correlated, and a naive t-test overstates confidence.
questions.deeper: Repeated cross-validation with several shuffles, plus a corrected resampled t-test or a paired bootstrap, gives a fairer comparison. In practice, a strong candidate also weighs B's steadier scores, from 0.82 to 0.84, as a mild reason to prefer it if the two cost the same to run.

questions.prompt: A company wants a model that ranks job applicants' CVs so recruiters only read the top 20%. It will be used for roles in the EU and trained on ten years of the company's past hiring decisions. Lay out the main risks and the controls you would put in place.
questions.answer: The biggest risk is learned bias. Past hiring decisions reflect past preferences, so the model can rank down groups that were hired less, often through proxies such as career gaps, names, school or postcode. It may also latch onto wording, not skill. Under the EU AI Act, systems used to filter or rank job applicants are high-risk, so the company faces duties such as risk management, data governance and bias checks, documentation, logging, human oversight and accuracy testing. Controls I would add: audit the training data and remove or test proxy features, measure selection rates and error rates by group before launch and on a schedule, have recruiters review a sample of rejected CVs, tell candidates an AI system is used and give them a way to ask for human review, keep logs and documentation, and limit personal data to what the task needs.
points: Historical hiring labels encode past bias, often via proxy features
Recruitment ranking is a high-risk use under the EU AI Act, with duties such as risk management, data governance, logging and human oversight
Fairness testing by group before launch and ongoing monitoring
Meaningful human review, including of rejected candidates
Transparency to candidates and a route to human review, since unread rejections may be solely automated decisions under GDPR
Data minimisation and privacy controls on CV data
questions.explanation:
The core problem is the label. A model trained on who was hired learns to copy past decisions, including their bias, and calling that ground truth hides it. Removing a protected attribute does not fix this, because other features often stand in for it. That is why fairness must be measured on outcomes by group, not assumed from the feature list.

The regulation point matters for an EU deployment. The EU AI Act lists AI used to filter, rank or evaluate job candidates as high-risk. The provider, here the company itself since it builds the tool, carries the main duties: risk management, data governance, documentation, logs, transparency, human oversight, accuracy and robustness. As the deployer it must also keep human oversight in place and tell people the system is used on them. Separately, under the GDPR, rejecting CVs that no person ever reads may count as a solely automated decision, which needs safeguards such as a right to human intervention.

The common mistake is to treat the human reviewer as the only safeguard. If recruiters only ever see the top 20%, nobody notices strong candidates the model buried. Reviewing a sample of rejections is what makes human oversight real. Another mistake is checking fairness once before launch and never again.
questions.deeper: Strong candidates also question the target. Predicting who was hired copies the past, while predicting performance a year in is closer to the real goal, though it is only seen for people who were hired. That selection bias is a good follow-up topic in interviews.

questions.prompt: You run k-means with features standardised, k set to the true number of groups, and 20 random restarts keeping the best result. Which dataset is k-means most likely to cluster wrongly?
options: Two concentric rings of points, a small ring sitting inside a larger ring
Three well-separated round blobs of similar size in a 20-dimensional space
Three well-separated round blobs, one holding twice as many points as each of the others
Three round blobs of equal spread whose outer edges touch each other slightly
questions.explanation:
k-means assigns each point to the nearest centroid, which carves space into straight-edged regions around each centre. That works when clusters are compact, roughly round and similar in spread. Two concentric rings share the same centre, so no pair of centroids can split them into inner and outer. k-means will cut both rings in half instead, and restarts cannot fix it because the problem is the shape, not the starting point.

Round, well-separated blobs in 20 dimensions are still easy, since distance to the centre separates them cleanly. A blob with twice as many points is fine when the groups are well separated. Very unequal sizes or spreads mostly cause trouble when clusters are close together. Touching edges cause a few border points to land in the wrong cluster, but the three groups are still found. Only the rings make k-means fail as a whole.
questions.deeper: Good follow-ups are what to use instead and how to choose k. DBSCAN or spectral clustering handle rings and other odd shapes, and Gaussian mixtures handle stretched clusters of different spreads. For k, teams look at the elbow plot or silhouette score, but in practice the business use of the segments often decides it.

questions.prompt: A job site uses a two-tower model to pull candidate jobs for each visitor from 8 million open postings. The user tower and the job tower each output a 128-number vector, and the score is their dot product. Which property of this design lets retrieval finish in a few milliseconds?
options: The two towers share all their weights, so a single forward pass scores the user against every posting at once.
The job tower is small enough that running it on all 8 million postings during each request is still cheap.
Job vectors do not depend on the user, so they are computed ahead of time and searched with a nearest-neighbour index.
User and job features are crossed inside the network, so the most relevant postings come out directly without any index.
questions.explanation:
The two towers only meet at the final dot product. Nothing about a job vector depends on who is searching, so the system can run the job tower over all 8 million postings offline and load the vectors into an approximate nearest-neighbour index. At request time it runs the user tower once and asks the index for the closest job vectors, which takes milliseconds.

Shared weights would not change the cost, since every posting would still need scoring. Running the job tower on 8 million postings per request, however small the tower, means millions of forward passes per visitor, which is far too slow. The option about crossed features describes the opposite of a two-tower model. Crossing user and job features inside the network is exactly what this design gives up. That loss of early interaction is the price of speed, and it is why a heavier ranker with cross features usually scores the few hundred retrieved jobs afterwards.
questions.deeper: Expect follow-ups on freshness and training. New postings need their vectors computed and added to the index quickly, or they are invisible. Training usually uses in-batch negatives, where other jobs in the batch act as negatives, and a strong candidate mentions correcting for popular items showing up as negatives too often.

questions.prompt: A single neuron computes f(w) = σ(w × x), where σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ) is the sigmoid. Take x = 2 and w = 0.5, and use σ(1) ≈ 0.7311. What is the derivative df/dw at this point? Give it as a decimal to 3 places.
questions.explanation:
The chain rule splits the derivative into an outer and an inner part. The outer function is σ(z) with z = w × x, and the sigmoid's derivative is σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)). The inner part is dz/dw = x. So df/dw = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)) × x.

With the numbers: z = 0.5 × 2 = 1, so σ(z) ≈ 0.7311 and 1 − σ(z) ≈ 0.2689. Their product is about 0.1966. Multiplying by x = 2 gives 0.3932, which rounds to 0.393.

The most common mistake is to stop at σ′(z) ≈ 0.197 and forget the inner derivative x. That is the derivative with respect to z, not w. Another slip is to evaluate the sigmoid at w = 0.5 instead of at z = 1.

Notice that σ(z)(1 − σ(z)) is at most 0.25, reached at z = 0. That cap is one reason deep stacks of sigmoid layers suffer from vanishing gradients.
questions.deeper: Backpropagation is this same chain rule applied layer by layer. A common follow-up is the gradient of the logistic loss with respect to z, which simplifies to σ(z) − y. That clean form is why sigmoid outputs are paired with cross-entropy rather than squared error, which keeps the small σ′ factor and slows learning.

questions.prompt: A team is choosing workflow patterns for several LLM features. Which pairings of pattern and task are a good fit? Select all that apply.
options: Prompt chaining for a product listing: write a draft, check length and banned words in code, then translate it.
Routing for document translation, where every request takes the same three steps in the same order.
Parallelization for contract review: separate calls check payment, liability and termination terms at the same time.
Orchestrator-workers for a code change where the files to edit are only known after reading the request.
Parallelization for a data migration, where each step needs the output of the step before it to begin.
Evaluator-optimizer for looking up the shipping status of an order, which is a single exact database read.
questions.explanation:
Prompt chaining fits tasks that split cleanly into fixed steps, and you can add a check in code between steps, as in the listing. Parallelization fits when parts of the work are independent. The three contract checks do not depend on each other, so running them at once cuts latency and lets each prompt focus on one risk. Orchestrator-workers fits when the subtasks cannot be known in advance. A central model reads the request, decides which files need changes, and hands them out to workers.

Routing only helps when inputs differ and need different handling. If every translation takes the same three steps, there is nothing to route, and the right pattern is plain prompt chaining. Parallelization fails for the migration because each step waits on the one before, so the steps cannot run at the same time. Evaluator-optimizer pays off when a grader can give useful feedback and a revision improves the result, as in polishing a translation. A single exact database read has nothing to refine, so a loop only adds cost and delay.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like candidates who start with the simplest pattern that works and add complexity only when it earns its place. A good follow-up answer: a fixed chain is cheaper and easier to test than a free-running agent, so move to orchestrator-workers or a full agent only when the steps truly cannot be planned ahead.

questions.prompt: An online store's search first uses a bi-encoder to fetch the top 100 products out of 5 million. Queries and products are embedded separately, and the nearest product vectors are returned. A cross-encoder then rescores those 100, and the top 10 are shown. Why is search built in two stages instead of using one model for everything?
options: The cross-encoder reads the query and product together, so it judges relevance better, but it is far too slow to run on all 5 million.
The cross-encoder's product vectors can be computed ahead of time, so it is the faster stage and it narrows the work for the bi-encoder.
The bi-encoder search is approximate, so the cross-encoder's job is to find relevant products that the first stage left out of its 100.
The cross-encoder can read whole product pages, so the reranking stage removes the need to chunk or truncate product descriptions.
questions.explanation:
A bi-encoder embeds each product once, offline. At query time it embeds only the query and runs a nearest-neighbour search, which takes milliseconds even over millions of items. The cost is accuracy: the query and the product never see each other, and each is squeezed into a single vector, so details such as "for kids", "without a cable" or an exact model number can get lost.

A cross-encoder takes the query and one product as a single input, so attention links every query word to every product word. That gives much better relevance scores, but it needs one full model pass per pair. Five million passes per search is impossible, while 100 passes is affordable.

The option about precomputed vectors describes the bi-encoder, not the cross-encoder, which has nothing to precompute because its score depends on the query. A reranker can only reorder what the first stage returned. It cannot bring back a product that was never fetched, so first-stage recall sets a ceiling on the whole system. Cross-encoders are transformers with input limits of their own, and their cost grows with input length, so they do not remove the need to chunk or truncate.
questions.deeper: Measure the two stages separately: recall@100 for the retriever and NDCG@10 after reranking. If recall@100 is low, a better reranker cannot help. Raising the shortlist size lifts the recall ceiling but adds reranker latency roughly in proportion, so teams tune it against a latency budget.

questions.prompt: A music recommendation model applies inverted dropout to a hidden layer, where each unit is zeroed with probability 0.4 during training. One unit's activation is 1.8 before dropout, and on this step it survives. What value does the unit pass to the next layer? Give the answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation:
Inverted dropout divides every surviving unit by the keep probability during training, so nothing needs to change at inference. The keep probability is 1 − 0.4 = 0.6, so the surviving value is 1.8 / 0.6 = 3.0.

Check the expected value. With probability 0.6 the unit outputs 3.0, and with probability 0.4 it outputs 0. The average is 0.6 × 3.0 + 0.4 × 0 = 1.8, exactly the original activation. That is the point of the scaling. The next layer sees inputs of the same average size in training and at inference, when dropout is off and the unit simply passes 1.8.

The most common mistake is dividing by the drop probability: 1.8 / 0.4 = 4.5, which makes the expected value 0.6 × 4.5 = 2.7, too large. Another is multiplying by the keep probability, 1.8 × 0.6 = 1.08. That is the scaling the original, non-inverted dropout applied at inference time, not something done to a surviving unit in training.
questions.deeper: Frameworks use the inverted form because it leaves the inference path free of dropout entirely. Interviewers sometimes push further: the expected value is preserved, but the variance is not. That shift in variance is one reason dropout placed just before a batch norm layer can hurt, since batch norm's running statistics are gathered with dropout on.

questions.prompt: A PyTorch weight `w` has `requires_grad=True`. A debugging loop runs three steps. Each step does a fresh forward pass and then calls `loss.backward()`, and each backward pass on its own gives `w` a gradient of 0.5. The loop never calls `optimizer.zero_grad()` or `optimizer.step()`, so `w` itself never changes. What is `w.grad` after the third step?
options: 1.5, because each `backward()` call adds its gradient into `w.grad`
0.5, because each `backward()` call replaces the value held in `w.grad`
None, because `w.grad` is only filled in once `optimizer.step()` runs
An error, because the graph is freed after the first `backward()` call
questions.explanation:
PyTorch records a graph of operations during the forward pass. `backward()` walks that graph and adds each leaf tensor's gradient into its `.grad` field. It never overwrites. Three backward passes of 0.5 each leave 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.5. That accumulation is deliberate, because it lets you sum gradients over several small batches, but it is why training loops call `optimizer.zero_grad()` every step.

The option claiming replacement describes what many people assume, and it is the reason forgetting `zero_grad()` is such a common bug. The option about `optimizer.step()` reverses the order. `backward()` fills `.grad` and `step()` only reads it to update the weight. The graph-freed option is half true. The graph is freed after `backward()`, but each step here builds a new graph with its own forward pass, so there is no error. Calling `backward()` a second time on the same graph is what usually fails, unless the first call passed `retain_graph=True`.

So after N debug passes without a reset, `w.grad` holds the sum of N gradients, not the latest one. That is why a gradient that looks several times too large is often a missing `zero_grad()`.
questions.deeper: Interviewers may ask when accumulation is useful. Gradient accumulation splits a large batch into micro-batches, calls `backward()` on each with the loss divided by the number of micro-batches, and only then steps and zeroes. A strong answer also mentions `detach()` for fixed targets, such as the target network in a DQN.

questions.prompt: Estimate how long a pretraining run takes. The model has 8 × 10⁹ parameters and trains on 2 × 10¹² tokens. Use training compute ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens FLOPs. Each GPU sustains 4 × 10¹⁴ FLOP/s of useful throughput, the run uses 512 GPUs in parallel with no downtime, and a day is 86,400 seconds. How many days does training take? Give the answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation:
Step 1, total compute: 6 × 8 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10¹² = 9.6 × 10²² FLOPs. Step 2, single-GPU time: 9.6 × 10²² ÷ (4 × 10¹⁴) = 2.4 × 10⁸ GPU-seconds. Step 3, GPU-days: 2.4 × 10⁸ ÷ 86,400 ≈ 2,778 GPU-days. Step 4, wall-clock time: 2,778 ÷ 512 ≈ 5.43, which rounds to 5.4 days.

The factor 6 comes from about 2 FLOPs per parameter per token for the forward pass and about 4 for the backward pass. The most common mistake is to use 2 × parameters × tokens, the forward-only cost used for inference, which gives about 1.8 days and badly underestimates the run. Another slip is to plug in the GPU's peak FLOP/s from a spec sheet. Real runs sustain only a fraction of peak because of communication, memory traffic and idle time between pipeline stages, so the sustained figure is the one to use.
questions.deeper: In a planning interview, add buffers. Restarts after hardware failures, evaluation runs and checkpointing all take time, so real schedules pad the estimate. A strong candidate also mentions model FLOPs utilization, the share of peak throughput actually achieved, and that recomputing activations to save memory adds FLOPs the 6ND rule does not count.

questions.prompt: A fraud-scoring model runs in int8. One activation tensor uses an affine scheme: a value x is stored as q = round(x / s) + z, clipped to the range −128 to 127, and read back as x̂ = s × (q − z). For this tensor the scale is s = 0.04 and the zero point is z = −20. An incoming value is x = 1.13. What is the absolute rounding error |x − x̂| after quantizing and reading the value back? Give it as a decimal to 3 places.
questions.explanation:
Work through the scheme one step at a time.

- Divide by the scale: 1.13 / 0.04 = 28.25
- Round to the nearest integer: 28
- Add the zero point: q = 28 + (−20) = 8, which is inside −128 to 127, so no clipping
- Read it back: x̂ = 0.04 × (8 − (−20)) = 0.04 × 28 = 1.12
- Error: |1.13 − 1.12| = 0.010

The most common mistake is to forget the zero point when reading the value back and compute 0.04 × 8 = 0.32, which gives an error of 0.81. The zero point must be removed on the way out exactly as it was added on the way in. Another slip is to add z again instead of subtracting it, which gives 0.04 × (8 + (−20)) = −0.48.

For any value inside the representable range, the rounding error is at most half a step, s / 2 = 0.02 here. Values outside the range get clipped, and their error can be far larger. The zero point lets the real value 0 map exactly to an integer, so zeros from padding or ReLU come back with no error at all.
questions.deeper: Choosing the scale is a tradeoff. A wide range avoids clipping rare large values but makes every step coarser, and a narrow range does the reverse. Calibration on sample data picks the range. A strong candidate also mentions per-channel scales for weights, which give each output channel its own step size.

questions.prompt: A hospital builds a model that predicts, at the moment a patient is discharged, whether they will be readmitted within 30 days. The training table was pulled from records six months later. Which feature should be removed because it would not be available when the model makes its prediction?
options: Home-care program enrolment, which nurses decide during the week after discharge
Emergency room visits the patient made in the 12 months before this admission
Length of the current stay in days, from admission up to the discharge decision
Kidney function results from blood tests reported on the last morning of the stay
questions.explanation:
The test for leakage is simple: at the exact moment of prediction, does this value exist yet? Home-care enrolment is decided in the week after discharge, so at discharge time it is unknown. Because the training table was built months later, the column is filled in for every row, and the model can learn from it. It is also likely to be tied to the outcome, since nurses may enrol patients who look unwell at the first follow-up. The model would score well offline and then fail in use, where the field is always blank.

The other three are safe. Past emergency visits happened before this admission. The length of stay is known once the discharge decision is made. Blood results reported on the last morning of the stay are on record before the patient leaves. Each can look suspicious because it is close to the outcome in time, but closeness is not the test. Availability at prediction time is.
questions.deeper: A good habit is to store a timestamp for when each feature value became known, then build training rows with a point-in-time join. In interviews, say you would also be suspicious of any single feature with very high importance, since leaked features often stand out that way.

questions.prompt: A decision tree node holds 16 users of a free app: 8 upgraded to the paid plan and 8 did not. A split on "used the export feature" sends 6 users left (all 6 upgraded) and 10 users right (2 upgraded, 8 did not). What is the information gain of this split, using entropy in bits (log base 2)? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Information gain is the parent's entropy minus the weighted average entropy of the children. Entropy is −Σ p log₂ p over the classes in a node.

Parent: 8 of 16 upgraded, so p = 0.5 and 0.5. Entropy is 1 bit, the maximum for two classes.

Left child: all 6 upgraded, so it is pure and its entropy is 0.

Right child: p = 0.2 and 0.8. Entropy = −0.2 × log₂ 0.2 − 0.8 × log₂ 0.8 = 0.464 + 0.258 = 0.722 bits.

Weighted child entropy: 6/16 × 0 + 10/16 × 0.722 = 0.451.

Gain: 1 − 0.451 = 0.549, which rounds to 0.55.

The common mistake is a plain average of the children, (0 + 0.722) / 2 = 0.361, which gives a gain of 0.64. That treats the 6-user child as if it mattered as much as the 10-user child. Using the natural log instead of log₂ gives the gain in nats, about 0.38, so the units must match the question.
questions.deeper: A good follow-up is the bias of information gain toward features with many values. A user ID splits every row into its own pure leaf, earns the maximum gain and is useless on new users. The gain ratio used in C4.5 corrects for this. In practice entropy and Gini pick nearly the same splits.

questions.prompt: An image-moderation model runs on 2 GPU instances that stay on all month (30 days, 24 hours a day). Suppose each instance costs $3.60 per hour. One instance can handle 20 predictions per second at full load, but average utilization over the month is 25%. What is the serving cost per 1,000 predictions? Give it in dollars to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation:
You pay for instance hours whether or not they are busy, but you only get the predictions that actually arrive.

- Hours in the month: 30 × 24 = 720
- Monthly cost: 2 × $3.60 × 720 = $5,184
- Predictions per second across both instances at 25% utilization: 2 × 20 × 0.25 = 10
- Predictions per month: 10 × 3,600 × 720 = 25,920,000
- Cost per 1,000: $5,184 / 25,920 = $0.20

The common mistake is to use full capacity, 40 predictions per second. That gives 103,680,000 predictions and $0.05 per 1,000, four times too cheap. Utilization divides straight into the unit cost, so a service that idles three quarters of the time costs four times as much per prediction as one that runs flat out.
questions.deeper: This calculation drives real setup choices. Strong answers name the levers: scaling down at night, batching requests on the GPU to raise throughput, a smaller or quantized model, or moving work that is not urgent to a batch job that runs near full utilization. They also note an online service cannot target 100%, since it needs headroom for spikes and latency targets.

questions.prompt: An internal company directory lets staff type a colleague's name and see a ranked list of profiles. Each query has exactly one correct profile, and people read from the top and stop at the first match. Which offline metric fits this search best?
options: MRR, since it scores each query by how high its one correct profile sits in the list.
Precision@10, since it counts how many of the top 10 results are the right person for each query.
NDCG@10, since it rewards graded relevance across the whole first page of results.
Recall@10, since what matters most is that the right profile appears somewhere on the first page.
questions.explanation:
With one correct answer per query and users who stop at the first match, what matters is the rank of that one profile. Reciprocal rank scores rank 1 as 1, rank 2 as 0.5 and rank 3 as about 0.33, and MRR averages this over queries. It tracks how far down people must read.

Precision@10 fits a different job. With one correct profile, its best possible score is 1 / 10 = 0.1, and it gives the same score whether the profile is at rank 1 or rank 10. Recall@10 has the same blind spot, since it only asks whether the profile made the first page. NDCG@10 is built for graded relevance spread across many results, and this directory has neither: one profile is right and the rest are simply wrong. With a single relevant item NDCG still rewards higher placement, but its gentle log discount scores rank 3 at 0.5, which suits a user who keeps scanning, not one who stops at the first match.
questions.deeper: If the team also cares how often the right person is the very first result, it can report success@1 next to MRR. For a product search where raters grade results as perfect, good or fair, NDCG becomes the better choice, and precision@k fits a feed with a fixed number of slots.

questions.prompt: An insurer fully fine-tuned a general assistant for 5 epochs at a high learning rate on 8,000 claim summaries and nothing else. Claim summaries improved a lot, but the model now writes poor emails and fumbles simple general questions it used to handle well. What is the most likely cause and a sensible fix?
options: Fine-tuning changed the tokenizer, so everyday words now split badly. Retrain the tokenizer on mixed text and keep the current fine-tuned weights.
Narrow updates overwrote general skills, which is catastrophic forgetting. Mix general data back in, cut the learning rate or epochs, or train LoRA adapters.
The model underfits general tasks because 8,000 examples is too few. Train for more epochs on the claim data until its general skills come back.
Weight decay during fine-tuning zeroed out general-purpose neurons. Turn weight decay off and rerun the same 5 epochs at the same learning rate.
questions.explanation:
Full fine-tuning updates every weight. Five epochs at a high learning rate on one narrow task push the weights far toward that task, and nothing in the data asks the model to keep its other skills. This is catastrophic forgetting. Mixing a share of general instruction data into training reminds the model of other tasks. A lower learning rate or fewer epochs limits how far the weights move. LoRA freezes the base weights and learns a small update, so the original model is kept and tends to forget less.

The tokenizer option is wrong because fine-tuning does not change the tokenizer, which is a fixed lookup built before training. The underfitting option gets the direction backwards: the model has fit the claim data too hard, and more epochs on that same data would make forgetting worse. The weight-decay option names a minor effect. Weight decay shrinks weights slightly, but it does not zero out skills, and rerunning with the same epochs and learning rate keeps the real cause.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate sets up a general regression suite before fine-tuning, such as a few hundred varied prompts scored before and after, so forgetting is caught early. Interviewers may ask how much general data to mix in. A small share is a common start, tuned against both the domain and the general evals.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain forecasts daily sales per store from three years of history. Features include sales lags and 7-day rolling averages. Shuffled 5-fold cross-validation gave an error of 6%, but the first month in production showed 14%. Which change to the validation setup best fixes the misleading estimate?
options: Use forward-chaining splits that train on earlier dates and validate on the dates right after.
Use stratified 5-fold so that each fold holds the same mix of high-sales and low-sales days.
Move to 10 folds so each validation fold is smaller and the error estimate becomes less noisy.
Keep the shuffled folds but fit feature scaling on each training fold only, never on validation rows.
questions.explanation:
Shuffling puts days from after a validation day into the training set. With lag and rolling features, neighbouring days share almost the same information, so the model is really filling in gaps between days it has already seen. That is much easier than forecasting the future, which is what production asks for. Forward-chaining splits (sometimes called rolling-origin or time series split) train only on the past and test on the period right after, so the validation task matches the real one.

Stratifying by sales level still shuffles across time, so the leak stays. More folds changes how noisy the estimate is, not the fact that each fold peeks at the future. Fitting the scaler on the training fold only fixes a real but much smaller leak. It does nothing about the model training on days that come after the days it is tested on.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds a gap between train and validation windows when features look back several days, so rolling averages near the boundary cannot see validation rows. They also make the validation horizon match production, for example a 14-day forecast window if the business plans two weeks ahead.

questions.prompt: A batch job calls an external geocoding API 15 times. Each call times out with probability 0.1, independently of the other calls. What is the probability that exactly 2 of the 15 calls time out? Give it as a decimal to 3 places.
questions.explanation:
The number of timeouts is binomial with n = 15 and p = 0.1. The probability of exactly k timeouts is C(n, k) × pᵏ × (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ.

Step by step: C(15, 2) = 15 × 14 / 2 = 105 ways to choose which two calls fail. Each such pattern has probability 0.1² × 0.9¹³. Here 0.1² = 0.01 and 0.9¹³ ≈ 0.2542. Multiplying gives 105 × 0.01 × 0.2542 ≈ 0.2669, which rounds to 0.267.

The most common mistake is dropping the C(15, 2) factor and answering 0.01 × 0.2542 ≈ 0.0025. That is the chance of one specific pattern, such as the first two calls failing and the rest succeeding. Another slip is to leave out the 0.9¹³ term, which says the other 13 calls must succeed. Without it you get 105 × 0.01 = 1.05, which is not even a valid probability.

As a sanity check, the expected number of timeouts is n × p = 1.5, so a result of 1 or 2 timeouts should be common, and it is.
questions.deeper: In practice you care more about "at least one" timeout, 1 − 0.9¹⁵ ≈ 0.79, which shows why a job with many calls needs retries even when each call is fairly reliable. The binomial also assumes independence. Real timeouts cluster during an outage, which makes jobs with several failures more common than this model predicts.

questions.prompt: A utility company's billing agent handles meter-reading disputes. On a test set, each attempt at a task succeeds with probability 0.85, independently of other attempts. The team's report shows pass@4, the chance that at least one of 4 attempts succeeds, which is above 99.9%. But a customer who raises the same kind of dispute 4 times expects it to be handled correctly every time. What is pass^4, the chance that all 4 of 4 attempts succeed? Give the answer as a percentage to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation:
The chance that all k attempts succeed is p to the power k, often written pass^k. With p = 0.85 and k = 4: 0.85 × 0.85 = 0.7225, then × 0.85 = 0.614125, then × 0.85 = 0.52200625, which is 52.2%.

pass@4 works the other way. The chance all 4 attempts fail is 0.15⁴ = 0.00050625, so the chance at least one succeeds is 1 - 0.00050625 = 99.95%. The same agent looks nearly perfect on one metric and close to a coin flip on the other.

The common mistake is to report pass@k for an agent that talks to customers. pass@k fits when you can try several times and keep the best, such as a coding agent whose patches are checked by tests before anyone sees them. A customer gets one attempt each time, so consistency is what matters, and pass^k measures it. As k grows, pass@k climbs toward 100% while pass^k falls toward 0.
questions.deeper: Strong candidates report both numbers and say which one matches how the product is used. Real attempts are not fully independent, since some tasks are hard every time, so measure pass^k directly by rerunning each task k times rather than trusting 0.85⁴. An interviewer may ask how to raise it: clearer tools and prompts, lower sampling temperature, and fixing the tasks that fail only some of the time.

questions.prompt: A city's model picks housing-benefit claims for fraud checks. Claims from applicants born abroad are selected at three times the rate of other claims, yet past audits found fraud no more common among them. Two fixes are proposed: a separate score threshold for each group at decision time, or retraining the model with a fairness constraint. Compare them and say what you would recommend.
questions.answer: Per-group thresholds are fast, exact and need no retraining. Raising the cut-off for one group closes the selection gap directly, and the cost is easy to measure: some fraud in that group goes unchecked and the overall hit rate may change. But they apply the protected attribute at decision time, which in many places counts as direct unequal treatment, and they hide the cause instead of fixing it. Constrained retraining builds the goal into the model and pushes it away from proxies, usually without needing the attribute when scoring. It takes more work, the trade-off is harder to tune, and error rates can still shift. I would first find why the model over-selects, likely proxies or labels from past audits that targeted the same group. Then I would fix the data and retrain with a constraint, cleared with legal, and monitor selection, hit and false positive rates by group every month.
points: Per-group thresholds are quick and exact but use the protected attribute at decision time
That may be unlawful direct unequal treatment, so legal review is needed
Constrained retraining tackles proxies in the model but costs more effort and tuning
Measure the accuracy cost: fraud missed and hit rate, by group
Find the root cause first, such as proxies or biased labels from past audits
Monitor selection, hit and false positive rates by group after the change
questions.explanation:
The fact that fraud is no more common among applicants born abroad matters. It means the extra checks mostly land on honest claimants, so this group faces a far higher false positive rate. Closing the selection gap here is not only about equal rates. It also reduces wrongful investigations.

A common mistake is to treat per-group thresholds as the obvious fix because they are simple. They work on the symptom, need the protected attribute for every decision, and can be challenged as treating people differently because of their origin. Another mistake is ignoring the labels. If past audits already targeted this group, the training data records more fraud found there simply because more people there were checked. A model trained on that copies the bias, and a fairness constraint on top only partly offsets it. Systems that public authorities use to assess eligibility for benefits are on the EU AI Act's high-risk list, and a fraud model that can lead to benefits being cut likely falls there too, so this analysis belongs in its documentation.
questions.deeper: Strong candidates suggest a randomized audit sample, checking a small random share of all claims. It gives unbiased fraud rates by group, which fixes the label problem and shows whether any remaining gap is justified. Interviewers value this because it turns a fairness argument into measurement.

questions.prompt: A support team classifies long chat transcripts with a vanilla RNN. It misses cues from the start of chats that run to 300 tokens, and training is slow on GPUs even with large batches. Which statement explains both problems correctly?
options: Gradients to early tokens pass through hundreds of multiplications by the recurrent weights and fade, and each state needs the previous one, so steps run in order.
An LSTM would fix both problems, because its gated cell state carries gradients across long gaps and its gates let all the time steps of one sequence run in parallel.
The RNN keeps a separate weight matrix for every time step, so long chats need far too many parameters to train well and far too much memory to batch on a GPU.
The RNN's cost grows with the square of the sequence length while self-attention grows only linearly, so long chats are slow and the early cues get diluted.
questions.explanation:
In a vanilla RNN, the hidden state at step t is computed from the state at step t − 1. Backpropagating from the last token to the first multiplies the gradient by the recurrent weight matrix and an activation derivative once per step. Over 300 steps that product usually shrinks toward zero, or sometimes explodes, so early cues barely affect learning. The same chain of dependencies blocks parallelism. Step 200 cannot be computed until step 199 is done, so a GPU cannot spread the work across time steps.

LSTMs and GRUs fix much of the first problem. Their cell state is updated mostly by addition, with a forget gate that can stay near 1, so gradients survive longer gaps. But they are still sequential, so the option claiming they run in parallel is wrong. RNNs share one set of weights across all time steps, so the parameter count does not grow with length. The complexity option is backwards. An RNN does work linear in sequence length, while self-attention compares every pair of tokens, which is quadratic. Transformers solve both problems because any token can attend to any other in one step, and all positions are computed at once in training.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds the trade-off in the other direction. An RNN generates each new token with fixed memory and cost, while a transformer's attention cost and cache grow with context length. That is why recurrent and state-space designs keep returning for very long sequences and on-device use.

questions.prompt: Design the click prediction model for an ad platform. Each auction ranks ads by bid times predicted click probability, and advertisers can also bid on conversions such as purchases. Cover the model and features, how labels arrive, how often you update the model, and what you monitor.
questions.answer: The auction multiplies bids by predicted probabilities, so the model must be calibrated, not just good at ranking. If it says 2% where the truth is 1%, ads are misordered and advertisers are mispriced. Use logistic regression or a deep model over very sparse features: user, ad, advertiser, placement, query and their crosses. Hash these into a fixed number of buckets to cap memory and handle unseen IDs, accepting some collisions. Clicks arrive within minutes, but conversions can take days, so either wait a set window before calling an example negative, or model the delay and correct labels when late conversions arrive. Ads and campaigns change daily, so update the model often, for example hourly and incrementally from streaming logs. If you downsample non-clicks for training, correct the predicted probabilities afterwards. Monitor log loss and the ratio of predicted to actual clicks by segment, and recalibrate when it drifts.
points: Calibration matters because bids are multiplied by the prediction
Very sparse ID and cross features, hashed into fixed buckets
Delayed conversions: a label window or a delay model
Frequent incremental updates as ads and campaigns change
Correct probabilities after negative downsampling
Monitor log loss and predicted-to-actual ratio by segment
questions.explanation:
Most ranking problems only need the right order. Ads are different because the predicted probability is a price input. An ad with a $2 bid and a 3% predicted click rate beats one with a $5 bid and 1%, so a systematic overestimate for one advertiser shifts real money. That is why log loss and calibration, not AUC alone, are the main offline checks.

The common mistake is to treat a conversion that has not happened yet as a negative. If you train on yesterday's clicks, many purchases are still to come, so the model learns that conversions are rarer than they are and ranks ads bid on conversions too low. A fixed attribution window or a delay model fixes this.

Feature hashing keeps the model a fixed size when there are billions of user and ad IDs, and lets brand-new IDs map somewhere instead of failing. Frequent updates matter because new campaigns launch every day and an ad's appeal fades quickly. Downsampling non-clicks speeds training, but it inflates predicted rates, so the scores must be scaled back down before the auction uses them.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask how to handle a brand-new ad with no history. Good answers use advertiser and creative features, a prior from similar ads, and some exploration. Strong candidates also mention checking calibration per advertiser, since an overall ratio of 1.0 can hide one advertiser at 1.5 and another at 0.6.

questions.prompt: A legal research assistant builds every request the same way. First comes a line with the current date and time to the second. Then comes a 5,000-token block of fixed instructions and worked examples. The user's question goes last. Prompt caching is turned on, yet the logs show almost no cache hits. What is the most likely cause?
options: The timestamp at the very start changes on every request, so no two prompts share a leading run of tokens to reuse.
The question at the end differs on every request, and a prompt cache only hits when the whole prompt is identical.
The fixed block is too long to cache, because a prompt cache can only hold short prefixes of a few hundred tokens at most.
Prompt caching only stores the generated output tokens, so the 5,000 input tokens are processed fresh every time.
questions.explanation:
A prompt cache stores the model's internal state for a leading run of tokens, so a later request that starts with exactly the same tokens can skip recomputing them. The match has to start at the first token, because the state for each token depends on every token before it. Here the very first line is a timestamp that changes every second. After that one difference, nothing that follows can be reused, even though the 5,000-token block is identical. Moving the timestamp below the fixed block, or rounding it to the day, would let almost every request hit the cache.

The option about the question at the end describes exact-match response caching, a different tool. A prefix cache is built for prompts that share a start and differ at the end, which is the normal case. Caches do not reject long prefixes. Many setups have a minimum length below which caching does not apply, and longer shared prefixes give larger savings. Prompt caching works on the input side. It saves the work of reading the prompt, not the work of generating output, which always depends on the new question.
questions.deeper: The general rule is to order a prompt from most stable to least stable: system instructions, tool definitions and examples first, then per-user context, then the current question. Watch for hidden changes in the prefix too, such as a request ID, a tool list in random order or reshuffled examples, which silently break caching.

questions.prompt:
Using scikit-learn 1.x, a churn model is trained on string labels. A teammate then treats `p[:, 1]` as each customer's churn probability. What does `p[:, 1]` actually hold?

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
X = [[1.0], [7.0], [2.0], [8.0], [1.5], [9.0]]
y = ["stay", "churn", "stay", "churn", "stay", "churn"]
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)
p = clf.predict_proba([[8.5], [1.2]])
```
options: The probability of "stay", since columns follow the sorted `clf.classes_`
The probability of "churn", since column 1 always holds the positive class
The probability of "churn", since it is the second label that appears in `y`
Nothing usable, since `fit` returns None and so `clf` is None at this point
questions.explanation:
A fitted classifier stores its labels in `classes_`, sorted the same way `np.unique` sorts them. Here that is `["churn", "stay"]`, because "churn" comes first alphabetically. Column j of `predict_proba` is the probability of `classes_[j]`, so column 1 is "stay". The teammate's feature is the chance a customer stays, the exact opposite of what they wanted.

The idea that column 1 is always the positive class comes from 0 and 1 labels, where 1 happens to sort last. scikit-learn has no notion of a positive class in `predict_proba`. The order in which labels first appear in `y` does not matter either, since the sort decides. The option about `fit` returning None is wrong because `fit` returns the estimator itself. That is why `LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)` can be chained and `clf` is a working model.

The safe pattern is `p[:, list(clf.classes_).index("churn")]`, or encoding the target as 0 and 1 before training.
questions.deeper: This bug slips through because metrics may still look plausible. ROC-AUC computed on the wrong column comes out as 1 minus the true AUC, so a strong model suddenly looks worse than random. Interviewers like candidates who print `classes_` before using probabilities.

questions.prompt: In plain data parallelism, each of 8 GPUs keeps a full copy of the weights, the gradients and the Adam state. A variant splits all three across the GPUs, so each GPU stores only one eighth of them and gathers the full weights for a layer just before it needs them. Give the common name or acronym for this approach: ______.
questions.explanation:
The approach is known as ZeRO, short for zero redundancy optimizer, or as fully sharded data parallel (FSDP). Both names describe the same idea. Plain data parallelism stores the same weights, gradients and optimizer state on every GPU, which wastes memory. Sharding gives each GPU one slice of each. Before a layer runs, the GPUs gather its full weights, use them and free them again. After the backward pass, each GPU keeps only the gradients for its own slice and updates only its share of the optimizer state.

A common mistake is to answer model parallelism or tensor parallelism. Those split the computation of the model, so each GPU does a different part of the work. Sharded data parallelism still has each GPU process its own slice of the batch through the whole model. It only splits where the state is stored. The price is more communication, since weights must be gathered for every layer in both passes.
questions.deeper: The stages are worth knowing. Sharding only the optimizer state already saves most of the memory, because Adam state is the largest part. Sharding gradients and then weights saves more but adds traffic. Strong candidates note that per-GPU memory falls roughly in proportion to the number of GPUs.

questions.prompt: Two versions of a news summarizer are being compared. Version A runs on a model from the same family as the LLM judge, and version B runs on a model from a different family. For each article, the judge sees both summaries and picks the better one. Which statements about the judge's biases and their fixes are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Judges often favour one position, frequently the first answer shown, so each pair should be judged in both orders.
Judges tend to prefer longer summaries, even when the extra length adds nothing the reader needs to know.
A judge may favour text from its own model family, so A's wins should be checked with another judge or with people.
Setting the judge's temperature to 0 removes position bias, because the judge then gives the same verdict every time.
Asking for a score from 1 to 100 instead of a pick removes the length preference, since finer scales are more precise.
Hiding which version wrote each summary fully removes self-preference, since the judge then cannot tell them apart.
questions.explanation:
Position bias is well documented. Shown the same pair in two orders, a judge often changes its verdict. Judging both orders and counting a win only when the verdicts agree, or averaging the two, cancels most of it. Verbosity bias means longer answers score higher even when the extra text is padding, which matters for summaries, where shorter is often better. Telling the judge to penalize padding and checking whether wins track length both help. Self-preference means a judge tends to rate text in its own family's style higher. Here that tilts the contest toward version A, so a second judge from another family, or a human sample, is needed before trusting the result.

Temperature 0 makes the judge consistent, not fair. It repeats the same position-biased verdict every time. A finer score scale does nothing about the cause of verbosity bias, and judges often use wide scales unevenly. Hiding the labels helps little, because the judge can still recognize its own family's phrasing and word choices, so self-preference survives blind labels.
questions.deeper: Before trusting any judge, measure its agreement with human labels on a sample of a few hundred items, and recheck it whenever the judge model or prompt changes. Interviewers like candidates who report the judge's agreement rate next to the win rate, because a win rate from an unchecked judge carries little weight.

questions.prompt: You are comparing two training recipes. A single run's validation accuracy varies from seed to seed with a standard deviation of 0.8 points. You want to average several runs so that the standard error of the averaged accuracy is 0.2 points. Assuming the runs are independent, how many seeds do you need?
questions.explanation:
The standard error of a mean of n independent values is σ / √n. Here σ = 0.8 and the target is 0.2, so √n = 0.8 / 0.2 = 4 and n = 16. Put another way, halving the error takes four times the runs, and quartering it takes sixteen times.

The option with 4 seeds treats the error as falling like 1/n. That is true of the variance, σ² / n, not of the standard deviation. Four seeds give 0.8 / √4 = 0.4, twice the target. The 256-seed option swaps the two quantities. It is the variance that falls like 1/n and the error, its square root, that falls like 1/√n. Using its rule, the variance must drop from 0.64 to 0.04, a factor of 16, so √n = 16 and n = 256, which wastes 240 runs. The option saying averaging cannot help confuses the noise of one run, which stays at 0.8, with the noise of the average, which shrinks as runs are added.

The independence assumption matters. If runs share hidden choices, such as the same data split, they are correlated and the error shrinks more slowly than 1/√n.
questions.deeper: Interviewers use this to probe whether you can tell a real gain from noise. If two recipes differ by 0.3 points and one run has seed noise of 0.8, a single run of each tells you nothing. A strong candidate runs several seeds per recipe, reports the mean with its standard error, and points out the 1/√n cost of extra precision.
options: 4 seeds, because the error of an average falls in direct proportion to the number of runs.
256 seeds, because the variance of the average, not its error, falls with the square root of the run count.
16 seeds, because the error of an average falls with the square root of the run count.
None, because seed noise is fixed and averaging more runs leaves the error unchanged.

questions.prompt:
Using pandas 3.x, you want a per-row feature for a payments model: each payment's amount divided by that user's average amount. How many rows do `a` and `t` have, and which should you divide `df["amount"]` by?

```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "user": ["u1", "u2", "u1", "u3", "u1", "u2"],
    "amount": [20, 50, 40, 10, 60, 10],
})
a = df.groupby("user")["amount"].agg("mean")
t = df.groupby("user")["amount"].transform("mean")
```
options: `a` has 3 rows and `t` has 6. Divide by `t`, since it lines up with `df` row by row.
`a` has 3 rows and `t` has 6. Divide by `a`, since pandas matches each row to its user.
`a` has 6 rows and `t` has 3. Divide by `a`, since it repeats the mean on every row.
Both have 6 rows with the same values. Either works, since both align to `df` alike.
questions.explanation:
`agg` reduces each group to one value, so `a` has one row per user, indexed by u1, u2 and u3. `transform` returns a result with the same index as the input, giving each row its own group's mean, so `t` has 6 rows indexed 0 to 5. Dividing `df["amount"]` by `t` pairs row 0 with row 0 and so on, which is exactly the per-row ratio you want.

The option that divides by `a` is the subtle trap. pandas aligns on index labels, not on the `user` column. The labels 0 to 5 never match u1, u2 or u3, so the result has 9 rows, all NaN, and no error is raised. The option with the lengths swapped mixes up which method reduces. The option claiming both have 6 rows assumes `agg` broadcasts back to the rows, which it never does.

If you already have `a`, `df["user"].map(a)` turns it into a row-aligned Series.
questions.deeper: In feature pipelines, `transform` is the tool for "compare each row with its group" features, such as z-scores within a store or a share of a user's spend. Interviewers like a follow-up: if these averages include the current or future payments, the feature leaks. In time-ordered data, use an expanding mean of earlier rows instead.

questions.prompt: An HR software company wants an LLM to turn a manager's rough notes into a performance-review summary with a fixed structure and a warm, specific tone. A detailed instruction prompt gets the structure right, but the tone drifts between generic and stiff. The team has 300 summaries that their HR experts approved and a few weeks of engineering time. Would you improve the prompt, add few-shot examples, or fine-tune? Explain how you would decide.
questions.answer: I would start cheap and measure. First I would hold out about 50 approved summaries, plus a rubric for structure and tone, as an eval set scored by experts or a checked LLM judge. Then I would try few-shot: two or three approved examples in the prompt, ideally retrieved for being similar to the current notes, because tone is easier to show than to describe. If that closes most of the gap at an acceptable prompt length, I stop there. I would fine-tune if few-shot plateaus below the bar, if the long examples make each request too slow or costly at our volume, or if we need very consistent style. The remaining 250 summaries are enough for a small supervised fine-tune, for example with LoRA. Fine-tuning shapes style and format well, but it adds training, versioning and retraining work, so it must clearly beat few-shot on the eval.
points: Build an eval set from held-out approved summaries before choosing
Try few-shot first, since tone is easier to show than describe
Fine-tune if few-shot plateaus or long prompts cost too much at volume
300 examples suit a small SFT or LoRA run for style
Weigh fine-tuning upkeep: retraining, versioning and serving
questions.explanation:
The behaviour wanted here is style, not new knowledge, and style is exactly what examples and fine-tuning teach well. Few-shot examples condition the model on the target tone with no training at all, so they are the fastest thing to try. Fine-tuning moves the style into the weights, which makes it more consistent and removes the need to send long examples with every request.

The common mistake is to jump straight to fine-tuning because it feels more serious, before there is any eval to show it helps. Without a held-out set, you cannot tell whether a fine-tuned model is better or just different. The reverse mistake is to keep adding instructions such as "be warm and specific", which rarely fixes tone because the words mean something vaguer to the model than to the HR team. A third slip is to train on all 300 examples and then test on the same ones, which hides overfitting.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often probe the data side. Approved summaries contain names and personal details, so they need PII handling before they are used for training or as examples. A strong candidate also asks what happens when the base model changes. A prompt usually moves to a new model with light edits, while a fine-tune must be redone.

questions.prompt: A support team wants to route tickets into five categories with logistic regression, which at heart is a binary model. Which statements about extending it to five classes are correct? Select all that apply.
options: One-vs-rest trains five binary models, each class against the rest, and picks the class with the top score.
A multinomial model trains jointly and turns five class scores into probabilities with a softmax.
With the softmax model, the five predicted probabilities for each ticket always add up to exactly 1.
With one-vs-rest, the five raw probabilities from the separate models always add up to exactly 1.
One-vs-one needs only five binary models in total, one built around each of the five classes.
Coding the classes as 0 to 4 and rounding a single linear regression output works just as well.
questions.explanation:
One-vs-rest trains a separate binary classifier per class and predicts the class whose model is most confident, so it is a valid extension. Multinomial logistic regression learns one weight vector per class and passes the five scores through a softmax, exp(zₖ) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ). By construction that gives positive values that add up to 1, so both statements about the multinomial model are correct.

The one-vs-rest models are trained separately, so nothing ties their outputs together. A ticket can get 0.7 from the billing model and 0.6 from the technical model. Libraries often rescale these to sum to 1 afterwards, but the raw outputs do not. One-vs-one trains a model for every pair of classes, which for five classes is 5 × 4 / 2 = 10 models, then takes a vote. Coding the classes as numbers and rounding a regression output invents an order and spacing, so the model treats the category coded 2 as halfway between those coded 1 and 3, which means nothing for ticket types.
questions.deeper: Multinomial is the usual default for logistic regression and tends to give better-calibrated probabilities, which matter if only confident tickets are routed automatically. One-vs-rest is handy when one category needs its own threshold. An interviewer may ask what changes if a ticket can belong to several categories at once. Then you want independent sigmoids, not a softmax.

questions.prompt: A support-triage agent makes 10 model calls per ticket. The first call's input is 3,000 tokens: system prompt, tool definitions and the ticket. After each call, the model's tool request plus the tool's result add 1,000 tokens to the history, and every call resends the whole history as input. Suppose input tokens cost $3 per million and there is no prompt caching. What is the input-token cost of handling 1,000 tickets, in dollars, as a whole number?
questions.explanation:
Each call's input is everything so far, so the inputs grow by 1,000 tokens per call: 3,000, 4,000, 5,000 and so on up to 12,000 on the 10th call.

- Tokens per ticket: 3,000 + 4,000 + ... + 12,000. That is 10 calls averaging 7,500 tokens, so 75,000 tokens.
- Tokens for 1,000 tickets: 75,000 × 1,000 = 75,000,000.
- Cost: 75 million × $3 per million = $225.

The most common mistake is to count each token once, as if the model only read new text: 3,000 + 10 × 1,000 = 13,000 tokens per ticket, which gives $39. Another is to use only the last call's size, 12,000 tokens, which gives $36. Both miss that the model has no memory between calls, so the app must resend the full history every time. That makes total input grow roughly with the square of the number of steps. Doubling the steps here to 20 would cost about 3.3 times as much, not twice as much.
questions.deeper: This is why long agent runs get expensive and why prompt caching matters, since the shared prefix is resent on every call. Trimming old tool results also pays off twice: it lowers the cost of every later call, not just one.

questions.prompt:
A colleague's PyTorch training loop for a demand-forecasting model looks like this:

```python
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
for x, y in loader:
    pred = model(x)
    loss = loss_fn(pred, y)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
```

What goes wrong when it runs?
options: Each `backward()` call adds to the stored gradients, so every step uses the sum of all past batch gradients, not just the current batch's gradient.
PyTorch clears the stored gradients inside `optimizer.step()`, so this loop trains exactly like one that calls `zero_grad()` on every iteration.
Each `backward()` call replaces the gradients from the previous batch, so the loop trains correctly and the missing reset only wastes a little memory.
The first `optimizer.step()` call raises a RuntimeError, because PyTorch will not apply gradients that were not zeroed before `backward()` ran.
questions.explanation:
In PyTorch, `loss.backward()` adds the new gradients into each parameter's `.grad` field rather than replacing what is there. Nothing in this loop clears that field, so after batch 50 the update uses the sum of all 50 batch gradients, each computed at older weights. The steps end up far larger than intended, and the loss usually oscillates or diverges. The fix is to call `optimizer.zero_grad()` once per iteration, before `loss.backward()`.

The option claiming the optimizer step clears gradients is a common belief, but the step only reads `.grad` and updates the weights. The option about replacing gradients describes how many people expect autograd to work, and it is exactly the wrong way round. No error is raised either.
