PyTorch accumulates on purpose, because that behaviour is what makes gradient accumulation across micro-batches possible.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate mentions the intended use of accumulation: run several micro-batches, call `backward()` on each loss divided by the number of micro-batches, then step and zero once. That simulates a larger batch on limited memory. Interviewers may also ask where `zero_grad()` belongs, and any point before the next `backward()` works.

questions.prompt: A legal team tests a model that scores emails for attorney-client privilege. On a tiny check set, the three privileged emails score 0.92, 0.70 and 0.45. The four non-privileged emails score 0.80, 0.45, 0.30 and 0.10. Compute ROC-AUC by comparing every privileged email with every non-privileged one, counting a tie as half a correct pair. Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
ROC-AUC equals the share of positive-negative pairs that the model orders correctly. With 3 privileged and 4 non-privileged emails there are 3 × 4 = 12 pairs.

- 0.92 beats all four negatives: 4 pairs.
- 0.70 loses to 0.80 but beats 0.45, 0.30 and 0.10: 3 pairs.
- 0.45 loses to 0.80, ties with 0.45 and beats 0.30 and 0.10: 2 + 0.5 = 2.5 pairs.

The total is 4 + 3 + 2.5 = 9.5 correct pairs, and 9.5 / 12 ≈ 0.79.

The most common slip is the tie. Dropping it gives 9 / 12 = 0.75, and counting it as a full win gives 10 / 12 ≈ 0.83. Counting a tie as half matches the area under the ROC curve, where a tied score moves the curve diagonally. Another mistake is to compare only neighbouring scores in the sorted list instead of every positive with every negative.
questions.deeper: This pair-counting view is the Mann-Whitney U statistic divided by the number of pairs. Nobody counts by hand in practice, but interviewers use small cases like this to check you know what AUC measures. It also explains why AUC is unchanged by any order-preserving change to the scores.

questions.prompt: A lender is building a CI pipeline that must pass before any new version of its loan approval model is deployed. Which checks belong in that pipeline? Select all that apply.
options: Unit tests on feature code, such as how `debt_to_income` handles an income of zero
Validation of training data schema, null rates and value ranges against set rules
A comparison of the candidate and the production model on the same recent holdout
A check that model size and p99 latency on a test machine stay within serving limits
A check that the candidate's holdout predictions exactly match the production model's
A check that the candidate's training loss is lower than the production model's was
questions.explanation:
Each true option guards a different way a model release can go wrong. Unit tests on feature code catch logic bugs, such as dividing by zero income, before they reach any model. Data validation stops a training run on broken data, such as a column that suddenly arrives empty. Comparing the candidate with the production model on the same recent holdout is the quality gate: a new model should ship only if it is at least as good on data both were tested on. Size and latency checks catch a model that is accurate but too big or too slow to serve within its limits.

Requiring exact prediction matches would block every real improvement, since a better model must predict differently. That kind of check fits a refactor that should change nothing, not a new model. Comparing training loss is a trap. Lower training loss can simply mean more overfitting, and two models trained on different data have losses that are not comparable at all.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds slice checks to the quality gate, such as no drop above a set margin for any region or loan type, since an average can hide a group that got worse. For lending, many teams also run a fairness check across protected groups before deploy.

questions.prompt: A school district's early-warning model flags students at risk of dropping out. In group A, 30% of students later drop out. In group B, 15% do. At the chosen threshold the flags have the same precision in both groups, 0.6, so a flag means the same thing whatever the group. The model also misses the same share of real dropouts in both groups, 30%. What follows for the false positive rate, the share of students who stay in school but are flagged anyway?
options: It must be equal in both groups, since precision and miss rate both match.
It must be higher in group B, since it has fewer real dropouts to find.
It must be higher in group A, the group where more students drop out.
It cannot be pinned down without each group's full score distribution.
questions.explanation:
Take 1,000 students per group. Group A has 300 dropouts. Missing 30% means 210 are flagged correctly. With precision 0.6, those 210 are 60% of all flags, so there are 350 flags and 140 are false. That is 140 of 700 students who stay, an FPR of 0.20. Group B has 150 dropouts, 105 caught, 175 flags and 70 false ones among 850 who stay, an FPR of about 0.08.

In general FPR = p / (1 − p) × (1 − precision) / precision × (1 − miss rate), where p is the base rate. Hold precision and miss rate fixed and FPR rises with p. So equal precision, often called predictive parity, plus equal miss rates forces unequal false positive rates whenever base rates differ and the model is not perfect.

Expecting equal FPRs is exactly the intuition this result breaks. Group B has fewer dropouts, which pushes its FPR down, not up. And the base rate, precision and miss rate together fix every cell of the confusion matrix, so the score distribution is not needed.
questions.deeper: This is the core of the well-known debate over criminal risk scores. One side showed equal precision across groups, the other showed unequal false positive rates, and both were right. The same clash holds for calibrated scores in general. In an interview, say the conflict is arithmetic, not a data problem, and that people affected and policy owners must choose which error to equalize.

questions.prompt: An ad model hashes the cross of `app_id` and `country`, which has about 3 million distinct values, into 2²⁰ (about 1 million) buckets. To save memory, an engineer cuts this to 2¹² (4,096) buckets. Which statement about hashing and this change is correct?
options: Apps first seen at serving time cannot be mapped, because the hash function was fit on training data
Collisions become rarer, because with fewer buckets each one receives more training examples
Far more values now share each bucket, so their effects get blended and accuracy usually drops
Memory now grows as new apps appear, because the hasher must store a table of the values it has seen
questions.explanation:
Feature hashing sends each value through a fixed hash function to a bucket index, and the model learns one weight per bucket. With 3 million values and 4,096 buckets, each bucket holds about 730 values on average, so a high-click app and a low-click app can share one weight. The model can only learn their blended effect, and accuracy usually falls. Even at 2²⁰ buckets there were already collisions, but far fewer per bucket.

The other statements describe hashing wrongly. A hasher stores no table of seen values. That is its main advantage: memory is fixed by the bucket count, whatever arrives. For the same reason it is never fit, so a brand new app at serving time still hashes to some bucket. Fewer buckets mean more values per bucket, so collisions become more common, not rarer. More examples per bucket does not help when those examples come from different values.
questions.deeper: Teams usually pick the bucket count by trying a few sizes and plotting validation loss against memory. A strong candidate also mentions signed hashing, used by scikit-learn's `FeatureHasher`, which lets colliding values partly cancel instead of always adding up.

questions.prompt: A document Q&A bot sends prompts of about 8,000 tokens, mostly retrieved passages, and gets answers of about 200 tokens, which it streams to the user. Users complain about a long pause before any text appears, but once text starts it flows quickly. Which explanation and fix fit best?
options: The pause is prefill, which processes all 8,000 prompt tokens at once and is compute-bound, so sending fewer retrieved passages shortens it most.
The pause is decode, which reads every weight for each token and is memory-bound, so quantizing the weights to 4 bits shortens it the most.
The pause is prefill, which reads all the weights once per prompt token and is memory-bound, so a GPU with faster memory shortens it most.
The pause comes from generating the 200 answer tokens, which all finish before streaming begins, so capping the answer length shortens it the most.
questions.explanation:
The time before the first token appears is mostly prefill. In prefill the model processes the whole prompt in one pass, with all 8,000 tokens going through each layer together. Every weight read from memory is reused across thousands of tokens, so the step is limited by compute, and its cost grows with prompt length. Cutting the retrieved context is the most direct fix. When part of the prompt repeats across requests, such as a long system prompt, caching its key and value states also helps.

Decode is the phase after the first token, and the users say that part is fast. 4-bit weights mainly speed up decode, so they target the wrong phase. The option claiming prefill reads the weights once per prompt token is wrong, because prefill reads them once for the whole prompt. That reuse is what makes it compute-bound rather than memory-bound. Capping the answer length helps total time, but with streaming the first token is shown as soon as it is generated, so the 200 tokens do not delay the first one.
questions.deeper: Serving dashboards should track time to first token and time per output token separately, since they have different causes and fixes. A strong candidate also mentions chunked prefill, which splits a long prompt into pieces so it does not stall the decode steps of other users on the same GPU.

questions.prompt: Two house price models were studied by retraining each on many bootstrap samples of the same size. In squared-error units, model A has bias² 0.04 and variance 0.10. Model B has bias² 0.09 and variance 0.02. The irreducible noise is 0.05 for both. Which model has the lower expected test error, and what could change that choice?
options: Model B, at 0.16 against 0.19. A much larger training set could flip this by shrinking A's variance.
Model A, since its bias² is less than half of B's, and bias is the error that more data cannot fix.
Model B, at 0.11 against 0.14. Adding the 0.05 noise term to both totals would flip the order to A.
Model A, since variance falls with training time, so A's 0.10 will drop once it trains for longer.
questions.explanation:
Expected squared test error is bias² + variance + noise. Model A gives 0.04 + 0.10 + 0.05 = 0.19. Model B gives 0.09 + 0.02 + 0.05 = 0.16. So B is better today. Variance usually shrinks as the training set grows, while bias depends mostly on the model family. If much more data cut A's variance to 0.04 and B's to 0.01, A would total 0.13 and B 0.15, and A would win.

Choosing A for its lower bias looks only at one term. Bias is often harder to fix, but the question is which model errs less now, and the totals decide that. The option claiming the noise term flips the order gets the sums without noise right, 0.14 and 0.11, but the same 0.05 is added to both, so the order cannot change. Variance here means how much the fitted model changes from one training sample to another. Training longer does not reduce it and often raises it for flexible models.
questions.deeper: In real work you rarely know these terms exactly, but bootstrap retraining or learning curves give rough estimates. An interviewer may ask what else lowers A's variance without new data: bagging, stronger regularization or fewer features. Bagging many copies of A is a classic way to keep its low bias and cut its variance.

questions.prompt: A grocery delivery service forecasts daily demand per product in 40 cities. Five large cities have three years of history. The other 35 launched in the last six months and have little data. Cities differ in holidays, weather and price levels, but most shopping patterns are shared. A team of three maintains the forecasts. Which modelling approach fits best?
options: Train 40 separate city models, since each city's demand pattern is different and a shared model would blur them.
Train one global model with no city features, so small cities borrow strength from large ones without any noise.
Train one global model with city features, and split off a city's own model only where error stays clearly worse.
Train a model on the five large cities only, and apply it to the 35 small ones without using their own short history.
questions.explanation:
A global model learns the shared patterns, such as weekly cycles and promotions, from all cities at once. Small cities borrow strength from large ones, which cuts the variance that would ruin a model trained on six months of data. City features, such as city ID, local holidays, weather and price level, let the same model learn where cities really differ. Splitting off a dedicated model only when one city's error stays clearly worse keeps the team at one pipeline in most cases.

Forty separate models give the small cities high variance, since each learns from little data, and they mean forty pipelines to retrain and monitor for a team of three. A global model with no city features goes too far the other way. It has high bias, because it cannot represent real differences like a regional holiday. Training only on the large cities ignores data that exists and assumes the small cities behave like big ones, which their different prices and weather suggest is not true.
questions.deeper: Interviewers may ask how you would check the choice. Compare per-city error on a time-based holdout for the global model against a per-city model where data allows. Strong candidates also mention that the global model needs one retraining schedule and drift checks per city, since a new city can shift faster than the rest.

questions.subtopic: where a verifier step pays off
questions.prompt: Your team is deciding where to add a verify-and-revise step after an agent's first attempt. For which of these tasks is such a step likely to improve results reliably? Select all that apply.
options: Writing a Python function for a ticket that comes with unit tests, where the step runs the tests and feeds any failures back.
Extracting invoice fields to JSON, where the step checks the output against a schema and confirms the line items add up to the stated total.
Answering a policy question with quotes, where the step checks that each quoted sentence really appears in the cited document.
Solving a pricing calculation, where the step asks the same model "Are you sure?" with no tool, data or test to check against.
Writing a playful subject line for a newsletter, where a second model call rates how catchy it sounds and asks for a rewrite.
questions.explanation:
A verifier step pays off when it brings a reliable signal from outside the model. Unit tests give a hard pass or fail and an error message the agent can act on, which is why code agents improve so much from a test-and-fix loop. A schema check and a sum check on invoice fields are cheap, exact and catch real errors such as missing fields or misread amounts. Checking that each quote appears in the source is a simple string match that catches invented quotes, a common failure in grounded answers.

Asking the same model "Are you sure?" with nothing new to check against tends not to help reliably. The model has the same knowledge and blind spots as before, and studies of self-correction without outside feedback find it often fails to fix errors and sometimes changes right answers to wrong ones. Rating how catchy a subject line sounds has no ground truth, and a model judging its own style tends to reward its own taste. A second call adds cost and latency and may just swap one acceptable line for another, so a quick human pick or an A/B test is the better check.
questions.deeper: A useful interview line is that verification is often easier than generation. When a cheap, reliable check exists, put it in the loop. When it does not, spend the budget on better prompts or human review instead of extra critique calls.

questions.prompt: A support team tests a classifier that marks tickets as urgent. On 1,000 tickets it has 30 true positives, 10 false positives and 50 false negatives. The rest are true negatives. What is the F1 score for the urgent class? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
First get precision and recall. Precision is 30 / (30 + 10) = 0.75. Recall is 30 / (30 + 50) = 0.375. F1 is their harmonic mean: 2 × 0.75 × 0.375 / (0.75 + 0.375) = 0.5625 / 1.125 = 0.50. A shortcut gives the same result: F1 = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN) = 60 / 120 = 0.50.

The common mistake is to take the plain average, (0.75 + 0.375) / 2 ≈ 0.56. The harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller of the two values, so a model cannot hide weak recall behind strong precision. Notice that the true negatives play no part at all. F1 only looks at the positive class, which is why it is popular for imbalanced problems.
questions.deeper: If missing an urgent ticket hurts more than a false alarm, F1 weights them wrongly. A strong candidate mentions F-beta, where beta above 1 leans toward recall, or simply reports recall at an agreed precision. Also remember F1 depends on the threshold you chose.

questions.prompt: You are training a model on 50 million examples on a single GPU. You compare full-batch gradient descent, mini-batch gradient descent with 256 examples per step, and stochastic gradient descent with 1 example per step. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation:
Mini-batch gradient descent is the standard choice because it balances three things. A batch of 256 is large enough to keep the GPU's parallel cores busy, small enough to fit in memory, and averaged enough for a stable step while still carrying some helpful noise.

Full-batch descent does give the exact gradient, but every step needs a pass over all 50 million examples. You get very few updates per hour, and the whole batch would not fit in GPU memory without accumulating gradients over many chunks. Low noise per step does not mean fast progress per second. Pure stochastic descent takes the cheapest steps, but a single example leaves most of the GPU idle, so it processes far fewer examples per second, and its gradients are very noisy. The claim about bias is backwards. A randomly sampled mini-batch gives an unbiased estimate of the full gradient, just like a single example, and averaging 256 examples cuts the variance of that estimate by a factor of 256.
questions.deeper: A common follow-up is how the learning rate should change with batch size. Larger batches give less noisy gradients and often allow a larger learning rate, roughly in proportion at first, usually with a warm-up period. Very large batches can generalize slightly worse, so teams tune batch size and learning rate together.
options: Full-batch steps give the cleanest gradient, so full-batch reaches a good model in the least time.
Mini-batch steps use the GPU's parallel cores well and fit in memory, with moderate gradient noise.
Single-example steps are the cheapest, so pure stochastic descent also makes the best use of the GPU.
Mini-batch gradients are biased estimates of the full gradient, unlike single-example gradients.

questions.prompt: A search engineer uses 2-dimensional vectors to explain a ranking change to a colleague. The query is q = [1, 0]. Document A is [3, 3] and document B is [0.9, 0.1]. The vectors are not normalized. Which statement is correct?
options: Cosine ranks B first and dot product ranks A first, and normalizing every vector to length 1 would make them agree.
Both rank A first, because A points in a direction closer to the query than B does, and both measure only direction.
Both rank B first, because for a single query the query length cancels out, so the two always give the same order.
Cosine ranks A first and dot product ranks B first, because cosine rewards long vectors and dot product removes length.
questions.explanation:
Work out both scores.

- Dot product: A gives 1×3 + 0×3 = 3. B gives 1×0.9 + 0×0.1 = 0.9. A wins.
- Cosine: A gives 3 / (1 × √18) ≈ 0.71. B gives 0.9 / (1 × √0.82) ≈ 0.99. B wins.

B points almost exactly along the query, while A sits at 45 degrees from it. The dot product equals length × length × cosine, so A's large length (about 4.24) outweighs its worse angle. Once every vector has length 1, the dot product equals the cosine and the two rankings match.

The option about the query length cancelling is the subtle trap. The query's length is the same for every document, so it cannot change the order. The documents' lengths differ, and they do change it. The option ranking A first on both measures gets the geometry wrong: A points further from the query than B, so it cannot win on cosine. The option that swaps the two measures has their roles reversed. Cosine divides length out, and the dot product keeps it.
questions.deeper: This bites in practice when an index is set to inner product but the embedding model's outputs are not normalized, or when old and new vectors were stored differently. Some recommenders keep unnormalized dot products on purpose, because vector length can encode popularity. Decide which behaviour you want, then normalize or not deliberately.

questions.prompt: You are setting up a churn model that several teammates will retrain and tune. The data has numeric columns with missing values, a few low-cardinality categorical columns, and a free-text `last_ticket` column that needs a custom cleaning step. How would you structure preprocessing and the model in scikit-learn so it is reusable and free of leakage?
questions.answer: I would build one Pipeline whose first step is a ColumnTransformer. Numeric columns go through SimpleImputer and StandardScaler, categorical columns through OneHotEncoder with handle_unknown="ignore", and the text column through a custom cleaning transformer followed by TfidfVectorizer. The custom step subclasses BaseEstimator and TransformerMixin, stores its settings in __init__ unchanged, learns anything it needs in fit and returns self, and only applies that in transform. The classifier is the last step. I would run GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV on the whole pipeline, with keys such as model__C and prep__text__tfidf__min_df. Because every learned step sits inside the pipeline, each fold refits the imputers, scalers, encoders and vocabulary on its training rows only, so validation rows never shape preprocessing. I would keep a final test set for one last check and save the fitted pipeline as a single artifact, so serving applies identical transforms.
points: One Pipeline with a ColumnTransformer routing each column type to its own steps
Custom transformer follows the estimator API: fit learns and returns self, transform applies
Hyperparameter search runs on the whole pipeline using step__param names
Each CV fold refits every learned step on training folds only, which prevents leakage
Save and serve the fitted pipeline as one object so training and serving match
questions.explanation:
The point of the design is that everything learned from data lives inside one estimator. Cross-validation and search then treat preprocessing as part of the model, which is what it is in production.

The most common mistake is to preprocess the full dataset first, for example imputing with the global median or fitting the TF-IDF vocabulary on all rows, and only then tune the model. Every fold then sees statistics computed partly from its own validation rows, so scores are optimistic and the chosen settings may not hold up. A second mistake is a custom transformer that does work in `__init__` or renames its arguments. `GridSearchCV` clones estimators by reading `get_params()`, so such a class breaks cloning or silently ignores the settings you search over.

A third is keeping preprocessing in a notebook and the model in a pickle. Serving code then re-implements the transforms by hand, and small differences cause training and serving skew.
questions.deeper: Two practical details impress interviewers. Pass the text column to the ColumnTransformer as a string, `"last_ticket"`, not a list, because TfidfVectorizer expects one-dimensional input. And if the cleaning step learns nothing, a FunctionTransformer is simpler than a full custom class.

questions.prompt: An LLM serving engine used to reserve one contiguous chunk of memory per request, sized for the maximum sequence length, and most of it sat unused. The engine now stores the KV cache in small fixed-size blocks that need not be next to each other, tracked by a per-request block table, much like virtual memory pages in an operating system. This technique is called ______.
questions.explanation:
PagedAttention borrows the idea of paging from operating systems. Each request's KV cache is a list of small blocks, for example 16 tokens each, and a block table maps the request's token positions to wherever those blocks live in GPU memory. A new block is taken only when the previous one fills up. Waste is limited to the unfilled part of the last block, instead of a large reservation for tokens that may never be generated. That freed memory lets the server run many more requests at once.

The common mistake is to answer FlashAttention. FlashAttention speeds up the attention computation by working in tiles that fit in fast on-chip memory, which avoids writing the full attention matrix to main memory. It does not decide how the KV cache is laid out across requests. Another near miss is simply KV cache, which is the thing being stored, not the technique for storing it.
questions.deeper: Blocks also make sharing cheap. Requests with the same system prompt, or several samples from one prompt, can point to the same physical blocks and copy a block only when they diverge. A strong candidate links this to prefix caching and to the higher batch sizes that continuous batching can then reach.

questions.prompt: A card issuer must answer each authorisation within 100 ms, and the fraud model gets 30 ms of that at p99. Two of its best features are the card's transaction count in the last hour and its average amount over 90 days. Today both come from SQL queries on the transaction database that take about 200 ms each. Which design best fits the budget?
options: Stream both aggregates into a feature store as payments arrive, look them up by card ID, and fall back to rules on timeout.
Run the two SQL queries in parallel on a read replica, so their time overlaps and the main database is not slowed down by them.
Cache each card's feature values for 24 hours after its first transaction of the day, and read them from memory after that point.
Approve each transaction at once and score it a few seconds later, then reverse the approval if the model flags it as likely fraud.
questions.explanation:
The real problem is that the features are computed when the request arrives. At about 200 ms per query, no tuning gets that under 30 ms. The fix is to compute the aggregates ahead of time. A streaming job updates each card's counts and averages as transactions happen and writes them to a key-value feature store. At request time the model does one lookup by card ID, which takes a few milliseconds. The rules fallback keeps authorisations flowing if the store is slow or down.

Running the queries in parallel only overlaps them. The request still waits about 200 ms, far over budget. A 24-hour cache is fast but stale. A one-hour transaction count frozen since the morning misses exactly the sudden burst of card testing it is meant to catch. Approving first and scoring later lets the fraudster walk away with goods or a digital purchase before the check runs, so the reversal often comes too late.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often follow up on consistency. The streaming job and the training pipeline must compute the aggregates the same way, or you get training-serving skew. A strong answer also states the fallback policy: what the rules check, how often the fallback fires, and an alert if that rate climbs.

questions.prompt:
An analyst clusters 30,000 delivery drivers on standardised features and tries k = 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.

- Inertia (within-cluster sum of squares): 9,100, 5,200, 4,700, 4,350, 4,050
- Mean silhouette score: 0.44, 0.51, 0.39, 0.33, 0.30

Which k do these numbers best support?
options: k = 6, since it gives the lowest inertia of all the values tried.
k = 2, since the largest single drop in inertia starts from k = 2.
k = 3, since inertia stops dropping fast and silhouette peaks there.
k = 4, since inertia keeps falling and silhouette is still close to 0.4.
questions.explanation:
The elbow method looks for the k after which extra clusters stop paying off. Going from 2 to 3 cuts inertia by 3,900. Each later step cuts it by only 300 to 500. So the bend is at k = 3. The silhouette score, which rewards points that sit close to their own cluster and far from the next one, also peaks at k = 3 with 0.51. Two separate signals agree, which is the best case you can hope for.

Picking k = 6 for its low inertia is the classic misuse. Inertia always falls as k grows and reaches 0 when every point is its own cluster, so the lowest value simply picks the largest k you tried. The big drop from 2 to 3 is evidence for 3, not 2, because it shows that k = 2 was merging two real groups. Moving to k = 4 lowers inertia only a little while silhouette falls to 0.39, so the extra cluster mostly splits an existing group.

Each tool can mislead on its own. Elbows are often blurry, and silhouette favours round, well-separated clusters, so it can prefer k = 2 on data with odd shapes or one dominant split.
questions.deeper: In real projects these numbers narrow the range and the business picks within it. If the operations team can only run two driver programmes, three segments may still be too many. A strong candidate also checks stability by rerunning with different seeds or on bootstrap samples and seeing whether the same groups come back.

questions.prompt: A churn model scored well offline but does poorly after launch. The team finds that `days_since_last_login` was computed for training by a nightly SQL job in UTC, while the live service computes it at request time, in local time, from a different table. This kind of problem is called ______.
questions.explanation:
Training-serving skew means the model receives features at serving time that are built differently from the ones it learned on. Here one feature name hides two pieces of code: a nightly batch job using UTC and one table, and a live service using local time and another table. The values can differ by a day or more for many users, and the model reads that as a real change in behaviour.

The common mistake is to call this data drift. Drift is a real change in the world, such as users logging in less often. Skew is a bug in your own pipelines, and it is often there from the first day of launch. The difference matters for the fix. Retraining on fresh data does not cure skew, because the training pipeline would still compute the feature the old way. You fix it by computing each feature from one shared definition, or by logging the features actually served and training on those logs.
questions.deeper: Feature stores exist largely to stop this bug, by giving training and serving one definition per feature. A quick test an interviewer may ask for: log the served features for a sample of requests, recompute the same rows with the training pipeline, and compare them column by column.

questions.prompt: A teammate builds a 10-layer ReLU network for credit risk scoring and sets every weight and bias to zero before training, to start from a neutral point. After many epochs the model still predicts the same default probability for every applicant. Explain what went wrong, and how schemes like Xavier and He initialization choose the scale of random starting weights.
questions.answer: With identical weights, all units in a layer compute the same value and get the same gradient, so they stay copies forever. This is the symmetry problem, and a layer of identical units is no better than a single unit. Zeros make it worse. ReLU(0) is 0, so every hidden output is 0, and with zero weights downstream every weight gradient is exactly 0. Only the output bias learns, so the model predicts the base default rate. Random weights break the symmetry, but the scale matters. Each layer multiplies the signal, so weights that are too small make activations shrink layer by layer and weights that are too large make them explode. Xavier sets the weight variance to about 2 / (fan_in + fan_out), which suits tanh or sigmoid. He sets it to 2 / fan_in for ReLU, doubling it because ReLU zeroes about half its inputs. Both keep activation and gradient variance roughly steady across layers.
points: Identical starting weights make units in a layer compute and update identically (symmetry)
With zeros and ReLU every weight gradient is zero, so only the output bias learns the base rate
Random initialization breaks symmetry, but its scale must be chosen with care
Too small a scale makes activations vanish across layers, too large makes them explode
Xavier uses variance about 2 / (fan_in + fan_out) for tanh or sigmoid, He uses 2 / fan_in for ReLU
questions.explanation:
Gradient descent can only make units different if something makes them different to begin with. With identical weights, every unit in a layer sees the same inputs, computes the same output and gets the same gradient, so after any number of updates they are still copies. Random weights are the simplest way to break that symmetry. Biases can start at zero as long as the weights are random.

The scale matters because each layer multiplies the signal by its weights. If each layer scales the activation variance by a factor a little below 1, the signal is tiny after 10 layers, and a factor a little above 1 makes it blow up. Xavier and He pick the variance so that factor is about 1. The factor of 2 in He initialization makes up for ReLU zeroing about half of each layer's inputs.

The common mistake is to say zero initialization only slows training down. Symmetry caps what the network can ever learn, and here it stops every weight from learning at all. Another mistake is to think any small random values are fine. A fixed standard deviation of 0.01 in a deep ReLU network makes activations shrink toward zero layer by layer.
questions.deeper: Frameworks apply sensible defaults to standard layers, so this mostly bites in custom layers or hand-written code. A useful habit is to log the mean and standard deviation of each layer's activations at step 0. A bad initialization shows up there before you spend a full training run.

questions.prompt: A retinal screening model is trained with log loss. The clinical team only cares about recall at a fixed score threshold of 0.3, and that is the number they report. A new engineer asks why the team does not train on recall directly. What is the best answer?
options: Recall at a fixed threshold changes in jumps as the weights move, so its gradient is zero almost everywhere.
Log loss always ranks models the same way recall does, so it is the same objective but faster to compute.
Recall can only be measured on held-out data, so it cannot be computed on the training set during fitting.
Training on recall would overfit, while log loss has a built-in penalty that keeps all of the weights small.
questions.explanation:
Recall at 0.3 counts how many true cases score above the line. A small change to the weights almost never pushes any score across 0.3, so recall stays flat, then suddenly jumps when one does. Its gradient is zero almost everywhere and undefined at the jumps, so gradient descent has nothing to follow. Log loss is a smooth stand-in. Every example gives a gradient that pushes its probability toward the true label. Recall on its own is also trivially maximised by flagging every patient, so it would need a second term anyway.

Log loss and recall can disagree. A model can have lower log loss and still lower recall at 0.3, which is why the team reports the metric it cares about. Recall can be computed on training data, it is just counting. Log loss has no built-in weight penalty. Regularization is a separate term you add to it.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds how the two meet: train on log loss, then choose the threshold on validation data to hit the recall the clinic needs. Class weights can tilt the loss toward missed positives. Log loss also tends to give well calibrated probabilities, which makes a threshold like 0.3 mean something.

questions.prompt:
A support team classifies ticket priority into low, medium and urgent. Using scikit-learn 1.x, what is the value of `w[2]`, the weight for urgent tickets, after this code runs? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.utils.class_weight import compute_class_weight

# 0 = low, 1 = medium, 2 = urgent
y = np.array([0] * 900 + [1] * 240 + [2] * 60)
w = compute_class_weight("balanced", classes=np.array([0, 1, 2]), y=y)
```
questions.explanation:
The balanced rule gives class c the weight n / (k × n_c), where n is the number of rows, k is the number of classes and n_c is the count of class c.

Working: n = 900 + 240 + 60 = 1,200 and k = 3. For urgent, n_c = 60, so the weight is 1,200 / (3 × 60) = 1,200 / 180 ≈ 6.67. The other weights are 1,200 / 2,700 ≈ 0.44 for low and 1,200 / 720 ≈ 1.67 for medium.

A common mistake is the simple ratio of the largest class to the rarest, 900 / 60 = 15. That gives the right relative sizes but on a different scale. The balanced formula is scaled so that each class carries the same total weight: 60 × 6.67, 240 × 1.67 and 900 × 0.44 each come to about 400. The weights over all 1,200 rows add up to 1,200, so the loss keeps its usual size and the learning rate and regularization behave as before.
questions.deeper: In practice you pass `class_weight="balanced"` to the model directly. Fully balanced weights often over-correct and hurt precision on the rare class, so treat the weight as a hyperparameter, and remember the scores are no longer calibrated probabilities.

questions.prompt: A review-sentiment model uses a bidirectional transformer encoder and averages its outputs. It was trained with position information accidentally switched off, and it gives "not good, actually great" and "not great, actually good" exactly the same score. Which option explains the failure and correctly describes how rotary position embeddings (RoPE) encode order?
options: Attention scores use only token contents, so a reordered input gives reordered outputs. RoPE rotates the value vectors by position, so outputs carry location while weights stay the same.
The softmax rescales every row, which erases where each score came from. RoPE adds a learned vector for each absolute position to the token embeddings before the first layer.
Attention scores use only token contents, so a reordered input gives reordered outputs. RoPE adds a fixed bias to every score that falls linearly with the distance between two tokens.
Attention scores use only token contents, so a reordered input gives reordered outputs. RoPE rotates queries and keys by angles set by position, so each score also depends on distance.
questions.explanation:
A score q·k depends only on what the two tokens are, not where they sit. So without position information, shuffling the input tokens just shuffles the outputs, and averaging them gives the same result. Both reviews contain the same tokens, so they get the same score. RoPE fixes this by rotating each pair of dimensions in the query and key by an angle proportional to the token's position. The dot product of two rotated vectors depends on the difference of their angles, so each score depends on how far apart the tokens are, which is relative position.

The option that rotates value vectors is wrong because RoPE acts on queries and keys. Rotating values would leave the weights blind to order. The softmax option gives a false reason, since normalizing a row does not lose which key each score belongs to, and its description is of learned absolute position embeddings. The option with a linear distance bias describes ALiBi, a different method that leaves queries and keys unchanged.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate notes why RoPE is popular: relative position is built into every score in every layer, and nothing is added to the embeddings. A common follow-up is how RoPE behaves past the training length, which leads into position interpolation and other context-extension tricks.

questions.prompt: A team runs random search over a large hyperparameter space. Assume each trial is drawn independently from the search distribution, and call a configuration good if it falls in the top 5% of that distribution by validation score. With 40 trials, what is the probability that at least one trial is good? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Work with the opposite event first. A single trial misses the top 5% with probability 0.95. Because trials are independent, all 40 miss with probability 0.95⁴⁰ = 0.1285. So the chance that at least one trial is good is 1 − 0.1285 = 0.8715, which is 0.87 to 2 places.

The most common mistake is 40 × 0.05 = 2.0. That is the expected number of good trials, not a probability, and it cannot be right since a probability cannot exceed 1. Another slip is 0.05⁴⁰, which is the chance that every single trial is good, a vanishingly small number.

The formula also shows the diminishing returns. 60 trials give 1 − 0.95⁶⁰ ≈ 0.95, and 100 trials give about 0.99. Each extra trial helps less than the one before.
questions.deeper: The 60-trial rule of thumb comes from this calculation. A strong candidate adds two caveats. Top 5% of the search distribution may still be well below the true best if the ranges are badly chosen. And if the good region is narrower, say 1%, about 300 trials are needed for the same 95% odds.

questions.subtopic: learning rate and number of trees
questions.prompt: A search team trains a gradient boosting model with a learning rate of 0.3 and 200 trees. A teammate lowers the learning rate to 0.03, keeps 200 trees, and validation loss gets worse. What is the most likely cause, and what should they do?
options: A smaller learning rate makes boosting overfit sooner, so go back to 0.3 and keep the 200 trees.
With smaller steps, 200 trees underfit, so allow far more trees and stop early on validation loss.
The tree count should match the training-loss minimum, so keep adding trees until training loss stops falling.
Shrinkage only changes training speed, not the final model, so the drop must come from a bad random seed.
questions.explanation:
The learning rate, also called shrinkage, scales each tree's contribution. At 0.03 each tree moves the predictions a tenth as far as at 0.3, so 200 trees now cover only a small part of the ground the old model did. The model is underfitting. Smaller steps need roughly proportionally more trees, here something near 2,000. The usual practice is to set a high cap on trees, watch loss on a validation set, and stop when it has not improved for a set number of rounds. A small learning rate with many trees often generalises a little better, at the cost of training time.

A smaller learning rate makes the model fit more slowly, so it overfits later, not sooner. Training loss keeps falling as trees are added, so choosing the count from training loss just picks a huge number and overfits. Shrinkage is not only about speed. With a fixed number of trees it changes the final model, as this drop shows.
questions.deeper: Treat learning rate and tree count as one pair of knobs. A typical recipe is to fix a small learning rate such as 0.05, let early stopping choose the tree count, then tune depth and regularisation. Remember that early stopping has seen the validation set, so report the final score on a separate test set.

questions.prompt:
The retriever of a bank's compliance assistant is tested on 50 questions. Each question has exactly one chunk that a reviewer marked as the correct source. For each question, the team records where that chunk ranked in the retriever's results:

- Rank 1: 22 questions
- Rank 2 or 3: 9 questions
- Rank 4 or 5: 6 questions
- Rank 6 to 10: 5 questions
- Not in the top 10: 8 questions

A question counts as a hit at k if its correct chunk is in the top k results. What is the hit rate at k = 5 (recall@5)? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Count the questions whose correct chunk sits at rank 5 or better, then divide by all questions.

- Hits at 5: 22 + 9 + 6 = 37
- Hit rate: 37 / 50 = 0.74

Two mistakes are common. One is to count only rank 1 and answer 22 / 50 = 0.44. That is the hit rate at 1, a much stricter measure, which matters when only one chunk goes into the prompt. The other is to include ranks 6 to 10 and answer 42 / 50 = 0.84, which is the hit rate at 10. The k should match how many chunks the system really passes to the model. If the prompt gets 5 chunks, a chunk at rank 7 helps no more than a missing one.

With one correct chunk per question, recall@5 and hit rate at 5 are the same number. When a question has several relevant chunks, recall@k is the share of them that were found, while hit rate asks only whether at least one was found, so the two can differ.
questions.deeper: The 8 questions with no match in the top 10 are where to look first. Reading them often reveals a chunking problem, vocabulary the embeddings miss, or a gap in the index. An interviewer may also ask for MRR on the same data, which rewards rank 1 more than rank 5 and so hints at whether a reranker would help.

questions.prompt: PCA on a data matrix whose columns have been mean-centred, but not scaled, finds the eigenvectors of the d × d ______ matrix, where d is the number of features. Each eigenvector is a principal component, and its eigenvalue is the variance of the data along that direction.
questions.explanation:
The covariance matrix holds each feature's variance on its diagonal and the covariance of each pair of features off the diagonal. For centred data X with n rows it is XᵀX / (n − 1). Its eigenvectors are the directions along which the data varies most, and each eigenvalue is the variance captured along that direction. Sorting by eigenvalue gives the first principal component, then the second, and so on. Libraries often reach the same result through a singular value decomposition of X, which avoids forming the matrix at all.

The common mistake is to answer the correlation matrix. That is right only when the features have also been scaled to unit variance, because the correlation matrix is the covariance matrix of standardized data. On unscaled data the two give different components, and features with large units dominate the covariance version. Another slip is the n × n matrix XXᵀ, which compares rows rather than features, so its size does not match d × d.
questions.deeper: A frequent follow-up is how PCA scales to wide data. Forming a 50,000 × 50,000 covariance matrix is expensive, so libraries work on the SVD of X directly, or use randomized SVD when only the top components are needed. A strong candidate also mentions scaling the features first when their units differ.

questions.prompt: Design the search ranking for a home goods store with 2 million products and 5 million searches a day. Cover how you find candidates, what the ranker uses, how you learn from user behaviour, and how you evaluate it offline and online.
questions.answer: Retrieve a few thousand candidates by combining keyword matching on titles and attributes with embedding search, which catches synonyms and vague queries, then filter out items that are out of stock. A learned ranker, such as gradient-boosted trees, scores them with features like query-to-product text match, category match, price, rating, stock and past click and purchase rates for similar queries. Labels come from logs, with purchases and add-to-cart worth more than clicks. Clicks carry position bias, so log the position shown, randomise a small slice of traffic or use propensity weights, and do not treat unclicked items low on the page as firm negatives. Offline, measure NDCG on human-judged queries and on held-out logs, split into frequent and rare queries. Online, A/B test conversion rate, revenue per search and the share of searches with no click, with latency as a guardrail.
points: Hybrid retrieval: keyword plus embedding search, then filters
A learned ranker over query-product match, quality, price and behaviour features
Graded labels from clicks, carts and purchases
Correct position bias in click data
Offline NDCG split by frequent and rare queries
Online A/B on conversion and revenue per search, latency as a guardrail
questions.explanation:
Search ranking is a two-stage problem like recommendation, except the query gives a strong signal of intent. Keyword matching is precise for exact terms such as "oak bookshelf", while embeddings rescue queries like "small table for a balcony" whose words may not appear in the title. The ranker then combines relevance with what makes a sale: price, rating, stock and how similar searches behaved.

The common mistake is to train on raw clicks as if they were relevance labels. Top results are clicked partly because they are on top, so a ranker trained this way learns to copy the old order. Weighting purchases above clicks and correcting for position bias gives cleaner signal.

Evaluation needs both sides. Offline NDCG lets you compare many ideas cheaply, but logs are shaped by the old ranker, so the launch decision comes from an online test. Splitting results by frequent and rare queries matters because rare queries make up a large share of traffic in total and are where models usually fail.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often probe rare queries and new products. Good answers mention query rewriting or spelling correction, content features for products with no history, and a small boost or exploration budget so new items can earn clicks. Watch the share of searches that end in reformulation, a strong sign of a bad result page.

questions.prompt:
Two moderators each label the same 200 posts as toxic or fine:

- Both say toxic: 42
- Both say fine: 118
- A says toxic, B says fine: 24
- A says fine, B says toxic: 16

What is Cohen's kappa for the two moderators? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Kappa compares observed agreement with the agreement you would expect by chance: κ = (pₒ − pₑ) / (1 − pₑ).

Observed agreement: (42 + 118) / 200 = 0.80.

Chance agreement: A says toxic on 42 + 24 = 66 posts, a rate of 0.33. B says toxic on 42 + 16 = 58 posts, a rate of 0.29. Both saying toxic by chance is 0.33 × 0.29 = 0.0957. Both saying fine is 0.67 × 0.71 = 0.4757. So pₑ = 0.5714.

Kappa: (0.80 − 0.5714) / (1 − 0.5714) = 0.2286 / 0.4286 ≈ 0.53.

The common mistake is to stop at 0.80. Raw agreement looks high because most posts are fine, and two people who both said fine most of the time would agree often even without reading the posts. Kappa removes that chance share. A value around 0.53 usually counts as only moderate agreement, a sign the guidelines for toxic need work.
questions.deeper: Kappa drops sharply when one class is rare, even with high raw agreement, so report it alongside per-class agreement. For more than two annotators, Fleiss' kappa or Krippendorff's alpha is the usual choice.

questions.prompt: An online furniture store has launched a shopping assistant agent that searches the catalogue, checks stock and builds a basket. Support says some conversations end badly, but nobody can tell why. What would you record for each agent run, and how would you use it?
questions.answer: I would give every run an id and record each step under it: the model's input, its output, which tool it called, the arguments, the tool result, the latency and any error. I would also record tokens and cost per step, the model and prompt version, and how the run ended: basket built, handed to a person, abandoned or step cap hit. Customer details would be masked before storage. With that, I can open a bad conversation and replay it step by step to find where it went wrong, such as a stock check that timed out. Across all runs, I would track tool error rates, steps and cost per run, and latency by step, with alerts on spikes. Bad runs would be labelled and added to the evaluation set.
points: One run id tying every step together
Per step: model input and output, tool name, arguments, result, latency, errors
Tokens, cost, model and prompt version, and the final outcome
Replay single bad runs to find the first failing step
Aggregate metrics and alerts on errors, cost and latency
Mask personal data and feed failures into the eval set
questions.explanation:
The common mistake is to log only the final reply, or only errors. Agent failures often start several steps before the bad answer. A search might return the wrong product, the agent builds on it, and the reply looks fluent but is wrong. Without each step's input and output you cannot see where the run went off course.

Per-step traces serve two uses. One is debugging a single run: read it like a story, find the first step where the agent's view of the world was wrong, and fix that tool, prompt or data. The other is monitoring across all runs. Rates of tool errors, runs that hit the step cap, and cost per run show problems no single ticket reveals, such as a slow stock service adding seconds to every run. Recording model and prompt versions matters too, because it lets you tie a jump in failures to a specific change.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like hearing that traces close the loop with evaluation: real failures become test cases, so the same bug is caught before the next release. A useful extra is sampling. Keep full traces for failed and flagged runs and a sample of successful ones, which controls storage cost while keeping what you need.

questions.prompt:
Using pandas 3.x, ad spend by channel comes from two systems and is added together. What does the last line return? Give a whole number.

```python
import pandas as pd
spend = pd.Series([100, 250, 80], index=["search", "social", "email"])
extra = pd.Series([40, 60, 20], index=["social", "video", "search"])
total = spend + extra
total.mean()
```
questions.explanation:
Arithmetic between two Series lines them up by index label, not by position. The result's index is the union of both: email, search, social and video.

- search: 100 + 20 = 120
- social: 250 + 40 = 290
- email: only in `spend`, so NaN
- video: only in `extra`, so NaN

`mean()` skips NaN by default, so it averages the two real values: (120 + 290) / 2 = 205.

There are three common wrong paths. Adding by position gives 140, 310 and 100, with a mean of about 183.3. Treating NaN as 0 but still counting it gives 410 / 4 = 102.5. Assuming a missing channel counts as zero spend, which is what `spend.add(extra, fill_value=0)` does, gives 120, 290, 80 and 60, with a mean of 137.5. The last one may be what the business wants, but it is not what `+` does.
questions.deeper: Alignment is a feature, not a bug, but it hides data problems. Two NaN rows here mean two channels were silently dropped from the average. In pipelines, check `total.isna().sum()` after combining sources, and decide on purpose whether a missing key means zero or unknown.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce team trains a recommendation model with item embeddings and dense layers. They switch the optimizer from plain SGD, which uses one learning rate for every parameter, to Adam. What does Adam add?
options: It keeps running averages of each parameter's gradient and squared gradient, and divides the first by the root of the second, giving per-parameter step sizes.
It keeps a running average of each parameter's gradient and multiplies the learning rate by it, so parameters with larger gradients always take much larger steps.
It estimates the diagonal of the Hessian for each parameter using finite differences, and divides the gradient by it to take an exact Newton step.
It keeps a running average of each parameter's squared gradient and adds it to the loss as a penalty, which keeps the weights small during training.
questions.explanation:
Adam keeps two moving averages per parameter. The first, m, is an exponential average of recent gradients. That is momentum: it smooths out noise and keeps moving in a consistent direction. The second, v, is an exponential average of recent squared gradients, a running estimate of how large that parameter's gradients usually are. The update is roughly lr × m / (√v + ε), after a bias correction for both averages starting at zero. Dividing by √v means a parameter with consistently small gradients still takes a reasonable step, and one with huge gradients is reined in. The size of each step stays roughly bounded by the learning rate, whatever the raw gradient scale.

Multiplying the learning rate by the gradient average gets the effect backwards, since large gradients would then cause even larger steps. Adam's second moment is not a Hessian. It tracks gradient size, not curvature, and there are no finite differences or Newton steps. Adding squared gradients to the loss confuses Adam with a penalty such as weight decay. Adam changes how the update is computed, not the loss itself.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask about memory. Adam stores two extra numbers per parameter, so a model with 1 billion parameters needs about 8 GB of fp32 optimizer state on top of the weights. For large embedding tables, some teams use sparse or lazy variants that only update the rows seen in a batch.

questions.prompt: A mobile app runs an image classifier on the phone. Post-training quantization to int8 cost a small, acceptable drop in accuracy. Pushing the same method to 4-bit weights causes a large drop. You still have the training code and data. Which of these steps is most likely to win back most of the lost accuracy?
options: Use quantization-aware training, which simulates the 4-bit rounding in the forward pass while training, so the weights adapt to it and much of the accuracy returns.
Switch to dynamic quantization, which computes activation scales on the fly for each input image, so every image gets scales that fit it and the 4-bit error goes away.
Rerun post-training quantization with a much larger calibration set of training images, so the value ranges are estimated better and the 4-bit rounding error mostly disappears.
Also quantize the activations to 4 bits, since the large drop comes from mixing 4-bit weights with higher-precision activations inside the same layers of the network.
questions.explanation:
Post-training quantization rounds the weights of a model that was trained in full precision and never had to cope with rounding. At int8 the rounding steps are small, so the damage is small. At 4 bits there are only 16 levels, and the errors add up across layers. Quantization-aware training inserts simulated quantization into the forward pass and keeps training, passing gradients straight through the rounding, so the network adjusts its weights to work well at low precision. It costs extra training time but usually recovers much of the gap.

Dynamic quantization only computes activation scales on the fly for each input. The weights are still rounded to the same 16 levels, so their error stays. A bigger calibration set gives slightly better value ranges, but calibration only sets ranges. It cannot restore the information lost when trained weights are rounded to 16 levels, which is why int8 was fine and 4 bits was not. Quantizing activations to 4 bits adds more rounding error, which makes accuracy worse, not better. Keeping the most sensitive layers at higher precision is another sound fix, but it is not among the options.
questions.deeper: In interviews, mention the cheaper options to try before full quantization-aware training: stronger post-training methods that minimize each layer's output error, keeping sensitive layers such as the first and last at higher precision, and per-channel scales. Always measure accuracy on slices, since quantization damage is often uneven across classes.

questions.prompt: A search team scores each results page by adding up graded relevance labels, dividing each label by log₂(position + 1), and then dividing the total by the score of the best possible ordering of those same results. A perfect ranking scores 1. This metric is called ______.
questions.explanation:
The prompt walks through the three parts of the name. Cumulative gain is the sum of relevance labels. Discounted means each label is shrunk by log₂(position + 1), so a relevant result at rank 1 counts more than the same result at rank 8. Normalized means dividing by the ideal DCG, the score you would get by sorting the results from most to least relevant. That last step puts every query on a 0 to 1 scale, so queries with many relevant results do not dominate the average.

The common mistake is to answer DCG, which has the discount but not the division by the ideal score. Others answer MRR or MAP. MRR only looks at the rank of the first relevant result, and MAP works with binary relevant or not relevant labels, so neither uses graded labels the way described here.
questions.deeper: In practice you report NDCG@k, such as NDCG@10, because users rarely scroll further. A good interview follow-up is where the graded labels come from: human raters, or clicks and purchases, which carry position bias and need correction before you trust the metric.

questions.prompt: A legal-tech team fine-tunes a model on 20,000 examples. Each one has a contract excerpt and a question as the prompt, about 1,500 tokens in all, followed by a 100-token answer written by a lawyer. Why would they usually compute the loss on the answer tokens only?
options: Masking the prompt tokens hides them from attention, so the model has to answer from what it already knows and learns legal facts more deeply.
Loss on the prompt tokens is always close to zero, so including them wastes compute but leaves the size and direction of the gradient unchanged.
The prompt tokens have no gradient path to the weights, so a loss computed on them would make the backward pass fail with an error during training.
Most of the training signal would go to predicting contract text the model never has to write, leaving only a small share for the answers that matter.
questions.explanation:
In supervised fine-tuning, the goal is to teach the model how to respond. Here each example has about 1,500 prompt tokens and only 100 answer tokens. If every token counts in the loss, about 94% of the signal trains the model to predict contract wording and user questions, text it will only ever read and never write. Keeping the loss on the answer tokens focuses learning on the behaviour you want, and it stops the model from learning to imitate the user side of the chat.

The option about hiding prompt tokens confuses two separate masks. Loss masking only removes positions from the loss. The answer tokens still attend to the full contract, which they need to answer. The option claiming the prompt loss is near zero is wrong because contract text is far from trivially predictable, so it would change the gradient a lot. The option about a failing backward pass is wrong because prompt positions are computed by the same weights, so a loss on them trains those weights normally.
questions.deeper: In code this usually means setting the label at prompt positions to an ignore value so the loss skips them. A strong candidate adds that multi-turn chats mask every user turn, and that some teams keep a small weight on prompt tokens when prompts are rare, high-quality text worth learning from.

questions.subtopic: online quality signals for LLM features
questions.prompt: An airline's customer chatbot answers baggage and booking questions. Live conversations come with no ground-truth labels. Which of these signals tell the team something useful about answer quality in production? Select all that apply.
options: The share of conversations where the customer asks to speak to a human agent
BLEU overlap between each live answer and the reference answer for that question
How often users click to regenerate an answer or rephrase the same question
Average answer length in tokens, with longer answers read as more helpful
Scores from an LLM judge on a daily random sample of chats, checked against human reviewers
The validation loss recorded at the end of the model's last fine-tuning run
questions.explanation:
With no labels, you look for behaviour that shows an answer failed, and for an independent grade on a sample of answers. A request for a human is a strong sign the bot did not solve the problem. Regenerating or asking the same thing again suggests the first answer missed. A judge model that scores a random sample against a rubric gives a direct quality reading at low cost, and checking it against human reviewers on part of the sample shows whether the judge can be trusted.

BLEU needs a reference answer, and live questions do not come with one, so it cannot be computed. Even with references, word overlap rewards matching phrasing rather than being correct. Answer length is not quality. Longer answers can be padded or wrong, and judges and users can be swayed by length. The last fine-tuning validation loss is a single fixed number from before launch. It cannot change as live traffic changes, so it tells you nothing about current answers.
questions.deeper: Explicit ratings help too, but few users leave them and those who do skew unhappy, so treat them as a trend rather than a score. A strong candidate adds that behavioural signals need care: a customer may ask for a human because policy requires it, so compare rates over time and by topic rather than reading one number alone.

questions.prompt: You run PCA on six standardized sensor features from a delivery fleet. The eigenvalues of the components, from largest to smallest, are 3.0, 1.5, 0.9, 0.4, 0.15 and 0.05. What is the smallest number of components that together explain at least 95% of the variance? Give it as a whole number.
questions.explanation:
Each eigenvalue is the variance along its component, and the total variance is their sum: 3.0 + 1.5 + 0.9 + 0.4 + 0.15 + 0.05 = 6.0. Each component's share is its eigenvalue divided by 6.0, and you add the shares from the top.

- One component: 3.0 / 6.0 = 50%
- Two: 4.5 / 6.0 = 75%
- Three: 5.4 / 6.0 = 90%
- Four: 5.8 / 6.0 ≈ 96.7%

Three components fall short of 95% and four pass it, so the answer is 4.

A common mistake is to divide by the largest eigenvalue instead of the total. Another is to count the eigenvalues above 1, the Kaiser rule, which gives 2 here. That rule answers a different question and promises no particular share of variance.

The total of 6.0 is no accident. Standardized features each have variance 1, so the eigenvalues add up to the number of features.
questions.deeper: In practice you read this off a cumulative explained-variance plot. A strong candidate adds that 95% of the variance is not 95% of the useful signal. A low-variance component can still carry the pattern that predicts the target, so the number of components is better tuned on the downstream validation score.

questions.prompt: A retailer has 80,000 product photos, each labelled with one of 30 categories. Spot checks suggest about 8% of the labels are wrong. Which are sound ways to find and handle the mislabeled rows? Select all that apply.
options: Drop every photo with a high training loss, since mislabeled rows are the only hard ones to fit
Flag disagreements using the final model's predictions on the same photos it was trained on
Flag photos where out-of-fold predictions from cross-validation confidently disagree with the label
Send the flagged photos to reviewers, starting with the most confident disagreements
Train with a noise-robust loss, such as generalized cross-entropy, that caps the pull of badly misfit rows
questions.explanation:
Out-of-fold predictions come from a model that never saw that photo, so when it confidently predicts a different category than the label, the label is a good suspect. This is the core idea of confident learning. Sending the most confident disagreements to reviewers first spends the relabelling budget where errors are most likely, and reviewers can fix a label rather than lose the photo. A noise-robust loss handles the errors nobody reviews. Generalized cross-entropy scales each row's cross-entropy gradient by the predicted probability of its label raised to a small power, so rows the model is confident are labelled wrong pull the weights much less. Label smoothing is a milder cousin. It only stops the model from becoming fully certain of any label, and does not down-weight rows it badly misfits.

High training loss also marks rare categories, unusual angles and other hard but correct photos. Dropping all of them removes the data the model most needs and can wipe out small classes. The final model's predictions on its own training photos are a poor detector, because a flexible model memorises wrong labels and then agrees with them.
questions.deeper: Fix the evaluation set first. If 8% of test labels are wrong, accuracy differences of a few points between models may be noise. Interviewers often ask how you would confirm the cleanup helped: retrain and compare on a small expert-checked test set.

questions.prompt: Four stores have true daily sales of A = 100, B = 120, C = 140 and D = 200. A gradient boosting model with squared loss starts by predicting the mean of the targets for every store. The first tree, fitted to the residuals, puts A and B in one leaf and C and D in another, and each leaf predicts the mean residual of its stores. With a learning rate of 0.1, what is the model's prediction for store D after this first tree? Give it as a whole number.
questions.explanation:
With squared loss, gradient boosting fits each new tree to the residuals, the true value minus the current prediction.

Step 1, the starting prediction: the mean of 100, 120, 140 and 200 is 560 / 4 = 140.

Step 2, the residuals: A = −40, B = −20, C = 0, D = 60.

Step 3, the leaf value for D: D shares a leaf with C, so the leaf predicts (0 + 60) / 2 = 30.

Step 4, the update: 140 + 0.1 × 30 = 143.

Two mistakes are common. Using D's own residual instead of the leaf value gives 140 + 0.1 × 60 = 146, but a tree outputs one value per leaf, shared by every row in it. Forgetting the learning rate gives 140 + 30 = 170. The small learning rate is deliberate. Each tree corrects only a tenth of the error it sees, and later trees keep chipping away at what remains, which tends to generalise better than one big jump.
questions.deeper: A good follow-up is how this changes for other losses. For log loss the trees fit the negative gradient, which is the label minus the predicted probability, and leaf values come from a Newton step rather than a plain mean. Libraries such as XGBoost also add a regularisation term that shrinks each leaf value.

questions.prompt: A sales assistant is asked "How many units of SKU-114, SKU-209 and SKU-377 are in stock?" In a single turn, the model returns three calls to `get_stock(sku)`, each with its own call ID. The stock service answers in the order 377, 114, 209, and each answer looks like `{"available": 12}` with no SKU in it. How should the app hand the results back?
options: Return all three results before the next model call, each one tagged with the ID of the call it answers.
Send each result as soon as it arrives and call the model after every one, so it sees fresh data sooner.
Join the three results into one text block in the order they finished, so the model can read them together.
Reject the turn and ask for one call at a time, since calls made in the same turn can race and corrupt each other.
questions.explanation:
The three lookups do not depend on each other, so the model can ask for them in one turn and the app can run them at the same time. The call IDs are how each result finds its way back. Because every answer looks like `{"available": 12}`, the ID is the only thing that tells the model which number belongs to which SKU. The model asked for three things in one turn, so it should get all three answers before its next step.

Calling the model after each result triples the model calls and leaves it working with a partial picture. It may answer with one SKU missing or ask again for calls that are already running. Joining results in the order they finished is the real trap here. The order was 377, 114, 209, not the order requested, and nothing in the content says which is which, so the model would likely give the wrong count for each SKU. Rejecting the turn is wrong for read-only lookups like these. Racing is only a worry when calls change shared state or when one call needs another's result, and in that case the model should ask for them in separate turns.
questions.deeper: A good follow-up point is dependent calls. If the model needs a customer ID before it can look up that customer's orders, those must run in sequence. Some teams also run parallel calls only for tools marked read-only, and serialize anything that writes.

questions.prompt: A one-feature model predicts delivery time as ŷ = w·x + b and is trained on the squared error L = (ŷ − y)². For one order, x = 2.5 and y = 4, and the current parameters are w = 0.8 and b = 0.5. What is ∂L/∂w at these values? Give the answer to 1 decimal place, with its sign.
questions.explanation:
Work forward first, then apply the chain rule backward.

- Forward: ŷ = 0.8 × 2.5 + 0.5 = 2.5, so ŷ − y = 2.5 − 4 = −1.5
- ∂L/∂ŷ = 2(ŷ − y) = 2 × (−1.5) = −3
- ∂ŷ/∂w = x = 2.5
- ∂L/∂w = −3 × 2.5 = −7.5

The negative sign says the loss falls if w grows, which makes sense because the prediction is too low. Gradient descent subtracts the gradient, so with a learning rate of 0.01 the new w would be 0.8 + 0.075 = 0.875.

The common mistakes are dropping the factor 2 from the square, which gives −3.75, and forgetting to multiply by x, which gives −3. That second value is actually the gradient for b, since ∂ŷ/∂b = 1. The other classic slip is a flipped sign, from differentiating (y − ŷ)² and forgetting the −1 from the inner term. A flipped sign sends the update the wrong way.
questions.deeper: Backpropagation in a deep network is this same move repeated: each node multiplies the gradient arriving from above by its own local derivative. Interviewers sometimes ask for the batch version in NumPy. For mean squared error over n rows, the gradient for the weights becomes (2/n) Xᵀ(ŷ − y).

questions.prompt: You review PyTorch training code for a 10-class image classifier and a separate price regressor, both trained on a CUDA GPU. Which of these are real bugs? Select all that apply.
options: The model is moved with `model.to("cuda")`, but each input batch stays on the CPU
The classifier ends in `softmax`, and that output is passed to `nn.CrossEntropyLoss`
The regressor outputs shape (batch, 1), its targets have shape (batch,), and both go to `nn.MSELoss`
Classifier targets are class indices of dtype long rather than one-hot vectors
`optimizer.zero_grad()` runs at the start of each step, before the forward pass
Validation runs under `model.eval()` and `torch.no_grad()`, then `model.train()` is called again
questions.explanation:
Three of these are bugs, and only one of them crashes.

- Model weights on the GPU and inputs on the CPU cannot be combined, so the first layer raises a runtime error about tensors on different devices. Each batch needs `.to(device)` too.
- `nn.CrossEntropyLoss` applies log-softmax itself and expects raw logits. Feeding it softmax output applies softmax twice. The inputs are squeezed into 0 to 1, gradients shrink and the model trains slowly or stalls, with no error.
- Shapes (batch, 1) and (batch,) broadcast to (batch, batch) inside `MSELoss`, so every prediction is compared with every target. PyTorch emits a UserWarning about the size mismatch but does not raise, so training runs on. The loss pulls every prediction toward the mean price of the batch, and the model learns little about individual items.

The other three are correct code. Class indices of dtype long are exactly the target format `CrossEntropyLoss` is built for. Zeroing gradients at the start of the step is as good as zeroing right after `step()`, since either way they are cleared before the next `backward()`. Switching to eval mode with `no_grad()` for validation, then back to train mode, is the textbook pattern.
questions.deeper: Silent bugs are what interviewers probe. A good habit is to assert shapes before the loss, overfit a single small batch to confirm the loss can reach near zero, and check that the initial classification loss is close to ln(10) ≈ 2.3 for 10 balanced classes.

questions.prompt: A job-matching site has 2 million job postings. A transformer encodes each posting into a vector once, offline, and stores it. When a candidate searches, the same kind of model encodes only the candidate's profile, and the site finds the nearest posting vectors. Because the query and each document are encoded separately and only meet as vectors at the end, this retrieval model is called a ______.
questions.explanation:
A bi-encoder runs the query and the document through the encoder separately and compares the two vectors with a similarity score such as cosine. The key benefit is that document vectors do not depend on the query, so all 2 million postings can be encoded ahead of time. At search time the system encodes one profile and runs a fast nearest-neighbour search, which takes milliseconds.

The common wrong answer is "cross-encoder", which is the opposite design. A cross-encoder takes the query and one document together as a single input, so attention can link every word in one to every word in the other. That gives more accurate relevance scores, but nothing can be computed ahead of time, and scoring 2 million postings would need 2 million model passes per search. This is why the two are often combined: the bi-encoder fetches a shortlist, and a cross-encoder reranks it. "Embedding model" describes what a bi-encoder produces, not the design the question asks about, which is encoding the two sides separately.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask how to make a bi-encoder more accurate without losing its speed. Good answers include fine-tuning it on your own query and match pairs, adding hard negatives that look relevant but are not, and putting a cross-encoder reranker on the top 50 to 100 results.

questions.prompt:
A support-ticket router sorts 1,000 tickets into three classes. For each class, here is how many tickets it predicted and how many of those predictions were right:

- Billing: predicted 600, correct 540
- Technical: predicted 350, correct 315
- Legal: predicted 50, correct 15

Each ticket gets exactly one predicted class. What is micro-averaged precision minus macro-averaged precision? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
