Macro averaging computes precision for each class, then takes the plain mean. Billing is 540 / 600 = 0.90, technical is 315 / 350 = 0.90 and legal is 15 / 50 = 0.30. The macro average is (0.90 + 0.90 + 0.30) / 3 = 0.70.

Micro averaging pools the counts first: (540 + 315 + 15) / (600 + 350 + 50) = 870 / 1,000 = 0.87. Since every ticket gets exactly one label, micro precision here equals plain accuracy.

The gap is 0.87 − 0.70 = 0.17. Micro weights each class by how often it is predicted, so the 50 legal predictions barely move it. Macro gives legal a full third of the vote, so its weak 0.30 drags the average down.

The common mistake is to weight each class precision by how many tickets that class predicted and call the result macro. (0.90 × 600 + 0.90 × 350 + 0.30 × 50) / 1,000 = 0.87, which is the micro figure again, and the gap wrongly disappears.
questions.deeper: Which average to report depends on what matters. If legal tickets carry the most risk, macro or a per-class table keeps their poor precision visible, while micro hides it behind the big classes. Scikit-learn also offers a weighted average, which weights each class by its number of true tickets.

questions.prompt: An ad click model uses logistic regression on 50,000 sparse one-hot features. You suspect only a few hundred features really matter, and you want a smaller model that is cheaper to serve and easier to inspect. Which regularization fits best, and why?
options: L1, because its penalty can push many weights to exactly zero and leave a sparse model.
L2, because its squared penalty pushes small weights to exactly zero faster than L1 does.
L2, because it keeps only one feature from each group of correlated features and drops the rest.
L1, because it shrinks every weight by the same fraction, so the ranking of features is kept.
questions.explanation:
L1 adds λ × Σ|w| to the loss. Its pull on each weight has the same size, λ, no matter how small the weight already is. So a weight that does not earn its keep gets pushed all the way to zero and stays there. You end up with a sparse model where most of the 50,000 weights are exactly zero, which is what you want for cheap serving and inspection.

L2 adds λ × Σw². Its pull is 2λw, which gets weaker as the weight shrinks, so weights get small but almost never reach exactly zero. That rules out the option claiming L2 zeros weights faster. Keeping one feature from a correlated group is closer to how L1 behaves. L2 spreads weight across correlated features instead. Shrinking every weight by the same fraction describes L2 in a simple case, while L1 subtracts a fixed amount and clips at zero.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often follow up with correlated features. L1 tends to pick one of a correlated group almost at random, which makes the chosen features unstable across retrains. Elastic net mixes L1 and L2 to get sparsity while keeping correlated groups together, and it is a common default in click and fraud models with huge sparse inputs.

questions.prompt: A travel company is adding LLM features in three places: suggesting city names as the user types in the search box, sorting incoming customer emails into 12 categories, and an assistant that builds multi-city itineraries that must respect a budget, layover limits and visa rules. A teammate wants to use a reasoning model, or chain-of-thought prompting, everywhere. Which features would you give extra reasoning to, and how would you decide?
questions.answer: I would not use reasoning everywhere, because it adds output tokens, cost and seconds of latency. City suggestions need answers in well under a second and are simple lookups, so a small fast model or plain search fits. Email sorting is mostly pattern matching, so I would start without reasoning and add it only if a held-out test shows gains on a hard slice, such as emails that raise several issues. The itinerary planner is a true multi-step problem with constraints that interact, so reasoning is likely to cut errors there, and users accept a few seconds of wait for it. To decide, I would build an eval set for each feature, compare accuracy with and without reasoning, and weigh the gain against the latency budget and token cost per request. I could also route only hard cases to the reasoning path and cap its reasoning budget.
points: Reasoning adds tokens, cost and latency, so it must earn its place
Autocomplete has a tight latency budget and a simple task, so no reasoning
Classification usually gains little, so test before adding it
Multi-step constrained planning is where reasoning helps most
Decide with per-feature evals that weigh accuracy against latency and cost
Route only hard cases or cap the reasoning budget
questions.explanation:
Chain-of-thought and reasoning models help when a task needs several dependent steps, such as checking a route against a budget, then a layover rule, then a visa rule. Writing out intermediate steps gives the model room to work before it commits to an answer. That help is paid for in generated tokens, which cost money and add latency roughly in proportion to their number.

The common mistake is to treat reasoning as a free accuracy boost and turn it on everywhere. For autocomplete, even a short reasoning trace breaks the response time users expect, and the task has no multi-step logic to gain from. For classification, gains are often small. The opposite mistake is to reject reasoning on cost alone, when one wrong itinerary that breaks a visa rule costs far more than a few thousand extra tokens. The right answer comes from measuring each feature, not from a blanket rule.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like candidates who frame this as a routing problem. A cheap model handles most traffic, and a classifier or confidence signal sends hard cases to the reasoning path. A strong answer also mentions tracking reasoning token counts in monitoring, since they can grow quietly and raise both latency and the bill.

questions.prompt: Design an image moderation system for a social app that receives 10 million uploads a day. The policy bans nudity, graphic violence and hate symbols. Cover the main components, how decisions get made, and how you would measure and improve the system.
questions.answer: Start with a written policy and labelling guide, since the model can only be as clear as the rules. On upload, run cheap checks first: hash matching against known banned images, then a fast classifier for each policy category. Images with high scores are removed at once, images with low scores are published, and the uncertain middle goes to human reviewers, with the most severe categories first in the queue. Set thresholds per category from the cost of each kind of error and the size of the review team. Users can appeal, and appeals go to a second reviewer. Reviewer decisions and appeal outcomes become new training labels. Measure precision and recall per category on audited samples, the prevalence of violating images that users saw, review queue time and the appeal overturn rate. Watch for evasion such as cropped or edited images, and audit error rates across user groups.
points: A clear policy and labelling guide as the foundation
A cascade: hash matching, fast classifiers, then humans for unclear cases
Thresholds per category, set by error costs and reviewer capacity
Human review for uncertain cases plus an appeals path
Review and appeal decisions feed back as training labels
Metrics: per-category precision and recall, prevalence, queue time, overturn rate
questions.explanation:
At 10 million uploads a day nobody can look at everything, and no model is accurate enough to act alone on every case. A cascade solves both problems. Cheap steps handle the clear cases at scale and people handle the hard ones. Hash matching catches re-uploads of known content almost for free. Thresholds turn scores into three outcomes: remove, publish or review.

The common mistake is to describe only the classifier. Interviewers want the system around it: who owns the policy, how much review capacity exists, how errors are found and how users can push back. Thresholds also differ by category. Missing a hate symbol and wrongly removing a beach photo carry very different costs, so one global cut-off is a weak design.

The feedback loop is what improves the system over time. But review labels only cover what the model sent to review, so you also need random audits of auto-approved images to measure what slipped through.
questions.deeper: Strong candidates bring numbers. If 2% of uploads land in the review band, that is 200,000 images a day, and at 1,000 reviews per reviewer per day you need about 200 reviewers. That figure often forces the thresholds to move. Good answers also mention reviewer wellbeing, since people will see graphic content all day.

questions.prompt: A fraud scoring service has an SLO that 99.95% of requests succeed over each 30-day month. It handles an average of 1,500 requests per second. How many failed requests can it have in a month and still meet the SLO? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation:
The error budget is the share of requests allowed to fail, applied to the month's total traffic.

- Seconds in 30 days: 30 × 24 × 60 × 60 = 2,592,000
- Requests in the month: 1,500 × 2,592,000 = 3,888,000,000
- Allowed failure share: 1 − 0.9995 = 0.0005
- Error budget: 3,888,000,000 × 0.0005 = 1,944,000 failed requests

The common mistake is reading 99.95% as leaving 0.5% to fail. That moves the decimal one place and gives 19,440,000, ten times too many. Another slip is using 0.05 instead of 0.0005 by forgetting to divide the percentage by 100.

Two million failures sounds large, but it is a fixed budget. A bad deploy failing 10% of requests would use 150 failures per second and burn the whole month's budget in about 3.6 hours.
questions.deeper: Teams use the budget to make decisions, not just to report. If half of it is gone in the first week, risky launches pause. A good interview answer also mentions burn-rate alerts, which fire when the budget is being spent fast enough to run out before the month ends.

questions.prompt: Fine-tuning a vision model on one GPU at a batch size of 64 fails with an out-of-memory error. Which of these changes reduce peak GPU memory during training? Select all that apply.
options: Mixed-precision training, which keeps most activations in 16-bit rather than 32-bit floats
Gradient checkpointing, which keeps only some activations in the forward pass and recomputes the rest during backward
Gradient accumulation, which runs several small micro-batches and sums their gradients before one optimizer step
Switching the optimizer from SGD with momentum to Adam, since Adam usually converges in fewer steps
Adding dropout after every layer, since it sets a share of the activations to zero during training
Raising the learning rate so the model reaches the target loss in fewer total training steps
questions.explanation:
Peak training memory is mostly weights, gradients, optimizer state and the activations saved for the backward pass. Mixed precision stores most activations in 16 bits, roughly halving them. Gradient checkpointing saves activations at only some layers and recomputes the rest during the backward pass, trading about one extra forward pass of compute for a large cut in activation memory. Gradient accumulation splits a batch into micro-batches, so only one micro-batch's activations are in memory at a time while the effective batch size stays the same.

Switching to Adam adds memory, because Adam keeps two running averages per parameter where SGD with momentum keeps one. Dropout frees nothing. The zeroed activations still occupy the same tensor, and the dropout mask is stored as well. Raising the learning rate may shorten training, but the number of steps does not change how much memory any single step needs.
questions.deeper: A common follow-up is why mixed precision does not halve weight memory: many setups keep an fp32 master copy of the weights plus fp32 optimizer state. For very large models, strong candidates mention sharding optimizer state, gradients and weights across GPUs, and offloading some of it to CPU memory.

questions.prompt: On a plant disease photo dataset, a plain 50-layer CNN ends up with higher **training** error than a plain 18-layer one, even though the deeper model could in principle copy the shallow one and make its extra layers pass their input through. Adding skip connections, so each block outputs x + F(x), lets the 50-layer model beat the 18-layer one. Why do skip connections help here?
options: The derivative of x + F(x) has an identity term, so gradients reach early layers directly, and a block can pass its input on by pushing F to 0.
Skip connections act as a regularizer much like dropout does, so the deeper network stops overfitting the training photos and generalizes better.
Skip connections reduce the number of trainable weights inside each block, so the deeper network has far fewer parameters that it needs to fit.
Adding the input back rescales each block's output to zero mean and unit variance, so activations stay stable much as they do with batch norm.
questions.explanation:
The puzzle in the prompt is the degradation problem. A deeper plain network should be able to match a shallower one, yet the optimizer fails to find that solution and training error gets worse. With a skip connection, the block computes x + F(x). Its derivative with respect to x is the identity plus ∂F/∂x, so during backprop the gradient from later layers reaches earlier ones through the identity term, not only through a long product of layer derivatives. The block also finds identity easy: if its layers are not useful, the optimizer only has to drive F toward zero, which is far easier than making a stack of nonlinear layers reproduce their input exactly.

The regularization option fails on the evidence. The deeper plain model was worse on training error, so the problem is fitting, not overfitting. An identity skip adds no weights and removes none, so the parameter option is wrong. Adding x to F(x) does not normalize anything. Without normalization the variance of the sum tends to grow with depth, which is why residual networks still use normalization layers.
questions.deeper: Transformers rely on the same idea, since every attention and feed-forward sublayer adds onto a residual stream. A strong answer notes that when a block changes the shape, the skip path uses a 1×1 convolution or a linear projection. Interviewers may ask why residual branches are often initialized to output near zero at the start of training.

questions.prompt: A food delivery app wants to predict, at the moment a customer places an order, how many minutes until it arrives. You have raw logs of orders (time, restaurant, customer location, items), restaurant events (order accepted, food ready) and courier events (GPS pings, assignment, pickup, drop-off). What features would you build, and what mistakes would you avoid?
questions.answer: Time features: hour of day, day of week and a holiday flag, with cyclical encoding if the model is linear. Order features: number of items, basket value and distance from restaurant to customer. Rolling aggregates computed only from events before the order time: the restaurant's median prep time over the last 7 days and last hour, how many orders are in its queue now, couriers free within 2 km, and recent average delivery time in the zone. For restaurant and zone IDs, use out-of-fold or past-only target encoding with smoothing, or let a tree model handle them. Avoid anything known only after the order is placed, such as the food-ready time, courier assignment or pickup time. Build training rows with point-in-time joins so each aggregate matches what the live system could compute, and use the same feature code offline and online.
points: Hour, weekday and holiday features
Distance and basket size from the order itself
Rolling prep time, queue length and courier supply computed only from earlier events
Leak-safe encoding of restaurant and zone IDs
Exclude post-order fields such as food-ready, assignment or pickup times
Point-in-time joins and shared feature code for training and serving
questions.explanation:
Delivery time is prep time plus courier wait plus travel, so good features describe each part as it looks at the moment of ordering. Rolling aggregates carry most of the signal: a restaurant that is slow tonight will likely stay slow for the next order.

The most common mistake is leakage from the logs themselves. Food-ready and pickup times are in the same tables and are extremely predictive, but they do not exist when the customer taps order. A model trained with them looks excellent offline and fails live. A subtler version is a rolling average computed over a full day, which includes deliveries that finished after this order was placed. Target encoding of restaurants leaks in the same way unless it uses only past data or other folds. Finally, if offline features come from a batch job and live ones from a different service, small differences in logic cause training-serving skew.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate also mentions updating the estimate after the order, when food-ready and pickup events arrive. That is a different model, or the same model with a prediction time per stage, and each stage may only use events before its own prediction time.

questions.prompt: A convolutional network spots defects in photos of circuit boards. It reaches 98% training accuracy but only 81% validation accuracy, and validation loss starts rising after epoch 12. Which actions are likely to reduce the overfitting? Select all that apply.
options: Collect more labelled board photos
Increase the weight decay (L2 penalty)
Stop training at the epoch with the lowest validation loss
Add more convolutional layers to the network
Train for more epochs until training loss reaches zero
Remove the dropout layers so every unit is always used
questions.explanation:
Overfitting means the model has learned details of the training photos that do not carry over to new ones. The fixes either give it more varied data or limit how closely it can fit.

More labelled photos make it harder to memorise individual examples, so the model has to learn patterns that hold across boards. Stronger weight decay penalises large weights and pushes the network toward simpler functions. Early stopping keeps the weights from the point where validation loss was lowest, before the model started fitting noise, which is exactly what the rising loss after epoch 12 signals.

Adding layers increases capacity, which usually makes overfitting worse. Training until training loss hits zero is the memorising this question is about. Removing dropout takes away a regularizer, since dropout forces the network not to rely on any single unit. All three wrong options push in the direction of more fitting, not less.
questions.deeper: In practice, data augmentation such as flips, small rotations and lighting changes is often the cheapest win for image models, because it adds variety without new labels. An interviewer may ask how to tell when more data will help: plot a learning curve and see whether validation error is still falling as the training set grows.

questions.prompt: A legal research tool ranks court rulings for each query. Each training query has 200 or so candidate rulings graded by lawyers from 0 (irrelevant) to 3 (key ruling). Users rarely read past the first page, so the team judges models by NDCG@10. Which training loss fits this goal best, and why?
options: A pointwise regression loss, because predicting each grade exactly is the same thing as getting the order right.
A pairwise loss that counts every wrongly ordered pair equally, because NDCG@10 also counts each swap the same.
A pointwise classification loss, because queries with many candidates would otherwise dominate a listwise loss.
A listwise loss, because it optimises a smooth stand-in for the list metric, so mistakes at the top cost most.
questions.explanation:
NDCG@10 cares about order, and mostly about order at the very top. A listwise loss looks at all candidates for a query together and approximates the list metric, so pushing a grade 3 ruling from slot 12 to slot 1 earns far more than tidying up slots 150 to 160. That matches the goal.

Pointwise regression treats each ruling alone. A model can predict grades fairly well and still order the top few wrongly, and it spends as much effort on rulings deep in the list as on the top ten. Plain pairwise loss is closer, since it learns order, but treating every swapped pair alike is the problem. NDCG discounts by position, so a swap at slots 1 and 2 matters far more than one at 180 and 181. A pairwise loss that weights each swap by how much it changes NDCG, as LambdaRank does, would also fit the goal, which is why the equal weighting in that option is the flaw. The claim about long queries is backwards. Pointwise losses let queries with many rows dominate, while listwise losses usually treat each query as one unit.
questions.deeper: A good follow-up is when pointwise is the right call: when you need calibrated scores, such as click probabilities for an ads auction, or when labels are sparse binary clicks. Strong candidates also mention LambdaRank-style methods, which weight pairwise gradients by the change in NDCG and sit between pairwise and listwise.

questions.prompt:
A courier's model predicts the chance that each parcel arrives late. Four parcels come back:

- Late, predicted 0.9
- On time, predicted 0.2
- Late, predicted 0.8
- On time, predicted 0.99

The numbers are the predicted probability of being late. Using the natural log, what is the mean log loss over the four parcels? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Log loss charges −ln of the probability the model gave to what really happened. For a late parcel that is −ln(p), and for an on-time parcel it is −ln(1 − p).

- Late at 0.9: −ln(0.9) ≈ 0.105
- On time at 0.2: −ln(0.8) ≈ 0.223
- Late at 0.8: −ln(0.8) ≈ 0.223
- On time at 0.99: −ln(0.01) ≈ 4.605

The sum is about 5.157, and the mean is 5.157 / 4 ≈ 1.29.

The last parcel does almost all the damage. The model was 99% sure it would be late, and it was not. Without it, the mean of the other three is only about 0.18. Log loss grows without limit as the probability given to the true outcome nears zero.

The common mistake is to use −ln(p) for every row, including the on-time parcels. That gives about 0.49, because it charges the confident wrong prediction almost nothing and charges the good 0.2 prediction heavily.
questions.deeper: This is why libraries clip probabilities away from exactly 0 and 1, and why one mislabelled row can wreck a leaderboard score. In an interview, mention that log loss judges calibration as well as ranking, so two models with the same AUC can have very different log loss.

questions.prompt: In a bank's customer chatbot, guardrails run before and after the main model call. Which statements about what these guardrails do are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An input moderation check can stop abusive or clearly harmful requests before the main model spends any tokens on them.
A PII filter on the output can mask an account number the model copied from a retrieved record before the user sees it.
Schema validation on the output can catch a tool call missing a required field before it reaches the payments code.
A topic limit on the input, which keeps the bot to banking, also stops it from making factual errors on banking questions.
Output checks add no delay to streamed replies, because they can run after the user has finished reading the reply.
A PII filter on the user's own message stops the model from revealing another customer's data in its reply.
questions.explanation:
Each guardrail catches one kind of problem at one point. Input moderation runs before the main call, so a blocked request costs only the small check, not a full model call. An output PII filter is the last chance to catch an account number that came in through retrieval and was copied into the reply. Schema validation checks the shape of a structured output, so a broken tool call is rejected or retried instead of crashing or misleading the code downstream.

A topic limit controls scope, not accuracy. The bot can stay on banking and still quote the wrong overdraft fee, which is a job for grounding and evaluation. Output checks on a streamed reply always cost something. You either hold text back until it passes, which adds delay, or check as you go and risk showing text you then have to withdraw. Checking after the user has read the reply defeats the purpose. A filter on the user's message protects what the user sends, but the leak here comes from retrieved data, so only an output check or access control on retrieval can stop it.
questions.deeper: Strong candidates weigh each check's cost. A small classifier or rule adds little delay, while an LLM-based check can add nearly as much as the main call, so input checks often run in parallel with it, accepting some wasted tokens on blocked requests in exchange for lower latency. They also track each guardrail's false-positive rate, since a filter that blocks real customers is a product failure.

questions.prompt: A chat model has 32 layers and 32 query heads per layer, but it uses grouped-query attention with 8 key-value heads per layer. Each head has dimension 128. The KV cache stores keys and values in fp16 (2 bytes per number). How much memory does the KV cache need for a batch of 16 sequences, each 4,096 tokens long? Give the answer in GB, where 1 GB = 10⁹ bytes, to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation:
For every token, every layer stores one key vector and one value vector for each key-value head. So the size is 2 (key and value) × layers × KV heads × head dimension × tokens × batch × bytes per number.

- Per token per layer: 2 × 8 × 128 = 2,048 numbers
- Per token across 32 layers: 2,048 × 32 = 65,536 numbers, or 131,072 bytes
- Tokens in the batch: 4,096 × 16 = 65,536
- Total: 131,072 × 65,536 = 8,589,934,592 bytes, about 8.6 GB

The most common mistake is to use the 32 query heads, which gives four times as much, about 34.4 GB. With grouped-query attention, several query heads share one key-value head, and only the shared key-value heads are cached. Another mistake is to forget the factor of 2 for keys and values, which gives about 4.3 GB. An answer of 8.0 means the bytes were divided by 2³⁰ instead of 10⁹.
questions.deeper: This calculation drives serving capacity. At long contexts the KV cache can outgrow the weights themselves, which limits how many requests fit on a GPU at once. Strong candidates mention the levers: grouped-query or multi-query attention, a quantized KV cache, paged cache allocation to cut fragmentation, and capping context length.

questions.prompt: A team plans a two-week A/B test of a new checkout flow on a fixed amount of traffic, with conversion rate as the metric. All else equal, which change would raise the test's statistical power?
questions.explanation:
Power is the chance that the test detects an effect that is really there. It rises with larger samples, larger true effects, less noise in the metric, and a higher significance level α. Moving α from 1% to 5% lowers the bar for calling a result significant, so a real effect clears it more often. The price is more false positives, the usual trade between type I and type II errors.

Each other option cuts power. Splitting traffic across three variants leaves each arm with a third of the users instead of half, so every comparison has a smaller sample. A noisier metric widens the spread of the estimated difference, so the same true effect is harder to tell apart from chance. Stopping after one week halves the sample, and power falls with it. Stopping early also tempts teams to peek at results, which inflates false positives unless the test uses a sequential design.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask for the four levers of power and then which ones a team actually controls. Sample size and α are choices, and metric noise can be cut with variance reduction such as CUPED. The effect size is mostly set by the product change itself, which is why teams fix a minimum detectable effect before launch.
options: Testing at the 5% significance level instead of the planned 1%.
Splitting the same traffic across three variants instead of two.
Making revenue per user, which is much noisier, the main metric.
Stopping the test after one week instead of two to ship sooner.

questions.prompt: A marketing tool writes a promotional email with one model call. A second call, with its own prompt, grades the draft against the brand's rules and returns specific feedback, such as "the discount is stated twice". The first call then revises, and the loop repeats until the grader passes the draft or 3 rounds are used up. Alongside prompt chaining, routing, parallelization and orchestrator-workers, this common workflow pattern is called the ______ pattern.
questions.explanation:
In the evaluator-optimizer pattern, one call generates and another evaluates, and the evaluator's feedback goes back to the generator for another try. It works when two things hold: there are clear criteria the evaluator can check, and a revision guided by feedback really does improve the output. Brand rules for an email meet both.

The common mistake is to answer reflection. Reflection usually means a model critiques and revises its own output, often inside one agent loop, and it is the broader idea behind this pattern. The named workflow pattern that sits in the same list as chaining and routing, with a separate grader call and a pass or fail gate, is evaluator-optimizer. Note also the round limit. Without a cap, a strict grader and a generator that cannot satisfy it will loop forever and burn tokens. The grader also needs to give specific feedback, since a bare fail gives the generator nothing to fix.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate mentions that the grader can be the weak point. If it shares the generator's blind spots, the loop polishes errors instead of catching them. Teams often mix code checks, such as length or banned phrases, with the model grader, and they measure whether later rounds actually raise quality before paying for them.

questions.prompt: A lender's default model went live three months ago. The label is whether a loan defaults within 12 months, and no loan has reached the end of that window yet. What can the team usefully monitor right now? Select all that apply.
options: The distribution of each input feature compared with training, for example with PSI
The distribution of predicted risk scores and the share of applicants approved
Null rates, out-of-range values and schema changes in incoming requests
Precision and recall on the 12-month default label for the loans issued so far
The share of approved borrowers who miss their first monthly payment
AUC on recent applications, using the model's own approve or decline decision as the label
questions.explanation:
Without labels you can still watch the inputs, the outputs and fast proxies for the outcome. Feature drift checks such as PSI show whether applicants now look different from the training data. Prediction drift, a shift in the score distribution or the approval rate, is often the first sign that something upstream changed. Data quality checks catch broken pipelines, such as a field that suddenly arrives empty, which can quietly wreck predictions. A missed first payment arrives within weeks and is strongly linked to later default, so it works as an early proxy.

Precision and recall on the 12-month label need that label, and no loan has it yet. Scoring the few early defaults against everyone else would count future defaulters as good loans. The AUC idea is a trap. Using the model's own decision as the label measures how well the model agrees with itself, so it will look excellent whatever the true quality is. None of the label-free signals prove the model is still accurate. They tell you where to look and when to worry.
questions.deeper: A strong answer also raises the selection problem. Declined applicants never get a loan, so their outcome is never seen, and the labels that do arrive come only from people the model approved. Some lenders approve a small random slice of borderline applicants to keep a less biased view of performance.

questions.subtopic: how mixture of experts saves compute
questions.prompt: A team plans to self-host a mixture-of-experts model with 16 experts in each MoE layer. A router sends every token to 2 of them. The model has 40B parameters in total, but only about 9B are used for any one token. What should they expect when serving it?
options: Compute per token is close to a 9B dense model, but GPU memory must hold all 40B parameters, as any token can be routed to any expert.
GPU memory only needs about 9B parameters, because just the experts picked for the current token are loaded while the rest wait on disk.
Compute per token matches a 40B dense model, because every expert processes every token and the router only weights their outputs.
Each expert is a full separate model, so a request runs end to end on the 2 best-matched experts while the other 14 stay idle for it.
questions.explanation:
In an MoE layer, the feed-forward block is replaced by many expert networks plus a router. For each token, at each MoE layer, the router picks the top 2 experts and only those run. That is why the active parameters, about 9B here, are far below the 40B total, and why compute per token is close to a 9B dense model. Shared parts such as attention and embeddings run for every token, which is why 9B is more than 2/16 of 40B.

Memory is the catch. Different tokens in the same batch, and even the same token at different layers, go to different experts, so every expert must be loaded and ready. Swapping experts in from disk for each token would be far too slow, so the option about holding only 9B is wrong. The option where every expert runs describes a dense model and would remove the compute saving. The option about routing whole requests is wrong because routing happens per token and per layer, not once per request.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often follow up on load balancing. If the router sends most tokens to a few favourite experts, those experts become bottlenecks and the others barely train, so MoE training adds an auxiliary loss that spreads tokens out. In serving, experts are often spread across GPUs, called expert parallelism, which adds communication between devices.

questions.prompt:
A fraud model scores each card transaction at the moment it happens. A teammate builds this pandas 3.x feature, gets 0.99 AUC offline, and then sees the model do much worse in production. What is the problem, and what is the right fix?

```python
tx = tx.sort_values(["card", "ts"])
tx["fraud_rate_3"] = (
    tx.groupby("card")["is_fraud"]
      .transform(lambda s: s.rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean())
)
```
options: Each row's window includes its own `is_fraud` label. Inside each card group, shift by one before rolling.
Early rows have fewer than three past values. Set `min_periods=3` so every window is full and fair.
The rolling window mixes transactions from different cards. Sort by `ts` alone before grouping.
Each row's window includes its own `is_fraud` label. Shift the whole column by one, then group and roll.
questions.explanation:
A rolling window ends at the current row and includes it. So `fraud_rate_3` for a transaction averages its own `is_fraud` label with the two before it. Any row labelled fraud gets a higher feature value, and the model learns to read its answer off the feature. In production that label does not exist yet when the transaction is scored, so the signal vanishes. The fix is `s.shift(1).rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean()` inside the per-card transform, so each row only sees earlier transactions on the same card.

The option that shifts the whole column before grouping finds the right problem but breaks the fix. The first row of each card would receive the last label of the previous card, which in this sort order is usually a later transaction from someone else. Setting `min_periods=3` only blanks early rows and still includes the current label. The claim that cards are mixed is false, because the groupby already keeps each card separate, and sorting by `ts` alone would not remove the leak.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds that fraud labels arrive late, often weeks later through chargebacks. Shifting by one row assumes the previous label was known at scoring time. A safer feature only uses labels whose confirmation date is before the current transaction, which is point-in-time correctness.

questions.prompt: A logistics team fits ordinary least squares to predict delivery time in minutes from route distance in km, number of stops and hour of day. They plan to report a 95% confidence interval and a p-value for each coefficient. Which assumptions does that inference rely on? Select all that apply.
options: The expected delivery time is a linear function of the features as entered in the model.
The errors on different deliveries are independent of one another.
The spread of the errors is about the same at every level of predicted time.
Each feature, such as route distance, follows a normal distribution.
No feature is an exact linear combination of the other features.
Delivery times, taken across all deliveries, follow a normal distribution.
questions.explanation:
OLS inference rests on assumptions about the errors and the form of the model, not about how the features are distributed.

Linearity matters because the coefficients only mean something if the expected target really is a weighted sum of the inputs as entered. You can still add squared or log terms. Independent errors matter because the standard error formula assumes each row adds new information. Deliveries by the same driver on the same day often break this, and the intervals then come out too narrow. Constant error variance matters because the usual formula uses one shared variance. If long routes have much noisier times, the standard errors are wrong. No perfect collinearity is needed for the coefficients to be unique at all. If one feature were an exact multiple of another, endless combinations of weights would fit equally well.

Normally distributed features are not needed. OLS treats the features as given, so they can be skewed, binary or anything else. A normal spread of delivery times across all deliveries is not needed either. That overall spread mixes short and long routes, so it can be skewed or have several peaks even when the model fits well. The assumption, where one is made, is about the errors left after the features explain what they can. Even normal errors only matter for exact small-sample tests. With many deliveries, the intervals hold approximately without them.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds the fixes. Use cluster-robust standard errors when rows are grouped, such as by driver, and heteroscedasticity-robust errors when the noise grows with the prediction. A plot of residuals against fitted values shows both problems. For pure prediction, most of these assumptions matter far less than for inference.

questions.prompt:
An insurance fraud model target-encodes `repair_shop_id`. One shop appears in only 8 training claims, and 6 of them were fraud. Across all training claims the fraud rate is 0.05. The encoding blends each shop's fraud rate with the global rate, treating the global rate as if it were backed by m = 20 extra claims:

(count × shop rate + m × global rate) / (count + m)

What encoded value does this shop get? Give it as a decimal to 2 places.
questions.explanation:
Step 1: the shop's own fraud rate is 6 / 8 = 0.75.

Step 2: the numerator is 8 × 0.75 + 20 × 0.05 = 6 + 1 = 7.

Step 3: the denominator is 8 + 20 = 28, so the encoding is 7 / 28 = 0.25.

Smoothing pulls rare categories toward the global rate. Eight claims is too few to trust a 75% fraud rate, since a couple of unlucky claims could produce it. With m = 20, the global rate gets more weight than the shop's own 8 claims. A shop with 800 claims would barely move from its own rate.

The common mistakes are using the raw 0.75, which lets a tiny sample dominate, or taking a plain average of the two rates, (0.75 + 0.05) / 2 = 0.40, which ignores how many claims back each one. The weights should depend on the counts.
questions.deeper: Smoothing reduces noise but does not stop leakage, because each claim's own label is still inside its shop's rate. Compute the encoding out-of-fold or from earlier data, and pick m by validation. scikit-learn's `TargetEncoder` does both cross-fitting and smoothing.

questions.prompt: A food delivery app shows an estimated delivery time at checkout and updates it until the food arrives. Customers are far more upset by late food than by early food. Design the prediction system: features, real-time inputs, the training loss and monitoring.
questions.answer: Split the estimate into parts: kitchen prep time, wait for a courier, and travel to the customer. Features include the restaurant's past prep times by hour and day, order size, distance, time of day and weather. Real-time inputs matter most: open orders at the restaurant, couriers nearby and live traffic. Keep these in a streaming feature store so the checkout call stays inside its latency budget, with historical averages as a fallback if a feed is down. Because late is worse than early, train with a quantile (pinball) loss at, say, the 80th percentile rather than mean squared error, which targets the average, so many orders arrive after the quoted time. After pickup, re-estimate travel from the courier's live location. Monitor mean absolute error, the share of orders later than promised, and bias by city, restaurant and time of day, with alerts when the late rate drifts.
points: Break the estimate into prep, courier wait and travel
Real-time signals: kitchen load, courier supply, traffic
Streaming feature store within the checkout latency budget, with fallbacks
Asymmetric loss such as quantile loss instead of mean squared error
Update the estimate as the order progresses
Monitor late-order rate and bias by segment, not just average error
questions.explanation:
The key design choice is the loss. Mean squared error is minimised by the average delivery time, so a large share of orders, often close to half, arrive after the estimate, which is the outcome customers hate most. A quantile loss at the 80th percentile charges 4 times more for being late than for being early, so the model learns to quote a time that is met about 80% of the time.

The common mistake is to describe a single model on static features. Delivery time depends heavily on what is happening right now: a kitchen with 30 open orders or a dinner rush with few couriers. Those signals must be fresh and fast to read, which is why a streaming feature store and a fallback belong in the design.

Splitting the estimate into parts also helps debugging. If late orders cluster at pickup, the prep model is wrong, not the routing. Monitoring by segment catches problems that a good overall average hides, such as one city that is always late.
questions.deeper: Strong candidates discuss the product trade-off. A padded estimate is rarely late but may scare off customers, so the percentile is a business choice tested online, using order conversion and late rate together. They also note a feedback effect: the quoted time changes courier behaviour and customer orders, so offline data does not fully predict it.

questions.subtopic: fitting a model onto a smaller GPU
questions.prompt: You must serve a 13-billion-parameter chat model on a single GPU with 24 GB of memory (1 GB = 10⁹ bytes). In fp16 its weights take 26 GB, and its KV cache in fp16 takes about 0.8 MB per token (1 MB = 10⁶ bytes). Product wants up to 8 conversations at once, each with a 4,096-token context. Lay out your plan and the checks you would run.
questions.answer: First the budget. The fp16 weights, 26 GB, do not fit, and a full KV cache needs 8 × 4,096 × 0.8 MB ≈ 26.2 GB, which is more than the whole GPU. So both must shrink. With 4-bit weights the model takes about 6.5 GB, say 7.5 GB with quantization scales. Leaving about 2 GB for activations and runtime overhead gives roughly 14 GB for the cache. An 8-bit KV cache halves it to 0.4 MB per token, so 8 full contexts need about 13.1 GB, which just fits. If that is too tight, I would cap the context lower or allow fewer concurrent chats, and use paged cache allocation so short chats do not reserve full-length space. Then quality: compare the compressed model with the fp16 model on a held-out chat eval set, including long-context and rare-topic slices, and measure latency. If quality drops too far, I would try 8-bit weights with a shorter context, or a smaller distilled model.
points: Do the memory budget: 26 GB of weights and about 26 GB of full KV cache, so neither fits as is
Quantize the weights to 4 bits, or 8 bits if quality needs it
Shrink the cache: 8-bit KV cache, a context cap or fewer concurrent chats, paged allocation
Leave headroom for activations and runtime overhead
Compare quality with the fp16 model on an eval set with slices, with a distilled model as fallback
questions.explanation:
This question tests whether you budget memory before choosing a technique. Serving memory is weights plus KV cache plus overhead, and the KV cache scales with concurrent requests times context length. Here the cache is as large as the weights, so shrinking only the weights is not enough.

The common mistake is to quantize the weights to 8 bits, see 13 GB, and declare that it fits. That leaves about 9 GB after overhead, room for about 11,000 fp16 cache tokens, while the requirement is 32,768. The service would load and then run out of memory under real traffic, usually at the worst moment. Another mistake is to skip the quality check. Four-bit weights and an 8-bit cache both add error, and the damage is often worst on long contexts and rare topics, so the evaluation needs those slices, not just an overall score.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often push on the tradeoffs. Strong candidates explain that cutting context hurts users with long chats, while cutting concurrency raises queueing at peaks. They might propose summarizing old turns to keep context short, and they set a hard admission limit so the server rejects or queues requests instead of crashing when the cache is full.

questions.prompt: At a grocery delivery company, `avg_basket_value_30d` is computed by a SQL job for training and written again in the checkout service's own code for live scoring. The two versions have drifted apart. The team moves the feature into a feature store. How does the feature store keep training and serving values consistent?
options: One feature definition fills both a history store for training and a fast lookup store for serving
Training and serving both read one shared table that keeps only the latest value for each customer
It compares training and serving values every night and retrains the model whenever the two disagree
It saves the model's predictions from training so checkout can reuse them instead of scoring live
questions.explanation:
The root cause was two pieces of code for one feature. A feature store removes that by having one definition, and the platform uses it to fill two stores. The offline store keeps timestamped history, so training can join each label to the feature value as it was at that moment. The online store keeps the latest value per customer in a fast key-value lookup, so checkout can fetch it in a few milliseconds. Same logic, two storage layouts for two access patterns.

A single table with only the latest value breaks training. Old labels would be joined to today's feature values, which leaks the future into the past. Nightly comparison and retraining might detect skew, but it does not prevent it, and retraining cannot fix a feature that is computed two different ways. Reusing training-time predictions makes no sense for live checkout, where the basket and customer are new and must be scored now.
questions.deeper: A good follow-up is point-in-time correctness. When building a training set, the offline store must return the value as of each label's timestamp, not the latest value. Strong candidates also mention logging the features actually served, which lets you check online and offline values against each other.

questions.prompt: A job board trains a new search ranker on click logs from its current ranker. On a held-out week of those logs, the new model predicts clicks better, with AUC 0.74 against 0.71. Most logged clicks happened in the top three slots. In a well-powered two-week A/B test, job applications per search do not change. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The logs reflect the old ranker's choices and slot order, so predicting those clicks better need not mean better rankings.
The held-out week came right after the training weeks, so it shared too much with them, and a week from months later would show no gain.
AUC ignores calibration, and applications depend on well-calibrated click probabilities, so offline log loss would have predicted the flat result.
The offline test scored single impressions while the A/B test split users, and that change of unit alone hides a real gain online.
questions.explanation:
Logged clicks are shaped by the old system. Users mostly click what sits in the top slots, partly because it sits there. That is position bias. And jobs the old ranker never showed have no clicks at all, which is a feedback loop. A new model can get better at predicting these biased clicks, for example by learning what the old ranker liked, without finding jobs that users would apply to. Clicks are also only a proxy for applications, the real goal.

The option about the held-out week has it backwards. A week right after training is the standard choice, and an older week drifts further from current users without removing the bias in the logs. The option about calibration misses that a ranker uses only the order of its scores, and log loss computed on the same biased click logs would share the same blind spot. The option about the unit of analysis is wrong because splitting by user is the normal way to test a ranker. If the new ranker really put better jobs on top, applications per search would rise under a user split too.
questions.deeper: Fixes include position-debiased training (inverse propensity weighting), a small slice of randomised results to collect unbiased labels, and interleaving tests that compare rankers on the same users. A strong candidate also asks whether the offline metric used applications or only clicks.

questions.prompt: A coding agent fixes failing tests in a large repository. Each time it runs the test suite, the full 3,000-line output goes into its context and stays there. After eight test runs, most of the context is old logs, and the agent has started editing code to fix failures that an earlier change already fixed. How should the test tool's output be handled?
options: Cut each test output to its first 200 lines, so the context stays small however large the test suite grows over time.
Return the failing tests and their errors, save the full log to a file, and drop older summaries after each run.
Keep every full output in context, since any earlier log might hold a clue and losing context costs more than tokens do.
Return only "passed" or "failed" for the whole run, so that no log text at all ever reaches the agent's context.
questions.explanation:
Good context engineering keeps what the next step needs and leaves the rest one tool call away. The next step needs to know which tests fail now and why, so a short summary of failing tests and their error messages is the right shape. The full log stays in a file the agent can open for the rare case the agent needs more detail. Dropping summaries from earlier runs stops the agent from acting on failures that no longer exist, which is the bug described here.

Cutting to the first 200 lines is blind truncation. Test runners usually print failures and the final summary near the end, so this keeps setup noise and throws away exactly what matters. Keeping every log is what caused the problem. Old failures sit next to new ones with nothing to tell them apart, and each call grows more costly. Returning only pass or fail goes too far the other way. The agent learns that something broke but not which test or why, so it has to guess or rerun the suite with no extra information.
questions.deeper: The same idea applies to any noisy tool, such as web pages, database dumps and build logs. Shape the output for the model the way you would shape an API response for a client. A strong candidate also mentions measuring the change with task success and tokens per task.

questions.prompt: A ride-hailing team has a month of pickup GPS points for one city. Busy pickup areas stretch along roads and around stations in irregular shapes, nobody knows how many there are, and many points are scattered one-offs that belong to no busy area. Which method fits best, and what do its main settings control?
options: k-means with a large k, since each centroid marks a busy area and far-off points get dropped as noise.
DBSCAN, where eps sets a neighbourhood radius and min_samples sets how many points make a dense core.
DBSCAN, where eps sets the number of busy areas and min_samples sets how far apart they must be.
A Gaussian mixture, since its components bend along roads and leave low-probability points unassigned.
questions.explanation:
DBSCAN builds clusters from density instead of centres. A point is a core point if at least min_samples points, counting itself in scikit-learn, lie within distance eps of it. Clusters grow by chaining core points that are within eps of each other, and they take in border points that sit near a core. Everything else is labelled noise. That fits this data: busy areas of any shape, no need to set how many there are, and the one-off pickups set aside.

k-means needs k up front, assumes round clusters around centres and assigns every point to some cluster, so the scattered pickups would pull centroids around rather than be dropped. The option that gives eps and min_samples the jobs of a cluster count and a minimum gap mixes up what they do. DBSCAN never takes a cluster count. eps is a radius, and the number of clusters falls out of the data. A Gaussian mixture fits ellipses, which cannot follow a curving road, and it gives every point a probability under each component rather than labelling noise by itself.
questions.deeper: The hard part in practice is choosing eps. A common trick is the k-distance plot: sort each point's distance to its min_samples-th nearest neighbour and look for the knee. One eps also struggles when busy areas differ a lot in density, such as downtown against the suburbs, which is where HDBSCAN helps. For raw GPS, use haversine distance.

questions.prompt: Delivery times for a grocery service are roughly normal, with a mean of 30 minutes and a standard deviation of 5 minutes. Using the 68-95-99.7 rule, what percentage of deliveries take longer than 40 minutes? Give it as a percentage to 1 decimal place.
questions.explanation:
First turn the cutoff into a z-score: (40 − 30) / 5 = 2. So 40 minutes is 2 standard deviations above the mean. The 68-95-99.7 rule says about 95% of values lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean, here between 20 and 40 minutes. That leaves 5% outside the band. The normal curve is symmetric, so half of that 5% is above 40 minutes and half is below 20. The answer is 2.5%.

The common mistake is answering 5%, forgetting that the 5% outside the band is split between two tails. Another is to use the 68% figure, which belongs to 1 standard deviation, or 35 minutes here. That would give 16%.

The rule is an approximation. The exact share above z = 2 is about 2.28%, because the true two-sided figure is 95.45%. For a quick estimate in an interview, 2.5% is the expected answer.
questions.deeper: Real delivery and latency times are usually right-skewed, with a long tail of slow cases. A normal model then understates how often the worst delays happen. For service targets, teams read percentiles such as p95 or p99 straight from the data rather than trusting a mean and a standard deviation.

questions.subtopic: what perplexity does and does not show
questions.prompt: A team compares checkpoints of a customer-support language model using perplexity on held-out text. Which statements about perplexity are correct? Select all that apply.
options: With the same tokenizer and held-out text, lower perplexity means the model gives that text higher probability.
Two models with different tokenizers can be ranked fairly by their per-token perplexity on the same documents.
Lower perplexity on general web text guarantees more helpful and more truthful answers in a support chat.
A perplexity of k means the model is about as unsure as picking evenly among k tokens at each step.
Perplexity can be measured on raw held-out text alone, with no human labels or reference answers.
A perplexity of 1.0 on the test set is the normal result for a well-trained model that generalizes well.
questions.explanation:
Perplexity is exp of the average negative log-probability per token. So with the tokenizer and text held fixed, lower perplexity means higher probability on that text. It reads as an effective branching factor: perplexity k is like guessing uniformly among k tokens. It needs only raw text, because each token's target is simply the next token, which is why it is cheap to track during training.

Ranking models with different tokenizers is unfair because the average is per token. A tokenizer that cuts text into more, easier pieces can get a lower per-token perplexity without modelling the text any better. To compare across tokenizers, normalize per byte or per word. Low perplexity on web text measures how well the model predicts typical text, not whether its answers are correct or useful, so helpfulness needs task evals or human ratings. A perplexity of 1.0 means the model was certain of every token, which on real held-out text points to test data leaking into training, not to good generalization.
questions.deeper: In practice perplexity is good for catching training problems and comparing checkpoints of one model. For a support bot, a strong candidate pairs it with task metrics such as resolution rate, answer accuracy on a labelled set, and human or model-graded quality reviews.

questions.subtopic: validating a judge before trusting it
questions.prompt: A team building a contract-summary tool wants an LLM judge to score each summary for accuracy and completeness, so they can compare prompt versions without paying lawyers to read every output. Which steps help show whether the judge can be trusted? Select all that apply.
options: Have lawyers label a few hundred summaries, then measure how often the judge's verdicts agree with theirs.
Test for bias, for example whether the judge favours longer summaries or whichever of two summaries is shown first.
Re-measure agreement with lawyer labels whenever the judge model or the judge prompt changes, not only once at launch.
Use the same model that writes the summaries as the judge, since it best understands what it meant to say.
Run the judge twice on each summary at temperature 0, and treat identical scores as proof that it is accurate.
questions.explanation:
An LLM judge is a measuring instrument, so you validate it the way you would validate any instrument: compare it with a trusted reference and look for systematic errors. Lawyer labels on a sample give that reference. Agreement with the lawyers, measured as raw agreement and ideally also with a chance-corrected statistic such as Cohen's kappa, tells you how far to trust the judge's scores. Bias checks matter because judges have known habits. They often prefer longer answers and, when shown two answers, the one in a particular position. Comparing short and long summaries of equal quality, and swapping the order of pairs, exposes these. The check must be repeated when the judge model or its prompt changes, because a new judge is a new instrument.

Using the writer model as its own judge is risky, not helpful. Models tend to rate their own style of output highly, which is called self-preference bias, and the judge would share the writer's blind spots. Identical scores across two runs show the judge is consistent, not that it is right. A judge can be perfectly repeatable and wrong in the same way every time.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like the follow-up "what agreement is good enough?" A strong answer compares the judge with how often two lawyers agree with each other on the same items. If lawyers agree with each other 85% of the time, a judge at 80% may be fine, and one at 60% is not.

questions.prompt: An interviewer says: "L2 regularization is just a Gaussian prior." Explain what that means using maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation, which prior L1 regularization corresponds to, and what the two priors say about why L1 gives sparse weights while L2 does not.
questions.answer: MAP picks the weights that maximise p(w given data), which is proportional to p(data given w) × p(w). Taking the negative log turns this into the negative log-likelihood plus −log p(w). The first term is the usual loss, such as log loss or squared error. If each weight has a zero-mean Gaussian prior with variance σ², then −log p(w) is Σw² / (2σ²) plus a constant, which is an L2 penalty. A smaller σ means a stronger belief that weights are near zero, so a larger λ. If the prior is Laplace with scale b, −log p(w) is Σ|w| / b plus a constant, an L1 penalty. The Laplace density has a sharp peak at zero, so the penalty has a kink there. Its pull toward zero stays the same size however small the weight gets, so the MAP solution can sit exactly at zero. The Gaussian is smooth at zero and its pull fades as w shrinks, so weights get small but not zero.
points: MAP maximises likelihood × prior, so the loss becomes negative log-likelihood minus log prior
A Gaussian prior gives a Σw² penalty, with strength rising as σ falls
A Laplace prior gives a Σ|w| penalty
The Laplace peak gives a kink at zero, so MAP weights can be exactly zero
The Gaussian is smooth at zero, so weights shrink but rarely reach zero
questions.explanation:
The link is just algebra on logs. Maximising a product of likelihood and prior is the same as minimising the sum of their negative logs, and the negative log of each prior is a familiar penalty. For linear regression with Gaussian noise of variance σₙ² and a Gaussian prior of variance σ_w², the penalty strength works out to λ = σₙ² / σ_w². A tight prior or noisy data both mean stronger regularization.

The most common mistake is to say the Laplace prior believes most weights are exactly zero. It does not. Under any continuous prior the chance of a weight being exactly zero is zero. Sparsity comes from taking the MAP point estimate, the peak of the posterior, which can land on the kink. The posterior mean under a Laplace prior is not sparse. A prior that truly puts mass at zero, such as spike-and-slab, expresses that belief directly.

Another slip is to forget the likelihood. The prior only adds the penalty. The data term is still the ordinary loss.
questions.deeper: Interviewers sometimes push on what full Bayesian treatment adds: instead of one MAP point, you average predictions over the posterior, which gives uncertainty estimates. A strong candidate also notes that weight decay in neural networks is the same Gaussian prior idea, though with adaptive optimisers like Adam, decoupled weight decay behaves differently from an L2 term in the loss.

questions.subtopic: fine-tuning a vision model on little data
questions.prompt: You fine-tune an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet to spot defects on circuit boards, with 1,500 labeled photos and a new classification head. Which practices are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Use a smaller learning rate for the pretrained backbone than for the new head.
Train the new head first with the backbone frozen, then unfreeze the top blocks a few at a time.
Normalize the photos with the same channel mean, standard deviation and color order used in pretraining.
Give the backbone a larger learning rate than the head, since it must move further away from ImageNet.
Turn off data augmentation, since pretrained features already generalize well on small datasets.
Apply strong weight decay to the backbone, since weight decay pulls weights back toward their pretrained values.
questions.explanation:
A small dataset cannot support big changes to millions of pretrained weights, so the sound practices all protect what the backbone already knows. A smaller backbone learning rate, often around 10 times lower than the head's, lets the features adapt gently while the new head learns fast. Training the head first matters because a randomly initialized head sends large, noisy gradients into the backbone at the start. Once the head is sensible, unfreezing the top blocks gradually lets the more task-specific layers adapt before the generic early ones. Matching the pretraining normalization keeps inputs in the range the first layers were trained on. A different scale or color order shifts every activation and quietly costs accuracy.

A larger backbone learning rate is the reverse of what helps and tends to erase the pretrained features. Turning off augmentation removes one of the best defenses against overfitting 1,500 images, and pretrained features do not remove that need. Weight decay pulls weights toward zero, not toward their pretrained values, so strong decay on the backbone drags it away from the starting point you wanted to keep. Penalties that pull toward the pretrained weights exist, but they are a different method.
questions.deeper: Lower rates for earlier layers and gradual unfreezing were popularized for fine-tuning language models and work for vision too. A practical gotcha is batch norm: with small fine-tuning batches, keeping the pretrained running statistics frozen is often safer than updating them from noisy batches.

questions.prompt: A support vector machine flags toxic product reviews. Its raw outputs are margin scores, not probabilities. The team holds out a calibration set, fits a logistic regression that takes the raw score as its only input and the true label as the target, and then reports that regression's output as the probability of toxicity. This recalibration method is called ______.
questions.explanation:
Platt scaling fits p = 1 / (1 + exp(−(a·s + b))), where s is the raw score and a and b are learned on held-out data. That is exactly a one-feature logistic regression on the score. Because the sigmoid is monotonic, the order of the reviews does not change, so ranking metrics such as ROC-AUC stay the same while the probabilities become usable.

The most common wrong answer is isotonic regression. It also recalibrates, but it fits a free-form, step-shaped increasing function instead of a sigmoid. It needs more calibration data and can overfit when the set is small. Some people answer temperature scaling, which divides a neural network's logits by one learned number and has no separate shift term. It is a close cousin, but the method described here, with a slope and an intercept on the score, is Platt scaling. Fitting the map on the training data instead of a held-out set is the other classic slip, because the model has already fitted those examples, so their scores are more extreme than scores on new reviews.
questions.deeper: A good follow-up is when to pick each method. Platt scaling suits small calibration sets and S-shaped distortion, which is typical of SVMs and boosted trees. Isotonic regression handles odd shapes but wants thousands of examples. Either way, check a reliability diagram before and after.

questions.prompt: A hospital pharmacy forecasts daily demand for a drug with a short shelf life. Running out costs about $90 per missing dose in emergency couriers and delays, while an unused dose costs about $10 when it expires. The current model is trained with mean squared error. What loss would you use instead, and how would it change the forecasts?
questions.answer: I would train with a quantile loss, also called pinball loss. It charges τ × (y − ŷ) when the forecast is too low and (1 − τ) × (ŷ − y) when it is too high. The model that minimises it predicts the τ quantile of demand rather than the mean. The right τ comes from the costs: τ = 90 / (90 + 10) = 0.9. With τ = 0.9, the loss is exactly the dollar cost divided by 100. The model will forecast the 90th percentile of daily demand, so it should run short on about 1 day in 10. Forecasts will sit above the mean, and further above it on days when demand is more uncertain. Mean squared error will look worse, so I would judge the model on total cost and on how often demand exceeds the forecast, which should be close to 10%.
points: Use a quantile (pinball) loss or another asymmetric loss
Set τ = 90 / (90 + 10) = 0.9 from the two costs
Forecasts move up to the 90th percentile of demand, not the mean
The gap above the mean grows on more uncertain days
Evaluate on total cost and on the shortfall rate, not MSE
questions.explanation:
Mean squared error treats a forecast 5 doses too low the same as one 5 doses too high, and its best answer is the average demand. With these costs that is wrong, because running short costs 9 times as much as overstocking. The pinball loss weights the two directions by τ and 1 − τ. Its best answer is the point where the chance of demand being higher is 1 − τ. Setting τ from the costs is the classic newsvendor result, and here the loss matches the real cost per dose.

The most common mistake is to keep MSE and add a fixed safety buffer, such as 10% on top. A flat buffer ignores that some days are far more uncertain than others, so it overstocks calm days and still runs short on volatile ones. Another is to weight under-forecasts 9 times inside squared error. That does shift forecasts upward, but its best answer is not a quantile, so the shortfall rate no longer lines up with the cost ratio.

At τ = 0.5 the pinball loss is half the absolute error, so mean absolute error, which targets the median, is the symmetric special case. If the costs might change, forecasting several quantiles lets the pharmacy pick τ later without retraining.
questions.deeper: Gradient boosting libraries support quantile objectives directly, which makes this cheap to try. A strong candidate also checks calibration of the quantile on a holdout: if demand beats the forecast on 25% of days instead of 10%, the model is not giving the 90th percentile it claims.

questions.prompt: A logistics company predicts delivery delay as one of 3 classes (on time, slightly late, very late) with a fully connected network. It takes 20 input features, then has a hidden layer of 64 units, a hidden layer of 32 units, and an output layer of 3 units. Every layer after the input has a weight matrix and a bias vector. How many trainable parameters does the network have? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation:
Each dense layer with n_in inputs and n_out outputs has n_in × n_out weights plus n_out biases.

- Input to first hidden layer: 20 × 64 + 64 = 1,344
- First hidden to second hidden layer: 64 × 32 + 32 = 2,080
- Second hidden layer to output: 32 × 3 + 3 = 99

The total is 1,344 + 2,080 + 99 = 3,523.

The most common mistake is to forget the biases, which gives 1,280 + 2,048 + 96 = 3,424. Another is to give the input layer its own weights or biases. The input layer only holds the 20 feature values and has nothing to learn. Activation functions such as ReLU add no parameters either.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often extend this to other layers. A convolution layer has kernel height × kernel width × input channels × output channels weights plus one bias per output channel, which is why convolutions need far fewer parameters than dense layers on images. Batch norm adds two learned parameters per channel, plus running statistics that are stored but not trained.

questions.prompt: A churn model gives a customer a 0.4 probability of leaving this month. If they leave, the company loses $200 in future profit. A retention call costs $10. For a customer who would otherwise leave, the call keeps them with probability 0.25. For a customer who would have stayed anyway, the call changes nothing. What is the expected gain in profit from calling this customer, compared with not calling? Give it in dollars as a whole number.
questions.explanation:
The call only earns money in one situation: the customer was going to leave and the call keeps them. That happens with probability 0.4 × 0.25 = 0.10, and in that case the company keeps $200. So the expected benefit is 0.10 × $200 = $20. The call costs $10 every time, whatever happens. The expected gain is $20 − $10 = $10, so calling is worth it on average.

The most common mistake is to skip the churn probability and compute 0.25 × $200 − $10 = $40. That treats every called customer as someone about to leave. Another slip is to forget the cost and answer $20. Listing each outcome with its probability and payoff, then summing, catches both.

The answer depends on the score. Calling breaks even when p × 0.25 × $200 = $10, which is p = 0.2. So a sensible rule is to call customers whose churn probability is above 0.2.
questions.deeper: This is why calibrated probabilities matter. The break-even threshold of 0.2 only works if a score of 0.4 really means a 40% chance of leaving. A strong candidate also asks where the 0.25 save rate came from, since it should be measured with a randomized holdout of called and uncalled at-risk customers, not guessed.

questions.prompt: A photo app finds visually similar images among 200 million image embeddings. Exact search, which compares the query with every stored vector, takes about 4 seconds per query. The team moves to a graph-based approximate index (HNSW) and gets about 20 ms per query, but on a test set it returns only 92% of the true top 10 neighbours that exact search finds. Product wants that closer to 99% without going back to exact search. What is the usual lever?
options: Raise how many candidates the index explores for each query, which lifts recall but makes every query slower.
Switch from cosine similarity to dot product, since graph indexes lose neighbours only when vectors are normalized.
Add more images to the index, since a graph index finds true neighbours more reliably as it grows.
Move to a cluster-based index such as IVF, since only graph indexes miss neighbours and cluster indexes are exact.
questions.explanation:
Exact search compares the query with all 200 million vectors, which is why it takes seconds. A graph index such as HNSW walks a graph that links each vector to some of its near neighbours, so it checks only a small fraction of the data. It is fast because it skips most vectors, and it misses some true neighbours for the same reason. The index has a setting for how many candidates to keep and explore during a search. Raising it checks more of the graph, so recall moves toward exact search, and each query gets slower. Teams pick the point on that curve that meets both a recall target and a latency budget.

Switching between cosine and dot product changes what counts as similar, not how thoroughly the index searches, and graph indexes handle normalized vectors routinely. Adding more images makes the search harder, because there are more vectors to miss at the same search effort. Cluster-based indexes such as IVF are approximate too. They search only the few clusters nearest the query, so a true neighbour sitting in an unsearched cluster is missed in the same way.
questions.deeper: A strong answer names the other knobs too: how densely the graph is connected and how much effort goes into building it, both traded against memory and build time. With a cluster-based index, the matching knob is how many clusters each query probes. Always measure recall against exact search on a sample, since latency alone hides the loss.

questions.prompt: A logistics team wants to know whether the `delivery_distance_km` feature has shifted since training. Their test builds the empirical cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the training sample and of last week's sample, then uses the largest vertical gap between the two curves as its statistic. This two-sample test is the ______ test.
questions.explanation:
The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test compares two samples of a numeric feature through their empirical CDFs. At every value x it asks what share of each sample is at or below x, and the statistic D is the largest gap between those two shares anywhere on the axis. D runs from 0 (identical curves) to 1 (no overlap). It needs no bins and makes no assumption about the shape of the distribution, which is why it is a common default for numeric drift checks.

The usual mix-up is with tests that look similar. The Wasserstein or earth mover's distance uses the whole area between the two CDFs, not the single largest gap. The chi-squared test and PSI both work on binned counts, so their answer depends on how you choose the bins. Also keep in mind that KS is a significance test. On very large samples it flags gaps too small to matter, so teams often report D itself alongside the p-value.
questions.deeper: Interviewers may ask when KS is a poor fit. It is meant for continuous features, so ties in discrete or heavily rounded values make its p-values less reliable, and categorical features need a chi-squared test or PSI instead. It is also most sensitive near the middle of the distribution, so a shift only in the tails can slip past it.

questions.prompt: A broadband provider wants an LLM chat assistant that answers customer questions and hands off to human agents when needed. It handles about 50,000 conversations a day. Design it, covering retrieval, routing and hand-off, guardrails, evaluation and cost per conversation.
questions.answer: A small classifier routes each conversation by intent and risk. Cancellations, billing disputes, complaints, safety issues and requests for a person go straight to an agent. For the rest, the assistant retrieves from help articles and network status, and reads the customer's own account through tools limited to that customer. It answers only from that context and cites its sources. Guardrails check inputs for prompt injection, mask personal data in logs, block promises outside policy such as unapproved credits, and check answers are grounded in what was retrieved. Hand off when retrieval finds nothing relevant, confidence is low or the customer repeats a question, passing a summary so they never start over. Evaluate offline on past conversations graded with a rubric by an LLM judge that is checked against human ratings. Online, track resolution without a repeat contact, hand-off rate and satisfaction. Cost per conversation is turns times tokens per turn times price, so cap context and cache common answers.
points: Route by intent and risk, with sensitive cases straight to people
Retrieval from help content plus scoped tools for account data
Guardrails: injection checks, personal data, policy limits, grounding
Clear hand-off triggers that pass a summary to the agent
