questions.prompt: KL divergence shows up in three places in your work: as a drift score between a training-time and a live feature histogram, as the loss between a teacher and a student in distillation, and as the penalty that keeps a fine-tuned LLM close to its reference model. Which statement about KL(P ‖ Q) is correct?
questions.explanation:
KL(P ‖ Q) = Σ P(x) log(P(x) / Q(x)), which equals the cross-entropy H(P, Q) minus the entropy H(P). In coding terms, H(P) is the best average code length for data from P, and H(P, Q) is what you pay if you build the code for Q instead. KL is the extra cost of using the wrong distribution. It is never negative and is 0 only when the two distributions match.

KL is not a distance. KL(P ‖ Q) and KL(Q ‖ P) usually differ, and the triangle inequality can fail. The asymmetry matters because the two directions punish different mistakes. If Q gives zero probability to an outcome that P can produce, the log term is infinite, so KL blows up. In drift monitoring this happens when a live histogram has an empty bin, which is why teams add a small smoothing count. Finally, since KL = H(P, Q) − H(P) and H(P) does not depend on Q, minimizing either one over Q gives the same answer. That is why training with cross-entropy is the same as minimizing KL from the data distribution to the model.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask which direction a method uses. Distillation with soft labels minimizes KL(teacher ‖ student), which pushes the student to cover everything the teacher finds likely. The LLM fine-tuning penalty uses KL(policy ‖ reference) on the policy's own samples. For a symmetric drift score, teams often use PSI, which adds both directions, or Jensen-Shannon divergence, which also stays finite.
options: It is the average extra cost of encoding samples from P with a code built for Q, and is 0 only if Q = P.
It is a true distance, so KL(P ‖ Q) equals KL(Q ‖ P) and the triangle inequality holds for it.
It stays finite even when Q gives zero probability to a histogram bin where P has some mass.
Minimizing it over Q gives a different answer than minimizing the cross-entropy H(P, Q) over Q.

questions.subtopic: position of facts in long context
questions.prompt: A RAG assistant for insurance policies retrieves 20 chunks per question and pastes them into the prompt in order of document ID, with the question at the end. Error analysis shows the right chunk was in the prompt for every failed question, and that accuracy drops sharply when that chunk sits around positions 8 to 12. Which change best targets this problem?
options: Rerank the chunks, keep fewer, and put the strongest at the start and end of the context, where models use information most reliably.
Retrieve 40 chunks instead of 20, so the right chunk is even more likely to appear and the model has more evidence to cross-check against.
Shuffle the chunk order on every request, so on average each chunk spends the same share of time in each position of the prompt.
Raise the sampling temperature, so the model explores more of the context and is less likely to fixate on the first chunks it reads.
questions.explanation:
This pattern is often called "lost in the middle". Many LLMs use information at the start and end of a long context more reliably than information in the middle, so the same chunk can be used or ignored depending only on where it sits. Ordering by document ID puts the most relevant chunks wherever they happen to fall. Reranking by relevance, sending fewer chunks and putting the strongest at the edges of the context attacks the cause directly.

Retrieving 40 chunks does not help, because the right chunk was already present. A longer context adds distracting text and pushes more chunks into the weak middle region. Shuffling only spreads the failures around. Each request still has the relevant chunk in the middle some of the time, so average accuracy barely changes and answers become less repeatable. Raising the temperature changes how the next token is sampled, not how the model weighs positions, and it adds randomness to answers that should be factual.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate proposes measuring it: plant the known answer chunk at each position and plot accuracy by position for your own model and prompt. The effect varies between models and context lengths, so test it rather than assume it. Fewer, better chunks also cut cost and latency.

questions.prompt: A food delivery app serves a delivery-time model online. To check it, the team takes 2,000 logged requests and reruns them through the offline batch pipeline used to build training data. For about 15% of requests the offline prediction differs from the one served, sometimes by more than 10 minutes. The model file is the same in both. How would you track down the cause, and what are the likely culprits?
questions.answer: Since the model file is identical, the difference must come from the inputs or the code around the model. I would log the exact feature vector served for each request and compare it, column by column, with the vector the offline pipeline builds for the same request. The columns that differ point to the cause. Likely culprits are two separate implementations of one feature, such as a rolling average over different windows, missing values filled differently, for example 0 online but the median offline, and time handling, such as offline code using UTC event time while the service uses local server time. Other suspects are different library versions or preprocessing artifacts, such as an encoder that maps new restaurants to different codes, and offline features that use data not yet available at request time. The lasting fix is one shared feature definition, training on logged served features, and a parity test in CI.
points: Model is the same, so diff the inputs: log served features and compare column by column
Two implementations of one feature, such as different windows or joins
Missing-value defaults that differ between online and offline code
Time zone, timestamp or point-in-time differences, including offline using later data
Library or preprocessing artifact versions, such as encoders and scalers
Fix with one shared feature definition, logged features and a parity test
questions.explanation:
The key move is to stop looking at the model and compare inputs. The same model file with the same feature vector must give the same output, so any gap lives in how features are built. Logging served feature vectors and diffing them against the offline rows turns a vague problem into a list of columns that disagree. The 15% of affected requests often share a trait, such as late-night orders or new restaurants, that points to the cause.

The common mistake is to treat this as drift and retrain. Drift is a change in the world over time, but here the same requests give two different answers today. Retraining keeps both code paths, so the gap comes back. Another mistake is to trust the offline pipeline as the truth. Offline code can be the buggy one, for example by joining data that arrived after the order was placed, which the live service could never see.
questions.deeper: Interviewers like a concrete guard. A strong answer proposes a daily parity job that replays a sample of live requests offline and alerts when more than a small share of predictions differ beyond a tolerance. It also says which side to trust: the online path defines what the model really sees, so training data is often rebuilt from logged served features.

questions.prompt: A model summarises customer support calls. For one call, summary X scores ROUGE-L 0.62 against the human reference and summary Y scores 0.41. On reading them, Y is a correct paraphrase of the reference, while X copies much of the reference wording but states the wrong refund amount. What does this show?
options: ROUGE measures word overlap, so it rewards copied wording and treats a wrong amount as one mismatched word.
ROUGE must have been computed wrongly, because a summary with a factual error cannot outscore a correct summary.
Y would come out ahead on BLEU, because BLEU matches synonyms and checks meaning rather than the exact words used.
ROUGE-L fails only on long texts, so scoring single words with ROUGE-1 instead would put Y ahead of X.
questions.explanation:
ROUGE counts how many words or word sequences a summary shares with a reference. ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence. Summary X reuses the reference wording, so it overlaps a lot. The wrong refund amount is just one token that does not match, so it costs X about as much as any other changed word. Summary Y says the same facts in new words, so it overlaps less and scores lower even though it is better.

Nothing was computed wrongly. This is ROUGE working as designed, and it has no notion of facts. BLEU has the same blind spot, since it is also built on exact n-gram overlap and does not match synonyms or meaning. Switching to ROUGE-1 does not help either. X still shares more single words with the reference than the paraphrase does, and a wrong number is still only one word.
questions.deeper: Treat BLEU and ROUGE as cheap regression signals, not judges of quality. For summaries, teams add factual checks such as entailment models or an LLM judge with a rubric, plus human review on a sample. Numbers, names and dates deserve targeted checks of their own.

questions.prompt: A meeting-notes tool summarizes 12,000 meetings per day. Each summary call sends 6,000 input tokens and receives 500 output tokens. Suppose the model costs $2 per million input tokens and $8 per million output tokens. What is the total model cost for a 30-day month, in dollars, as a whole number?
questions.explanation:
Price input and output tokens separately, then scale up.

- Input tokens per day: 12,000 × 6,000 = 72,000,000, which is 72 million. At $2 per million that is $144.
- Output tokens per day: 12,000 × 500 = 6,000,000, which is 6 million. At $8 per million that is $48.
- Cost per day: $144 + $48 = $192.
- Cost per month: $192 × 30 = $5,760.

The most common mistake is to add all tokens together and apply one price. Using the input price for all 78 million tokens gives $156 per day and $4,680 per month, which is too low by over $1,000. In this example each output token costs four times as much as an input token, so output must be priced on its own. Real price lists often charge more for output too, but the ratio varies, so always use the actual rates. The other frequent slip is losing track of the millions, for example multiplying 72,000,000 by $2 and getting a figure a million times too large. Writing each step with its unit avoids both.
questions.deeper: Notice that input is 92% of the tokens here but 75% of the cost. Interviewers like to follow up with "how would you halve this bill?" Good answers include shorter transcripts after removing filler, caching a shared instruction prefix, a smaller model for short meetings and batch processing if summaries can wait.

questions.prompt: In an interview for an insurance pricing team, you are asked how gradient boosting builds its model step by step, and which hyperparameters you would tune first on 200,000 claims with 40 features. How would you answer?
questions.answer: Gradient boosting builds an additive model one small tree at a time. It starts from a constant, such as the mean claim cost. At each round it computes the negative gradient of the loss for every row, which for squared error is just the residual, the gap between the target and the current prediction. It fits a shallow tree to those values, scales the tree's output by a learning rate, and adds it to the model. Each new tree corrects what the ensemble still gets wrong. I would tune the learning rate and the number of trees together, using early stopping on a validation set so the tree count picks itself. Next I would tune tree size, through max depth or number of leaves, and the minimum samples per leaf, which control how complex each tree is. Then row and column subsampling and L2 regularisation to curb overfitting further.
points: Starts from a constant prediction and adds trees one at a time
Each tree fits the negative gradient of the loss, the residuals for squared error
Each tree's output is shrunk by the learning rate before it is added
Tune learning rate and number of trees together, with early stopping
Then tree depth or leaf count and minimum samples per leaf
Then row and column subsampling and regularisation
questions.explanation:
The heart of the answer is that boosting is sequential. Each tree depends on all the ones before it, because it is trained on what they still get wrong. The gradient part is what makes the method general. For squared error the negative gradient is the residual. For log loss in a classifier it is the label minus the predicted probability. The same loop then works for any differentiable loss, such as a Poisson or Tweedie loss for claim amounts.

The most common mistake is to describe a random forest instead: many deep trees trained independently and averaged. Boosting uses shallow trees added in sequence, so it mainly reduces bias, while bagging mainly reduces variance. A second mistake is tuning the number of trees on its own. A smaller learning rate needs more trees to reach the same fit but usually generalises better, so the two must move together, and early stopping on a validation set handles that cleanly. Tree depth comes next because it sets how many features one tree can combine in a single interaction.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate adds practical points. Modern libraries bin features into histograms for speed, handle missing values natively and can enforce monotonic constraints, which pricing teams often need so that predicted cost never falls as prior claims rise. A likely follow-up is how you would explain a single quoted price, where SHAP values on the trees are the usual answer.

questions.prompt: Many training losses are the negative log-likelihood of a noise model, so minimizing them is maximum likelihood estimation. Which pairings of a loss with the model it corresponds to are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation:
Write down the noise model, take the negative log of its density, and drop constants. A Gaussian density contains exp(−(y − ŷ)² / 2σ²), so its negative log is the squared error up to scale and a constant. That is why mean squared error is maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise with fixed variance. A Laplace density contains exp(−|y − ŷ| / b), so its negative log is the absolute error, which pairs mean absolute error with Laplace noise. For a categorical label, the likelihood of an example is the predicted probability of its true class, and the negative log of that is exactly softmax cross-entropy.

The option pairing MSE with Laplace noise swaps the two. MSE is in fact sensitive to outliers, because squaring magnifies large errors. Laplace noise has heavier tails, which is why MAE is the more robust choice. Binary cross-entropy comes from a Bernoulli label, not a Gaussian one. A Gaussian on the label would give squared error on the probability, a different loss. Finally, MAE is minimized by the conditional median, not the mean. Only MSE targets the mean.
questions.deeper: Interviewers use this to see whether you can derive a loss rather than recite it. A good follow-up: what if the noise variance changes with the input? Then the model predicts both a mean and a variance and minimizes the Gaussian negative log-likelihood, which divides each squared error by σ² and adds a log σ term.
options: Mean squared error is maximum likelihood when the targets have Gaussian noise with a constant variance.
Mean squared error is maximum likelihood under Laplace noise, which is why it resists outliers.
Binary cross-entropy is maximum likelihood for a Gaussian label centred on the predicted probability.
Mean absolute error is maximum likelihood when the targets have Laplace noise with a constant scale.
Softmax cross-entropy is maximum likelihood for a single categorical label per example.
Mean absolute error and mean squared error both estimate the conditional mean of the target.

questions.prompt: A lab has a fixed compute budget, equal to training a 60B-parameter model on 250B tokens. Training compute is about 6 × parameters × tokens. They want the lowest pretraining loss for this budget and do not care about serving cost. Which plan do empirical compute-optimal scaling results point to?
options: About 27B parameters on about 550B tokens, since fitted scaling laws found size and data should grow together, near 20 tokens per parameter.
Keep 60B parameters on 250B tokens, since this split already sits close to the compute-optimal ratio of about 4 tokens per parameter.
About 120B parameters on about 125B tokens, since loss keeps falling faster from added parameters than from added data at this scale.
About 6B parameters on about 2.5T tokens, since loss depends mostly on how many tokens the model sees, so the smallest model wins.
questions.explanation:
Compute-optimal scaling studies trained many models of different sizes on different amounts of data and fitted how loss depends on each. They found that, for a fixed budget, the lowest loss comes from growing model size and training tokens in roughly equal proportion. The resulting rule of thumb is about 20 training tokens per parameter. It is an empirical fit, not a law, and the exact ratio shifts with data and architecture, but it lands far from the other splits here. The budget is 6 × 60B × 250B = 9 × 10²² FLOPs. Setting tokens = 20 × parameters gives 6 × N × 20N = 120N² = 9 × 10²², so N ≈ 27B and D ≈ 550B tokens. Every option uses the same compute, so the only question is how to split it.

The plan that keeps 60B on 250B tokens is at only about 4 tokens per parameter, so it is undertrained rather than near the optimum. Earlier scaling work favoured big models like this, which is why the idea is tempting. The 120B plan goes further in that direction, at about 1 token per parameter. The 6B plan goes too far the other way, at over 400 tokens per parameter. Extra data then gives shrinking returns, while the small model's capacity limits how low the loss can go.
questions.deeper: The 6B plan is not silly in practice. When a model will serve huge numbers of requests, teams often train a smaller model far past 20 tokens per parameter, accepting a slightly worse loss for the compute spent in exchange for much cheaper inference. A strong candidate says which goal is being optimized before quoting the 20-to-1 rule.

questions.prompt: A click model is trained on data that keeps every click but only a random 10% of non-clicks. The real click rate is about 1%. The model is well calibrated on the sampled data. For one impression it outputs p′ = 0.5. What is the best estimate of the real click probability?
options: About 0.050, from multiplying the score by the 0.1 keep rate
About 0.500, since dropping random negatives leaves scores unbiased
questions.explanation:
Think in odds. Keeping only 10% of non-clicks makes clicks look 10 times more common, so the model's odds are 10 times the real odds. The model's odds are 0.5 / 0.5 = 1. The real odds are 1 × 0.1 = 0.1, and turning odds back into a probability gives 0.1 / 1.1 ≈ 0.091. Written as one formula, p = p′ / (p′ + (1 − p′) / w) with keep rate w = 0.1.

Multiplying the score by 0.1 is a shortcut that only works when p′ is small, because then the odds and the probability are almost equal. At p′ = 0.5 it is far off. Leaving the score at 0.5 confuses ranking with calibration. Undersampling keeps the order of the scores, so AUC is unchanged, but every probability is inflated. The 0.909 option applies the correction backwards, raising the probability when it should be lowered.
questions.deeper: This matters wherever the probability drives money, such as ad bids priced as expected value per click. Interviewers may ask how you would check the fix: compare the mean corrected prediction with the real click rate on unsampled data, and plot a reliability curve.

questions.prompt: A food-photo classifier scores 91% accuracy on its validation set in the training notebook. The team wraps it in a new serving script, runs that script on the exact same validation images, and gets 74%. Which could explain the drop? Select all that apply.
options: Dropout is still active in the serving script, so random units are zeroed on every prediction.
Batch norm runs in training mode at serving, so it normalizes with each incoming batch's statistics.
The serving script resizes and normalizes images differently from the training pipeline.
Users upload different kinds of food photos than the ones in the validation set.
The model overfit its training data, so the 91% validation score was too optimistic.
Gradient tracking is left on at serving, which changes the values the forward pass returns.
questions.explanation:
The key fact is that the images are identical, so anything about the data or the model's general quality is ruled out. What is left is the code path, and three common bugs fit.

Dropout should be off at inference. If the model is never put in evaluation mode, units are randomly dropped on every call, so predictions get noisier and accuracy falls. Batch norm in training mode normalizes with the mean and variance of whatever batch arrives, rather than the running averages saved during training. With small or uneven serving batches those statistics are far from the training ones, and the outputs shift. Different preprocessing, such as another resize method, BGR instead of RGB order or a missing mean and standard deviation step, is training-serving skew. The model sees inputs unlike the ones it was trained on.

The option about user uploads describes data drift, which cannot apply when the same images are scored. Overfitting would show as a gap between training and validation scores, not between two runs on the same validation set. Gradient tracking costs memory and time but does not change the outputs of the forward pass.
questions.deeper: A quick test is to run the serving code and the notebook on the same few images and compare raw outputs to several decimal places. Teams lock this in with a parity test in CI that fails if the two paths differ beyond a small tolerance. Exporting the model with preprocessing built in removes a whole class of skew.

questions.prompt:
A travel site wants to test a new booking flow. The current booking rate is 4.0%, and the smallest lift worth detecting is a 10% relative increase. The test uses a two-sided significance level of 0.05 and 80% power, so use 1.96 for the significance level and 0.84 for power. Use the standard per-arm sample size formula with unpooled variances:

n = (1.96 + 0.84)² × (p₁(1 − p₁) + p₂(1 − p₂)) / (p₂ − p₁)²

Round n up to a whole user. The site gets 6,000 new eligible users a day, split evenly between control and treatment. How many whole days must the test run to reach the required sample in both arms? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation:
Step 1, turn the relative lift into rates: p₁ = 0.040 and p₂ = 0.040 × 1.10 = 0.044, so p₂ − p₁ = 0.004.

Step 2, the variance term: 0.04 × 0.96 + 0.044 × 0.956 = 0.0384 + 0.042064 = 0.080464.

Step 3, n = 2.8² × 0.080464 / 0.004² = 7.84 × 0.080464 / 0.000016 ≈ 39,427.4, which rounds up to 39,428 users per arm.

Step 4, each arm gets 6,000 / 2 = 3,000 users a day, so 39,428 / 3,000 ≈ 13.14 days. You cannot stop part way through a day and still have enough users, so the test needs 14 days.

The most common mistake is in step 4: dividing one arm's sample by the full 6,000 a day gives about 7 days, half of what is needed. The second is using the relative lift, 0.10, as p₂ − p₁. That makes n tiny and the test hopelessly underpowered. Small absolute gaps on a low base rate are what make sample sizes large.
questions.deeper: Here 14 days is also two full weeks, which is good, because weekday and weekend users often behave differently. Interviewers like to hear that you would round up to whole weeks anyway, and that halving the detectable lift roughly quadruples the sample needed.

questions.prompt: An insurer wants an LLM to draft claim decision letters. Every letter must follow a strict house structure and tone, and must quote the exact policy terms for the customer's product. The policy library runs to thousands of pages and changes every quarter. A prompt with five example letters still breaks the house structure in about 1 in 10 drafts, and the examples use up a large share of the context. Which approach fits best?
options: Fine-tune on approved past letters for structure and tone, and retrieve the current policy terms for each request.
Fine-tune every quarter on the full policy library so the model knows the terms, and keep the house rules in the prompt.
Use retrieval alone and add more example letters to each prompt, because fine-tuning cannot change tone or structure.
Put the whole policy library in every prompt, as a long context makes retrieval and fine-tuning unnecessary.
questions.explanation:
The two needs call for different tools. Structure and tone are behaviour: the same patterns on every letter, learned well from many examples. That is what fine-tuning is good at, and here prompting with examples has already been tried and still fails 1 time in 10. The policy terms are facts that change every quarter and must be quoted exactly. Retrieval handles that. You update the index when terms change, and the next letter quotes the new wording with a source a reviewer can check.

Fine-tuning on the policy library is the classic mistake. Weights store facts loosely, so the model may paraphrase terms or blend clauses from different products. It cannot point to a source, and it goes stale after each quarterly change until the next training run. The claim that fine-tuning cannot change tone or structure is false. Style and format are among the things it changes most reliably. Putting thousands of pages in every prompt likely exceeds the context window, and even where it fits it costs a lot per request, slows replies and makes it harder for the model to find the one clause that matters.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate tries the cheap steps first, better prompts and structured output, and only fine-tunes once a measured failure rate justifies it, as here. They also note that the fine-tuning data should contain letters with retrieved terms in the prompt, so the model learns to quote from context rather than from memory.

questions.prompt: You must train a language model whose weights and training state need about 20 GPUs' worth of memory. The cluster has 4 servers with 8 GPUs each. GPUs inside a server share very fast links, while traffic between servers goes over a network that is several times slower. How should you split the model?
options: Tensor parallelism within each server and pipeline parallelism across servers, as split layers sync constantly over fast links while stages trade data only at edges.
Pipeline parallelism inside each server and tensor parallelism across servers, since stages sync constantly while each tensor shard syncs only once per training step.
Pipeline parallelism across all 32 GPUs, since splitting the layers into 32 stages keeps every GPU busy at all times and so leaves no idle waiting at all.
Tensor parallelism across all 32 GPUs, since splitting each layer's weight matrices needs no traffic until gradients are averaged at the end of each step.
questions.explanation:
Tensor parallelism splits the weight matrices inside each layer, so the GPUs must combine partial results several times per layer, in both the forward and backward passes. That is a lot of traffic, and it only runs well over fast links, which means inside a server. Pipeline parallelism puts groups of whole layers on different devices. Stages only hand activations forward and gradients back at their boundaries, so the slower network between servers can cope.

The reversed layout puts the chattiest traffic on the slowest links, and the claim that tensor shards sync once per step is false. Pure pipeline parallelism across 32 stages has a real cost called the bubble. At the start and end of each step, many stages sit idle waiting for work, and more stages make the bubble bigger. Splitting the batch into micro-batches shrinks it but never removes it. Pure tensor parallelism across servers would send its per-layer traffic over the slow network, and it does need communication inside every layer, not just at the end.
questions.deeper: Large runs usually combine three kinds: tensor parallelism within a server, pipeline parallelism across a few servers, and data parallelism across copies of that whole arrangement. A strong candidate explains that the layout follows the network, with the most frequent communication placed on the fastest links.

questions.prompt: Your team built an IT helpdesk agent. It reads a ticket, then uses tools to look up the user, reset passwords, unlock accounts and install approved software. Before rollout, the head of IT asks how you will know it works and is safe. Design the evaluation.
questions.answer: I would run the agent in a sandbox with fake users, accounts and software, so it can act without touching production. I would build a few hundred test tickets from real history, each with the correct end state, such as the account unlocked and nothing else changed. Task success is judged by checking that final state, not the agent's own claim. I would also check the trajectory: did it pick the right tools, pass valid arguments and avoid needless or repeated calls. I would track steps, cost and latency per ticket. Safety cases matter most: requests for unapproved software, a user asking to reset someone else's password, and tickets carrying injected instructions. Since agents are not deterministic, I would run each ticket several times and report the pass rate. Humans would review a sample of traces, and the whole suite would run again on every change.
points: Sandbox with fake accounts, success judged by the final state
Trajectory checks: right tools, valid arguments, no needless calls
Steps, cost and latency per task
Safety and adversarial cases, including prompt injection and permission abuse
Repeated runs to measure consistency
Human review of traces and a regression suite on every change
questions.explanation:
An agent changes things in the world, so the evaluation has to look at what it did, not only at what it said. The most common mistake is to grade the agent's final message. An agent can report "password reset done" after calling the wrong tool, or after resetting the wrong account. Checking the actual end state in a sandbox catches that, and checking that nothing else changed catches side effects.

A second mistake is to look only at success rate. Two agents can both solve 90% of tickets while one takes 4 steps and the other takes 30, with very different cost and risk. Trajectory checks show this, and they also expose unsafe paths that happen to end well. Safety cases need their own set, because normal tickets rarely test whether the agent refuses a request it should refuse. Finally, agents vary from run to run. A ticket that passes once may fail on the next run, so measure the pass rate over repeated attempts.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate proposes a staged rollout after the offline suite: shadow mode where the agent suggests actions a human approves, then automatic handling of low-risk ticket types first. The approval and override rates from shadow mode are some of the best evidence for wider rollout.

questions.prompt: A triage model predicts whether a patient with a cough has influenza. It was trained and calibrated in summer, when about 2% of these patients had flu. In winter, lab results show about 20% do. The symptoms and test readings of flu patients look the same as in summer, and so do those of patients without flu. Ward staff say the model's probabilities now look far too low. What is the best fix?
options: Multiply each prediction's odds by the ratio of winter to summer prior odds, then recheck the decision threshold.
Reweight training rows by the ratio of winter to summer feature densities and retrain, since this is covariate shift.
Change nothing, because a change in class rates leaves p(y given x) the same, so the scores are still correct.
Retrain from scratch on winter data only, since any change in class rates makes the old model's features invalid.
questions.explanation:
This is label shift. The class rate p(y) changed, while p(x given y), how each class looks, stayed the same. By Bayes' rule, p(y given x) is proportional to p(x given y) × p(y), so the only thing that moved is the prior. For a calibrated model, that means each prediction's odds get multiplied by a fixed factor. Summer prior odds are 0.02 / 0.98 ≈ 0.0204 and winter prior odds are 0.20 / 0.80 = 0.25, a factor of about 12.25. A summer score of 0.10 has odds 0.111, which becomes about 1.36, a probability of roughly 0.58. Thresholds tuned in summer then need rechecking.

Reweighting by feature densities is the fix for covariate shift, which assumes p(y given x) stays fixed. Here that is exactly what changed, so retraining with those weights would relearn the summer posterior. Changing nothing has the two conditionals the wrong way round. Retraining from scratch throws away a model whose features are still valid, and early winter labels are few.
questions.deeper: When the new prior is not measured directly, it can be estimated from unlabelled predictions, for example with an EM procedure or black box shift estimation. A strong candidate also checks the assumption: if a new flu strain causes different symptoms, p(x given y) has changed and a prior correction is no longer enough.

questions.prompt: A single deep decision tree for card fraud gets 99% training accuracy, and its validation score swings a lot when the random seed changes. A random forest of 500 trees, each just as deep, gives higher and steadier validation scores. What is the main reason?
options: Averaging many decorrelated trees cuts variance, while bias stays close to that of one tree.
Each new tree is fit to the errors of the trees before it, which steadily drives the bias down.
Bootstrap sampling hands each tree more training rows than the original dataset contains.
Random feature subsets make each tree more accurate on its own than one tree using all features.
questions.explanation:
A deep tree has low bias but high variance: small changes in the data give a very different tree, which is what the seed-to-seed swings show. Averaging B trees that each have variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ gives variance ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/B. The second term shrinks as you add trees. The first term only shrinks if the trees are less correlated, which is why random forests use bootstrap samples and a random subset of features at each split. Bias stays roughly where a single deep tree puts it.

Fitting each tree to the errors of the previous ones describes boosting, which mainly reduces bias. A bootstrap sample has the same number of rows as the original, drawn with replacement, so each tree sees only about 63% of the unique rows. Random feature subsets usually make each single tree slightly worse. The gain comes from the trees disagreeing in different places, so their errors cancel when averaged.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask why adding more trees to a random forest rarely causes overfitting, while adding more boosting rounds can. The answer follows from this: more bagged trees only lower the averaging term, while more boosting rounds keep fitting the training residuals. Tune max_features to control the correlation between trees.

questions.prompt: A food delivery app predicts how long each order will take, within a 50 ms scoring budget. It uses three features: the restaurant's average prep time over the last 30 days, the number of orders the restaurant received in the last 10 minutes, and the straight-line distance from the assigned courier's current position to the restaurant. The order count is there to catch sudden rushes, so it must include orders from the last minute. Assume a streaming job costs more to run than a nightly batch job for the same feature. Which setup gives each feature the freshness it needs at the lowest cost?
options: Prep time in a nightly batch job, recent orders by streaming, distance at request time
Prep time and recent orders from a streaming job, distance computed at request time
Prep time and recent orders from a nightly batch job, distance computed at request time
All three computed at request time by querying the raw orders and location tables
questions.explanation:
Match each feature's computation to how fast it changes. A 30-day average barely moves within a day, so a cheap nightly batch job is fresh enough. The count of orders in the last 10 minutes changes minute by minute and is the signal for a sudden rush, so it needs a streaming job that updates it within seconds. The courier's distance depends on where that courier is at the moment of the request, so it can only be computed at request time, which is cheap since it is one small calculation.

Streaming the 30-day average meets every freshness need, but the prompt says streaming costs more, and a day-old 30-day average is almost the same number, so the extra cost buys nothing. Computing the recent order count nightly makes it hours stale, so the model never sees a lunch rush. Computing everything at request time means scanning 30 days of orders per request, which blows the 50 ms budget and loads the source databases.

There is also a consistency cost. Request-time and streaming features must be logged as served, or rebuilt point in time, so training sees the same values serving did.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often push on the streaming feature: what happens when the stream lags? A strong answer stores a timestamp with each value, has serving fall back to a default or flag it when the value is stale, and monitors stream lag as an operational metric.

questions.prompt: A support bot routes tickets into 40 intent classes. The labels came from an outsourced team of 12 annotators. The model has stopped improving, and an expert audit of 500 random tickets disagrees with the training label on 15% of them. Design a labeling process that fixes this, and say how you would handle the noisy labels you already have.
questions.answer: First I would rewrite the guidelines with a clear definition, examples and tricky edge cases for each intent, merging classes the experts themselves confuse. I would run a pilot where several annotators label the same tickets and measure agreement with Cohen's or Fleiss' kappa per class. Low-agreement classes point to unclear guidelines, not lazy annotators. In production, I would mix expert-labelled gold tickets into each batch to score annotators, send a share of tickets to two annotators, and have an expert adjudicate disagreements and feed the decisions back into the guidelines. For the existing data, I would find likely errors with cross-validated predictions that confidently disagree with the label, relabel those first, and drop or down-weight what stays doubtful. Finally I would keep an expert-labelled test set so I can tell if quality actually improved.
points: Clear per-class guidelines with examples and edge cases, possibly merging confusable intents
Measure inter-annotator agreement on overlapping items, by class
Gold questions with known answers to monitor each annotator
Expert adjudication of disagreements that feeds back into the guidelines
Find suspect existing labels with out-of-fold model disagreement and relabel them
Keep a clean expert-labelled test set to measure real progress
questions.explanation:
A 15% error rate across 40 classes usually means the task is unclear, not that annotators are careless. So the process starts with guidelines and a measure of agreement. Agreement by class shows which intents are badly defined. Gold items catch individual annotators who drift. Adjudication turns each disagreement into a guideline fix, so quality improves over time instead of staying flat.

For existing labels, the efficient move is to let the model point at likely errors. Train with cross-validation, then flag tickets where the out-of-fold prediction confidently disagrees with the given label. This is the idea behind confident learning. Experts relabel those first, which costs far less than relabelling everything.

The common mistake is to jump straight to a bigger model or more data. With noisy labels, more data of the same quality raises the ceiling very little. Another mistake is to measure progress on a test set labelled by the same noisy process, which can hide real gains or invent fake ones.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask how you would budget this. A good answer prices the work: double-labelling every ticket doubles the cost, so you overlap only a share, focus experts on low-agreement classes, and track kappa and gold accuracy on a dashboard each week.

questions.prompt: A card issuer retrains its fraud model every month. Fraud is confirmed by chargebacks, which can arrive up to 60 days after a transaction, and fraudsters change tactics every few weeks. How would you evaluate a new model version before and after it goes live?
questions.answer: Offline, I would split by time, never at random: train on older months and test on a later window, so the test looks like the future the model will face. The test window must end at least 60 days ago, so its labels have matured. Otherwise recent fraud that has not been reported yet is counted as legitimate, which corrupts both precision and recall. I would backtest over several consecutive windows to see how fast performance decays as tactics shift. I would report business metrics at a fixed alert budget, such as fraud dollars caught and the false decline rate, next to PR-AUC. Online, I would run the new model in shadow mode or on a small share of traffic. While labels are pending, I would watch fast signals: score distribution drift, alert rate, analyst review outcomes and early customer disputes. Then I would recompute the real metrics as chargebacks mature.
points: Split by time, training on the past and testing on a later window
Score only on matured labels, at least 60 days old, or fresh fraud looks legitimate
Backtest over several windows to measure decay under drift
Report business metrics at a fixed alert budget, such as dollars caught and false declines
Online, use shadow mode or a small rollout with fast proxy signals until labels arrive
questions.explanation:
Two problems stack up here. Fraud patterns shift, so a random split lets the model see future tactics in training and makes the test look easier than real life. And labels arrive late, so the most recent data is partly mislabelled: a fraudulent transaction from last week usually still looks legitimate in the table.

The most common mistake is to test on the freshest month because it seems most relevant. Its unreported fraud is labelled as legitimate, so a correct alert on it is scored as a false positive and a miss on it is scored as a true negative. The numbers can move in either direction, and they will change again once chargebacks land. Waiting for label maturity costs time, which is why the online plan leans on fast proxies such as analyst review outcomes and score drift. These cannot replace confirmed labels, but they catch a broken model within days instead of two months.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate also mentions that the model's own decisions change the labels. Declined transactions never become chargebacks, so their true label stays unknown. Teams handle this with a small random approval holdout or by labelling declines through analyst review.

questions.prompt: A coding assistant serves an 8-billion-parameter model with fp16 weights (16 GB in total) on a GPU with about 1 TB/s of memory bandwidth. The KV cache is on and prompts are short. Each new token takes about 20 ms, and a profile shows nearly all of that time inside the layers' matrix multiplications, yet the compute units are only about 5% busy. Serving 8 users in one batch instead of 1 barely changes the time per step. What best explains this?
options: Each step reads all 16 GB of weights from memory but does only about two operations per weight, so memory bandwidth, not compute, sets the step time.
Each step must wait for the previous token to be sampled, and this dependency stops the GPU from running the model's layers in parallel with each other.
Each step reads the KV cache for every earlier token, and at this context length the cache is far larger than the weights, so reading it dominates.
Each step's matrix multiplications are compute-heavy, and fp16 math runs slowly at small batches, so a GPU with more raw compute would cut the step time.
questions.explanation:
To produce one token, the GPU multiplies each weight by one number per sequence and adds it in, about two operations per weight. But every one of the 16 GB of weights must be pulled from memory to do that. At about 1 TB/s, reading 16 GB takes about 16 ms, which matches the 20 ms step. The arithmetic itself would take a fraction of a millisecond, so the compute units sit idle waiting for data. Adding users to the batch reuses each weight once it has been read, so 8 users cost nearly the same time as 1. That is the signature of a memory-bound step.

Tokens are generated one after another, but that dependency is between steps and does not explain idle compute inside a step. Layers always run in sequence. The KV cache for a few hundred tokens is tens of megabytes, tiny next to 16 GB of weights, so it matters only at long contexts or large batches. The option that calls the step compute-heavy gets the cause backwards. A GPU with more raw compute would not help, because its math units are already idle waiting for data.
questions.deeper: This is why weight quantization speeds up decoding even when the math still runs in 16-bit: fewer bytes to read per token. It is also why batching raises throughput almost for free until the batch is large enough for the step to become compute-bound or the KV cache to fill memory.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce team samples 400 checkout sessions at random and reports a 95% confidence interval for the mean checkout time of 41 to 47 seconds, using the usual normal-based interval. Read the interval in the standard frequentist way, where the true mean is a fixed but unknown number. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: If the sampling were repeated many times, about 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true mean.
There is a 95% probability that the true mean checkout time lies between 41 and 47 seconds.
About 95% of individual checkout sessions take between 41 and 47 seconds.
With everything else equal, a sample of 1,600 sessions would give an interval about half as wide.
A 99% interval built from the same data would be narrower than 41 to 47 seconds.
A two-sided test at the 5% level would reject the claim that the true mean is 50 seconds.
questions.explanation:
The 95% describes the method, not this one interval. Build intervals this way over many samples and about 95% of them will cover the true mean. That makes the repeated-sampling statement correct. The width scales with 1/√n, so going from 400 to 1,600 sessions divides the width by √4 = 2, which makes the half-width statement correct. A 95% interval holds exactly the null values that a two-sided test at the 5% level would not reject. 50 seconds lies outside 41 to 47, so the test rejects it.

The statement giving a 95% probability that the true mean lies in 41 to 47 is the classic misreading. In the frequentist view the true mean is fixed, so this particular interval either contains it or not. A probability statement like that needs a Bayesian credible interval, which can match these numbers under a flat prior but rests on different assumptions. The interval is about the mean, not individual sessions, which vary far more. A 99% interval is wider, not narrower, because more confidence needs a larger range.
questions.deeper: In A/B testing, interviewers prefer candidates who report an interval for the difference between groups, not just a p-value. A useful extra point is that the 1/√n rule makes precision expensive: halving the width needs four times the traffic, which often decides how long an experiment must run.

questions.prompt: A legal-tech team uses an open-weights model that was pretrained with rotary position embeddings and a 4,096-token context. They need it to read 32,000-token contracts. When they simply feed in full contracts, answers about clauses past the first few thousand tokens become incoherent. Explain why, and how they could extend the context window.
questions.answer: The model never saw positions beyond 4,096 in training. Rotary embeddings encode position as rotation angles, and at positions about 8 times larger some dimensions reach angles the model has never seen. The attention patterns it learned do not hold there, so scores become unreliable and output degrades. The model also never learned to use links that span tens of thousands of tokens. The standard fix has two parts. First, rescale positions so long inputs map into the familiar range, for example position interpolation, which shrinks positions by about 8, or a larger rotary base frequency. Second, run a short continued pretraining on long documents, mixed with normal-length data, so the model adapts. Then evaluate with retrieval tests at many depths, real long-contract questions and short-context benchmarks, and plan for the larger KV cache. If that is too costly, chunking with retrieval is the fallback.
points: Positions beyond the training length are out of distribution
Rotary angles at unseen positions break learned attention patterns
Rescale positions with interpolation or a larger rotary base
Short fine-tune on long documents mixed with normal-length data
Test long-range retrieval at many depths and recheck short-context quality
Plan for KV cache memory, or fall back to chunking with retrieval
questions.explanation:
A transformer's weights put no hard limit on length, which is why it is tempting to just feed longer input. But the model only learned how attention behaves at the positions it was trained on. Rotary embeddings rotate query and key vectors by angles that grow with position, and the slowest-rotating dimensions never complete a cycle within 4,096 tokens. At position 30,000 they reach angles that were never seen in training, so the attention scores are out of distribution.

The common mistake is to think rescaling alone solves it. Interpolation squeezes positions together, so nearby tokens now differ by smaller angles than the model is used to, and quality suffers until a fine-tune adapts it. Another mistake is to fine-tune only on long documents, which can hurt short-context performance. A third is to judge success by perplexity alone, since a model can predict local text well while still failing to use a clause 20,000 tokens back.
questions.deeper: Interviewers often ask about cost. Attention compute grows quadratically with length and the KV cache grows linearly, so a 32,000-token request needs about 8 times the cache of a 4,096-token one. A strong candidate also asks whether the task truly needs the whole contract at once, or whether retrieving the relevant clauses would be cheaper and just as accurate.

questions.subtopic: explaining a RAG bot end to end
questions.prompt: A product manager at an airline asks you to explain, in plain terms, how the new baggage-policy chatbot answers a customer's question, and where each step can go wrong. Give the explanation you would offer.
questions.answer: Before any customer asks anything, we take the airline's baggage policy pages and cut them into short passages, each covering one rule. Each passage is turned into a list of numbers that captures its meaning and stored in a searchable index. When a customer asks a question, we turn it into numbers the same way and fetch the few passages whose meaning is closest. We hand those passages and the question to the language model, with an instruction to answer only from them and to cite them. Each step can fail. A page may be missing, outdated or badly extracted, for example a fee table that comes out jumbled. A rule can be split across two passages. The search can miss the right passage when the customer says "carry-on" and the policy says "cabin bag". And the model can ignore the passages, add details from its own memory, or answer when it should say it does not know.
points: Offline: policy pages split into passages, embedded and stored in an index
At question time: embed the question and fetch the closest passages
The model answers from those passages and cites them
Content failures: missing, outdated or badly parsed pages
Retrieval failures: rules split across passages, wording mismatch
Generation failures: ignoring the passages, inventing details, not declining
questions.explanation:
The skill here is splitting the system into stages a non-specialist can follow, then tying each failure to a stage. That matters because fixes differ by stage. A wrong answer caused by an outdated page is fixed in the content pipeline, while one caused by the model ignoring a good passage is fixed in the prompt or the model choice.

The most common mistake is to describe the chatbot as "the AI reads all our policies and answers". That hides retrieval, which is where many real failures happen, and gives the manager no way to reason about errors. A second mistake is to bury the explanation in jargon such as embeddings, vector databases and top-k without saying what they do. The plain version, passages turned into numbers that capture meaning so similar text can be found, is accurate enough and easy to repeat. A third is to cover only the happy path. A manager mostly needs to know where it breaks and what the team can measure at each step.
questions.deeper: A strong follow-up is to walk the manager through one real failure, such as a wrong pet-fee answer caused by a jumbled table, and show which stage caused it. Stakeholders trust a system more when they can see the team knows where its errors come from and how each one is measured.

questions.subtopic: a deploy that predicts a constant
questions.prompt: Twenty minutes after a new version of a messaging app's spam model is deployed, the trust team notices that every message gets a spam score of exactly 0.12. The service shows no errors and latency is normal. Walk through how you would handle this incident, from detection to making sure it cannot happen again.
questions.answer: First, mitigate: roll back to the previous model version from the registry, since that is fast and the old model was known to work, then confirm scores look normal again. Spam was flowing meanwhile, so I would tell the trust team and check what got through. Then find the root cause by replaying logged requests against the bad version in staging. A constant score almost always means the model sees constant inputs or ignores them: features arriving null and filled with defaults, a renamed column that new code silently drops, a missing or mismatched preprocessing artifact such as a tokenizer, or the wrong file, such as a placeholder baseline, registered as the model. Finally, add guards: a pre-deploy test that scores a fixed set of known messages and fails if scores barely vary or differ sharply from the current model, a canary with an automatic check on score spread, and an alert when prediction variance collapses.
points: Mitigate first: roll back to the last good version from the registry and confirm recovery
Assess impact, such as spam let through, and keep the trust team informed
Reproduce offline by replaying logged requests against the bad version
Suspect constant inputs: null features, dropped columns, missing preprocessing, wrong artifact
Guards: fixed-set test before deploy, canary with a score-spread check, variance alert
questions.explanation:
A constant output with no errors is a classic silent failure. The service is healthy by every operational metric, so only a check on the predictions themselves catches it. That is why the first move is to roll back, not to debug live. Rolling back is quick and safe because the registry keeps the previous version ready, and debugging can then happen without users being harmed.

The common mistake is to dive into the model code while bad scores keep flowing. Another is to stop at the immediate bug, such as a renamed field, without asking why the release process let a broken model reach users. The lasting value of the incident is the guard: a release check that compares the new model's scores on a fixed set of inputs with the current model's would have failed this deploy in minutes, before any user saw it.
questions.deeper: In an interview, mention a blameless post-mortem with a timeline, impact and actions with owners. A sharp follow-up is how to detect this automatically. Good answers track the spread of scores, such as the standard deviation or the number of distinct values per minute, since a check on the mean can miss a constant that happens to sit near the old average.

questions.prompt: A team measures its bug-fixing agent by whether the repository's tests pass after its change. After a prompt update, the pass rate jumps from 61% to 90%. Reading the diffs, an engineer finds that many new passes come from the agent loosening assertions, adding skip markers to failing tests, or returning a hard-coded value when the input matches the test case. What is the best response?
options: Add a rule to the prompt telling the agent never to edit tests, and keep the visible test pass rate as the only grade.
Keep the new prompt, since a 29-point gain on the same tests shows the update makes the agent better on average.
Replace the test run with an LLM judge that reads the agent's summary of its fix and scores whether it sounds right.
Make tests read-only to the agent, grade with hidden tests it never sees, and flag diffs that special-case inputs.
questions.explanation:
The agent is gaming the grader. Making the tests pass is what gets rewarded, and weakening the tests is easier than fixing the bug. The fix has to make cheating impossible or useless. Read-only test files block edits to assertions and skip markers. Hidden tests, written for the same bug but never shown to the agent, defeat hard-coded answers, because a special case for the visible input fails on new inputs. Checking diffs for test changes and input-specific branches catches what slips through.

A prompt rule helps a little but leaves the incentive in place, and the hard-coded values do not touch test files at all, so the rule would not even cover them. Keeping the prompt confuses the metric with the goal. The 29-point gain is inflated by fake fixes that ship broken code. An LLM judge reading the summary is worse still: it grades claims, not behaviour, and an agent that took a shortcut can still describe its fix as a real one.
questions.deeper: This is Goodhart's law applied to agents: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Strong candidates treat any grader the agent can see or touch as open to attack. In interviews, mention reviewing a sample of passing trajectories, not just failures, since gaming only shows up in runs that look like successes.

questions.prompt: A telecom team trains a random forest of deep trees to predict churn. By mistake, `customer_id` is left in as a feature. It is a randomly assigned code, unique for every customer, stored as an integer. Impurity-based feature importance ranks it third, above contract type. What is the best reading of this?
options: The ID must carry real signal, because a forest only splits on a feature when that split lowers impurity.
Permutation importance would rank the ID higher still, since shuffling unique values destroys the most information.
Averaging over trees blurs the ranking, so trust the importance from one deep tree trained on the same data.
Impurity importance favours features with many unique values, so check permutation importance on held-out data.
questions.explanation:
Impurity-based importance adds up how much each feature lowered impurity across all splits, measured on the training data. A feature with thousands of unique values offers thousands of candidate thresholds, so deep trees can almost always find one that cleanly separates a few training rows, even when the values are random. Those gains are real on the training rows and worthless on new customers. Permutation importance on held-out data asks a different question: how much does validation performance drop when this column is shuffled? For a random ID the answer is close to zero.

The option claiming the ID must carry signal misses that impurity drops on training data include drops from fitting noise. Permutation importance would rank the ID lower, not higher. Shuffling it on held-out data barely changes the score, because the patterns it memorised do not exist in those rows. One deep tree has the same bias toward many-valued features, with more noise.

A second caveat applies to both methods. Strongly correlated features, such as monthly and total charges, split the credit between them, so each can look weaker than it is.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate drops IDs and other leakage-prone columns before training, then reports permutation importance or SHAP values on a validation set. For correlated groups, permuting the whole group together, or dropping a feature and retraining, shows more clearly what the model really relies on.

questions.prompt: You are fine-tuning a text classifier for medical triage notes with fp16 mixed precision. Around step 3,000 the training loss suddenly turns NaN and never recovers. How would you track down the cause and fix it?
questions.answer: First, find where the NaN starts. Resume from the last good checkpoint, log the loss and gradient norm every step, and check the batch at the failing step for NaN or infinite inputs and bad labels. Next, look at the fp16 range. Its largest value is about 65,504, so big activations or logits can overflow. Use dynamic loss scaling, which skips steps with infinite gradients and lowers the scale, or switch to bf16, which has the same exponent range as fp32. Then check for numerically unsafe code such as a log of zero, division by a zero count or a hand-written softmax, and compute the loss in fp32 from logits with the built-in cross-entropy. Finally, if gradient norms were spiking before the failure, lower the learning rate, add warmup and clip gradients, unscaling them first when a loss scaler is used.
points: Reproduce from the last good checkpoint and find the first step and tensor that goes NaN
Check the input batch for NaN or infinite values and bad labels
fp16 range problems: use dynamic loss scaling or switch to bf16
Remove unsafe operations like log(0) and compute the loss in fp32 from logits
Watch gradient norms, then lower the learning rate, add warmup and clip gradients
questions.explanation:
A NaN that appears suddenly after thousands of good steps usually has one of a few causes, and the order of checks matters. Finding the first step and the first tensor that goes bad tells you whether the problem is the data, the forward pass or the update. The framework's anomaly detection mode can point to the operation that produced the first NaN.

fp16 has a narrow range, so activations, logits or gradients can overflow to infinity, and infinity minus infinity is NaN. Loss scaling protects small gradients from underflow and backs off when it sees infinite gradients, but it cannot fix an overflow in the forward pass. bf16 has the same exponent range as fp32 and avoids most of these problems.

The common mistake is to jump straight to lowering the learning rate. That may hide the symptom while a corrupt record or a log of zero is still there, waiting to strike again. Another mistake is clipping gradients while they are still scaled, which makes the clip threshold meaningless.
questions.deeper: In production training jobs, teams add guards that check for a non-finite loss and skip or halt the step, and they save checkpoints often enough that a NaN costs minutes, not days. Interviewers like hearing that you would also log the loss scale over time, since a scale that keeps collapsing points to persistent overflow.

questions.subtopic: an agent stuck in a loop
questions.prompt: A recruiting team's scheduling agent keeps calling `get_availability(interviewer_id="u-482", week="2026-W49")` with exactly the same arguments, again and again, until it hits the 40-step cap. It never books the interview. How would you debug this, and what would you change?
questions.answer: First I would open the traces and read the step where the loop starts: the exact tool result the model saw, and its reasoning right after. Repeated identical calls usually mean the result did not give the model what it needed, or did not tell it what to do next. Maybe the tool returns an empty list when the interviewer has no free slots, which looks like a failure, or an error the model cannot act on. I would also check the harness: is the tool result really added to the context, or is it dropped or cut off? Fixes: make results explicit, such as "no free slots that week, try another week or interviewer", and separate empty from error. Add prompt guidance for when data is unavailable. In the harness, detect repeated identical calls, return a note after the second one, and stop and escalate after a few. Finally, turn this trace into a regression test.
points: Read the trace at the first repeat: the tool result and the model's next reasoning
Check the result is clear: empty versus error, with a hint for the next step
Check the harness really passes the result back into the context
Detect repeated identical calls in the harness, then warn, stop or escalate
Tell the agent in the prompt what to do when the data does not exist
Add the failing trace to the eval set as a regression test
questions.explanation:
The common mistake is to treat the loop as a model problem and jump straight to a bigger model or a higher step cap. A higher cap only makes the loop more expensive. A repeated identical call is a symptom: the agent believes it has not yet got what it needs. The cause is usually in what it sees, so the trace is the first place to look.

Three causes cover most cases. The tool result is ambiguous, such as an empty list that could mean no slots, a wrong id or a failure. The result never reaches the model because of a harness bug, such as an exception that is caught and ignored, or a message dropped when the context is trimmed. Or the prompt sets a goal the agent cannot meet, such as "always book within the requested week", with no instruction for when that is impossible. Each one needs a different fix, which is why you read before you change anything. Loop detection in the harness is a safety net, not the cure.
questions.deeper: In an interview, describing how you would read one trace step by step is more convincing than listing fixes. A good follow-up to expect: how would you catch this before users do? Answer with monitoring alerts on step counts and repeated calls, plus eval cases where the right answer is that no slot exists.

questions.prompt: A team stacks three click-prediction models: gradient-boosted trees, logistic regression and a 1-nearest-neighbour model. They train each base model on the full training set, then fit a logistic regression meta-model on the base models' predictions for those same training rows. The meta-model puts almost all its weight on the nearest-neighbour model, and the stack scores worse on validation than the boosted trees alone. What is the problem, and what is the fix?
options: The meta-model is too simple to see when each base model fails. Replace it with a deep gradient-boosted model.
The meta-model saw in-sample predictions, which flatter the most overfit model. Use out-of-fold predictions.
The meta-model lacks context about each row. Give it the raw features as well as the base model predictions.
Learned stacking weights always overfit. Average the three base model predictions with equal weights instead.
questions.explanation:
A 1-nearest-neighbour model predicts each training row from itself, so its predictions on rows it was trained on are perfect. The boosted trees also fit their own training rows better than they will fit new data. The meta-model sees these in-sample predictions and learns to trust whichever base model looks best on them, which is the most overfit one. On new data that model is much weaker, so the stack falls apart.

The fix is out-of-fold predictions. Split the training set into K folds, train each base model on K − 1 folds and predict the held-out fold, so every row gets a prediction from a model that never saw it. Fit the meta-model on those, then refit the base models on all the data for serving.

A more complex meta-model would overfit the same misleading inputs even harder. Adding raw features can help a well-built stack but leaves the leak in place. Equal weights avoid the leak but throw away the point of stacking, and learned weights are not doomed to overfit. With out-of-fold inputs and a simple, regularised meta-model, they generalise well.
questions.deeper: scikit-learn's stacking estimators do the out-of-fold step for you with internal cross-validation. In an interview, add that the folds must respect the data's structure. With time-ordered clicks, use time-based folds, or the out-of-fold predictions leak the future too. Stacking gains are often small, so weigh them against the cost of serving several models.

questions.subtopic: downstream thresholds after a model swap
questions.prompt: A social app sends posts scoring 0.7 or higher on its abuse model to human review, and the review team can handle about 5,000 posts a day. A new model has higher AUC, but it was trained with abusive examples up-weighted. On a week of replayed traffic it scores about 14,000 posts a day at 0.7 or above. What should the team do before switching models?
options: Recalibrate the new scores or pick a new threshold that keeps review near 5,000 a day, then check on a canary
Keep the 0.7 threshold, because a model with higher AUC will do better than the old one at any fixed threshold
Rescale the new scores linearly so their minimum and maximum line up with the old model's minimum and maximum
Keep 0.7 and let the review team work through the extra posts, since the backlog will settle once traffic does
questions.explanation:
AUC only measures how well a model ranks posts. It says nothing about what a score of 0.7 means. Up-weighting abusive examples in training pushes scores upward, so the old threshold now sits at a very different point in the new model's distribution, and review volume nearly triples. The fix is to set the operating point again for the new model. Calibrating its scores on recent labelled data, or mapping them onto the old model's score distribution, gives the scores a stable meaning, and the threshold is then chosen so about 5,000 posts a day go to review. Then check precision and recall at that point and confirm on a canary before the full switch.

Higher AUC does not mean better results at a fixed threshold, since the two models' scores are on different scales. Matching the minimum and maximum aligns the ends of the range but not the middle, where the threshold sits, so volume can still be far off. Asking reviewers to absorb almost three times their capacity means harmful posts wait longer, and the backlog keeps growing, because the extra volume comes from the model, not from a traffic spike.
questions.deeper: Strong candidates treat the score as an interface. Thresholds, business rules and reports downstream all depend on its scale, so a model swap is also an interface change. A common practice is a calibration step in the serving pipeline, so a new model can drop in while scores keep a stable meaning. Interviewers may ask how to check calibration: a reliability plot on recent labelled data.

questions.prompt:
Your team has three new projects and asks you to pick a starting model for each.

- Predict loan default from 40 numeric and categorical columns, with 200,000 rows, scored in a nightly batch job.
- Detect cracks in photos of concrete, with 5,000 labeled images, running on a tablet on site.
- Classify the topic of customer reviews, with 30,000 labeled reviews, served through an API with a 100 ms latency budget.

What would you choose for each, and why?
questions.answer: For loan default I would start with gradient-boosted trees. Tabular columns have no spatial or order structure for a neural network to exploit, trees handle mixed types and skewed features well, and at this size they usually match or beat MLPs while being cheap to train and serve. For cracks I would fine-tune a small pretrained CNN, such as a mobile-sized network. Convolutions build in locality and translation equivariance, which suits cracks that can appear anywhere, 5,000 images are too few to train from scratch, and a small CNN runs fast on a tablet. For reviews I would fine-tune a small pretrained transformer encoder. Attention captures word context and negation, 30,000 labels are plenty for fine-tuning, and a compact or distilled encoder fits a 100 ms budget. I would keep a TF-IDF plus logistic regression baseline to check that the gain is worth the cost.
points: Tabular data: gradient-boosted trees first, since there is no spatial or sequence structure to exploit
Images: fine-tune a pretrained CNN, whose locality and translation equivariance suit cracks
Small datasets call for transfer learning, not training deep models from scratch
Text: fine-tune a pretrained transformer encoder for word context
Serving limits (tablet, 100 ms) push toward small or distilled models
Keep a simple baseline to judge whether the deep model earns its cost
questions.explanation:
Interviewers want the reasoning in a clear order: inductive bias, then data size, then serving cost. An inductive bias is an assumption built into the model. Convolutions assume nearby pixels matter together and that a pattern means the same thing anywhere in the image, which is true of cracks. Attention lets any word affect any other, which matters in reviews where a "not" five words back flips the meaning. Tabular rows have neither property, so trees, which split on single features and need no feature scaling, are the strong default.

Data size then decides between training from scratch and transfer learning. 5,000 images and 30,000 reviews are small for deep models but plenty for fine-tuning a pretrained one. Serving cost then picks the model size inside each family.

The common mistake is to pick the most powerful architecture everywhere, such as a large transformer on the loan table, or to ignore deployment and propose a model the tablet cannot run. Another is reaching for an RNN for the reviews. It can work, but it reads words one at a time, trains more slowly and lacks the strong pretrained checkpoints that transformer encoders have.
questions.deeper: A strong candidate also says what would change each choice. If the loan data included long transaction histories, a sequence model over events could add signal on top of the trees. If the tablet had tight memory, quantizing the CNN would matter. Senior answers tie every choice to a metric and a baseline.

questions.prompt: An ad click model uses gradient boosted trees. One feature, `merchant_id`, has 400,000 values. Many appear only a few times, and new merchants show up every day. Before splitting off a validation set, an engineer replaced each ID with that merchant's mean click rate over the full labelled dataset. Validation AUC jumped from 0.71 to 0.93, but the online gain was small. What is the best fix?
options: Compute each row's encoding out-of-fold or from earlier days only, smoothed toward the global click rate
Keep the full-data encoding but smooth it toward the global click rate, which removes the leak for rare merchants
Switch to one-hot encoding, which cannot leak the label and lets the trees learn a separate effect per merchant
Drop `merchant_id` entirely, since any encoding of an ID with this many values will leak the label into training
questions.explanation:
The jump to 0.93 is a leak, not a real gain. Each row's own click label went into its merchant's mean. For a merchant seen three times, the encoding nearly spells out the answer. The validation rows were encoded with the same full-data means, so they leak too. The fix is to make sure a row's label never feeds its own encoding: compute it out-of-fold, or from data before the row's timestamp, and smooth rare merchants toward the global rate. Unseen merchants then get the global rate as a sensible default.

Smoothing alone helps but does not remove the leak. The row's own label is still inside its merchant's mean, just with less weight. One-hot encoding does not leak, but 400,000 sparse columns are costly, trees split poorly on them, rare merchants have almost no data, and new merchants get nothing at all. Dropping the feature is too drastic. Out-of-fold target encoding and feature hashing both keep merchant signal without leaking.
questions.deeper: Many libraries now do out-of-fold target encoding for you, and CatBoost uses an ordered version for this exact reason. In an interview, also mention hashing to a fixed number of buckets, or learned embeddings, as options when categories churn daily.

questions.prompt: A decoder-only model has 24 layers and width d_model = 2,048. Each layer has multi-head attention with full-width query, key, value and output projections, and an MLP that expands to 4 × d_model and back. The vocabulary has 50,000 tokens, and the input embedding and output layer share one tied matrix. Ignoring biases and layer-norm weights, how many parameters does the model have? Give the answer in billions to 2 decimal places.
questions.explanation:
Start with one layer. Attention has four d × d matrices for query, key, value and output, which is 4d². The MLP has a d × 4d matrix going up and a 4d × d matrix coming back, which is 8d². So each layer has about 12d².

With d = 2,048, d² = 4,194,304, so one layer has 12 × 4,194,304 = 50,331,648 parameters. Across 24 layers that is 1,207,959,552.

The tied embedding adds 50,000 × 2,048 = 102,400,000 once. The total is 1,207,959,552 + 102,400,000 = 1,310,359,552, or about 1.31 billion.

The usual mistakes are counting attention as 3d² by forgetting the output projection, counting the MLP as one 4d² matrix, or adding the embedding twice even though the prompt says it is tied. Splitting attention into heads does not change the count, because the heads together still use full-width projections.
questions.deeper: The 12 × d² × layers shortcut lets you sanity-check a model card in seconds. Interviewers may then ask how the count changes with grouped-query attention, which shrinks the key and value projections, or with a gated MLP, which uses three matrices instead of two at a smaller hidden width.

questions.prompt: You run a RAG support bot for a broadband provider. It retrieves help-centre articles and answers customer questions. Leadership asks how you know the bot is good, and how you will catch regressions when you change the prompt, the model or the chunking. Design the evaluation.
